title: Where to Find robots.txt and What the File Reveals About Crawling
description:
You find robots.txt at the root of a site's host, which means you append the filename to the bare domain: example.com/robots.txt, never to a subfolder path. Google for Developers states the rule plainly, and everything confusing about this file follows from it. Most people who go looking for robots.txt are chasing a symptom, not a file. A page stopped ranking, a Search Console report threw an error, an /inurl:robots.txt search returned a wall of unrelated results. They find the file within a minute. Then they stare at four lines of text and have no idea which one is costing them traffic.

That gap is the whole point. Locating the file is a two-minute mechanical task that never needed a consultant, and the file itself is the least interesting part of a crawl audit. What matters is what the rules are doing to your URLs, and whether the assumptions you made when you wrote them survive contact with how search engines actually behave. If you already know what a disallow line is, you still may not know that it does far less than its name suggests. This piece is about the second half of the job.

Type the bare host into the address bar and add the filename. That is the entire procedure for the common case, and it works on your own site and on anyone else's. A robots.txt lookup is a read operation on a public file, so no credentials, no tool, and no plugin are involved in retrieving it.

Three quirks trip people up. The first is that most frameworks serve the file from a route rather than from disk, so the content you see may be generated. The second is that a Content Delivery Network can intercept the request and return a cached copy that no longer matches what the origin serves. The third is that a redirect chain can quietly send you to a different host, and the rules you are reading then belong to a site you do not own. If the URL resolves through two hops, verify the final destination before you conclude anything about your own crawl rules.

You should also read what you found instead of scanning for the word disallow. The rules that hurt are usually the ones you wrote years ago and never revisited.

  • What the File at the Root Actually Does
  • How Crawlers Read What You Wrote
  • Checking Any Site in Under Two Minutes
  • Six Dimensions That Separate a Working File From a Decorative One
  • Where Site Owners Fool Themselves
  • Reading the Signals Before You Rewrite Anything
  • Frequently Asked Questions

What the File at the Root Actually Does

Robots.txt is a plain-text set of instructions addressed to automated crawlers, published at a fixed location so that any robot can find it without being told. It is a convention, not a gate, and that distinction decides how much weight to give it. The file tells well-behaved crawlers which paths they may request. It cannot enforce anything, and it never controls what a page does once a crawler has it. The robots.txt collection rules exist to make the location predictable, which is the only reason a file with this little syntax works at all.

The adjacent concept people confuse it with is the meta robots tag. That tag lives inside a page, and it governs indexing rather than fetching. A noindex directive removes a URL from results. A disallow rule removes your ability to crawl it. They solve different problems, and mixing them up is how a site ends up with thousands of pages that Google can see in the index but has never actually read. We have written elsewhere about robots.txt disallow rules do far less than most site owners assume, and that page digs into the indexing consequences in detail.

The file serves two audiences with opposite needs. Search engines read it to know where not to go. Everyone else reads it to learn what a site considers off-limits: staging environments, internal search, cart funnels, admin panels. The second audience is why a robots.txt is semi-public by design, and why writing confidential paths into it is a mistake rather than a security measure.

How Crawlers Read What You Wrote

A crawler requests the file before it requests anything else on a host, caches it, and then applies the rules to every subsequent fetch. A single file per host, protocol, and port covers the whole site, so there is no reason to look anywhere else once you have the root copy in front of you. That combination rule matters because http and https versions of the same site can each carry their own file, and so can a non-standard port. If your site moved to HTTPS and the old file was never cleaned up, the http copy still exists and still applies to the http host.

Directives are grouped by user-agent, and the specificity logic is not a priority ranking. A crawler picks the most specific group that names it, and ignores more general groups entirely when a specific match exists. An asterisk group is the fallback for every crawler without a named group. If you wrote a wildcard block and later added a Googlebot block, crawlers matching Googlebot read only the Googlebot block. Everything in the wildcard group stopped applying to them the moment you saved that change.

Path matching is prefix-based and case-sensitive. Disallowing a directory blocks every URL that starts with that string, which is usually what you want and occasionally a disaster. Disallowing a single dynamic parameter string can catch thousands of filter combinations you never intended to block. Query strings complicate this further: a rule that blocks a URL with parameters does not automatically block the parameter-free version, and vice versa.

The file is also parsed leniently. A malformed line is skipped rather than crashing the parse, which is forgiving until it means a rule you depended on simply stopped existing. There is no rewrite, no validation warning, and no error surfaced anywhere unless you go looking for the report.

Checking Any Site in Under Two Minutes

The sequence below is the one worth running on your own domain every quarter, and on any domain you are about to compete against.

  1. Open the bare host in a browser and append the filename to the root, so you are requesting the file from the host itself rather than through a search result. If the address bar shows a path segment before the filename, the request is wrong and the file you get back is meaningless.
  2. Hard-refresh the page. Browser caches and CDN caches both serve stale copies, and a file that shows yesterday's rules while tomorrow's live ruleset is already deployed will send you chasing the wrong problem.
  3. Confirm which host, protocol, and port you actually landed on, since a redirect can move you off the origin you meant to inspect.
  4. Read the file top to bottom and note where each user-agent group begins and ends. A line that looks global may be sitting under a named group that only applies to one crawler.
  5. Cross-check the file against Search Console's robots.txt report, which shows the version Google last fetched and flags syntax errors the file itself will never tell you about. Search Console's robots.txt report is the fastest way to see what a crawler actually received rather than what you intended to send.

Two minutes is honest. Ten seconds gets you the file. The rest is checking whether the version you are reading is the version that is live.

Six Dimensions That Separate a Working File From a Decorative One

A robots.txt that exists is not a robots.txt that works. These are the dimensions worth scoring any file against, whether it is yours or a competitor's.

Dimension What to look for
Placement The file resolves at the host root, not at a subfolder, and not only behind a redirect
Coverage Named user-agent groups exist for the crawlers that matter, and no stale wildcard block silently overrides them
Path specificity Disallow patterns block exactly the paths intended, with no accidental prefix collisions on shared directory names
Indexing alignment Pages that must not appear in results carry a noindex directive, not just a disallow rule
Freshness The live file matches what Search Console last fetched, and there is a process for updating it when the site changes
Error visibility Syntax is clean enough that the Search Console report shows no warnings, and someone actually reads that report

Most audits fail on two of these at once. Coverage and indexing alignment are the usual pair: a team adds a Googlebot block to protect a staging path, then forgets that the same path is linked from production and still indexed. Placement failures are rarer but more expensive, because a file at the wrong address has no effect at all while giving the team a false sense of protection.

The freshness dimension is the one that decays fastest. Sites get restructured, content moves under new directories, and the disallow list keeps pointing at paths that no longer exist while the new ones go unprotected. A robots.txt is not a set-and-forget artifact. It is a configuration file, and it drifts.

Where Site Owners Fool Themselves

The belief that hurts most is the one about secrecy. Teams treat robots.txt as a way to hide internal paths from competitors, then list staging subdomains, admin routes, and API endpoints by name. A file intended to reduce crawl load becomes a directory of everything worth probing. If a path needs protection, it needs authentication, not a line in a text file that is deliberately public.

A subtler mistake is assuming that a disallow rule prevents indexing. It does not. Crawlers cannot read a page they are told not to fetch, but the URL itself can still be indexed if other pages link to it with anchor text. The result is a search result with no snippet, which looks like a penalty and is not one. The disallow did exactly what it said it would do, and the indexing happened anyway through signals the page never controlled.

Teams also write rules against the wrong host. An old robots.txt sitting on the plain-http version of a site looks harmless until you realise the crawler fetches it for that host. Configuration templates make this worse: a starter file copied from a framework's documentation can reference directory structures that exist in the template and nowhere in your actual site.

Then there is the caching blind spot. A CDN configured to cache aggressively can keep serving an old robots.txt for hours after a deploy, so a rule change appears not to have taken effect. Teams respond by editing the file again, layering a second set of contradictory rules on top of the first, and now two versions of the same directive are in circulation.

The final one is quieter. Some teams disallow a path to reduce crawl budget, check that rankings held steady, and conclude the rule was harmless. Nothing was measured, nothing was verified, and the rule stays because no one wants to be the person who unblocked something that seems to be working.

Reading the Signals Before You Rewrite Anything

You face a specific decision once you have the file open: leave it alone, edit it, or rebuild your crawl rules from scratch. The signals tell you which.

Leave it alone when the file is clean, the paths it blocks are genuinely private, Search Console shows no fetch errors, and your indexed pages are the ones you want indexed. A working configuration does not need attention just because you looked at it.

Edit it when you find a specific, nameable problem. A disallow rule catching a directory of content pages. A stale wildcard block shadowing a newer named group. A path that moved six months ago while the rule stayed pointed at the old one. These are surgical fixes, and they take minutes.

Rebuild when the file has become a museum of decisions no one remembers. If nobody on the team can explain why a group exists, what it was protecting, or when it was last relevant, the ruleset is not a configuration, it is an archaeology site. Start from a short list of paths that genuinely must not be crawled, write groups only for the crawlers you care about, and check each one against a live URL before you publish.

The trigger worth acting on immediately is a mismatch between what you intend and what Search Console reports. If the live file shows rules you did not write, or the fetched version is weeks old while your deploy was this morning, stop editing and diagnose the caching layer first. Changing rules against a stale copy is how a small problem becomes two.

There is a version of this job that scales past one domain. When you are running multiple sites, the manual quarterly check turns into a crawl-health process, and that is a different kind of work: watching for coverage drops, tracking which URLs stopped getting fetched, and reacting before a blocked path has been blocked long enough to lose its rankings. That is what GrowGanic is for, and it treats crawl visibility as one input among many rather than a one-off checklist item. On paid plans, a rank drop triggers a fresh read of the search results and a refresh of the page that slipped, which is a faster loop than a quarterly reminder in a calendar.

The routine inspection is still yours, and it should be. Finding the file takes two minutes and tells you something no dashboard can: whether the rules you set years ago still describe the site you run today.

Free gets you an article. Pro publishes thirty a month. Business publishes a hundred and fifty. Current pricing: growganic.io/pricing. Stop writing articles. Start shipping them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where do I find the robots.txt file?

Append the filename directly to a site's root domain, so the request goes to the host itself rather than to any path beneath it. Google's documentation on creating the file specifies that it must sit at the host root to apply. If a subfolder version exists, it controls nothing beyond that folder's own host context, and the root copy is the one crawlers actually read.

Does robots.txt still work?

It works for its stated purpose: telling compliant crawlers which paths not to request. It does not enforce anything, block a determined scraper, or prevent indexing on its own. A disallowed URL can still appear in results when other pages link to it, because the rule governs fetching rather than indexing. Treat it as a load-management convention with indexing side effects, not as access control.

How to get robots.txt from a website?

Request it from the bare host in a browser and hard-refresh to bypass any cached copy. If you want to know what a search engine actually received, the Search Console robots.txt report shows the last fetched version along with any syntax warnings. For a domain you do not own, the browser request is the whole method and needs no tooling at all.

How to fix blocked by robots.txt error?

Read the file first and find the user-agent group that matches the crawler reporting the error. Look for a disallow pattern that prefixes the blocked URL, then check whether the live file still matches what Search Console shows as fetched. If no rule explains it, the cause usually sits outside the file: password protection, a firewall rule, or a hosting-level restriction. Remove the specific rule, redeploy, and request a re-fetch rather than deleting the file wholesale.

Sources

  1. Google for Developers
  2. Google Search Console Help

title: Rumpelstiltskin Dance AI: Locking a Tip-Toe Barn Meme Template
description:
How I shipped a 1–2 photo → tip-toe barn meme dance on Cloudflare Workers — template lock, guest Stripe, Seedance via TryAllAPI.

rumpelstiltskindance.video turns 1–2 adult photos into a tip-toe / “Wing In My Jawwdinz”-adjacent meme dance short with sound. Independent fan tool (2026), 18+. The homepage does not ask users to storyboard; it locks the motion template and sells the render.

Angle for this post: template lock done with an optional second dancer — similar family to party sites, different farm/barn beat. Prices and model ids change; treat live site / console as source of truth.

Locked motion, optional friend

Create panel pattern:

  1. Photo 1 · Lead — required, clear front face.
  2. Photo 2 · Friend — optional, only with permission.
  3. Fixed tip-toe dance motion template.
  4. 720p default messaging; pay once.

Copy on-site refuses celebrity / MV stills. That is load-bearing product policy for face tools — not a legal afterthought.

Live pricing verified: 500 credits · $8.88 · 720p, with multi-packs (e.g. $16.99, larger tiers). Guest Stripe. Always re-check the create button.

Why template lock wins on meme dances

Meme dances are recognizable moves. If you let users rewrite the choreography prompt, you get mush that does not match the sample. Locking the motion:

  • Makes demos honest.
  • Stabilizes Seedance payloads.
  • Shrinks the UX to “good photos + pay.”
  • Cuts support threads that start with “why doesn’t it look like the viral clip?”

Stack overview

Layer Choice Role
Front / SSR TanStack Start (Vite) Landing, upload panel, generation status
Runtime Cloudflare Workers Edge deploy, secrets, API routes
DB Cloudflare D1 Credits, orders, task rows (table prefixes if DBs are shared)
Payments Stripe Checkout One-time packs + optional larger packs; guest checkout
Video upstream TryAllAPI → Seedance Async create + poll
Analytics GA Funnel sanity check 
lead (+ optional friend) → tip-toe template
→ check credits (else Stripe)
→ Worker creates Seedance task via TryAllAPI
→ poll until MP4 URL → store / show
→ on failure: refund credits

Why a video API aggregator

Operational checklist after register / top-up:

  1. Confirm available USD balance in the console (not only the checkout success page).
  2. Create a token in pay-as-you-go style billing.
  3. Enable the video / Seedance-related channel group on that token. Wrong group → “no available channel” even when the model id looks right.
  4. Prefer separate keys per product (rumpel-prod vs sandbox).
  5. Put the key only in Workers Secrets (for example TRYALLAPI_API_KEY). Never in the frontend bundle or a blog post.

Conceptually the call shape looks like this (field names follow the aggregator’s v3 contents API; always re-check current docs):

POST /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks
Authorization: Bearer <TRYALLAPI_API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept-Encoding: identity

GET /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks/{id}

I send Accept-Encoding: identity from the Worker because some gateways behave badly with transparent decompression. Model ids used in production look like Seedance 2.x family strings — treat console ids as source of truth, not this paragraph.

Seedance parameters that matter for tip-toe templates

A few details that bit me across this family of sites:

  • Pass duration as an explicit integer. Some models default to “smart length.” Omitting duration can silently lengthen the clip and the bill.
  • resolution and ratio. Cost tracks resolution tier and duration more than portrait vs landscape. Match whatever the create UI offers (often 480p/720p and 9:16 for Shorts).
  • generate_audio. When the product ships “finished” downloads, leave audio on; creators who want a trending sound can mute later.
  • Status machine. Expect something like queued → running → succeeded / failed. Success URLs are often short-lived signed links — download/rehost on your side before handing the file to the user.
  • Decent failure. On supply_unavailable or hard failures: refund credits, show a short human message, log the detailed upstream error server-side, optionally fall back to another Seedance tier.

Rough mental model for upstream cost (illustrative only — use your own usage fields and invoices):

tokens ≈ duration_sec × width × height × fps / 1024
cost   ≈ tokens × price_per_million_tokens

Price the site after you measure a few real runs with retry margin, Stripe fees, and failed-job refunds — not from a spreadsheet fantasy of 0% failure.

Map lead vs friend roles consistently. Rehost short-lived result URLs. Separate keys if you operate a matrix of dance domains.

Credits, Stripe, and the “can charge money” line

Demo UIs are easy. The line between toy and product is:

  1. User hits Create → check credit balance.
  2. If short → Stripe Checkout Session (guest allowed).
  3. Webhook (plus a return-URL sync check) grants credits.
  4. Pre-debit / lock credits, create upstream task, persist task_id in D1.
  5. Poll until done; succeed → show MP4; fail → refund credits.

Two books of account stay separate: USD balance at TryAllAPI (your cost) vs site credits (what you sold). Mixing them in one mental ledger is how you underprice or invent “mysterious” losses.

When several products share one Stripe account, isolate webhooks by endpoint or by metadata (site / product). Callbacks pointed at the wrong apex domain are a classic multi-site footgun.

Secrets stay in Workers: TRYALLAPI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, webhook secret, auth secrets. The browser only ever sees publishable Stripe keys if needed.

Deploy notes (Workers + D1)

Typical loop on this template family:

pnpm install
# wire D1 database_id, production env, custom domain in wrangler
pnpm cf:deploy

Before calling a deploy “done”:

  • D1 binding is correct; shared DBs use table prefixes, not a new database per micro-idea (free-tier DB counts are limited).
  • AUTH_TRUSTED_ORIGINS and Stripe return / webhook URLs match the production HTTPS origin.
  • GA id is set for a coarse funnel (land → upload → pay → wait → download).
  • One real end-to-end path on production or a staging Worker: upload → pay → render → download.

Production origin: https://rumpelstiltskindance.video.

Product rules that are not optional

Face-based generation is not “just another SaaS CRUD app”:

  • Require an explicit 18+ / rights-to-use confirmation on upload.
  • Block minors and refuse celebrity / stranger misuse in copy and policy.
  • Expect upstream safety refusals; refund and explain.
  • Keep privacy policy honest about retention; do not train on user media by default.
  • Market as an independent fan-style tool for a trend format — not as an official tie-in unless you actually have that deal.
  • Use your own sample renders in marketing.

Those constraints belong in the product, not in a footnote you add after the first dispute email.

What I would reuse on the next tip-toe / barn meme site

  1. Lock the recognizable move; do not open a choreography IDE.
  2. Lead required + optional friend keeps the funnel simple.
  3. Guest one-time pack from ~$8.88 beats subscribe-first.
  4. Credits with automatic refund on failed generation.
  5. Self-hosted samples sell faster than SEO adjectives.

Consumer: watch the sample on rumpelstiltskindance.video, upload authorized photos, pay once. Builders: TryAllAPI, prove create+poll, then wrap credits. Lock the tip-toe; meter the GPU.

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Weights Drop Nov 4: Licence, Size, How to Run
description:
On November 4, 2026, Moonshot AI is scheduled to do something no lab has done before: hand the public the complete weights of a 2.8-trillion-parameter AI model that independent testing currently ranks as the strongest open model in the world. Kimi K3.1 Pro has been live through Moonshot's apps and API since October 23, but the downloadable release — the one that lets anyone outside Moonshot run, inspect, fine-tune and redistribute the model — is still a promise with a date on it. We checked Moonshot's Hugging Face organisation while writing this article: there is no K3.1 Pro repository yet. The newest thing there is still the older Kimi K3. So this is the guide to read before the drop: what exactly is landing, the licence question that will decide what "open" really means here, the terabyte-scale hardware reality, the two controversies hanging over the release, and a checklist for the day itself. For the launch story — benchmarks, pricing and how the model performs — start with our Kimi K3.1 Pro launch guide; this article is about the weights.

What exactly is dropping on November 4

Kimi K3.1 Pro is not a new architecture. It is a heavily post-trained version of Kimi K3, the model Moonshot released in the summer: a mixture-of-experts system with 2.8 trillion total parameters, of which about 104 billion are active on any given token. It uses Moonshot's Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals design, reads text, images and video in a single model, and works across a context window of one million tokens. What the extra post-training bought is measurable: on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, K3 scored 44; K3.1 Pro scores 55, fourth of every model the evaluator tracks and only three points behind the best closed model, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5.

"Full model weights" is the phrase that matters. A weight file is the trained model itself — the numbers that encode everything it learned. With the weights, the model stops being a service you rent from Moonshot and becomes a file you possess: you can run it on hardware you control, fine-tune it on your own data, inspect its behaviour without an API in between, and keep it forever even if Moonshot changes its prices, its terms, or its mind. That is why a weights release is a different event from an API launch, and why the October 23 launch, impressive as it was, is only half the story.

Two things about the drop are still unknown, and both matter. First, Moonshot has not said whether the faster K3.1 Pro Highspeed variant is part of the weights release or stays a hosted-only product. Second — and this is the big one — Moonshot has not named the licence. More on that below, because there is a very good precedent to read in the meantime.

Here is what the family looks like side by side. The K3 column is verified from the actual Hugging Face repository; the K3.1 Pro column is what is known or reasonably expected before November 4, and every expectation is labelled as one.

Kimi K3 (already out) Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights due Nov 4)
Total / active parameters 2.8 trillion / ~104 billion 2.8 trillion / ~104 billion (same base)
Context window 1 million tokens 1 million tokens
Input Text, images, video Text, images, video
Weight format MXFP4 weights, MXFP8 activations Not yet published; MXFP4 expected
Download size on Hugging Face 1.56 TB across 96 files Not yet published; similar scale expected
Licence Kimi K3 License (custom) Not yet announced
Serving vLLM and SGLang, official recipes Not yet published; same stacks expected
API price $3 / $15 per million tokens $2 / $10 per million tokens

The licence question — and what K3's licence actually says

Everything about this release hinges on a document that does not exist yet. "Open weights" tells you the file is downloadable; it says nothing about what you are allowed to do with it. That is the licence's job, and Moonshot's announcement named none. The honest position today is: unknown, decided on November 4.

But we are not guessing in the dark, because Kimi K3 shipped under a licence Moonshot wrote for exactly this model family, and you can read it in full in the Kimi K3 repository on Hugging Face. It is a short, unusually readable document, and if K3.1 Pro follows the same pattern — which is an expectation, not a fact — this is what "open" will mean in practice.

The Kimi K3 License starts like the famous MIT licence: permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software — explicitly including the weights, the code and the right to fine-tune and build derivative works — free of charge. For researchers, hobbyists, and the overwhelming majority of companies, that is the whole story: download it and build.

Then come two conditions aimed at the very top of the market. The first is the "Model as a Service" clause. If you or your affiliates run a business that gives third parties API-style access to model inference or fine-tuning — where those third parties meaningfully control inputs, parameters or training data — and that business's aggregate revenue exceeds 20 million US dollars over any consecutive twelve months, you must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before using the model commercially. Note what the clause deliberately does not cover: products that merely embed the model inside specific features, and simple relays of requests to models hosted by others. The second condition is a branding rule: if the model powers a commercial product with more than 100 million monthly active users, or more than 20 million dollars in monthly revenue, the name "Kimi K3" must be prominently displayed in that product's interface.

A final carve-out softens both conditions: they do not apply to purely internal use — anything that never exposes the model, its outputs or its capabilities to third parties — nor to use through Moonshot's own products and certified inference partners. And the licence closes with the standard "as is" disclaimer and a contact address for licensing questions.

So when the K3.1 Pro licence appears, the checklist is short and specific. Is it the same Kimi K3 License with the name swapped, or a new document? Is the Model-as-a-Service revenue threshold still 20 million dollars? Does the branding rule survive? Has anything been added — an acceptable-use list, a geographic restriction, a research-only tier? Five minutes of reading on November 4 will answer all of it, and until those five minutes happen, any article that tells you what you may do with these weights — including confident claims that they are "fully open" or "not really open" — is getting ahead of the document.

One and a half terabytes: the hardware reality

The second reality check is physical. The Kimi K3 weights on Hugging Face occupy 1.56 terabytes, spread across 96 files, in MXFP4 format — a compact 4-bit representation that Moonshot bakes in during training rather than squeezing down afterwards. K3.1 Pro is the same architecture at the same parameter count, so a similar footprint is the reasonable expectation. To put 1.56 terabytes in perspective: it is roughly twenty-five times the size of a typical 70-billion-parameter model download, and it will not fit on the drive of most workstations, let alone in the memory of a gaming GPU.

Running it is a data-centre conversation, and the arithmetic is not complicated. The weights alone need about 1.6 terabytes of fast memory before you have processed a single token; on top of that sits the key-value cache for that million-token context, which grows with every conversation you serve. A top-end data-centre GPU carries around 141 to 192 gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory. Divide the weights by that and you land in the region of ten to twelve flagship GPUs just to hold the model — one full high-end server node, or a couple of smaller ones linked together — with more headroom needed for comfortable serving. This is not a criticism; it is the honest category of the thing. K3.1 Pro is open in the sense that a power station's blueprints are open: nothing stops you, provided you have a power station.

Three practical consequences follow. First, the first wave of real usage will come from inference providers and well-equipped labs, not individuals — watch for hosted endpoints appearing within days of the drop, the same pattern that followed the Mistral Large 4 open-weights release in late October. Second, community quantisation projects will immediately try to squeeze the model smaller; how much intelligence survives aggressive shrinking of a model that is already 4-bit native is a genuine open question, and early claims should be treated as claims. Third, for almost everyone reading this, the API at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens will remain the rational way to use K3.1 Pro for the foreseeable future — the weights matter to you because they cap Moonshot's pricing power and guarantee the model's survival, not because you will host it yourself.

How you will actually run it

If you do have the hardware, the path is already paved, because K3 set it up. Moonshot's K3 release shipped with official support in the two serving stacks that dominate open-model deployment: vLLM, which carries a Moonshot-maintained recipe for the model, and SGLang, which documents it in its cookbook. Day-one support for K3.1 Pro in the same stacks is the reasonable expectation — the architecture is unchanged — but "reasonable expectation" is doing real work in that sentence, and the model card on November 4 is the document that will confirm versions, flags and known issues.

Preparation, if you intend to be ready on the day, is mostly logistics. You need roughly 1.6 terabytes of fast local storage free, a Hugging Face account that has accepted any licence gate the repository carries, and your serving stack installed and tested in advance — K3 itself is the perfect rehearsal download if bandwidth is cheap for you, since its tooling, file layout and deployment guides mirror what is coming. One warning from experience with every major drop: the first hours bring download congestion and a flood of re-uploads, mirrors and repackaged versions from unknown accounts. Download from the official moonshotai organisation only, and let other people be the first to discover which community conversion is broken.

The scoreboard moved: Index v5 and the speed problem

Anyone preparing to evaluate the drop should know that the measuring stick changed last week. On October 27, Artificial Analysis replaced its Intelligence Index with version 5, built mostly on private tests. Under the new index, K3.1 Pro scores 46 — ninth overall, and the highest score of any open-weights model, three points behind the best closed systems on that chart. Some of Artificial Analysis's own task-level measurements are striking: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, the tough terminal-based coding-agent test, they measured K3.1 Pro at 67 percent — the highest they had recorded — and on their GDPval-AA measure of economically valuable knowledge work it ranks third. Moonshot's own reported Terminal-Bench figure, 65.7 percent against Claude Opus 5.5's 66.4, is close behind.

The same independent testing exposes the model's real weakness, and it is not intelligence. It is speed. Artificial Analysis measured K3.1 Pro's output at about 41 tokens per second, ranking 188th of 192 models for output speed. For batch work and offline analysis that hardly matters. For interactive products — a coding assistant answering in real time, an agent loop making hundreds of calls — it matters a great deal, and it is part of why OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra, launched October 26 at half the per-token price of the model it replaces and scoring 48 on the new index, is a serious rival for the same workloads. The Highspeed variant exists precisely because Moonshot knows this; whether self-hosting the weights improves or worsens the speed picture will be one of the first things the community benchmarks after November 4. Our comparison of the best AI coding assistants is a useful map of the field this model is entering.

Two controversies hanging over the drop

An honest preview has to include the two stories that broke around this model in the last week, labelled for exactly what they are.

The first is a report, not a finding. On October 28, The Information reported — and Reuters followed on October 29 — that according to people with direct knowledge, Moonshot relied heavily on outputs from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to train K3.1 Pro, with a similar claim made about DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash. Training one model on another's outputs, called distillation, sits in contested legal and ethical territory and is restricted by most providers' terms. What is established: the report exists, it is attributed to unnamed sources, and as of October 29 neither Moonshot, OpenAI nor DeepSeek had publicly commented on it. What is not established: whether it is true, and if so, to what degree. It changes nothing about the file that lands on November 4, but it may shape how enterprises' lawyers read the licence — one more reason that document matters.

The second story is Moonshot's own disclosure, and it is stranger: for the open-weight release, the company deliberately made its model worse at hacking. Moonshot says it identified and removed cyberattack-related material from both the mid-training data and the reinforcement-learning tasks, because capability at finding and exploiting software flaws was rising with scale and weights, once published, cannot be recalled. On its internal exploit benchmark, the filtered model scores 81.0 percent; an identical pipeline without the filtering scores 90.5 percent. Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin publicly defended the approach, arguing that restraint now beats the identity-check regimes that a wave of AI-powered attacks could trigger. The open question — and it can only be answered after November 4 — is whether the reduction survives contact with the research community: outside teams will test whether fine-tuning restores the removed capability, and at least one company has already publicly announced plans to try stripping the safeguards. Moonshot's published before-and-after numbers make this the first open release in history whose safety claim arrives with its own test attached.

A third, smaller allegation deserves a sentence for completeness: VentureBeat reported screenshots, which it could not authenticate, purporting to show a paid-promotion brief for Kimi creators that included an instruction not to label posts as paid partnerships. Moonshot had not responded in the reporting. Unverified documents are not evidence — but if you see suspiciously synchronised praise on drop day, you will know the context in which to read it.

Meanwhile, K2 closes its doors today

One dated detail is easy to miss in the drop coverage: the previous generation is being retired on a schedule that starts now. Moonshot's pricing pages indicate the K2 series closes to new users from October 31 — today — and is due to be fully retired by the end of December. If your product still routes traffic to a K2 model, the weights drop is not your only November deadline; migration to K3 or K3.1 Pro belongs on the same calendar page. Moonshot also had a smaller operational stumble this week, apologising for rate limits on K3.1 Pro and resetting a portion of user quotas — a useful reminder that demand for this model, even hosted, is currently outrunning the supply pointed at it.

Your November 4 checklist

When the repository appears, these are the checks that separate knowing from repeating — the same checks we will run before updating this article:

  1. The licence file. Name, Model-as-a-Service threshold, branding rule, anything new. Read the document, not the summaries.
  2. The repository itself. Official moonshotai organisation, exact repo names — and whether Highspeed is included or hosted-only.
  3. Formats and size. MXFP4 as expected? Total terabytes? Any official smaller variants?
  4. The model card. Shipped context length, serving-stack versions, known limitations, and any stated difference between the API model and the released weights.
  5. Independent numbers. Artificial Analysis and community evaluations run on the released weights — not the API — including whether the cyber-capability reduction is measurable.
  6. First endpoints. Which inference providers list it, at what price per token, within the first week.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are the Kimi K3.1 Pro weights out now?

No. As of October 31, 2026, Moonshot's Hugging Face organisation has no K3.1 Pro repository — the newest release there is still Kimi K3. Moonshot's announcement promises the full weights "will be released by Nov 4, 2026", and until the repository appears, the model is available only through Kimi's apps and Moonshot's API.

What licence will the K3.1 Pro weights use?

Moonshot has not announced one. The best guide is the precedent: Kimi K3 shipped under the custom Kimi K3 License — broadly MIT-style freedom to use, modify and sell, with a separate-agreement requirement for Model-as-a-Service businesses earning over $20 million a year, and a branding rule for products above 100 million monthly users or $20 million in monthly revenue. Whether K3.1 Pro uses the same licence can only be confirmed from the licence file in its repository on November 4.

How big will the download be?

Kimi K3's weights occupy 1.56 terabytes on Hugging Face in MXFP4 format across 96 files. K3.1 Pro shares the same 2.8-trillion-parameter architecture, so a similar size is expected — but the exact figure is only known when the repository is published. Plan for roughly 1.6 terabytes of free, fast storage.

Can I run Kimi K3.1 Pro on my own computer?

Realistically, no — and that is about physics, not permission. The weights alone need around 1.6 terabytes of memory to load, which means roughly ten to twelve flagship data-centre GPUs before serving a single request. Community quantisation projects will try to shrink it after release, but a model that is already natively 4-bit has limited room to shrink. For individuals and most teams, the API at $2/$10 per million tokens is the practical route.

Is it true K3.1 Pro was trained on GPT-6 outputs?

It has been reported, not proven. The Information reported on October 28, 2026, citing people with direct knowledge, that Moonshot relied heavily on GPT-6 Astra outputs to train K3.1 Pro; Reuters carried the report on October 29. Moonshot, OpenAI and DeepSeek had issued no public comment as of October 29. Treat the claim as an unconfirmed allegation until a company statement or stronger evidence appears.

Conclusion

Strip away the hype and November 4 is a document release as much as a model release. The model itself is already proven in public: fourth on the old independent index, top of the open field on the new one, priced a third below its predecessor, and slow enough that speed — not smarts — is its honest weakness. What nobody outside Moonshot has seen is the paperwork and the files: the licence that decides whether "open" means MIT-free or free-with-conditions, the repository that decides whether Highspeed is included, and the released weights that decide whether the much-discussed cyber-capability reduction is real. Our launch guide covers what K3.1 Pro is; this article will be updated with what the drop actually contained — licence first — as soon as the repository is live and verified. If Moonshot keeps its date, that update lands on November 4.
