title: Next.js 16 `use cache` Directive: Granular Caching at the Function Level and What It Replaces
description:
Next.js 16 use cache Directive: Granular Caching at the Function Level and What It Replaces

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Next.js 16 eliminates the framework's most confusing aspect: implicit caching. Previous versions cached fetch requests automatically, left developers guessing when route segments became static, and buried cache configuration inside fetch options. The new use cache directive makes every cache decision explicit. Developers mark what to cache, set expiration with cacheLife(), and invalidate with cacheTag().

The old model failed because developers could not predict cache behavior. A fetch call with no options might cache forever or not cache at all, depending on whether the route contained dynamic functions. Route segments became static or dynamic based on heuristics the compiler inferred from your code. Production bugs emerged when a component that worked dynamically in development suddenly rendered statically in production, serving stale data for hours.

Problem: implicit caching causes unpredictable cache behavior and stale data

Next.js 16 solves this with use cache. When you add the directive to a function or component, the framework caches its return value. When you call cacheLife('hours'), the cache expires in one hour. When you call cacheTag(['products']), you can invalidate that cache entry on demand. The mental model becomes: mark what you cache, state when it expires, name it for invalidation.

Solution: explicit use cache directive gives predictable control

This post covers what use cache replaces, how function-level and component-level caching work, migration patterns from unstable_cache, the cache hierarchy Next.js now uses, and production gotchas around cache storage.

Key Takeaways

  • use cache replaces unstable_cache, fetch cache options, and all implicit caching; every cache decision is now explicit.
  • You can cache at the function level (data fetching) or component level (entire UI trees), with arguments and closures becoming part of the cache key automatically.
  • cacheLife() sets expiration windows; cacheTag() enables on-demand invalidation; both pair with use cache to control freshness.
  • Cache storage defaults to in-memory per instance; use cache: remote moves entries to a shared durable handler for high hit rates.
  • Migration requires converting unstable_cache wrappers to use cache directives and replacing fetch next.revalidate with cacheLife() calls.

What use cache Replaces: unstable_cache, fetch Options, and Implicit Caching

use cache supersedes three caching mechanisms from Next.js 15 and earlier.

unstable_cache: developers wrapped functions in unstable_cache(fn, keyParts, options) to cache database queries or API calls. The wrapper returned a new function that memoized results. The name signaled instability; the API never graduated to stable. Next.js 16 removes it entirely.

fetch cache options: developers passed { next: { revalidate: 3600 } } to fetch calls to cache HTTP responses. The framework intercepted fetch, stored the response in a data cache, and served cached data until expiration. This worked only for fetch calls. Database queries and third-party SDK calls required unstable_cache.

Implicit route caching: Next.js analyzed route segments at build time. If a segment contained no dynamic functions (cookies, headers, searchParams), the compiler marked it static and prerendered it. If any child component called a dynamic function, the entire segment became dynamic. Developers could not see this decision; they inferred it from build output or production behavior.

All three mechanisms are gone. use cache handles every scenario.

Diagram showing old caching mechanisms replaced by use cache

The removal creates a single model. You mark cacheable operations with use cache, set expiration with cacheLife(), and invalidate with cacheTag(). The compiler generates cache keys from function arguments and captured closures. No wrapper functions, no fetch-specific options, no implicit heuristics.

This unification matters because developers now reason about caching the same way everywhere. A database query, a fetch call, and a React Server Component all use identical syntax. The cache key derivation follows the same rules. The expiration model applies uniformly.

How use cache Works: Function-Level and Component-Level Caching

The use cache directive applies to async functions and React Server Components. When Next.js encounters it, the framework serializes the function's return value into an RSC payload and stores that payload in a cache.

Function-level caching targets data operations. Add use cache to the top of an async function that fetches from a database, calls a third-party API, or performs expensive computation:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  const product = await db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = $1',
    [id]
  );

  return product;
}

The compiler generates a cache key from the function identity and its arguments. In this example, the key includes getProduct and the id value. Calling getProduct('123') creates one cache entry; calling getProduct('456') creates another. The framework does not cache the function itself; it caches the result for each unique set of arguments.

Component-level caching targets UI trees. Add use cache to an async component that renders JSX:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export default async function ProductList() {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');

  const products = await db.query('SELECT * FROM products');

  return (
    <ul>
      {products.map(product => (
        <li key={product.id}>{product.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

The framework caches the entire RSC payload for the component. The payload includes the rendered JSX, serialized props, and any data the component loaded. When Next.js renders the same component again within the cache window, it returns the cached payload without executing the component body.

Content image showing cache key generation and payload storage

How use cache generates keys and stores payloads

The cache key includes arguments and any values captured from parent scopes. If a component reads a variable from a closure, that variable becomes part of the key. This ensures different inputs produce separate cache entries.

Arguments and return values must be serializable. You cannot cache functions, class instances with methods, or objects containing Symbols. The framework serializes primitives, plain objects, arrays, and React elements. Attempting to cache non-serializable values throws a runtime error.

Components marked with use cache cannot directly call cookies(), headers(), or access searchParams. These APIs provide request-time data that varies per request. Calling them inside a cached function creates a contradiction: the cache expects stable inputs, but runtime APIs return dynamic values. If you need runtime data, pass it as an argument to the cached function from a non-cached parent component.

Using cacheLife() for Granular Cache Control

cacheLife() sets the expiration policy for a cached function. Without it, Next.js applies a default profile. The default provides basic time-based invalidation, but production apps need explicit control.

The function accepts a named profile or a custom configuration object. Next.js 16 ships with four built-in profiles:

Profile Revalidate Expire Stale
seconds 15 seconds 15 seconds 1 minute
minutes 5 minutes 5 minutes 1 hour
hours 1 hour 1 hour 1 day
days 1 day 1 day 7 days

Revalidate determines when the cache entry becomes stale. After this window, Next.js marks the entry for refresh but continues serving the stale value while fetching a new one in the background.

Expire sets the hard limit. After this window, the cache entry becomes invalid. Requests cannot use it; Next.js must fetch fresh data synchronously.

Stale controls client-side caching. The browser keeps the RSC payload fresh for this duration when prefetching or navigating.

Use a built-in profile when the default windows fit your data freshness requirements:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

Use a custom configuration when you need precise control:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getInventory(warehouseId: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife({
    revalidate: 300,    // 5 minutes
    expire: 600,        // 10 minutes
    stale: 3600,        // 1 hour
  });

  return await inventoryApi.getStock(warehouseId);
}

The configuration accepts seconds as numbers. The example caches inventory for 5 minutes, expires it after 10 minutes, and allows the browser to use stale data for 1 hour during navigation.

Pairing cacheLife() with cacheTag() enables on-demand invalidation:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  cacheTag('products', `product-${id}`);

  return await db.products.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

When you call revalidateTag('products') from a Server Action, Next.js invalidates all cache entries tagged with products. The next request for any product executes the function and generates a fresh cache entry.

Migration Patterns: Converting Legacy Caching to use cache

Migrating from Next.js 15 caching requires three steps: remove unstable_cache wrappers, replace fetch cache options, and add explicit use cache directives.

Step 1: Remove unstable_cache wrappers

Old pattern with unstable_cache:

import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

const getCachedUser = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => {
    return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  },
  ['user'],
  { revalidate: 3600, tags: ['users'] }
);

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  return await getCachedUser(id);
}

New pattern with use cache:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  cacheTag('users');

  return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

The directive goes inside the function body. The cache key now derives automatically from the function identity and arguments. You do not specify key parts manually.

Step 2: Replace fetch cache options

Old pattern with fetch options:

export async function getProducts() {
  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products', {
    next: { revalidate: 300, tags: ['products'] }
  });
  return response.json();
}

New pattern with use cache:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProducts() {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');
  cacheTag('products');

  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products');
  return response.json();
}

The fetch call no longer carries cache options. The use cache directive controls caching for the entire function, including the fetch call and any subsequent processing.

Content image showing migration from old caching patterns to use cache

Step 3: Add explicit directives to previously implicit routes

Routes that relied on implicit static optimization need explicit use cache directives. If a page component performs data fetching that should cache, add the directive:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  const { id } = await params;
  const product = await db.products.findUnique({ where: { id } });

  return <div>{product.name}</div>;
}

The migration flow moves all cache control to the function level. You see caching decisions in the code where they apply, not in build output or framework internals.

Migration flow from old caching patterns to use cache

use cache vs Data Cache vs Full Route Cache: Understanding the Cache Hierarchy

Next.js 16 maintains three cache layers: function-level cache (via use cache), prerendered HTML, and browser cache. Each serves a different purpose in the request lifecycle.

Function-level cache stores RSC payloads for individual functions and components. When you mark a function with use cache, Next.js caches its serialized return value. This cache applies during rendering. If a component calls a cached function multiple times in a single request, the framework returns the cached result after the first call.

Prerendered HTML stores complete pages generated at build time or during incremental static regeneration. When Next.js prerenders a page, it executes all cached functions, generates the RSC payload, renders HTML, and writes the HTML to disk. Subsequent requests serve the HTML directly without executing Server Components. The cacheLife expire window controls when the HTML becomes stale and triggers a background revalidation.

Browser cache stores RSC payloads the client receives during navigation or prefetching. When a user navigates to a new page, Next.js sends the RSC payload. The browser caches this payload according to the cacheLife stale window. During that window, navigating back to the page uses the cached payload without a server request.

Cache hierarchy showing function-level, HTML, and browser caches

These layers work together. A request hits the browser cache first. If the cached payload is stale, the browser requests from the server. The server checks for prerendered HTML. If the HTML is stale or missing, Next.js executes the page component. The component calls cached functions, which check the function-level cache. If a function's cached result is stale, the framework executes the function and updates the cache.

The distinction matters when you configure cacheLife. Setting revalidate to 5 minutes means the function-level cache refreshes every 5 minutes. Setting expire to 10 minutes means the prerendered HTML becomes invalid after 10 minutes. Setting stale to 1 hour means the browser uses its cached payload for 1 hour without checking the server.

Cache layer Storage location Invalidation trigger Controlled by
Function-level In-memory or remote handler revalidate window or revalidateTag() cacheLife() revalidate
Prerendered HTML Disk or platform storage expire window or deployment cacheLife() expire
Browser Client memory stale window or user action cacheLife() stale

The default cache handler stores function-level entries in memory per instance. This works for small apps but does not share cache across instances. For apps with multiple servers or serverless functions, use use cache: remote to store entries in a shared handler. The remote handler requires a network roundtrip for each cache hit, so it only pays off when the hit rate is high and the cached operation is expensive.

Production Gotchas: Cache Storage, Edge Runtime, and Common Mistakes

Production environments introduce cache storage constraints, edge runtime limitations, and developer mistakes that do not surface in local development.

Cache storage defaults to ephemeral in-memory per instance. When you deploy to a platform like Vercel, each serverless function instance maintains its own cache. Cache entries do not persist across cold starts. If an instance scales down and later scales up, the new instance starts with an empty cache. This differs from development, where next dev maintains a single long-running process with a persistent in-memory cache.

For durable shared caching, configure a cache handler in next.config.ts:

const nextConfig = {
  cacheHandlers: {
    default: {
      handler: './cache-handler.js',
    },
  },
};

export default nextConfig;

The cache handler must implement the Next.js cache handler interface. The official Redis handler provides a reference implementation. Using a remote cache introduces latency; each cache hit requires a network roundtrip to the cache store. Profile your cache hit rate before migrating. If the hit rate is low, the network overhead exceeds the benefit.

Edge runtime does not support all cache operations. Functions deployed to the edge can use use cache, but they cannot write to a durable cache handler that requires a persistent connection. The edge runtime allows only stateless HTTP requests. If your cached function must run at the edge, limit cache storage to the edge instance's memory. Cache entries do not persist across edge locations or instance restarts.

Common mistakes include caching non-serializable values, accessing runtime APIs inside cached functions, and misunderstanding cache key derivation.

Attempting to cache a class instance fails at runtime:

// This crashes when Next.js tries to serialize the cache entry
export async function getUserService(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  return new UserService(id);
}

The framework can only serialize plain objects, arrays, primitives, and React elements. Extract the data from the class instance and cache the data:

export async function getUserData(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  const service = new UserService(id);
  return await service.getData();
}

Accessing cookies() inside a cached function throws an error:

// This crashes because cookies() is a runtime API
export async function getSessionUser() {
  'use cache';
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const sessionId = cookieStore.get('session');
  return await db.sessions.findUnique({ where: { id: sessionId.value } });
}

Runtime APIs provide request-specific data. Caching request-specific data breaks the cache model. Move the runtime API call to a parent component and pass the value as an argument:

export async function Page() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const sessionId = cookieStore.get('session')?.value;

  if (!sessionId) {
    return <div>Not logged in</div>;
  }

  const user = await getCachedUser(sessionId);
  return <div>Hello {user.name}</div>;
}

async function getCachedUser(sessionId: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');

  const session = await db.sessions.findUnique({ 
    where: { id: sessionId },
    include: { user: true }
  });

  return session?.user;
}

The cached function receives sessionId as an argument. Different session IDs produce different cache entries. The cache key includes the session ID, so each user gets their own cached entry.

Production flow showing cache handler, edge limitations, and error paths

Cache key derivation includes function identity, arguments, and captured closures. If a closure captures a value from a parent scope, that value becomes part of the key. This can produce unintended cache misses if the captured value changes frequently:

export default async function ProductList({ category }: { category: string }) {
  const baseUrl = process.env.API_URL;

  // The cache key includes both category and baseUrl
  async function fetchProducts() {
    'use cache';
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/products?category=${category}`);
    return response.json();
  }

  return <div>{await fetchProducts()}</div>;
}

If API_URL changes between deployments, the cache key changes and all entries become invalid. For stable cache keys, pass environment variables as arguments or read them inside the cached function without capturing them from closures.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should you use use cache: remote instead of the default in-memory cache?

Use use cache: remote when your app runs on multiple serverless instances or containers and the cached operation is expensive enough to justify a network roundtrip. The remote cache shares entries across instances, but each cache hit requires fetching from the remote store. Profile your cache hit rate first; if it is below 80%, the network overhead likely exceeds the benefit.

Can you cache Server Actions with use cache?

Server Actions cannot use use cache directly because they are not idempotent operations; they mutate state rather than fetch data. You can pass Server Actions through cached components to Client Components without invoking them inside the cacheable function. The cached component treats the action as a serializable prop.

What happens when you call revalidateTag() with a tag that does not exist?

Calling revalidateTag() with a non-existent tag succeeds silently without invalidating anything. The framework does not track which tags exist; it only invalidates cache entries that match the tag. If no entries match, the call has no effect. This makes tag-based invalidation safe to call speculatively.

How does Next.js handle cache entries when you redeploy your app?

A new deployment generates a new build ID, which becomes part of the cache key for all use cache entries. When the build ID changes, all previous cache entries become inaccessible. This applies to both in-memory and remote caches. The new deployment starts with an empty cache, even if you use a durable cache handler.

Can you use use cache in Client Components?

Client Components cannot use use cache because they run in the browser, which has no server-side cache. The directive only works in Server Components and server-side async functions. If you need to cache data in a Client Component, fetch it in a Server Component, cache the Server Component with use cache, and pass the data as props.

Conclusion: Building a Mental Model for Next.js 16 Caching

The mental model for Next.js 16 caching reduces to three principles: mark what you cache, state when it expires, name it for invalidation. Every cache decision is explicit. No framework heuristics infer whether a route should cache. No fetch calls carry hidden cache options. No compiler analysis determines static versus dynamic rendering.

Add use cache to functions that fetch data or render UI. Call cacheLife() to set expiration windows. Call cacheTag() to enable on-demand invalidation. The compiler generates cache keys from function identity, arguments, and captured closures. Arguments and return values must be serializable. Runtime APIs like cookies() cannot be called inside cached functions.

Migration from Next.js 15 requires removing unstable_cache wrappers, replacing fetch cache options, and adding explicit directives. Production deployments need cache handler configuration for durable shared caching. Edge deployments limit cache to in-memory per instance. Cache entries do not persist across deployments because the build ID becomes part of the cache key.

The result is a caching model where developers control every aspect. You see caching decisions in the code where they apply. You reason about cache behavior the same way everywhere: functions, components, routes. You configure freshness requirements once, at the function level, rather than in multiple places with conflicting options. For teams managing complex data dependencies, this clarity eliminates an entire class of production bugs.

title: How to Test an MCP Server: Vitest, In-Memory Transport, Streamable HTTP and the Inspector CLI
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Testing an MCP server means checking three layers: the pure functions behind your tools, the MCP contract (tool list, schemas, results and errors), and the transport your clients actually use. You can cover all three with Vitest and the official TypeScript SDK, without starting an AI client, and the whole suite below runs in about 300 ms.

I wrote this while building Benchline, my set of browser tools that are also a stateless MCP server. Every tool there is a pure function first and an MCP tool second, and that split is what makes testing easy. Below is a small, complete example server you can copy, the tests I run against it, and the MCP Inspector CLI commands for manual checks. Everything was run with @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.32.2, Vitest 5.0.5 and Node 22.20, and I re-ran the full suite on October 31, 2026 (1.32.2 is still the latest SDK release) with the same result.

TL;DR

  • Unit-test the logic as plain functions. Most bugs live there, and these tests need no MCP at all.
  • Contract-test the server in memory with InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair() and a real SDK Client: list tools, check schemas, call each tool, and assert on errors.
  • Test the transport once over Streamable HTTP: the SDK client connects, initialize returns 200, wrong Accept headers get 406, GET gets 405 on a stateless server.
  • Check by hand with npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli <url> --transport http --method tools/list.
  • In SDK 1.32.2, a schema failure and an unknown tool both came back as a tool result with isError: true, not as a thrown error. Write your assertions so they hold either way.

The server under test

Two read-only tools: slugify, with a typed output schema, and json_format, which must report bad input as an error result instead of crashing.

```ts title="src/server.ts"
import { McpServer } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js";
import { z } from "zod";

export function slugify(input: string) {
return input.normalize("NFKD").replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, "").toLowerCase()
.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-").replace(/^-+|-+$/g, "");
}

export function createServer() {
const server = new McpServer({ name: "demo-tools", version: "1.0.0" });

server.registerTool("slugify", {
title: "Slugify",
description: "Turn a title into a URL slug (lowercase ASCII, words joined by hyphens).",
inputSchema: { text: z.string().min(1).max(500) },
outputSchema: { slug: z.string() },
annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, idempotentHint: true, openWorldHint: false },
}, async ({ text }) => {
const slug = slugify(text);
return { content: [{ type: "text", text: slug }], structuredContent: { slug } };
});

server.registerTool("json_format", {
title: "Format JSON",
description: "Pretty-print a JSON string with the given indent. Returns an error result for invalid JSON.",
inputSchema: { json: z.string(), indent: z.number().int().min(0).max(8).default(2) },
annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, idempotentHint: true, openWorldHint: false },
}, async ({ json, indent }) => {
try {
return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(json), null, indent) }] };
} catch (e) {
return { isError: true, content: [{ type: "text", text: Invalid JSON: ${(e as Error).message} }] };
}
});

return server;
}




The key design choice is that `slugify` is exported on its own. The MCP handler is a thin wrapper, so the logic is tested like any other function.

## Layer 1: unit tests for the tool logic



```ts title="test/unit.test.ts"
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { slugify } from "../src/server.ts";

describe("slugify (pure function)", () => {
  it("lowercases and joins words", () => expect(slugify("Hello, MCP World!")).toBe("hello-mcp-world"));
  it("strips accents", () => expect(slugify("Crème Brûlée")).toBe("creme-brulee"));
  it("trims separators", () => expect(slugify("  --a--  ")).toBe("a"));
});

Nothing MCP-specific here, and that is the point. In Benchline, each tool folder has a pure lib/ covered by Vitest. The MCP layer only maps inputs and outputs.

Layer 2: contract tests with the in-memory transport

The SDK ships InMemoryTransport, which links a client and a server inside one process. You test the real protocol (JSON-RPC messages, schema validation, result shapes) with no ports and no network.

```ts title="test/mcp.test.ts"
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from "vitest";
import { Client } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js";
import { InMemoryTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/inMemory.js";
import { createServer } from "../src/server.ts";

let client: Client;
beforeAll(async () => {
const [clientT, serverT] = InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair();
await createServer().connect(serverT);
client = new Client({ name: "test", version: "1.0.0" });
await client.connect(clientT);
});
afterAll(() => client.close());

describe("MCP contract (in-memory)", () => {
it("lists tools with object schemas and descriptions", async () => {
const { tools } = await client.listTools();
expect(tools.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
for (const t of tools) {
expect(t.name).toMatch(/^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$/);
expect(t.description?.length).toBeGreaterThan(20);
expect(t.inputSchema.type).toBe("object");
expect(t.annotations?.readOnlyHint).toBe(true);
}
expect(new Set(tools.map((t) => t.name)).size).toBe(tools.length);
});

it("returns structured content that matches the output schema", async () => {
const r = await client.callTool({ name: "slugify", arguments: { text: "Hello MCP" } });
expect(r.isError).toBeFalsy();
expect(r.structuredContent).toEqual({ slug: "hello-mcp" });
});

it("applies schema defaults", async () => {
const r = await client.callTool({ name: "json_format", arguments: { json: '{"a":1}' } });
expect((r.content as any)[0].text).toBe('{\n "a": 1\n}');
});

it("reports bad input as a tool error, not a crash", async () => {
const r = await client.callTool({ name: "json_format", arguments: { json: "{oops" } });
expect(r.isError).toBe(true);
expect((r.content as any)[0].text).toMatch(/^Invalid JSON/);
});

it("rejects arguments that fail the input schema", async () => {
const r = await client.callTool({ name: "slugify", arguments: { text: "" } }).catch((e) => e);
if (r instanceof Error) expect((r as any).code).toBe(-32602);
else expect((r as any).isError).toBe(true);
});

it("errors on unknown tools", async () => {
const r = await client.callTool({ name: "nope", arguments: {} }).catch((e) => e);
expect(r instanceof Error ? true : (r as any).isError).toBe(true);
});
});




What these tests catch:

- **Schema regressions.** Every tool must have an object `inputSchema` and a useful description. A model picks tools by name and description, so an empty description is a real bug.
- **Annotation drift.** If a tool is meant to be read-only, assert `readOnlyHint`. Clients can use annotations to decide when to ask the user for confirmation.
- **Duplicate names** after a refactor.
- **Error shape.** A handler that throws on bad input is worse than one that returns `isError: true` with a clear message, because the model can read the message and retry.

Two results surprised me, so I logged them before writing the assertions. With SDK 1.32.2, calling `slugify` with an empty string (which fails `min(1)`) and calling a tool that doesn't exist both resolved to a result with `isError: true`. The unknown-tool text was `MCP error -32602: Tool nope not found`. Older SDK versions and other server frameworks may throw a JSON-RPC error instead, so the tests accept both shapes.

## Layer 3: the Streamable HTTP transport

Clients like Cursor, Claude Code and VS Code connect over HTTP, so test that path once. This server is stateless: a new `McpServer` and transport per request and no session ID. Benchline's public endpoint is stateless in the same way: no API key and no session.



```ts title="src/http.ts"
import { createServer as createHttpServer } from "node:http";
import { StreamableHTTPServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/streamableHttp.js";
import { createServer } from "./server.ts";

// Stateless Streamable HTTP: a new server + transport per request, no session id.
export function startHttp(port = 0) {
  const http = createHttpServer(async (req, res) => {
    if (req.url !== "/mcp") { res.writeHead(404).end(); return; }
    if (req.method !== "POST") { res.writeHead(405, { Allow: "POST" }).end(); return; }
    const chunks: Buffer[] = []; for await (const c of req) chunks.push(c as Buffer);
    const body = JSON.parse(Buffer.concat(chunks).toString() || "null");
    const server = createServer();
    const transport = new StreamableHTTPServerTransport({ sessionIdGenerator: undefined, enableJsonResponse: true });
    res.on("close", () => { transport.close(); server.close(); });
    await server.connect(transport);
    await transport.handleRequest(req, res, body);
  });
  return new Promise<{ url: URL; close: () => void }>((resolve) =>
    http.listen(port, "127.0.0.1", () => {
      const { port } = http.address() as { port: number };
      resolve({ url: new URL(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}/mcp`), close: () => http.close() });
    }));
}

if (import.meta.url === `file://${process.argv[1]}`) {
  const { url } = await startHttp(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3321));
  console.log(`MCP server on ${url}`);
}

```ts title="test/http.test.ts"
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from "vitest";
import { Client } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js";
import { StreamableHTTPClientTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/streamableHttp.js";
import { startHttp } from "../src/http.ts";

let srv: Awaited>;
const url = () => process.env.MCP_URL ? new URL(process.env.MCP_URL) : srv.url;
beforeAll(async () => { if (!process.env.MCP_URL) srv = await startHttp(); });
afterAll(() => srv?.close());

const init = { jsonrpc: "2.0", id: 1, method: "initialize",
params: { protocolVersion: "2025-06-18", capabilities: {}, clientInfo: { name: "curl", version: "1" } } };

describe("Streamable HTTP transport", () => {
it("works with the official SDK client", async () => {
const c = new Client({ name: "http-test", version: "1.0.0" });
await c.connect(new StreamableHTTPClientTransport(url()));
const { tools } = await c.listTools();
expect(tools.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
await c.close();
});

it("answers initialize without a session id (stateless)", async () => {
const r = await fetch(url(), { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify(init),
headers: { "content-type": "application/json", accept: "application/json, text/event-stream" } });
expect(r.status).toBe(200);
expect(r.headers.get("mcp-session-id")).toBeNull();
});

it("rejects a client that does not accept both content types", async () => {
const r = await fetch(url(), { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify(init),
headers: { "content-type": "application/json", accept: "application/json" } });
expect(r.status).toBe(406);
});

it("returns 405 for GET when there is no SSE stream", async () => {
const r = await fetch(url(), { headers: { accept: "text/event-stream" } });
expect(r.status).toBe(405);
});
});




All four passed. Facts worth pinning in tests, because a framework upgrade can silently change them:

- `initialize` returned **200** with no `mcp-session-id` header, so clients don't need to track a session.
- A request with `Accept: application/json` only returned **406**. The Streamable HTTP spec requires clients to accept both `application/json` and `text/event-stream`, and some hand-written clients and proxies don't.
- `GET /mcp` returned **405**, which tells clients there is no server-to-client SSE stream on a stateless server.
- In stateless mode, `tools/list` worked without an `initialize` call first. A raw curl got back a 1,120-byte JSON response for the two tools.

Set `MCP_URL` to run the same file against a deployed server: `MCP_URL=https://your-host/mcp npx vitest run test/http.test.ts`. I ran it against the local server started with `node src/http.ts`, and all 4 tests passed.

Response size is worth a test too. Everything in `tools/list` is sent to the model, so it costs context on every conversation. I measured why that matters in [MCP vs API](https://fabwaseem.com/blog/mcp-vs-api).

## Manual checks with the MCP Inspector CLI

The [MCP Inspector](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/inspector) has a web UI and a CLI mode. The CLI is handy in a terminal or a CI smoke step (I first ran it with version 2.12.0, and the same commands gave the same output with 2.13.0, the latest release on October 31, 2026):



```bash title="Inspector CLI"
# list tools
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://127.0.0.1:3321/mcp \
  --transport http --method tools/list

# call one tool
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://127.0.0.1:3321/mcp \
  --transport http --method tools/call --tool-name slugify --tool-arg 'text=Hello MCP World'

The call printed:

{
  "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "hello-mcp-world" }],
  "structuredContent": { "slug": "hello-mcp-world" }
}

And raw curl, for when you suspect the client:

```bash title="curl"
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3321/mcp \
-H 'content-type: application/json' \
-H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
-d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list"}'




## Running it in CI



```json title="package.json (scripts)"
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "vitest run",
    "test:remote": "vitest run test/http.test.ts"
  }
}

npm test runs all three layers. In 3 test files and 13 tests, Vitest reported a duration of 295 ms. Run test:remote with MCP_URL set after each deploy as a smoke test. It catches a broken proxy, a missing route or a CDN that strips headers, which is exactly what unit tests can't see.

What to test, as a checklist

  • Every tool: unit tests for its logic, including edge cases and bad input.
  • tools/list: unique names, object input schemas, descriptions long enough to be useful, expected annotations.
  • Each tool through callTool: one happy path, one error path that returns isError: true with a readable message.
  • Output schemas: structuredContent matches what you declared.
  • Transport: SDK client connects; initialize status and session header; Accept handling (406); GET behavior (405 when stateless).
  • Auth, if you have it: no token gets 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header, and a wrong-audience token is rejected. The MCP security guide covers the cases worth testing.
  • Size: keep an eye on the tools/list byte count as you add tools.

If you are building your first server, start with how to build an MCP server in Next.js and stateless MCP servers. Then connect it to your editor with how to add a remote MCP server.

FAQ

How do I test an MCP server without an AI client?

Use the official SDK's Client class in your test runner. Connect it to your server with InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair() for fast in-process tests, or with StreamableHTTPClientTransport for the HTTP path, then call listTools and callTool and assert on the results. No model or editor is needed.

What is InMemoryTransport in the MCP SDK?

InMemoryTransport, exported from @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/inMemory.js, creates a linked pair of transports inside one process. Connect your server to one end and a Client to the other, and they exchange real JSON-RPC MCP messages without any network, which makes contract tests fast and deterministic.

How do I use the MCP Inspector CLI?

Run npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli followed by the server URL, --transport http and a method. For example --method tools/list lists tools, and --method tools/call --tool-name slugify --tool-arg 'text=Hello' calls one. It prints the JSON result, which makes it useful for scripts and CI smoke checks.

Should an MCP tool throw or return isError?

Return a result with isError: true and a clear text message for expected failures such as invalid input. The model can read the message and try again. In my tests with SDK 1.32.2, even schema validation failures and unknown tool names came back as isError results.

Why does my MCP server return 406 Not Acceptable?

The Streamable HTTP transport requires the client to send an Accept header listing both application/json and text/event-stream. A request with only Accept: application/json got 406 from the SDK's server transport in my test. Fix the client or the proxy that rewrites the header.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: CH-Ops Pro Scheduled Archival: Move ClickHouse® Data to S3
description:
Table of Contents

  1. What is CH-Ops?
  2. Introducing the CH-Ops Scheduled Archival
  3. Creation of an Archival Job
  4. Choose How Data Should Be Archived
  5. Configure the Watermark Column
  6. Starting Point and File Partitioning
  7. Choose the Storage Format
  8. Where the Job Runs, and Where It Writes To
  9. Scheduling and Getting Notified
  10. Defining the Restore Shape Upfront
  11. Managing a Job After It's Created
  12. A Complete Archival Example
  13. Restore Archived Data
  14. Explore Archived Files
  15. A Simple End-to-End Flow
  16. Why This Is Worth Setting Up
  17. Further Reading

What is CH-Ops?

CH-Ops is a browser-based operations platform built for managing ClickHouse® deployments. Instead of relying entirely on the command line or HTTP APIs, it provides a unified interface for executing SQL queries, monitoring clusters, managing users, backups, alerts, dashboards, and much more — all from a single web application.

One of the features available in the CH-Ops Pro version is Scheduled Archival, which moves aging data to S3-compatible storage on a schedule instead of letting it grow indefinitely inside the cluster.

Let's explore how Scheduled Archival works and how you can use it to automate ClickHouse data archival.

Introducing the CH-Ops Scheduled Archival

A ClickHouse® cluster tends to grow in one direction: up. Old rows rarely get deleted, and most of them are barely queried once they age past a certain point.

Scheduled Archival, under the Backups section in CH-Ops, gives you a way to move that cold data out to S3-compatible storage on a schedule, in a columnar format, without writing your own export scripts.

It allows you to create jobs that periodically archive data from ClickHouse to S3-compatible storage. A job runs a plain SELECT query against your cluster on a schedule, writes the result to S3-compatible storage, and — depending on the mode you choose — keeps track of what it has already archived so the next run only picks up new rows.

You write the query once. CH-Ops handles the window, the file format, the compression, and the schedule around it.

Three tabs organize the feature:

Tab What it's for
Jobs Create, run, pause, and monitor archival jobs
Restore Bring an archived snapshot back into a ClickHouse table
Archive Explorer Browse the folder structure of what has actually been written to storage

Creation of an Archival Job

Start by creating a new job from Scheduled Archival → New Job.

Give the job a name and provide a normal SELECT query describing the data you want to archive.

For example:

SELECT *
FROM uk.uk_price_paid

The archival window is handled automatically by the engine, so the query itself does not need to contain a time filter for an incremental job.

Before creating the job, you can use Test (describe) to inspect the query and its columns.

Choose How Data Should Be Archived

The Mode determines how each archival run handles the data.

The Mode dropdown gives you two options:

  • Incremental (windowed): Archives only new rows each run, tracked with a watermark column.
  • Full snapshot: Exports the entire result of the query every run.

Incremental is the one you will use for anything that grows over time, like an events or transactions table. Full snapshot suits smaller, slowly changing tables where re-exporting everything each time is cheap enough not to matter.

Configure the Watermark Column

For incremental archival, CH-Ops uses a watermark column to determine what data should be included in each window.

The interface allows you to pick a column that increases on both INSERT and UPDATE, something like updated_at. The archival engine uses this value to track progress between runs.

If your only candidate is a String column, CH-Ops warns you first, because ClickHouse compares strings byte-wise, which only matches logical order under specific conditions.

Starting Point and File Partitioning

The Start from value determines where the first archival window begins. The initial run can catch up on the historical data from the selected starting point, while subsequent runs continue from where the previous run stopped.

This is particularly useful when setting up archival for an existing dataset rather than starting from newly inserted records.

An optional partition expression, like toDate(created), drives a third folder level in storage, so archived files land in date-based (or otherwise expression-based) folders instead of one flat run.

Leave it blank and you get a single folder per run instead.

A Check button lets you validate the expression before saving the job.

Choose the Storage Format

CH-Ops lets you select the format used for archived files.

The available formats shown in the interface include:

Setting Options
Format Parquet, ORC, Avro
Codec zstd, snappy, gzip, lz4, brotli, none
Max rows per file Specify the maximum number of rows that should be written to each archive file, for example, 5,000,000
Insert threads Configure the number of threads used during the archival operation. Use 1 for an exact split; more threads provide faster but approximate splitting

This gives you control over the balance between storage size and processing requirements.

Parquet with zstd is a reasonable default: columnar, well compressed, and widely readable by downstream tools.

Where the Job Runs, and Where It Writes To

Run on node decides which cluster node executes the job every time, defaulting to whichever node is selected in the navbar.

The Test and partition check also run on this node, so the columns you see while configuring the job match what the scheduled run will actually use.

The Storage Profile determines where the archived files are stored. In the example configuration, the job uses an S3 storage mvp-poc profile.

Once the storage profile is selected, CH-Ops can write the generated archival files to the configured object storage location.

This separates long-term archived data from the primary ClickHouse storage while keeping the data available for later exploration or restoration.

Scheduling and Getting Notified

The schedule is entered as a standard cron expression, evaluated in UTC, not server local time, so it lines up with the archival window, which itself seals at the start of day UTC.

Something like 0 * * * * runs hourly.

Notification channels reuse whatever alert channels you have already configured, like Google Chat or email, with an option to notify on failure only, so you are not paged for every successful run.

Defining the Restore Shape Upfront

Before you save the job, you also define the shape a restored table will take: an engine (MergeTree is the default), the ORDER BY columns, and an optional PARTITION BY.

This is used to build the CREATE TABLE statement automatically when you restore later, and the column list comes from the Test step, so it is worth running Test with your final query before finishing this section.

Once everything is filled in, Create saves and enables the job.

Managing a Job After It's Created

Each job appears as a card showing its name, mode (windowed or full snapshot), the underlying query, schedule, format and codec, target node, watermark column, and status.

From there, you can:

  • Run it immediately, outside its schedule.
  • Pause it without deleting it.
  • Resume it if needed again.
  • History to see past runs.
  • Backfill to catch up a range that was missed or never covered.
  • Edit or Delete the job entirely.

A Complete Archival Example

Here is an example configuration for a scheduled archival job:

Setting Value
Name testing1
Node replica2 (10.X.X.X.X)
Query SELECT * FROM uk.uk_price_paid
Mode Incremental
Watermark created_at (DateTime)
Start from 01/01/2026 12:42
Storage profile s3
Format / Codec Parquet / zstd
Max rows per file 5,000,000
Schedule 0 * * * * (02:00 UTC daily)
Notifications #Testing-channel, on failure only

The first run archives everything from January 2026 up to the start of the current day, which might be a few hundred million rows in one large snapshot.

Every run after that picks up one day.

Restore Archived Data

Archiving is only useful if the data can be retrieved when needed.

The Restore tab allows you to select an archival job and choose a snapshot to restore.

You can specify:

  • Destination database
  • Destination table
  • Optional ON CLUSTER clause

CH-Ops can also build the required DDL for the restored table using Build DDL.

This provides a straightforward path from archived files back into ClickHouse.

Explore Archived Files

The Archive Explorer provides a visual view of the archived data stored in the configured storage location.

Instead of navigating through object-storage paths manually, you can browse the available archive folders directly from CH-Ops.

The interface identifies archives based on the configured job and storage format, making it easier to locate archived datasets.

A Simple End-to-End Flow

The complete workflow brings together the key steps:

  1. Create an archival job and define the SELECT query.
  2. Choose incremental archival or full snapshot mode.
  3. Configure the watermark column and starting point when using incremental mode.
  4. Select the storage format, compression codec, and file partitioning options.
  5. Choose the execution node and S3-compatible storage profile.
  6. Configure the schedule and notification channels.
  7. Define the restored table's engine, sorting key, and optional partitioning.
  8. Create the job and monitor its runs.
  9. Explore archived files or restore a snapshot when needed.

Why This Is Worth Setting Up

Manually exporting cold data to S3 usually means a cron job somewhere, a script that tracks its own watermark, and a separate process for restoring anything back.

CH-Ops Pro's Scheduled Archival brings these steps into a single workflow.

With incremental and full-snapshot modes, configurable storage formats and compression, scheduled execution, notifications, restoration, and archive exploration, it provides a practical way to manage long-term ClickHouse data in S3-compatible storage.

Further Reading

  • CH-Ops Installation Guide
  • CH-Ops Official GitHub Repository
  • CH-Ops Demo Video

title: If you're looking for what comes after wire, take a look at kanna-di
description:
For a long time, compile-time DI in Go meant google/wire. But wire is no longer taking new features, and every so often the question comes up: what do you use instead?

This post introduces kanna-di, which I wrote to sit in that spot. Like wire, the generated code is plain Go and imports nothing at run time. The difference is that you register no providers.

What was tedious

Think about what you write for wire:

  • a wire.go with //go:build wireinject, where you declare the injector's signature yourself
  • wire.NewSet to collect providers, passed to wire.Build
  • wire.Bind for every interface
  • and every time you add a constructor, you add it to some set

In other words, telling wire which functions to use is a separate job, living somewhere other than the code. Constructors already sit next to their types. You're listing them a second time.

How kanna-di thinks about it

With kanna-di, you mark the struct that will be the container, and that's it. It looks at each field's type, finds the constructor next to that type, follows that constructor's parameters recursively, and writes a constructor that calls everything in order.

Take a layered application. The register-user use case depends on a repository for persistence and a sender for the welcome mail. Each layer keeps its constructors next to its types, as usual:

// package user, the domain
type Repository interface {
    Save(ctx context.Context, u User) error
    Find(ctx context.Context, id ID) (User, error)
}

// package mail, the domain
type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, m Message) error
}

// package usecase
func NewRegisterUser(repo user.Repository, mailer mail.Sender) *RegisterUser
func NewGetUser(repo user.Repository) *GetUser

// package postgres, the infrastructure
func NewUserRepository(db *sql.DB) *UserRepository

// package sendgrid, an external API
func NewSender(cfg config.Config) *Sender

// package handler
func NewUser(registerUser *usecase.RegisterUser, getUser *usecase.GetUser) *User

// package config
func Load() (Config, error)

The composition root already has a struct that holds what the program is made of: the server. Mark it //kanna:container.

package main

//go:generate go tool kanna-di

//kanna:container
type server struct {
    _ user.Repository `di:"with=postgres.NewUserRepository"`
    _ mail.Sender     `di:"with=sendgrid.NewSender"`

    users *handler.User
}

func (s *server) routes() http.Handler {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("POST /users", s.users.Register)
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", s.users.Get)
    return mux
}

func openDB(cfg config.Config) (*sql.DB, func(), error) {
    db, err := sql.Open("pgx", cfg.DSN)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    return db, func() { db.Close() }, nil
}

What only this root can decide is written next to it: which implementation serves each of the domain's two interfaces (with=), and how to open what the standard library provides (openDB). Nothing else.

go generate ./... writes di_gen.go:

// Code generated by kanna-di. DO NOT EDIT.

package main

import (
    "example.com/shop/internal/config"
    "example.com/shop/internal/handler"
    "example.com/shop/internal/infra/postgres"
    "example.com/shop/internal/infra/sendgrid"
    "example.com/shop/internal/usecase"
)

// newServer initializes dependencies and constructs server.
func newServer() (*server, func(), error) {
    cfg, err := config.Load()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    db, cleanup, err := openDB(cfg)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    repo := postgres.NewUserRepository(db)
    mailer := sendgrid.NewSender(cfg)
    registerUser := usecase.NewRegisterUser(repo, mailer)
    getUser := usecase.NewGetUser(repo)
    users := handler.NewUser(registerUser, getUser)

    return &server{
        users: users,
    }, cleanup, nil
}

*usecase.RegisterUser comes from usecase.NewRegisterUser. *sql.DB comes from openDB, next to the container. user.Repository and mail.Sender come from the implementations the container named. config.Config is loaded once and shared by openDB and sendgrid.NewSender. Nothing is registered anywhere. When a constructor's parameters change, the next go generate changes the code that calls it.

func main() {
    s, cleanup, err := newServer()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer cleanup()

    log.Print(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", s.routes()))
}

How providers are found

"The function next to the type" has a precise definition. When a type is needed, kanna-di takes the first of these that has one:

  1. an argument of the constructor (di:"arg")
  2. the provider the container chose for the type (di:"with=...")
  3. an exported field of a struct the container embeds or declares as _
  4. a function in the container's own package
  5. an exported function in the package declaring the type, when that package is in your module or go.work

Finding none stops generation. So do two at the same level. A helper in a testutil package or a fixture returning the same type changes nothing unless the container names it. The standard library and other modules are never searched: io does have a function returning an io.Writer, and you would not want it picked for you.

Errors say which field

The part of DI that eats your time is when resolution fails. kanna-di's errors trace the need back to the field it started from.

The most common mistake with an interface is forgetting with=:

./server.go:12:2: error: nothing provides mail.Sender, which usecase.NewRegisterUser needs
  via server.users → handler.NewUser → usecase.NewRegisterUser
  return one from a function in package main, take it with di:"arg", or choose a provider with di:"with=..."

When there are two candidates, both positions are shown along with how to choose:

./server.go:11:2: error: 2 functions in package usecase return *usecase.GetUser
  usecase.NewGetUser (../../internal/usecase/get_user.go:12:6)
  usecase.NewCachedGetUser (../../internal/usecase/get_user.go:30:6)
  via server.users → handler.NewUser
  choose one with _ *usecase.GetUser `di:"with=usecase.NewGetUser"`

Typos get a did you mean, and if the implementation chosen with with= does not satisfy the interface, the error names the missing method.

Taking a container apart in tests

This is where I think the difference from wire is largest.

In tests you want the repository swapped for an in-memory one and the mail sender for something that only records. With wire, that means another injector and another set. With kanna-di, you declare a container in a _test.go file and embed the production server.

//kanna:container
type testServer struct {
    *server

    _ user.Repository `di:"arg"`
    _ mail.Sender     `di:"arg"`
}

func TestRegisterUser(t *testing.T) {
    sent := &mailtest.Recorder{}
    s := newTestServer(memory.NewUserRepository(), sent)
    srv := httptest.NewServer(s.routes())
    defer srv.Close()

    // POST /users ...

    if len(sent.Messages) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("want 1 welcome mail, got %d", len(sent.Messages))
    }
}

Embedding a container from the same package rebuilds it here, field by field. Because the two interfaces are now declared as arguments, the with= bindings are unused, and nothing needs *sql.DB or config.Config anymore. So openDB, config.Load, and sendgrid.NewSender are never called, and newTestServer returns neither a cleanup nor an error. In production the root chooses the implementations; in tests you pass them in. That's all.

The output goes to di_gen_test.go. The chicken-and-egg problem, where the test calls newTestServer before it has been generated, is handled by kanna-di: it type-checks once more with what it is about to write in place, so a call to a not-yet-generated constructor does not stop it.

In a real application

showcase is a gRPC todo service that uses kanna-di across its layers:

  • internal/di holds the Config and Infra containers; NewInfra assembles the pgx pool and the transactor
  • each operation in usecase is a container of its own; NewPutTodo and NewDeleteTodo are generated
  • the handler container bundles the use cases into NewHandler

A use case looks like this:

//kanna:container
type DeleteTodo struct {
    _ *infra.Deps // infra.NewDeps provides it; its Transactor and Todos fill the fields below

    transactor tx.Transactor
    todos      repository.Todo
}

A struct in a _ field is not stored; it only serves the container. The use case takes exactly what it needs from what the infrastructure bundled.

A struct with no fields, such as the todov1.UnimplementedTodoServiceServer a gRPC handler embeds, is left at its zero value. No provider is needed for it.

Cleanup

Providers returning T, func() or T, func(), error have their cleanups collected into one. They run in reverse order, and when a provider fails, the cleanups of those that ran before it are called before the error is returned. Same behavior as wire. Anything taken as an argument or drawn from an embedded struct belongs to the caller and is never closed.

The honest part

  • Requires Go 1.26. It is designed to be installed with go get -tool
  • It is v0, written by one person, and the API still moves
  • A generic struct cannot be a container: there is no way to choose its type arguments
  • Within one directory, test containers can live in either the in-package test package or the external _test package, not both
  • Rule 5 (searching the type's own package) only covers your module and go.work. Constructors in dependencies are never picked up automatically. This is deliberate

kanna-di is one of the kanna family of generators, but it stands on its own. It shares nothing with the other tools, and the generated code calls only your functions.

Try it 

go get -tool github.com/go-kanna/di/cmd/kanna-di

Mark the struct with //kanna:container, add //go:generate go tool kanna-di, run go generate ./....

If you're coming from wire: the functions you listed in wire.NewSet are, most likely, already next to their types. wire.Bind becomes _ Iface \di:"with=pkg.NewImpl"``, and the injector declaration goes away.

The repository has an example/ directory with the layout from this post, runnable as is.

Disclosure: kanna-di is a rewrite of mickamy/injector, an earlier tool of mine. The idea is the same: a container struct, and constructors found next to their types. The inject tag became di, the directive became //kanna:container, and embedded test containers and cleanup handling were added. injector is archived; development continues here.
