Rare queries are left out of the lists by design. A long tail of low-click pages shows up in the totals only. Sitemaps and URL inspection are not ingested. The README lists these.

Try it

The example is in packages/connector/google-search-console/examples/. You need a Google Cloud project with the Search Console API enabled, an OAuth client of type Desktop app, and a verified property. The README walks through it.

If you point it at a property with real traffic, I would love to hear what breaks.

title: Run your own model endpoint on a rented GPU with vLLM: your own API key, an SSH tunnel, and an optional LoRA adapter
description:
Short answer: rent a GPU with SSH access, install vLLM in a fresh Python environment, start it so it listens only on the instance's own localhost, require an API key of your own, and reach it from your machine through an SSH tunnel. If you have a LoRA adapter for the same base model, vLLM can serve it next to the base model under its own name. When you are done, copy out what you need and destroy the instance.

Disclosure: I work on CloudGPU, and the GPU rental in this guide is ours. Each step ends with a "What to check" line, because versions, flags and defaults change.

Which kind of endpoint is this?

CloudGPU's terms (section 6) say that each running instance with a service URL gets a public HTTPS address; these URLs are "hard to guess but they are not authenticated by default", and if you need authentication you configure it inside your instance, for example an API key on your Ollama deployment. The docs say that templates that serve an API, such as Ollama and ComfyUI, get such a URL.

This guide takes a different route on purpose. You rent a raw GPU, run vLLM on it, and do not publish any URL: the server listens only on the instance's own localhost, requires your own API key, and you reach it through an SSH tunnel from your machine. That gives you an endpoint only you can use, as long as you keep the SSH access and the key to yourself.

vLLM's own security guide is clear about the limits of the key: --api-key protects only the endpoints under the /v1, /v2, /inference and /cohere prefixes, other endpoints on the same server are not covered, and it says not to rely on --api-key alone. It also notes that some underlying components may listen on all network interfaces. So treat the key as one layer, keep the tunnel as the way in, and do not send anything to the instance that you would not put on a rented machine.

Read these things first

  1. The license of your base model. An adapter sits on top of a base model, so the base model's license applies to what you serve. The walkthrough uses Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, whose model card lists the Apache-2.0 license (read 2026-10-27). If you use a small Llama or Gemma model instead, read the Llama 3.2 Community License or the Gemma Terms of Use first, including what they say about derivative models. This guide gives no legal conclusions.
  2. What your adapter was trained on. Use only data you have the right to use; CloudGPU's acceptable use policy (section 1.8) prohibits training on datasets you do not have rights to use. If your adapter was trained on text generated through DeepSeek's API and you publish its outputs, DeepSeek's Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026) require you to label published outputs as AI-generated (section 3.1).
  3. CloudGPU's terms. Read the terms before you rent. Section 1 says compute comes from third-party data centres and supplier networks, which can change, so this guide does not claim your data stays on any particular machine.

What you need

  • A CloudGPU account with balance. GPU instances are billed per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum, and billing stops when you destroy the instance (terms). Rates are on the pricing page. Payment is by card or USDT (payments).
  • A terminal with ssh, scp and Python 3 on your own machine.
  • Optional: a LoRA adapter trained on Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, stored in the usual Hugging Face PEFT layout (a folder with adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors), for example the one from the self-critique guide in this series. Without an adapter, do everything below and skip the adapter parts; you will serve the base model only.

What to check: ssh -V prints a version, and python3 --version prints a version. If you have an adapter, its folder contains the two files above.

Step 1: make your endpoint key and look at your adapter (on your own machine)

The key is a long random string that only you and the server know. Generate one:

python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"

Keep it in a password manager. Make a new one for every instance; never reuse a key from another service.

If you have an adapter, open adapter_config.json in its folder and note two fields: base_model_name_or_path and r (the LoRA rank).

What to check: the command printed a long random string that you have stored somewhere other than a shell history you share. For an adapter, base_model_name_or_path is mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (if not, the adapter belongs to another base model and this guide's command will not match it), and r is a number you can compare with the rank limit in Step 4.

Step 2: rent a raw GPU

On Deploy, choose Raw GPU and a card. The CloudGPU docs say that every template is a ready-made image with root SSH and that for anything a template does not cover you rent a raw GPU (Deploy â†’ Raw GPU) and install what you need over SSH. The docs' GPU table lists 16 GB as the minimum VRAM for models from 0.5B to 8B parameters; vLLM also needs Linux and an NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 7.5 or higher, according to its installation page. A 7B model in 16-bit needs memory for the weights plus a cache for requests, so a card with more than the minimum is the easy fix if the server reports it cannot fit.

Connect with the SSH details of your running instance. If you have an adapter, upload its folder from your own machine (scp takes the port with a capital -P):

scp -r -P <ssh-port> ./adapter-selfloop <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>:/workspace/

What to check: ssh -p <ssh-port> <ssh-user>@<ssh-host> connects, nvidia-smi lists a GPU, and (with an adapter) ls /workspace/adapter-selfloop shows adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors.

Step 3: install vLLM in a fresh environment

The vLLM installation page recommends uv for the Python environment. uv can be installed from PyPI (see the uv installation page). On the instance:

pip install uv
cd /workspace
uv venv --python 3.12 --seed --managed-python
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto

These lines follow the vLLM page as read on 2026-10-27; if the page now shows different commands, use its commands.

What to check: with the environment active, vllm --version prints a version, and python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" prints True. If the install stops with an error, read the error text and the troubleshooting parts of the vLLM page.

Step 4: start the server on localhost, with your key

Use your own key in place of <your-endpoint-key>. With an adapter:

cd /workspace && source .venv/bin/activate
nohup vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --api-key <your-endpoint-key> \
  --tokenizer-mode hf \
  --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 16 \
  --lora-modules selfloop=/workspace/adapter-selfloop \
  > /workspace/vllm.log 2>&1 &

Without an adapter, remove the --enable-lora, --max-lora-rank and --lora-modules lines.

What the flags do, from the vLLM serve reference and LoRA page: --host 127.0.0.1 keeps the HTTP server on the instance's localhost; --api-key makes requests under /v1 carry that key; --tokenizer-mode hf uses the Hugging Face tokenizer instead of letting auto pick the mistral_common tokenizer for Mistral models; pinning it is meant to match how an adapter was trained with the Hugging Face tokenizer, so drop the flag if your adapter was trained another way; --lora-modules name=path registers the adapter under the name selfloop; --max-lora-rank must be at least the adapter's r and the docs list the allowed values (the default is 16), so if your r from Step 1 is larger than 16, use the next allowed value. The key is visible in the instance's process list while the server runs, which is one more reason to use a fresh key per instance.

Wait until the log says the server is ready before you send a request. If the process exits, read the end of the log with tail -n 50 /workspace/vllm.log. A message about memory for the cache is fixed by adding --max-model-len 8192 or by choosing a card with more memory.

What to check: on the instance, curl -s -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models | head -n 1 prints an HTTP status line that is not a success (an authentication error is expected, because you sent no key), and curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-endpoint-key>" http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models prints JSON that lists the base model and, with an adapter, selfloop.

Step 5: open the tunnel and call your endpoint (on your own machine)

In one terminal, open the tunnel. Nothing is printed while it runs; leave it open:

ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 -p <ssh-port> <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>

If local port 8000 is already used, pick another local port (for example -L 8001:127.0.0.1:8000) and use it in the URLs below. In a second terminal:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-endpoint-key>"

Now the same request through the OpenAI SDK (pip install openai on your own machine). Put this in a file named ask.py:

import os
import sys

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key=os.environ["ENDPOINT_KEY"])

BASE = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3"
ADAPTER = "selfloop"  # delete this name from the loop below if you started without an adapter

question = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

for name in (BASE, ADAPTER):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=name,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        temperature=0,
        max_tokens=300,
    )
    print("==", name)
    print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
    print()

Run it with the key in an environment variable, not in the file:

export ENDPOINT_KEY="<your-endpoint-key>"
python3 ask.py "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

Any tool that lets you set an OpenAI-compatible base URL and a key can use the same two values (http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 and your key) while the tunnel is open.

What to check: the curl call lists the model names you expect; ask.py prints one answer per model name; and a call with a wrong or missing key is refused rather than answered. If the tunnel command prints "address already in use", use another local port. Reading two answers is not a test of your adapter; for that, use questions the adapter never saw and compare them yourself, as in the self-critique guide.

Step 6: stop, copy out what you need, destroy

Close the tunnel with Ctrl+C in its terminal. Before you destroy anything, copy what you want to keep. The docs have a section called "What to save before you destroy an instance"; read it in the CloudGPU docs. For example, copy the server log from your own machine:

scp -P <ssh-port> <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>:/workspace/vllm.log ./

Then destroy the instance from your Dashboard (the docs: "You can destroy an instance at any time"). Minutes spent copying are billed like any other minute, and billing stops once the instance is destroyed. The endpoint key was meant for this instance only; do not reuse it.

What to check: the instance no longer appears as running in your Dashboard, and the curl call from Step 5 now fails to connect.

Privacy and access, in plain terms

  • This is your own endpoint, with your own API key, reached through your own SSH tunnel. It is not a public URL.
  • Per CloudGPU's terms (section 5), you keep ownership of any data, models, code or output you create on or upload to an instance, and CloudGPU says it does not access, inspect, copy or back up the contents of your instance except in three listed cases: a credible report of a violation of section 3, valid legal process, or to protect the safety of users or third parties.
  • Per the same terms, destroying an instance permanently deletes its local storage, and you are responsible for backing up what you want to keep.
  • Whatever you send to the endpoint is processed on that rented instance. Do not send secrets or personal data you would not put on a rented machine.
  • If you call a model through CloudGPU's AI API instead of your own instance, the request is forwarded to the model provider and its terms apply; see the privacy policy.

Sources

All read on 2026-10-27 (UTC+8).

  • vLLM: installation (NVIDIA CUDA), serving LoRA adapters, serve command reference, security guide.
  • uv: installation.
  • Licenses: Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 model card, Llama 3.2 Community License, Gemma Terms of Use.
  • DeepSeek: Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026).
  • CloudGPU: terms, acceptable use policy, privacy policy, docs, pricing.

title: Planning a CMS Closed Beta: Test Scenarios for Web Studios
description:
A useful closed beta is not a race to click every control. It is a chance to learn whether a real team can complete a small task, hand it to someone else, and explain what happened when the result differs from expectations.

Morlix CMS is collecting applications from web studios for a future closed beta. Testing has not started, and participation is subject to review and approval. The public release target is March 11, 2027; it may change and is not a beta start date or an invitation deadline.

The exercises below are a preparation framework for studios. They are not an announced beta test protocol, a list of features guaranteed in a future build, or a report of completed participant tests.

Choose a small scenario

Start with a fictional service website: a home page, one service page, and a short news item. Assign a developer, a designer, and an editor to it, even if one person plays several roles. Write down the job each person needs to complete.

For example, an editor wants to change the opening paragraph of a service page, have a colleague review the result, and understand the next step. A useful test asks whether the allowed workflow is clear and whether the result matches expectations. It does not assume a particular approval feature exists.

Before attempting any scenario, read the terms and instructions for the build you actually receive. Only use actions and environments permitted by the project. If a feature is unavailable, mark the scenario as unavailable rather than trying to bypass a restriction.

Capture the starting conditions

A test result becomes more useful when someone else can repeat it. Record the supplied build version, relevant environment, browser, device, assigned permissions, and any configuration choices. If an instruction is unclear, note the exact step and the information needed to proceed.

Use synthetic content and a separate test environment. Do not place a real client's site, personal data, credentials, or private keys into an experimental setup merely because access is available. Any exception requires the actual test rules and the relevant client's agreement.

The live Morlix website already has published pages and a blog with categories and tags. That is evidence about one installation, not a guarantee that every beta participant will receive the same components or configuration.

Four workflow checks worth preparing

Content and handover

If the provided build allows it, prepare a page with headings, a link, and an image. Save the work and check the rendered result. Ask a colleague unfamiliar with the setup to find the content and explain what they would do next.

Compare what happened with the expected outcome. Was the text preserved? Is the link still correct? Can the colleague identify where help is needed? Treat the availability of drafts, publication rights, and review steps as questions for the actual version, not assumptions.

Design across page sizes

Prepare two sample pages and agree on a few visual rules: heading hierarchy, image proportions, and readable spacing. Where permitted, make a small change and compare the output on a phone and a desktop.

Separate a design preference from an interface that is difficult to understand and from a reproducible defect. They need different follow-up, even when a screenshot shows all three.

Components and changes

If the beta rules allow extension testing, record the components in the starting configuration. Change one component at a time, then rerun the same small set of permitted tasks. This makes it easier to identify when a change affects another part of the project.

A single successful combination does not prove compatibility with every theme, extension, server, or future version. Ask which dependencies and update conditions apply to the actual components.

Access and recovery

Create a simple responsibility matrix: who prepares content, who reviews it, and who manages configuration. If the build provides relevant accounts and the rules permit the test, check that each participant can perform their intended actions without gaining unrelated access. Do not try other people's accounts or bypass permissions.

For backups, first agree on the permitted scope. If a recovery test is available, record the initial state, make a safe test change, and restore to an isolated environment following the supplied instructions. Check content, files, and settings only where they are part of the allowed scenario. Creating a backup file alone does not establish that restoration works.

Write feedback that can be reproduced

A concise report can follow five fields:

  1. Goal: what the person was trying to accomplish.
  2. Conditions: build, environment, account permissions, and device, where available.
  3. Steps: the smallest sequence that demonstrates the issue.
  4. Expected and actual result: what you thought would happen and what you observed.
  5. Impact: whether work is blocked, a workaround is needed, or the issue is a smaller inconvenience.

Include an anonymised sample or screenshot only when the test rules allow it and secrets have been removed. An unexpected result may come from an unsupported scenario or an environment setting, so state the observation before suggesting a cause.

For product feedback, describe the need and context. “An editor needs to know who reviewed a change” is more useful than asserting that a particular button must exist. It does not imply that the feature has been promised.

Interpret a successful test carefully

Passing one scenario on one build says little about untested environments. An issue-free limited beta is not proof that there are no security defects. An invitation is not a guarantee that the system is ready for every client or that a particular support arrangement exists.

Before a production decision, studios still need to confirm licensing, component compatibility, data ownership, backup and recovery responsibilities, and agreements with the customer for the actual product and version.

Web studios can apply through morlix.ru and follow Morlix on Telegram for updates. The public release target remains March 11, 2027 and may change. Read the original Russian article.

Original article (Russian)

title: A Free Google Scholar Alternative API: Search 250M Papers With OpenAlex in Python
description:
Google Scholar has no API, and its terms don't allow scraping. If you need research papers in a script (for a literature review, a reading list, or a RAG pipeline), use OpenAlex instead. It's a free, open catalog of over 250 million scholarly works (the successor to Microsoft Academic), and its data is CC0, so you can reuse it however you like.

The script

Search titles and abstracts, keep papers from 2015 on, and sort by citations:

"""Search scholarly papers with the free OpenAlex API. Usage: python3 paper_search.py '"growth mindset"'"""
import json
import sys
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request

query = sys.argv[1]
params = {
    "filter": f"title_and_abstract.search:{query},publication_year:2015-",
    "sort": "cited_by_count:desc",
    "per-page": 10,
    # "api_key": "YOUR_KEY",  # free at openalex.org/settings/api ($1/day of usage)
}
url = "https://api.openalex.org/works?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(params)
data = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30))

print(f"{data['meta']['count']:,} papers match {query}. Most cited since 2015:\n")
for w in data["results"]:
    venue = ((w.get("primary_location") or {}).get("source") or {}).get("display_name", "")
    pdf = (w.get("best_oa_location") or {}).get("pdf_url") or ""
    print(f"{w['cited_by_count']:>6}  {w['publication_year']}  {w['title']}")
    print(f"        {venue}  {pdf}")

Real output (October 2026):

$ python3 paper_search.py '"growth mindset"'
9,092 papers match "growth mindset". Most cited since 2015:

  1694  2019  PISA 2018 Results (Volume I)
        Programme for international student assessment/Internationale Schulleistungsstudie
  1511  2019  A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
        Nature  https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1466-y.pdf
  1259  2019  Mindsets: A View From Two Eras
        Perspectives on Psychological Science
  1054  2016  Motivation to learn: an overview of contemporary theories
        Medical Education  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1111/medu.13074

Quotes around the phrase matter. Without them, OpenAlex matches the words anywhere, and "most cited" fills up with unrelated famous papers.

Useful details

  • Abstracts come as an "inverted index" ({"word": [positions]}). Rebuild the text by sorting positions: " ".join(w for _, w in sorted((i, w) for w, idx in inv.items() for i in idx)).
  • Free PDFs: best_oa_location.pdf_url links to a legal open-access copy when one exists. Add is_oa:true to the filter to keep only those.
  • Filters chain with commas: type:review, cited_by_count:>100, publication_year:2020-2024.
  • DOI lookups: filter=doi:10.1038/s41586-019-1466-y|10.1177/1529100612453266 fetches up to 50 at once.
  • Limits: without a key, you share a small free daily budget with everyone on your IP. A free key (openalex.org/settings/api) gives you $1/day of usage, where a search costs $0.001 for up to 100 results. That's plenty for most projects.

No-code version

If you'd rather get a spreadsheet, I wrapped this as Research Paper Search on Apify. Type queries or paste DOIs, set filters (year, citations, type, open access), and export CSV or Excel with authors, institutions, journal, citations, the full abstract, topic, and PDF link. It costs $2 per 1,000 papers, and no key is needed.

The script is yours either way. Happy reading.

title: Why My IQ Test Has a 15-Minute Timer (and Why That's Harder Than It Sounds)
description:
Why My IQ Test Has a 15-Minute Timer (and Why That's Harder Than It Sounds)

When I published my first post here about how the scoring on IQCognify works, a few people asked about the other design decision that shapes every result: the timer. The test gives you 15 minutes for the full run. That number wasn't picked to create pressure. It exists because of what the test is trying to measure — and enforcing it fairly in a browser turned out to be one of the harder engineering problems in the whole project.

Timing is part of the measurement

Working memory and processing speed are real components of cognitive ability, and every standardized test accounts for them. An untimed puzzle test mostly measures how long you're willing to sit there. A timed one measures something closer to how you actually think: pattern recognition under mild constraint, decisions made without infinite deliberation.

But the moment you add a timer, you take on an obligation: the clock has to be fair. A fair timer never punishes someone for a slow network, a background tab, or a laptop that decided to run a virus scan mid-test.

The three ways a browser timer lies

1. Tab switches. Browsers throttle JavaScript timers in inactive tabs — a setInterval that fires every second in the foreground may fire once a minute in the background. Count ticks and your clock drifts. The fix is to never count ticks at all: record a start timestamp, and compute elapsed time from Date.now() differences every time the UI updates. Throttling then affects how often the display refreshes, never how much time has actually passed.

2. Slow asset loading. If question images load lazily, a user on a slow connection spends their 15 minutes watching spinners. Every question asset in the test is tiny and preloaded before the clock starts, so the measured time is thinking time, not download time.

3. Server round-trips. If the timer lives on the server, latency becomes part of the test. The whole run — questions, timing, scoring — happens client-side. The server never gets a vote on how long you took.

The edge case nobody warns you about

Sleep. A laptop closing mid-test can produce a four-hour "elapsed time" on wake. The honest handling is to detect a discontinuous jump in elapsed time and end the session rather than score it — an unscored attempt is a better outcome than a garbage score presented as real. Silent data corruption is worse than a lost session, in testing and everywhere else.

Why 15 minutes

Long enough that the constraint is mild for most people, short enough that speed still differentiates. It's a calibration choice, and like the scoring model, it should be a deliberate one — if you build anything similar, decide what your timer is for before you decide how long it is.

The test itself is live at IQCognify if you want to see the timer behave — 27 questions, no signup, and your time is measured by timestamps, not ticks.

title: Find out why your Spring Boot + React request is slow, from the click to the SQL
description:
You click Checkout. It takes almost a second. Yesterday it took a quarter of that.

The usual next step is to open five tools: the Network tab, the Spring Boot logs, a SQL log, maybe a profiler, maybe Postman. Each one shows you one layer. You become the glue, lining up timestamps and guessing which layer is to blame.

This post shows a different way. We'll trace one click from React, through Spring Boot, down to the SQL, and back to the React state update, then read the trace to find the cause. The tool is Causeline, an open-source (Apache 2.0) debugger I've been building for exactly this stack.

It takes about five minutes to set up.

What you need

  • JDK 21+ and Spring Boot 4.1
  • React 18 or 19, Node 22
  • An app where the React front end calls the Spring Boot API

Step 1: Add the Spring Boot starter

<dependency>
  <groupId>dev.causeline</groupId>
  <artifactId>causeline-spring-boot</artifactId>
  <version>0.1.0-alpha.4</version>
</dependency>

Using Gradle

implementation("dev.causeline:causeline-spring-boot:0.1.0-alpha.4")

Step 2: Switch it on in a dev profile

src/main/resources/application-dev.yml:

causeline:
  enabled: true

Causeline is off unless you enable it, and it refuses to start when a prod or production profile is active. That matters, because it captures a lot: headers, bodies and SQL values. It's meant for your laptop and your QA environment.

Using Spring Security?

Permit /causeline/**. Causeline protects those paths with its own access token:

http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
    .requestMatchers("/causeline/**").permitAll()
    /* ...your rules... */);

Step 3: Start the app

./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev

The log prints a link with a fresh access token:

Causeline UI: http://localhost:8080/causeline/?token=...

Open it and call any endpoint. You'll already see server-side traces: controller, repositories, SQL with values, and outbound HTTP calls.

Want your service methods as separate rows? Use Micrometer's standard annotation; there's no Causeline-specific one:

@Observed
public Order createOrder(OrderRequest request) { ... }

Step 4: Add the React SDK

npm install @causeline/react@alpha


import { CauselineProvider } from '@causeline/react';

createRoot(root).render(
  <CauselineProvider endpoint="/causeline/api/spans">
    <App />
  </CauselineProvider>,
);

The provider does nothing in production builds, so it's safe to leave in.

Proxy /api and /causeline to Spring Boot so requests stay same-origin. With Vite:

// vite.config.ts
server: {
  proxy: {
    '/api': 'http://localhost:8080',
    '/causeline': 'http://localhost:8080',
  },
},

Step 5: Name the click

Wrap the handler in trace(), and use useTracedState for the state you care about:

import { trace, useTracedState } from '@causeline/react';

const [status, setStatus] = useTracedState('checkoutStatus', 'idle');

const onCheckout = () =>
  trace('Checkout', async () => {
    const response = await fetch('/api/orders', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify(cart),
    });
    setStatus(response.ok ? 'paid' : 'failed');
  });

The React SDK adds a standard W3C traceparent header to the request. Spring Boot picks it up through Micrometer Tracing, so the browser and server spans land in one trace.

Click the button. Open the newest trace.

Reading the trace: why is it slow?

The waterfall reads top to bottom as one tree: the Checkout action, the browser request, the Spring request, OrderController.createOrder, the transaction, OrderService.createOrder, the cache, the repository, the INSERT, the payment call.

Two columns matter:

  • Duration is inclusive: a span plus everything under it.
  • Self is the time a span spent on its own work, not waiting on its children.

Duration tells you where the time passed. Self time tells you who spent it.

The controller shows 914 ms, but only 8 ms of that is its own. It's waiting. Causeline ranks bottlenecks by self time, so it skips the parents and points at the span doing the work:

Bottleneck: POST localhost/fake-payment/charge · 844 ms · 88%

It also flags a second problem: the database transaction was open for 907 ms, and 844 ms of that was waiting for the payment call. That holds a database connection the whole time. The fix is to make the call before or after the transaction.

One detail I cared about: self time subtracts the union of child intervals. If a span starts three requests in parallel, their overlap is counted once, not three times. Otherwise the ranking would lie whenever things run concurrently.

When it fails: where was it thrown?

When the payment provider times out, the failing path turns red, from the HTTP client up to the controller. Below the waterfall you get the exceptions with their class, message and location in your code (PaymentClient.java:36), and an Open link that jumps to that line in VS Code, IntelliJ or Cursor.

This also works for exceptions your code catches and logs, as long as they're logged at WARN or ERROR with the exception attached. Those are often the ones that hide.

Did the fix work? Replay and compare

After a change, you don't need to click through the UI again. Replay resends the captured request (method, path, headers, body) to your app, and Compare with… puts any two runs side by side:

Every span shows then vs now, and the ones that changed are marked. Here the whole slowdown traces back to PaymentClient.charge; the rest of the request is unchanged. It also tells you when the response body differs.

Bonus: let your coding agent read the trace

Causeline has an MCP endpoint, so Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and other MCP clients can read the same traces. Your agent can find what failed and where, fix it, then replay the request and compare the runs itself. Causeline runs no AI of its own.

The startup log prints the command. For Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http causeline http://localhost:8080/causeline/mcp --header "X-Causeline-Token: <token>"

The agent sees traces the way an export shows them: credentials, sensitive values and SQL literals are redacted. By default it can only replay GET and HEAD requests. Anything else needs an allowlist in your configuration (causeline.mcp.*), which the agent can't change.

What else is in there

  • N+1 queries and long transactions are flagged automatically
  • Explain a slow SELECT to see its query plan
  • Copy as cURL, MockMvc test or k6 script
  • OWASP Top 10 hints on the traffic you already captured
  • Load replay: send a request many times and see which span grew

How it stays safe

  • It runs inside your app at /causeline. No account, no agent to install, no cloud.
  • Off by default, and it refuses to start in production.
  • The UI and API need an access token.
  • Anything leaving the app (exports, bug reports, OpenTelemetry export, MCP) is redacted by default.
  • Every kind of captured data can be switched off with causeline.capture.*.

Known gaps

It's an alpha, so here's what it doesn't do well yet:

  • A cancelled fetch shows as a failed request (AbortError), not clearly as "cancelled".
  • A retry shows as a second request, not linked to the first attempt.
  • Exceptions swallowed without logging can't be seen.
  • Next.js is supported through @causeline/next, but only on the Node.js runtime, not Edge.

Try it and tell me what broke

https://github.com/causeline/causeline

Website: https://causeline.dev/

If you build with Spring Boot and React, I'd really value your feedback. Try it on a real app and tell me in the comments what broke, or what you expected to see in the trace and didn't.

title: How to Get Every Open Job From a Company's Careers Page (Greenhouse, Lever & Ashby APIs)
description:
Most tech companies don't build their own careers page. They use an applicant tracking system (ATS), and the three big ones (Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby) each publish a free, public JSON API for every company's job board. They exist so companies can show their jobs on their own sites, so there's no scraping, no login, and no API key.

If you know the company's board name (usually just the company name), one request gets you every open job.

ATS Public endpoint
Greenhouse https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{company}/jobs
Lever https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{company}?mode=json
Ashby https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{company}

How do you find the name? Open the company's careers page and click any job. The link will contain boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb, jobs.lever.co/spotify, or jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp.

The script (standard library only)

It tries all three platforms, keeps the one with the most jobs, and saves a CSV.

"""Every open job at a company, from its public job-board API. Usage: python3 company_jobs.py airbnb"""
import csv
import json
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

BOARDS = {
    "greenhouse": "https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{}/jobs",
    "lever": "https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{}?mode=json",
    "ashby": "https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{}",
}


def get(url):
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "jobs-script"}), timeout=30) as r:
            return json.load(r)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError:
        return None  # no board with that name


def rows(ats, data):
    if ats == "greenhouse":
        return [(j["title"], j["location"]["name"], j["absolute_url"]) for j in data["jobs"]]
    if ats == "lever":
        return [(j["text"], j["categories"].get("location", ""), j["hostedUrl"]) for j in data]
    return [(j["title"], j.get("location", ""), j["jobUrl"]) for j in data["jobs"]]


def jobs_for(company):
    # A company name can exist on more than one platform (often an old, nearly empty board), so keep the biggest
    found = [(ats, rows(ats, data)) for ats, url in BOARDS.items() if (data := get(url.format(company)))]
    return max(found, key=lambda f: len(f[1]), default=(None, []))


company = sys.argv[1]
ats, jobs = jobs_for(company)
if not ats:
    sys.exit(f"No Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby board found for {company}")
with open(f"{company}-jobs.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["title", "location", "url"])
    w.writerows(jobs)
print(f"{company} ({ats}): {len(jobs)} open jobs saved to {company}-jobs.csv")

Real runs (October 2026):

$ python3 company_jobs.py airbnb
airbnb (greenhouse): 201 open jobs saved to airbnb-jobs.csv
$ python3 company_jobs.py spotify
spotify (lever): 89 open jobs saved to spotify-jobs.csv

The gotcha: stale boards

My first version returned the first platform that answered. For Ramp, that was a Greenhouse board with exactly 1 job. Ramp's real board is on Ashby, with 170. Companies switch ATS and leave the old board up, so check every platform and keep the biggest. That's what the max() line does.

Other things to know:

  • Descriptions are in the full responses: Greenhouse needs ?content=true, Lever has descriptionPlain, and Ashby has descriptionPlain.
  • Salary shows up on Ashby (?includeCompensation=true) and Lever (salaryRange) when the company publishes it.
  • Lever EU companies live at api.eu.lever.co.
  • Be polite: cache results, and don't hammer the endpoints. Job boards change a few times a day at most.

Tracking new jobs (no code)

The script is enough for a one-off export. If you want many companies, more platforms, and only the jobs posted since yesterday, I packaged it as a Company Jobs Scraper on Apify. It covers Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable, SmartRecruiters, and Recruitee in one format, with title, location, remote, and date filters. It has a "only new jobs since the last run" mode for schedules, and costs $1.40 per 1,000 jobs with no subscription. People use it for job alerts, recruiting research, and hiring signals ("who's hiring ML engineers this week?").

Either way, the script above is yours to copy.

title: React: carga accesible sin saltos visuales
description:
Un botón que cambia a “Cargando…” parece un detalle pequeño, pero puede decidir si un formulario se siente confiable o roto. En interfaces de registro y verificación he visto que el problema no suele ser la petición HTTP: es que el usuario no sabe si su acción fue recibida, el contenido salta y el lector de pantalla no recibe una señal clara.

Cuando trabajo en React, trato el estado de carga como parte del contrato de la interfaz. La pantalla debe conservar su forma, explicar que está ocurriendo y ofrecer una salida si la operación tarda demasiado. Esto vale igual para un formulario de contacto que para un flujo que prueba un correo temporal para Facebook en un entorno aislado. La palabra clave, incluso si aparece en un análisis de contenido como tempmailso, no debe dictar una experiencia confusa.

El estado de carga tambien es parte del diseño

Una carga robusta tiene al menos cuatro estados explícitos:

  • Listo: los controles pueden recibir interacción.
  • Enviando: la acción se está procesando y no debe duplicarse.
  • Éxito: la interfaz confirma qué paso terminó.
  • Error: se explica el problema y se indica cómo continuar.

El estado “enviando” no debería borrar todo el formulario ni reemplazarlo por un spinner sin contexto. Mantener las etiquetas y reservar espacio para el mensaje ayuda a que el usuario conserve el mapa mental de la página. También evita que el foco termine en un lugar inesperado.

Para errores de validación, conviene mostrar el mensaje cerca del campo y asociarlo con aria-describedby. Esta forma de presentar errores inline sin mover el formulario es especialmente útil en pantallas pequeñas, donde un salto de layout puede ocultar la causa del fallo.

Un contrato pequeño para React

El componente no necesita una máquina de estados grande para ser predecible. Incluso un objeto simple deja claro qué puede renderizarse:

function SubmitButton({ status }) {
  const labels = {
    idle: "Continuar",
    loading: "Guardando…",
    success: "Guardado",
    error: "Intentar de nuevo",
  };

  return (
    <button type="submit" disabled={status === "loading"}>
      {labels[status]}
    </button>
  );
}

Deshabilitar el botón durante la petición reduce dobles envíos, pero no basta por sí solo. El texto debe cambiar y el contenedor del estado debe tener una señal para tecnologías de asistencia:

<p role="status" aria-live="polite" className="form-status">
  {message}
</p>

role="status" comunica cambios que no son urgentes. Para un error que bloquea la siguiente acción, un role="alert" puede ser más adecuado. No conviene usar ambos sin pensar: demasiadas notificaciones hacen que la experiencia sea ruidosa.

CSS que reserva espacio y respeta preferencias

Un hueco estable para el mensaje evita que el formulario crezca cuando llega una respuesta. No hay que fijar una altura enorme; basta con reservar el espacio razonable para el caso normal:

.form-status {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
  margin-block: 0.5rem;
  color: var(--text-muted);
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms;
    animation-iteration-count: 1;
    scroll-behavior: auto;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms;
  }
}

El min-height no resuelve todos los casos: un mensaje de dos líneas necesita espacio adicional y el diseño debe poder crecer. La meta es que una respuesta normal no empuje los controles. Para el indicador visual, una barra de progreso o un texto breve suele ser mas útil que un spinner aislado.

También reviso contraste, foco visible y orden de tabulación. Un color gris claro puede verse elegante en el mockup y desaparecer en producción. Si la interfaz usa animación para entrar o salir, debe ser decorativa, no la única forma de saber que la petición terminó.

Como probar el flujo completo

Las pruebas deben cubrir más que una captura del estado final. En React Testing Library comprobaría que:

  1. el botón comienza habilitado;
  2. pasa a un estado ocupado después del clic;
  3. el mensaje se anuncia con el rol correcto;
  4. un segundo clic no dispara otra petición;
  5. el error conserva los valores introducidos;
  6. el foco llega al primer campo inválido cuando corresponde.

En integración, simularía respuestas rápidas, lentas y fallidas. Una respuesta rápida puede esconder problemas de accesibilidad que aparecen con una red lenta. Para flujos de email, los reintentos de verificación sin duplicados ayudan a separar la lógica del servidor de la señal que ve la persona.

También añadiría un caso con texto imperfecto de prueba, como “tamp mail com”, para confirmar que el contenido se muestra como texto normal y no termina accidentalmente convertido en un enlace. Es un detalle poco glamuroso, pero evita sorpresas en revisiones de contenido.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Debo ocultar el formulario mientras carga?

Normalmente no. Mantenerlo visible permite revisar lo que se envió y conserva la estructura. Solo bloquearía los controles que podrían duplicar la operación.

¿Un spinner es suficiente?

No. Acompáñalo con texto o una señal accesible, y asegúrate de que el cambio sea observable sin depender del color o del movimiento.

¿Qué métrica mirar?

Además del tiempo de respuesta, observa errores de validación repetidos, abandonos durante el envío y cambios inesperados de layout. Una interfaz rápida que no explica su estado sigue pareciendo lenta.

Cierre

Los estados de carga son una oportunidad para unir diseño, accesibilidad y rendimiento. En React, un contrato pequeño, espacio reservado en CSS y pruebas con respuestas lentas suelen producir una mejora visible sin reescribir la aplicación. La interfaz no necesita prometer que todo será instantáneo; necesita decir la verdad, mantener el contexto y dejar claro cuál es el siguiente paso.

title: How to Find Broken Links on Any Website (Free Python Script + No-Code Option)
description:
Broken links quietly hurt a site. Readers hit dead ends, and search engines waste crawl time on pages that don't exist. Most broken-link checkers are browser extensions that check one page, or SEO suites that cost $100+ a month.

Here's a free Python script that checks every link on a page, using only the standard library, no installs. After that, a no-code option for checking a whole site.

The script

It does three things:

  1. Downloads the page and pulls out every <a href>.
  2. Checks each link with a HEAD request, falling back to GET because some servers refuse HEAD.
  3. Prints anything that returns 4xx/5xx or doesn't connect at all. 
"""Find broken links on one web page. Usage: python3 find_broken_links.py https://example.com"""
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from html.parser import HTMLParser

UA = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (link checker)"}


class Links(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.hrefs = []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        href = dict(attrs).get("href")
        if tag == "a" and href:
            self.hrefs.append(href)


def status(url):
    for method in ("HEAD", "GET"):  # some servers refuse HEAD
        try:
            req = urllib.request.Request(url, method=method, headers=UA)
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=15) as r:
                return r.status
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            if method == "GET" or e.code not in (403, 405, 501):
                return e.code
        except Exception as e:
            return f"error: {getattr(e, 'reason', e)}"


page = sys.argv[1]
html = urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(page, headers=UA), timeout=15).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
parser = Links()
parser.feed(html)
links = {urllib.parse.urldefrag(urllib.parse.urljoin(page, h))[0] for h in parser.hrefs}
links = sorted(u for u in links if u.startswith("http"))

with ThreadPoolExecutor(10) as pool:
    results = list(zip(links, pool.map(status, links)))

broken = [(u, s) for u, s in results if not isinstance(s, int) or s >= 400]
print(f"Checked {len(links)} links on {page}: {len(broken)} broken")
for u, s in broken:
    print(f"  {s}  {u}")

Run it:

python3 find_broken_links.py https://www.python.org/about/apps/

Real output (October 2026):

Checked 119 links on https://www.python.org/about/apps/: 3 broken
  error: [Errno 61] Connection refused  http://mcsp.wartburg.edu/zelle/python/
  error: [Errno 61] Connection refused  http://pragprog.com/book/gwpy2/practical-programming
  404  http://wiki.python.org/moin/TkInter

Even python.org has a few. Old links rot: domains expire, wikis move, and http:// links stop answering.

Things that will trip you up

  • False alarms from social sites. LinkedIn, X, and Instagram often answer automated requests with 999, 403, or 520 even when the page works fine in a browser. Treat those as "check by hand", not "broken".
  • Redirects. urllib follows them silently. A link that redirects to a 404 shows as 404, which is what you want. A long redirect chain is still worth fixing.
  • JavaScript sites. If a site builds its pages with JavaScript, the raw HTML has no links in it. You'd need a headless browser.
  • Be polite. Ten threads is fine for one page. For a whole site, limit requests per server and respect robots.txt (urllib.robotparser exists, but it mishandles * wildcards and some ? rules, so test it).

Checking a whole site (no code)

The script checks one page. For a full site you need the list of pages (from the sitemap), deduplication across pages, "which page is this broken link on?", and the false-alarm handling above.

I packaged all of that as a Broken Link Checker on Apify. Type a domain and it reads the sitemap (or follows internal links), checks every link, marks bot-blocking sites as restricted instead of broken, and tells you which page each broken link is on. It costs $0.80 per 1,000 links checked, with no subscription, and you can schedule it weekly. On python.org, 30 pages and 2,000 links took about a minute and found 4 broken links. It also respects each site's robots.txt, so it skips what sites ask crawlers not to touch, and doesn't charge for those.

If you also want titles, meta descriptions, and H1s checked, the same idea powers a Website SEO Audit that scores each page and lists fixes.

Either way, the script above is yours. Copy it, change it, run it on a schedule.

title: Human-in-the-loop: designing the review queue
description:
"Doubtful cases go to a human" is easy to say and easy to get wrong. If the review queue is slow, confusing or endless, people stop trusting it, start rubber-stamping, and the accuracy you measured in the pilot quietly disappears. Here is how I would design the queue so it holds up.

What goes into the queue

Two kinds of items belong there:

  1. Low confidence. Anything below the threshold you agreed on. In my ticket-triage demo (public data, test numbers) about 24% of tickets fall below the line, and that share is a design input, not a surprise.
  2. Hard rules. Items that must always be checked regardless of confidence: amounts above a limit, a failed checksum, a customer flagged as sensitive.

Keep the two reasons separate in the record. They have different fixes later.

Size the queue before you build it

A queue is a workload, so do the arithmetic early:

items_per_day × share_to_review × minutes_per_review / 60 = reviewer_hours_per_day

If that number is bigger than the people available, either the threshold or the scope is wrong. Better to find out on paper.

Show the reviewer what they need in one screen

  • The item itself, and the system's proposed answer.
  • Why it is in the queue: low confidence, which rule fired.
  • The evidence: the cited passage, the extracted field highlighted in the source, the runner-up answer.
  • One-click actions: accept, correct, reject. Correcting should take fewer clicks than rewriting.

If the reviewer has to open three other systems to decide, the average review time doubles and your cost model breaks.

Order and age

Don't sort by arrival only. Sort by deadline and by risk. Show the age of each item and alert when anything sits longer than your service level. An unattended queue is an outage in slow motion.

Make the queue teach the system

Every correction is a labelled example. Store the original proposal, the final answer, who changed it and when. Then:

  • Re-tune the threshold monthly on the fresh labels.
  • Look at the top confusions (the pairs the model mixes up) and fix those first.
  • Track the override rate: how often reviewers change the proposal. A rising rate is an early warning that quality is drifting.

Guard against rubber-stamping

If reviewers accept 99.5% of items in two seconds each, they are not reviewing. Seed a small share of known-answer items into the queue and measure whether they are caught. It is an honest check on the human half of the system.

Takeaways

  1. Define why an item enters the queue, and record the reason.
  2. Compute reviewer hours before building.
  3. Give the reviewer evidence and one-click actions on one screen.
  4. Treat every correction as training data and track the override rate.
  5. Test the humans too, with seeded items.

Portfolio and contacts: @Kotenev01_bot.

I write about practical, measurable AI adoption for business: demos on test data, no invented case studies. Telegram channel: @kotenev01_en

title: A Tiny Eval Harness for Picking Between GPT, Gemini and Claude
description:
"Which LLM is best?" is the wrong question. The useful one is: which model performs best on my feature's real inputs, at a speed and token cost I can live with? You can answer that with a small harness and an afternoon.

The setup

You need three things:

  1. A rubric. Three to five pass/fail or 1–5 criteria. Example for an extraction task: valid JSON, all fields present, numbers match the source.
  2. A dataset. 30–50 real inputs (PII masked). Mix typical cases with edge cases: very long inputs, mixed languages, malformed text, requests that should be refused.
  3. One interface. A single function your app and your harness both call.

Keep the model behind one function

The key design rule: the rest of your codebase never knows which provider it's talking to. With OROO Blue (one API, one OROO key for OpenAI, Google and Anthropic models), the model is just a string.

MODELS = ["oroo-chatgpt", "oroo-gemini", "oroo-claude"]

function generate(prompt, model):
    # same gateway, same key, only the model name changes
    request = {
        model: model,
        prompt: prompt,
        temperature: CONFIG.temperature,    # identical for every model
        max_tokens: CONFIG.max_tokens,
        idempotency_key: hash(prompt + model)  # safe retries
    }
    return oroo_gateway.call(request, key = env.OROO_KEY)

for case in dataset:
    for model in MODELS:
        start = now()
        out = generate(case.input, model)
        record(case.id, model, out.text, out.tokens, now() - start)

The idempotency key matters: if a request times out and your harness retries, OROO Blue's idempotency handling prevents a double charge.

Score blind

Export results with the model column hidden or shuffled, then score against the rubric. Unblind only after scoring. It's surprisingly easy to "see" quality in a model you already like.

Compare on three axes

For each model, look at:

  • Quality: average rubric score, and specifically how it did on edge cases
  • Latency: median and slowest responses
  • Tokens: average per request, which drives running cost

Pick based on the feature. High-volume, simple tasks often favour the faster, lighter option.

Guardrails while you experiment

  • Use a dedicated eval key with per-key model, token and rate limits.
  • Key secrets are shown once and stored hashed, so put the key straight into an env var or secrets manager.
  • Add an IP allowlist, and revoke the key when you're done.
  • Spend comes from OROO Mint, a prepaid INR wallet topped up via Razorpay, and you pay only for tokens used.
  • OROO doesn't store prompts or completions.

Re-run on every model update

Commit the dataset and rubric to the repo. When a model changes, re-run the harness. Because MODEL lives in config, switching in production is a one-line change you can roll back.

More at orooblue.com.

Originally published on the OROO Kids blog: https://orookids.blogspot.com/2026/10/gpt-gemini-or-claude-how-to-pick-right.html

title: JSX in React – What and Why?
description:
JSX stands for JavaScript XML.

JSX is a syntax extension used in React that allows us to write HTML-like code inside JavaScript.

In simple words, JSX helps us write UI elements using HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript.

  1. What is JSX? Without JSX, we create UI elements using JavaScript's React.createElement() method.

Without JSX:

import React from "react";

function App() {
  return React.createElement(
    "h1",
    null,
    "Hello World"
  );
}

export default App;

With JSX:

function App() {
  return <h1>Hello World</h1>;
}

export default App;

Both produce the same UI.

Easy to understand
JSX makes React code cleaner and easier to read.

  1. Why do we use JSX? Imagine you are developing an e-commerce website.

You need:

  • Navigation bar
  • Product cards
  • Search bar
  • Add to cart button
  • Footer If you use only JavaScript methods like React.createElement(), creating complex UI structures becomes difficult to read.

JSX makes this easier.

Main advantages:

  1. Easy to write HTML-like UI inside JavaScript.
  2. Makes code readable and maintainable.
  3. Supports JavaScript expressions.
  4. Helps create reusable React components.
  5. Makes dynamic UI development easier.

title: Teaching an AI assistant to forget a deleted Figma comment
description:
Picture this.

A team spends a week arguing in the comments of a Figma file about whether the sign-up button should be a pill. They settle it, the designer deletes the thread to tidy up, and a month later your AI assistant is still telling new hires that "the team agreed on a pill, see the comments". The comment is gone from Figma. The memory of it is not.

Nothing crashed. The assistant just remembers something that no longer exists, and design decisions are exactly the kind of thing people ask it about.

For Mergetober I built a Figma connector for Cognee with that in mind. The code is in PR #372 for issue #4552.

What it does

Cognee turns documents into a knowledge graph an agent can search. The connector feeds it from Figma:

  • Each file becomes one document: its type, folder, page names, frame and section names, and the text of every text layer. FigJam stickies count too.
  • Each comment thread becomes one document: the comment and its replies in time order with their authors, which frame it is pinned to, and whether it is resolved.
  • Geometry, images, hidden layers and default layer names like "Frame 12" are never read. A Figma file is a canvas, not prose, so only the text is kept.
  • A deleted file, a deleted comment, or a folder you deselect is forgotten on the next sync. 
source = figma_source(token, folder_ids=["<folder id>"])
await cognee.remember(source, dataset_name="figma")

Files and their comments share one node set per folder, so a search can be limited to one folder. There is also an optional OAuth integration that plugs into Cognee's connect and folder-picker flow.

What the API does not give you

Figma has no change feed and no delete feed. The folder listing gives each file's last_modified, not its version number, and the part that costs is GET /v1/files/:key, the whole node tree, which sits in Figma's strictest rate-limit tier. Figma's docs list 10 to 20 requests a minute for Dev and Full seats and about 20 a month for View and Collab seats. Comments do not move a file's timestamp. You cannot list a user's teams. Listing folders needs a private OAuth app, because public apps are not allowed the folders:read scope.

So each run lists the selection, fetches only the files whose last_modified moved, and serves the rest from a cache. Comments are read every run, one cheap request per file, because they never change the stamp. Cognee does the incremental part by content: a document whose text is unchanged keeps its id and never reaches the LLM again.

Two things my first design got wrong

I found both by reading my own code the way a reviewer would.

It cached too much. The cache kept whole rendered rows, title and folder name included. A rename or a folder move may not change a file's timestamp, so the cache would have kept serving the old title. Now the cache holds only what the node tree contributes, and the title and folder come from the fresh listing every run.

It could never finish a big team. When Figma returned a 429 that outlasted the retries, the whole run failed and the next run started from zero, hitting the same wall. Now at most 100 node trees are fetched per run, and a rate limit stops the fetching cleanly. Files not reached keep the text they were last synced with, so nothing is forgotten, and the next run carries on. The sync counts say so with failed_budget or failed_rate_limit.

I also made it stricter than it needed to be. An empty selection raises, because an empty list must never mean "forget everything". A selection that suddenly lists no files, when files were synced before, raises too. Earlier reviewers on my Stripe connector pointed out that a node set per record makes a big graph, so I used one per folder.

How I tested it

There are 68 tests on Python 3.10 and 3.12. Figma is an in-memory fake behind dlt's real HTTP stack. 8 of them run the whole Cognee pipeline with a mocked LLM: deleted files and comments leave the graph, an unchanged re-sync makes no LLM call, a sync cut short by the budget keeps what it has, and a file and its comments share a node set.

Then I ran it against a real Figma account on the free plan: a folder with two design files and one comment thread with a reply.

  • First sync: both files and the thread came in, and a search answered correctly from the design text.
  • Re-sync with nothing changed: 0 file downloads and 0 LLM calls.
  • A new comment: only that thread went to the LLM.
  • A deleted comment: forgotten.
  • A text edit in one file: only that file was fetched again, the new text was in the graph and the old text was gone.
  • A file moved to the trash: forgotten on the next sync, the rest untouched.

The only surprise was timing. My first sync after the edit saw nothing, because Figma saved the change a few seconds after I read the folder. The next run caught it.

What I did not test

The OAuth connect flow, because it needs a private Figma app. Large files and long syncs: I used two small files. Paid plans, and the actual rate limits of the free plan. All of that is covered by the fake, not by Figma.

Try it

The example is packages/connector/figma/examples/example.py. You need a personal access token (Settings, Security) with the scopes file_content:read, file_comments:read, folders:read and file_metadata:read, plus a folder id or a team id. Use a separate dataset, and tell me what breaks.

title: Analyzing 454 Express Entry draws with pandas: what IRCC's own data says about Canada's CRS cut-offs
description:
Canada's Express Entry system publishes every "round of invitations" it runs: the date, the program or category, how many people were invited and the lowest Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score that got an invitation. IRCC puts this in a JSON feed behind its rounds of invitations page. I cleaned that feed into three CSV files and put them on GitHub, so I wanted to see what you can learn from it with a few lines of pandas.

Everything below runs as is against the public CSVs. The outputs are pasted straight from my terminal (pandas 3.0, data through round #453 on October 28, 2026).

1. Load the data 

import pandas as pd
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 10)

BASE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/izafar0999-gitup/canada-express-entry-draws/main/"

draws = pd.read_csv(BASE + "express_entry_draws.csv",
                    parse_dates=["date"], dtype={"round_number": "string"})
print(draws.shape)
print(draws["date"].min().date(), "to", draws["date"].max().date())
print(draws[draws["round_number"].str.contains("[a-z]", regex=True)]
      [["round_number", "date", "invitations"]])

(454, 9)
2015-01-31 to 2026-10-28
    round_number       date  invitations
362          91b 2018-05-30          200
363          91a 2018-05-30          500

First gotcha: round_number is not an integer. On May 30, 2018 IRCC ran two rounds on the same day and numbered them 91a and 91b. Reading it as string on purpose makes that explicit and stops anyone from casting it to int later and crashing on 91a.

2. Rounds and invitations per year 

draws["year"] = draws["date"].dt.year
yearly = draws.groupby("year").agg(
    rounds=("round_number", "size"),
    invitations=("invitations", "sum"),
    median_cutoff=("crs_cutoff", "median"),
)
print(yearly)

      rounds  invitations  median_cutoff
year                                    
2015      23        31063          469.0
2016      27        33782          482.0
2017      30        86023          438.5
2018      28        89800          442.0
2019      26        85300          459.5
2020      37       107350          471.0
2021      42       114224          712.0
2022      24        46539          692.0
2023      42       110266          486.0
2024      52        98903          524.5
2025      58       113998          533.5
2026      65       149409          514.0

2026 is not over, and it already has the most rounds (65) and the most invitations (149,409) of any year in the data.

Second gotcha: that median_cutoff column is misleading. Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) rounds only invite people who already have a provincial nomination, and a nomination is worth 600 CRS points on its own (see IRCC's CRS criteria page). In 2021 IRCC ran only program-specific rounds, 25 of the 42 of them PNP, so the median jumps to 712. Drop PNP rounds before you compare years:

no_pnp = draws[draws["category"] != "Provincial Nominee Program"]
print(no_pnp.groupby("year")["crs_cutoff"].median().loc[2019:])

year
2019    459.5
2020    469.0
2021    401.0
2022    510.0
2023    486.0
2024    499.0
2025    504.5
2026    475.0
Name: crs_cutoff, dtype: float64

Even this still mixes very different draws. The 2021 figure includes round #176 (February 13, 2021), a Canadian Experience Class round that invited 27,332 people with a cut-off of 75, which is still the largest and lowest round in the file. A median per year is a rough summary at best. Group by category if you want a number someone could plan around.

3. The end of the "general" draw

IRCC labels each round as General (all programs), Program-specific (one program, such as CEC or PNP) or Category-based (for example French speakers or healthcare workers). A pivot table shows how the mix changed:

share = (draws.pivot_table(index="year", columns="round_type",
                           values="invitations", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
              .pipe(lambda t: t.div(t.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100)
              .round(1))
print(share.loc[2019:])

last_general = draws[draws["round_type"] == "General"].sort_values("date").iloc[-1]
print("Last general round:", last_general["round_number"], last_general["date"].date(),
      last_general["invitations"], "ITAs, cut-off", last_general["crs_cutoff"])

round_type  Category-based  General  Program-specific
year                                                 
2019                   0.0     98.8               1.2
2020                   0.0     63.4              36.6
2021                   0.0      0.0             100.0
2022                   0.0     76.8              23.2
2023                  23.5     69.6               7.0
2024                  42.9     14.6              42.4
2025                  59.0      0.0              41.0
2026                  54.1      0.0              45.9

Last general round: 294 2024-04-23 2095 ITAs, cut-off 529

In 2019 almost every invitation came from a general round. In 2025 and 2026, none did. The last general round was #294 on April 23, 2024. If you only look at the cut-off column without round_type, you will compare a French-language round with a CEC round and draw the wrong conclusion.

4. 2026 by category 

d26 = draws[draws["year"] == 2026]
summary = (d26.groupby("category")
              .agg(rounds=("round_number", "size"),
                   invitations=("invitations", "sum"),
                   min_cutoff=("crs_cutoff", "min"),
                   max_cutoff=("crs_cutoff", "max"))
              .sort_values("invitations", ascending=False))
print(summary)

                                               rounds  invitations  min_cutoff  max_cutoff
category                                                                                  
French language proficiency                        12        60500         382         435
Canadian Experience Class                          18        57750         507         523
Healthcare and social services occupations          3        11500         467         475
Provincial Nominee Program                         21        10814         697         805
Trade occupations                                   2         6500         476         477
Senior managers with Canadian work experience       3         1000         389         429
Physicians with Canadian work experience            3          891         169         223
Transport occupations                               2          450         470         477
Skilled military recruits                           1            4         368         368

The spread is the story: CEC cut-offs stayed in a tight 507 to 523 band all year, while French-language rounds closed between 382 and 435. Same system, same year, a gap of roughly 100 points depending on which door you are eligible for.

5. Where the pool sits

The second file is the CRS score distribution IRCC publishes with most rounds: how many profiles are in the pool in each score band.

pool = pd.read_csv(BASE + "express_entry_crs_score_distribution.csv",
                   parse_dates=["date", "distribution_as_of"])
latest = pool.sort_values("date").iloc[-1]
bands = ["candidates_601_1200", "candidates_501_600", "candidates_451_500",
         "candidates_401_450", "candidates_351_400", "candidates_301_350", "candidates_0_300"]
snap = latest[bands].astype(int)
print("Snapshot as of", latest["distribution_as_of"].date(), "total", int(latest["candidates_total"]))
print((snap / int(latest["candidates_total"]) * 100).round(1).to_string())

Snapshot as of 2026-10-25 total 228724
candidates_601_1200     0.3
candidates_501_600      9.0
candidates_451_500     31.1
candidates_401_450     27.8
candidates_351_400     20.9
candidates_301_350      7.5
candidates_0_300        3.3

Only 9.3% of the 228,724 profiles score above 500. CEC rounds in 2026 needed at least 507, so most of the pool is below the line for those rounds, and the biggest single band is 451 to 500 (31.1%). Two caveats if you use this file: IRCC often reuses the same snapshot for several rounds in one week, so drop_duplicates("distribution_as_of") before you plot a time series, and the bands are fixed by IRCC, so you cannot compute an exact count above, say, 519.

6. Draws come in clusters 

d26 = d26.sort_values("date")
weeks = d26["date"].dt.isocalendar().week
per_week = d26.groupby(weeks).size()
print("2026 rounds:", len(d26), "| weeks with at least one round:", per_week.size)
print(per_week.value_counts().sort_index().rename("weeks").rename_axis("rounds_in_week"))
gaps = d26["date"].diff().dt.days.dropna()
print("Longest gap:", int(gaps.max()), "days, ending", d26.loc[gaps.idxmax(), "date"].date())

2026 rounds: 65 | weeks with at least one round: 21
rounds_in_week
1     1
2     3
3    10
4     7
Name: weeks, dtype: int64
Longest gap: 25 days, ending 2026-06-22

The 65 rounds of 2026 fell in just 21 calendar weeks. In 17 of those weeks IRCC ran three or four rounds back to back (typically PNP, then CEC, then a category round). So "how many draws were there" is a less useful question than "how many draw weeks were there". If you are building any kind of "next draw" estimate, model the week, not the individual round.

Things to know before you build on this

  • PNP cut-offs include the 600 nomination points. Subtract 600 if you want to compare them with other rounds, or just keep them separate.
  • From November 3, 2026, IRCC changes how Canadian work experience and job offers are scored, and says it will pause rounds for up to two weeks while it recalculates every profile (source: IRCC's CRS criteria page and its October 2026 backgrounder on high-wage occupations). Cut-offs after that date will not be directly comparable with earlier ones, so add a rules_version column before you mix them.
  • Tie-breaking timestamps are ISO 8601. A trailing Z means IRCC gave the time in UTC.

Get the data

  • GitHub: https://github.com/izafar0999-gitup/canada-express-entry-draws (CSV files, data dictionary and the build script that regenerates them from IRCC's JSON feed)
  • Source: IRCC rounds of invitations, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations.html, under the Open Government Licence â€“ Canada

If you would rather read the pool numbers than compute them, I keep a plain-English version on the Express Entry pool statistics page. And if you want to turn the scoring tables themselves into code, the step-by-step CRS calculation guide walks through every factor with a worked example.

Zafar Iqbal maintains crscalcu.ca, an independent site that is not affiliated with IRCC. Always confirm rules on canada.ca before making immigration decisions.

title: What Abstraction Does React Introduce?
description:
JavaScript could already update the DOM.

So why did we need React?

In my previous post, we discussed the history of Web UI and how it evolved from HTML to React.

But there are many misconceptions about React.

One of them is that React removes DOM manipulation.

That’s not the proper way to understand it.

Instead, React abstracts DOM manipulation.

So, what is abstraction?

The bigger picture of React's abstraction is where you describe UI declaratively as a function of application state, organize UI into components, and then let React handle the synchronization between that description and the React rendering environment.

That is about the overall abstraction, which abstracts many underlying tasks.

Let's understand that.

Abstractions

1. DOM Mutations

DOM mutations mean abstracting low-level concepts and thinking about that abstraction.

Before React, you need to think about the DOM nodes, properties, DOM methods, and DOM events.

React abstracts that and introduces concepts like Components, Props, UI, and State.

This is similar to how higher-level programming languages abstract machine instructions.

2. Declarative UI

Declarative means you describe what the result should be.

You are describing the desired UI.

You don't need to explicitly describe:

  • Create dashboard DOM.
  • Insert dashboard.
  • Update Button.

Instead, React tracks your declaration and manages the transition between them.

This separates "What" from "How".

3. Component and State Abstraction

Before React, you needed to create reusable JavaScript functions intentionally.

But React makes UI itself composable.

This introduces the component abstraction.

State abstraction abstracts the tracking of what changed, which element depends on it, and what should I update.

4. Abstraction as a Contract

In React, you describe the UI corresponding to the current state.

Now React is responsible for reconciling that description with the rendered UI.

Now the developer's responsibility becomes:

  • What should the UI look like?
  • What state does it depend on?
  • How are components composed?

And React manages the responsibility for rendered work, reconciliation, scheduling, commit, and host environment updates.

title: StudyLoop: turn your markdown notes into flashcards that can't lie to you
description:
I keep my notes in markdown. Hundreds of files: RFC summaries, postmortems, the bits of HTTP caching I have to re-learn every time a CDN misbehaves. Writing them is easy. Remembering them is not. Two months later I'm searching my own notes and still getting no-cache and no-store mixed up.

Flashcards fix the remembering part, but making them by hand takes so long that I never kept it up. Asking an LLM to make them is fast, but it's risky. Sometimes the model invents an answer that sounds right and isn't in the notes, and then you memorize something false.

So I built StudyLoop, a small terminal tutor that treats your notes as the only source of truth. It is open source (MIT), pure Python stdlib, and has no runtime dependencies: github.com/bayuh85/studyloop.

The real use case: learning HTTP caching from my own notes

The repo ships examples/http-caching/notes.md, a short set of notes on freshness, Cache-Control, validators, conditional requests and Vary. Here is the loop I actually run:

export ATMOROUTER_API_KEY=...        # only card generation needs a key
python3 -m studyloop add examples/http-caching/notes.md --deck caching
python3 -m studyloop study --deck caching --limit 10
python3 -m studyloop ask "what does no-cache mean" --deck caching

On a live run this morning, add cut the file into 14 passages and the model proposed 32 cards. StudyLoop kept 30 and rejected 2:

passages 14  new 14 · moved 0 · unchanged 0 · removed 0
cards 30 accepted · 2 rejected
  rejected  quote not in passage  484e52b3fc7bd77d  What does the `immutable` Cache-Control extension actually do...
  rejected  quote not in passage  484e52b3fc7bd77d  How does `stale-while-revalidate` work...

Those two rejections show the whole idea working. The model wrote reasonable questions about immutable and stale-while-revalidate, but the passage it was given didn't support its answers. So those cards never got into my deck.

How a card is kept or rejected

Each passage is sent on its own, and the model has to return JSON: front, back, and a quote. A card is stored only if:

  • the quote is a contiguous excerpt of that passage (whitespace may differ, words and order may not),
  • at least half of the content words in back appear in the passage, so a real quote attached to an invented answer still fails,
  • any citation the model names matches the passage's own [file:start-end].

Every card carries its line range, so when you review it you can jump straight to the source.

Passages that survive edits

Each passage id is a SHA-256 over the source path plus the exact passage text. If you insert a line near the top of the file, the line ranges shift but the ids stay the same, so your review history stays put. If you edit a passage, it becomes new work. If you delete one, its cards go too. Running add again only sends passages the model hasn't seen yet, so re-syncing a notes folder costs almost nothing.

Review with SM-2, ask with BM25

study is classic SuperMemo SM-2: ease starts at 2.5 and never goes below 1.3, intervals run 1 day, 6 days, then grow by ease, and an again grade puts the card back in the current session.

ask makes no network call. It ranks passages with Okapi BM25 (k1 = 1.5, b = 0.75; hyphenated directives like max-age count as one token) and answers in your notes' own words:

`no-cache` does not mean "do not store this". A cache may store a no-cache
response, but it must revalidate with the origin before every reuse.
[examples/http-caching/notes.md:37-43]

The answer is never made up, because it's your own sentences with a line citation.

Try it without a key

There's an offline demo server that stands in for the model, and the 46-test suite runs against it:

python3 -m studyloop.demo_server --port 8766
python3 -m studyloop add examples/http-caching/notes.md --deck caching \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8766/v1 --api-key demo

Provider

Card generation uses the standard OpenAI chat-completions request, so --base-url works with any compatible server. By default it points at AtmoRouter, a cheap AI API gateway and OpenRouter alternative: 155 models behind one OpenAI-compatible key, pay per token, at up to 89% below official prices. The default model is cc/claude-sonnet-4-6. Turning a whole notes folder into cards costs about as much as a coffee, and asking questions is free because it runs locally.

Repo: github.com/bayuh85/studyloop. Issues and PRs welcome, especially chunking for other heading styles.

title: GPT summarization workflow: combining batch processing for Node.js hiring rubrics
description:
Short answer: treat candidate scoring as a batch job behind an application-owned contract, not as a vendor-shaped feature. For an e-commerce hiring team, the useful unit is a rubric decision with a traceable tenant, input version, model choice, and result status. Batch processing is efficient for large summarization workloads, but the queue and result format must remain replaceable.

The operational constraint is per-tenant cost visibility. A single monthly total cannot tell me whether one marketplace, recruiter, or rubric is producing the spend. I would attach the tenant and rubric version before submission, retain the provider request ID, and export a status report that can be reconciled without opening five vendor consoles. That decision matters more than shaving a few seconds from a non-interactive workflow.
