Infrai fits this boundary when a team wants one REST surface, one credential, and per-call accounting metadata attached to the tenant ledger. It is not the right answer when a provider's specialized batch controls, cloud-native governance, or model-specific guarantees are more important than a unified backend account.

Keep the contract small.

In practice, that means the first record written for a profile is more valuable than the first request sent to a model. I would persist tenant_id, work_item_id, rubric_version, a content hash, and an application-generated idempotency key before a worker sees the item. The worker can then construct whatever batch line the selected provider requires, but the result consumer never has to infer ownership from a prompt or a filename. Suppose a retry returns after the original result has already been exported: the consumer looks up the work item, sees the terminal export state, records the duplicate provider response for audit, and does not create a second score. Suppose the rubric changes while the batch is running: the old version remains attached to the old item, and the new rubric creates a new item rather than mutating history. Suppose one tenant's 1,000 profiles keep a shared batch open while another tenant has only 18: the scheduler can split the work by tenant or reporting window without changing the scoring contract. This is more bookkeeping than a direct SDK call, but it is the bookkeeping that makes per-tenant cost visibility and migration possible. A provider adapter should be replaceable precisely because these decisions live above it.

That is the whole test.

The limitation is important: a unified surface does not make a provider's batch behavior identical to another provider's behavior. The trade-off is an extra adapter and a readiness check in exchange for a simpler credential and accounting boundary. If the hiring platform already has strict AWS controls, Bedrock is the better choice; if it needs a GPT-specific batch contract, OpenAI is the better choice. I would not recommend an aggregation layer merely because it has more routes.

The lesson is an invariant, not a claim about a particular provider: every submitted item needs a stable application ID, tenant ID, rubric version, and outcome state. If a retry creates a second result, the reporting layer cannot distinguish a late answer from double billing. If a result arrives without its input version, a recruiter can read a plausible summary produced against yesterday's rubric. Plausible is not correct.

The incident lesson: the batch boundary is the product

Consider a bounded production scenario: an e-commerce platform receives candidate profiles for several tenants and scores each profile against a job rubric. The daytime path accepts the profile, normalizes the rubric, and records a work item. A later batch groups those items for summarization and scoring. One tenant has 1,000 profiles; another has 18. They should not disappear into one unlabelled blob.

I initially wanted the batch provider's object to be the system record. That is convenient until migration day. The safer boundary is an application record whose provider fields are optional: queued, running, succeeded, failed, and exported are ours; provider batch IDs and raw responses are attached evidence. This leaves room to change the transport while preserving audit and cost joins.

The advice has a boundary. Interactive candidate feedback, strict ordering, or a workflow that must fail within a short request deadline belongs on a synchronous path. Batch is the right lane for deferred summaries and rubric evidence, where throughput and accounting matter more than immediate display.

How should a GPT summarization workflow combine batch processing?

The contract should expose the business operation rather than the vendor vocabulary. I use an input object like CandidateScoringRequest, a result object with rubric-versioned evidence, and a separate usage record. The provider adapter can map those objects to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a cloud batch API, or a plain REST batch service.

OpenAI's Batch API is a natural reference for asynchronous requests and is useful when the rest of the application already uses its client conventions. Google Vertex AI Batch Prediction is a stronger fit for teams already operating on Google Cloud and wanting its job and storage controls around batch inference. Anthropic Message Batches is a credible choice when the scoring prompt is built around Claude and the team accepts an Anthropic-specific batch lifecycle. Amazon Bedrock batch inference belongs on the shortlist when governance and model access already live in AWS.

Those are not interchangeable claims of capability. They differ in authentication, input-file handling, completion semantics, model availability, and how usage is exposed. I would verify those details against the provider's current contract before writing an adapter. A comparison table is useful precisely because it keeps the decision conditional:

There is a practical failure mode here that deserves more room than the vendor names: a batch can finish successfully while the business export is still wrong. Imagine a tenant's rubric changes after submission, a worker retries a timed-out request, and a result arrives with a provider ID but no local work-item match. The model response may be perfectly readable, yet the platform must quarantine it, preserve the old rubric version, and report the item as unresolved rather than silently attach it to the newest job. That is why I keep provider status, normalized outcome, and export state as separate fields, and why a migration test should replay duplicate, late, and unknown results before anyone compares model quality.

Option Good fit Migration risk to isolate
OpenAI Batch API Existing OpenAI request shapes and a GPT-centered workflow Batch object and JSONL conventions can leak into application code
Vertex AI Batch Prediction A Google Cloud estate with storage and IAM already standardized Cloud-specific job and artifact assumptions
Anthropic Message Batches Claude-oriented summarization and scoring Provider-specific message and result semantics
Bedrock batch inference AWS governance and centralized model access AWS job, location, and model-routing concerns
A REST aggregation layer One credential and one accounting surface across backend capabilities The adapter still needs a clear capability and readiness check

A managed aggregation layer is worth considering for the last row when the platform team's real problem is operational sprawl. Infrai's public discovery surface is self-describing, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that makes contract inspection and adapter generation less dependent on a private SDK. Its broader positioning is one REST API, one key, and one bill across backend services. For this workflow, the concrete value is being able to join per-call cost metadata and request IDs to the tenant ledger while keeping the application-facing interface in my code.

My recommendation is specific: teams that need one accounting surface for deferred candidate summaries should try Infrai behind an application-owned batch adapter, provided the required batch capability is live in their region and its discovered schema matches the payload they intend to send. A direct provider is the better choice when the organization needs a provider's specialized batch controls, model-specific guarantees, or cloud-native governance more than it needs a unified backend account.

The preventative path in Go

The following small client shows the part I want to make boring: authenticate from the environment, use an explicit method, respect Retry-After on 429, and surface non-success bodies. It inspects the batch catalog rather than inventing a submit payload. The submit schema should come from the discovered capability contract; copying guessed fields into production is how an adapter becomes a liability.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func listBatches(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/batch/list", nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done(): timer.Stop(); return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("batch list failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("batch list exceeded retry limit")
}

func main() {
    body, err := listBatches(context.Background(), &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second})
    if err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

For submission, I would generate an idempotency key from the application work-item ID plus the rubric version, persist it before the request, and make the adapter map the discovered request and response schema. The same key must be reused after a timeout. The worker then polls the provider's status, checks each result, and writes a tenant-tagged usage record before marking the work item exported. Error checking is part of the workflow, not a cleanup task after the happy path.

How do cost controls become operational controls?

Cost visibility needs a ledger shape that survives vendor changes. Store tenant, job, work-item, rubric version, provider, model, request ID, input and output accounting fields when supplied, status, and timestamps. Keep raw result payloads separately from the normalized score. That gives finance a reconciliation path and gives SRE a way to distinguish a provider retry from an application retry.

I would set an SLO for completion reporting, not pretend that batch latency is an interactive SLA. For example, define the target as the percentage of accepted work items that reach a terminal state and appear in the export within the agreed reporting window. Track queued, running, succeeded, failed, and unknown separately. A missing result is a state to page or reconcile, not a zero score.

The capacity question is similarly concrete: how many profiles arrive per tenant during the peak window, how many tokens does a rubric prompt add, and how many concurrent batches can the selected provider absorb? The answer determines whether to split by tenant, rubric, or time window. One giant batch may reduce coordination overhead while making a single tenant dominate the completion window. Many tiny batches improve isolation while increasing polling and bookkeeping. I would choose the partition that keeps the largest tenant within the reporting SLO, then measure queue age and result export lag.

A unified REST surface can reduce the number of credentials and invoice joins, and Infrai's documented convention includes per-call cost, latency, vendor, cache-hit, and request-ID metadata. That is useful evidence for the ledger. It does not remove the need to test the exact batch schema, check readiness, or decide which failures are retriable. The adapter remains the ownership boundary.

The decision rule

Use a batch API for deferred summarization and rubric scoring when the result can arrive later, the work is partitionable, and the application owns idempotency and accounting. Keep the domain contract provider-neutral. Compare OpenAI, Vertex AI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and an aggregation layer against your existing cloud controls and migration cost, not against a single unit price.

For this e-commerce workflow, I would choose the unified REST option only when per-tenant visibility and a single backend credential materially simplify operations, and only after discovery confirms the required capability. I would choose a direct specialist when its batch semantics or governance are the actual requirement. That is a reversible decision because the scoring contract, ledger, and export format remain ours.

If that boundary fits your system, start by inspecting the documented batch capability and discovery contract before implementing the adapter.

Sources

  • OpenAI Batch API
  • Google Cloud Vertex AI batch prediction
  • Anthropic Message Batches
  • Amazon Bedrock batch inference
  • Cohere Rerank documentation
  • Infrai discovery

title: hotellobby (LobbyDuo): UX Notes on Preview-Before-Pay AI Booth Videos
description:
How I shipped a two-photo → Hotel Lobby booth duo on Cloudflare Workers — optimizing framing preview before Stripe, with Seedance via TryAllAPI.

Trend video products usually fail at the same moment: the user pays, then discovers their faces are cropped wrong. For tryhotellobby.app (product name hotellobby / LobbyDuo) I optimized the UX before the charge, not another prompt textarea.

Upload two adult face photos → ~15s orange COLORS-style booth duo (9:16 / 16:9 / 21:9, 480p or 720p) with original/AI booth audio. Independent tool — not affiliated with any artist group. This post is the builder + UX walkthrough. Prices and model ids change; treat live site / console as source of truth.

UX thesis: preview framing, then unlock Create

The homepage copy is blunt: free scene preview before you pay — upload two photos, check framing in the orange booth layout, then unlock Create with a one-time pack.

That sequence matters more than fancy motion poetry:

  1. Photo 1 → left of the booth duo.
  2. Photo 2 → right.
  3. Local/layout preview of how faces sit in the booth.
  4. Only then: Stripe → credits → Seedance render.

Users who can see “my face is too small / off-center” before paying convert better and refund less. Free-form “make a hotel video” prompts do the opposite: ambiguity first, charge second, regret third.

Live packs verified on-site while writing: Single $8.88 (≈ 500 credits / one 720p), 3-pack $16.99, plus larger packs (and occasional cheaper 480p messaging). Guest Stripe — no account for a single video. Always re-check the create CTA before you screenshot a price for a friend.

Why left/right roles beat a single “upload faces” dump

Booth memes are spatial. If the UI does not say who stands where, users invent their own convention and then complain the sample “looks different.” Fixed seats:

  • Remove “who is who?” support tickets.
  • Stabilize the locked template prompt sent upstream.
  • Make demos honest — the sample matches the seats.

Aspect ratio is a first-class control (9:16 default for Reels/TikTok; 16:9 / 21:9 for other cuts). Original/AI booth audio means the download is shareable without hunting a track.

Stack overview

Layer Choice Role
Front / SSR TanStack Start (Vite) Landing, upload panel, generation status
Runtime Cloudflare Workers Edge deploy, secrets, API routes
DB Cloudflare D1 Credits, orders, task rows (table prefixes if DBs are shared)
Payments Stripe Checkout One-time packs + optional larger packs; guest checkout
Video upstream TryAllAPI → Seedance Async create + poll
Analytics GA Funnel sanity check 
two faces → booth layout preview
→ check credits (else Stripe)
→ Worker creates Seedance task via TryAllAPI
→ poll until MP4 URL → store / show
→ on failure: refund credits

Demo clips are self-hosted. Do not hotlink someone else’s sample MP4 for marketing.

Why a video API aggregator

Operational checklist after register / top-up:

  1. Confirm available USD balance in the console (not only the checkout success page).
  2. Create a token in pay-as-you-go style billing.
  3. Enable the video / Seedance-related channel group on that token. Wrong group → “no available channel” even when the model id looks right.
  4. Prefer separate keys per product (hotellobby-prod vs sandbox).
  5. Put the key only in Workers Secrets (for example TRYALLAPI_API_KEY). Never in the frontend bundle or a blog post.

Conceptually the call shape looks like this (field names follow the aggregator’s v3 contents API; always re-check current docs):

POST /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks
Authorization: Bearer <TRYALLAPI_API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept-Encoding: identity

GET /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks/{id}

I send Accept-Encoding: identity from the Worker because some gateways behave badly with transparent decompression. Model ids used in production look like Seedance 2.x family strings — treat console ids as source of truth, not this paragraph.

Seedance parameters that matter for booth duos

A few details that bit me across this family of sites:

  • Pass duration as an explicit integer. Some models default to “smart length.” Omitting duration can silently lengthen the clip and the bill.
  • resolution and ratio. Cost tracks resolution tier and duration more than portrait vs landscape. Match whatever the create UI offers (often 480p/720p and 9:16 for Shorts).
  • generate_audio. When the product ships “finished” downloads, leave audio on; creators who want a trending sound can mute later.
  • Status machine. Expect something like queued → running → succeeded / failed. Success URLs are often short-lived signed links — download/rehost on your side before handing the file to the user.
  • Decent failure. On supply_unavailable or hard failures: refund credits, show a short human message, log the detailed upstream error server-side, optionally fall back to another Seedance tier.

Rough mental model for upstream cost (illustrative only — use your own usage fields and invoices):

tokens ≈ duration_sec × width × height × fps / 1024
cost   ≈ tokens × price_per_million_tokens

Price the site after you measure a few real 720p runs with retry margin, Stripe fees, and failed-job refunds — not from a spreadsheet fantasy of 0% failure.

Booth-specific: map two reference images to left/right seats consistently; same-person clones in both seats look wrong — the UI should say so.

Credits, Stripe, and guest checkout

Demo UIs are easy. The line between toy and product is:

  1. User hits Create → check credit balance.
  2. If short → Stripe Checkout Session (guest allowed).
  3. Webhook (plus a return-URL sync check) grants credits.
  4. Pre-debit / lock credits, create upstream task, persist task_id in D1.
  5. Poll until done; succeed → show MP4; fail → refund credits.

Two books of account stay separate: USD balance at TryAllAPI (your cost) vs site credits (what you sold). Mixing them in one mental ledger is how you underprice or invent “mysterious” losses.

When several products share one Stripe account, isolate webhooks by endpoint or by metadata (site / product). Callbacks pointed at the wrong apex domain are a classic multi-site footgun.

Secrets stay in Workers: TRYALLAPI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, webhook secret, auth secrets. The browser only ever sees publishable Stripe keys if needed.

Deploy notes (Workers + D1)

Typical loop on this template family:

pnpm install
# wire D1 database_id, production env, custom domain in wrangler
pnpm cf:deploy

Before calling a deploy “done”:

  • D1 binding is correct; shared DBs use table prefixes, not a new database per micro-idea (free-tier DB counts are limited).
  • AUTH_TRUSTED_ORIGINS and Stripe return / webhook URLs match the production HTTPS origin.
  • GA id is set for a coarse funnel (land → upload → pay → wait → download).
  • One real end-to-end path on production or a staging Worker: upload → pay → render → download.

Production origin for Checkout / auth trust: https://tryhotellobby.app (alternate brand hostnames may exist — keep allowlists in sync with the URL users actually pay on).

Product rules that are not optional

Face-based generation is not “just another SaaS CRUD app”:

  • Require an explicit 18+ / rights-to-use confirmation on upload.
  • Block minors and refuse celebrity / stranger misuse in copy and policy.
  • Expect upstream safety refusals; refund and explain.
  • Keep privacy policy honest about retention; do not train on user media by default.
  • Market as an independent fan-style tool for a trend format — not as an official tie-in unless you actually have that deal.
  • Use your own sample renders in marketing.

Those constraints belong in the product, not in a footnote you add after the first dispute email.

What the UX taught me

  1. Preview-before-pay reduces “bad crop” chargebacks more than shaving another dollar off the Single pack.
  2. Locked booth layout beats free-form hotel prompts.
  3. Guest Single pack (~$8.88) matches “I need one clip tonight.”
  4. Credits with automatic refund on failed generation is table stakes.
  5. Measure land → upload → pay → wait → download before rewriting marketing adjectives.

Consumer path: tryhotellobby.app — watch the sample, upload two authorized adult faces, preview framing, pay once. Builder path: TryAllAPI, top up, prove create+poll, then polish the preview UX. Sell confidence in framing first; sell GPU second.

title: What SEBI's retail algo circular means for your order layer
description:
SEBI's 4 February 2025 circular, "Safer participation of retail investors in Algorithmic trading", is mostly a compliance document. But if you build trading software, most of it lands on one place in your code: the layer that sends orders to a broker. Here is what it changes in practice. I'm writing this as a developer, not as a lawyer, so read the circular itself before you design anything.

  1. No more open API keys The circular does not permit open APIs. A broker may give API access only through an API key that is specific to the vendor and the client, together with a static IP the broker has whitelisted. The aim is traceability: the broker should be able to say which algo provider and which end client sent any order.

For your system this means API keys and IPs are per client records, not global settings, and your order traffic has to leave from a fixed, known address.

  1. Orders need to be tagged Brokers have to detect and tag algo orders using identifiers the exchange specifies, and this also applies to algos a broker offers to its own clients. Where the broker's API has an order tag field, you can pass a compact tag yourself. Kite Connect, for example, accepts an optional alphanumeric tag of up to 20 characters that comes back in the order book.

A pattern that works: encode the strategy ID and version in the tag, so one look at the broker's order book tells you which rule set sent the order.

  1. Versions must be frozen
    An approved algo that changes needs fresh approval. In software terms, a strategy version should become immutable once it is approved, and a change creates a new version with a new record. If your strategies are edited in place, you cannot prove later what was running when an order went out.

  2. Keep an audit trail you can actually read
    For every order, store the client, strategy ID and version, the rule that triggered it, the request you sent and the broker's response. This is the record you will want when a client asks why an order fired.

  3. Login is OAuth and two-factor
    The framework asks for OAuth-based authentication and two-factor authentication. Most brokers already work this way. The practical effect is a daily login step: for example, Kite Connect's access token expires at 6 AM the next day. Plan for a re-login prompt and pause live strategies for any client whose token has lapsed, instead of letting orders fail silently.

What is still moving
Secondary sources disagree on when parts of this apply, and the exchanges have issued their own operational rules (for example on static IP changes). Check the SEBI and NSE notices for the current dates before you commit a launch plan.

Where we wrote this up in more detail
We build algo trading software for brokers, strategy providers and trading educators, and we keep a longer technical guide with the Kite Connect login and order flow table, the order-layer audit design and cost drivers: Algo trading software development in India. If you are planning an app around it, the trading app development guide covers the client side.

Sources: SEBI circular text (reproduced by TaxGuru), Zerodha Kite Connect documentation on user login and orders.

Reviewed by Ranjeet, Technical Reviewer at Brandzivio.

title: How to Uninstall GBase Database(GBase 8a): A 5-Step Clean Removal Guide
description:
Wrong software version, completed POC, or server migration? These situations often require a clean GBase Database(GBase 8a) uninstall.

GBase Database provides an uninstall script, but running it in the wrong order can leave services running, processes holding files, or installation directories behind.

Follow these five steps to safely uninstall GBase Database. Run the commands as the DBA user and prepare the required uninstall password in advance.

Step 1: Back Up All Database Data

Before uninstalling GBase Database, back up everything you need to retain. The uninstall script deletes database data and does not preserve it for recovery.

Make sure you back up:

  • Database tables and other required data
  • Configuration files
  • Installation and troubleshooting logs
  • External table definitions and source files
  • Any load files stored outside the database

Pay special attention to external tables and load source files. Confirm their actual storage paths and make separate copies if necessary.

Do not proceed until the backup is complete and verified.

Step 2: Check for Active Business Connections

Before stopping GBase Database services, confirm that no business connections, running queries, or data loading operations remain.

Stopping services while data loading is in progress may leave incomplete files or interrupt ongoing operations.

Even in a POC environment, check for active workloads before continuing.

Step 3: Stop GBase Database Services

Stop services in reverse startup order: stop GCluster first, followed by GCware.

gcluster_services all stop
gcware_services all stop

Stopping the compute and SQL service layer before the underlying cluster management service helps ensure an orderly shutdown.

For multi-node GBase Database clusters, verify that services have stopped on every node. Stopping services on the first node does not automatically guarantee that remote nodes are clear.

Step 4: Run the GBase Database Uninstall Script

Navigate to the gcinstall directory extracted from the original installation package.

Run the uninstall script in silent mode using the original demo.options configuration file:

cd /opt/gcinstall
./unInstall.py --silent=demo.options

The script uses the existing configuration rather than requiring you to enter all installation parameters again.

Be prepared to enter the required password when prompted. The exact interaction and supported parameters may vary by GBase Database version, so consult the corresponding installation manual.

Important: Do not interrupt the uninstall process. Stopping it midway may leave the cluster in a partially removed state and require manual cleanup.

Step 5: Verify the Uninstall and Clean Up Remaining Files

After the uninstall script finishes, verify that the GBase Database processes have exited and the installation directory has been removed.

Check running processes:

ps -ef | grep -E "gcluster|gcware" | grep -v grep

Check the installation directory:

ls -ld /opt/gbase

A clean result should show no remaining GCluster or GCware processes belonging to this cluster and no remaining installation directory.

If processes remain, identify which cluster they belong to before stopping or killing them. Other database instances or services may share the same host.

If the machine will be reused, also review:

  • Old environment variables and profile settings
  • Scheduled jobs and automatic startup entries
  • The DBA user and its associated configuration
  • Residual files and directories
  • System parameters modified during environment preparation

Only remove shared users, directories, or system settings after confirming that no other application depends on them.

Additional Notes: Preserve Configuration and Installation Records

The GBase Database uninstall script relies on demo.options. Archive this file together with the installation logs and backup records.

Also remember that system-level settings modified by environment preparation scripts may not be automatically restored during uninstall.

Whether these settings need manual restoration depends on the operating system and GBase Database version. Record all relevant changes in the deployment handover documentation.

For production environments, perform uninstall operations through the approved change management process. Uninstallation is irreversible, and a verified backup is the recovery path.

Final Checklist: GBase Database Uninstall

Before marking the uninstall as complete, confirm:

  • [ ] Database data and required files are backed up.
  • [ ] No active business connections or loading operations remain.
  • [ ] GCluster and GCware services are stopped on every node.
  • [ ] unInstall.py completes successfully.
  • [ ] No related service processes remain.
  • [ ] The installation directory is removed.
  • [ ] Environment settings and startup entries are reviewed.
  • [ ] demo.options and installation logs are archived.

The key takeaway: A clean GBase Database uninstall is more than running unInstall.py. Back up data, stop services in reverse startup order, execute the uninstall script, and verify every node before returning the machine to service.

Keep these five steps in your GBase Database deployment runbook to make future reinstalls, server replacements, and POC environment cleanup more predictable.

title: How to Route Password Reset Email Templates — An Ownership Decision for Signup SREs
description:
How to Route Password Reset Email Templates — An Ownership Decision for Signup SREs

The page says password_reset_delivery_failed, and the on-call sees a signup queue growing while users wait for a verification link. The least complex fix is usually a single reusable template behind a stable application contract. Keep the reset token, recipient, and expiry owned by the signup service; let the delivery provider own rendering and transport only when that boundary is worth the operational trade.

Short answer: choose a provider-hosted template when several teams need consistent copy and you can accept provider-specific template management. Choose an application-rendered template when review, localization, or portability requires the source to live with the code. Infrai is a reasonable option for the first shape: its template-create and email-send capabilities let the application keep the delivery contract stable while the service behind it changes.

This is a system-shape decision, not a contest for the cheapest message. A reset email is part of account recovery. A duplicate can confuse a user; a late message can make a valid link look broken.

What did the page fire before the email failed?

Start with the alert, then walk backwards. The useful page is not “the provider returned an error.” It is “a signup reached the verification deadline without a delivered reset message.” That distinction changes what gets measured.

For each reset request, emit a request ID, template revision, provider request ID, and timestamps for created, accepted, delivered, bounced, and expired. Keep the reset token itself out of logs. The event list is enough to reconstruct the path when an engineer is covering both the queue and the signup service.

I would alert on the ratio of expired reset attempts and on queue age, with a separate low-volume alert for a sudden bounce increase. A provider timeout is a signal to retry; an expired recovery attempt is the user-visible failure. Those are related, but they are not the same metric.

The threshold needs a human check. A short classroom enrollment window may create a burst of legitimate resets. Page on every small bounce spike and the alert becomes noise; wait for a large expired-attempt ratio and the support queue has already grown. False positives spend attention. False negatives spend trust.

Which template should own the contract?

There are two viable architectures. Both can deliver the same verification link. Their invariants differ.

The short version: the template owns presentation, while the signup service owns recovery policy.

In the provider-owned shape, the signup service sends a template identifier plus data such as the user’s display name, reset URL, and expiry text. The template service owns markup and presentation revisions. The invariant is that every published revision accepts the same data contract. If a designer changes the button or footer, the application should not need a deployment.

In the application-owned shape, the service renders the message from a versioned template in the repository, then submits the rendered subject and body to the email API. The invariant is stronger: the exact content for a release is reviewable beside the code, and a rollback restores both behavior and copy. The cost is operational. Localization, previewing, and template editing now belong to the application team.

The rule I use is simple: provider ownership fits when content changes are frequent and the variable contract is stable; application ownership fits when regulated review or release reproducibility matters more than editor convenience. Do not let a template editor become an untracked production deployment.

How do you make retries boring?

A reset send is a write. The worker must assume the network can fail after the provider accepted the request. Retrying without an idempotency key can produce two messages, and two valid-looking links are a support ticket waiting to happen.

The following Go example keeps the decision boundary explicit. It calls the documented send route, builds a stable request identity from the signup event, reads the key from the environment, and treats a non-success response as an error. The template payload is deliberately supplied by the caller so the provider’s current schema remains the source of truth.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func deliveryKey(signupID, templateRevision string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(signupID + ":" + templateRevision))
    return "password-reset-" + hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func sendEmail(body []byte, signupID, templateRevision string) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    idempotencyKey := deliveryKey(signupID, templateRevision)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
            return fmt.Errorf("email API returned HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody)
        }
        if retryAfter, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second)
        } else {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 100 * time.Millisecond)
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("email API retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    err := sendEmail([]byte(`{"template_id":"reset-v3"}`), "signup-2026-10-31-0042", "reset-v3")
    fmt.Println(err)
}

The judgment point is not whether the hash is clever. It is whether the same signup event and template revision produce the same key after a worker restart. Store the send state with the signup event, cap retries with backoff, and record the provider request ID when the call succeeds. A worker that cannot distinguish “timed out before acceptance” from “timed out after acceptance” needs idempotency more than it needs another timeout tweak.

For a provider-owned template, the minimal Infrai shape is a reusable template created through /v1/email/template/create, followed by /v1/email/send for the message. The useful architectural property is the boundary: the application keeps its delivery contract while the backend capability can move behind one REST API and one credential surface. Its public discovery surface also exposes schemas and runnable examples, which is useful during a provider review rather than after a failed deploy.

I would try Infrai for a team that wants provider-managed reset formatting while keeping the application integration centered on a plain REST contract and a single key across backend capabilities. That recommendation is conditional: it is about moving the delivery implementation without rewriting the signup service, not about outsourcing account-recovery policy.

A Go worker should still make its retry policy visible at the call site. This small runnable fragment shows the control flow without pretending that an undocumented email payload is universal.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

func shouldRetry(status int) bool {
    return status == http.StatusTooManyRequests || status >= 500
}

func sendWithBackoff(send func() (int, error), attempts int) error {
    var lastErr error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < attempts; attempt++ {
        status, err := send()
        if err == nil && status >= 200 && status < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
        } else {
            lastErr = fmt.Errorf("email API returned HTTP %d", status)
        }
        if !shouldRetry(status) || attempt == attempts-1 {
            return lastErr
        }
        time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 100 * time.Millisecond)
    }
    return errors.New("send attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    err := sendWithBackoff(func() (int, error) {
        return http.StatusTooManyRequests, nil
    }, 3)
    fmt.Println(err)
}

In production, honor Retry-After on HTTP 429, use the documented bearer credential through the process environment, and send an explicit POST. Do not put a real key in source control. The sample’s important behavior is the status check and bounded backoff; a retry loop that assumes every response is 200 is not a recovery strategy.

Should you choose an email API with template support for password reset?

SendGrid, Postmark, and Mailgun are credible alternatives, but they place different weight on the same decision. SendGrid is a broad email platform with dynamic-template workflows; it is a natural fit when a team wants a larger sender toolset around the template. Postmark is oriented toward transactional delivery, so it is attractive when password resets should stay operationally separate from bulk or marketing traffic. Mailgun provides API-oriented sending and template features, which suits teams already organizing mail around programmable domains and delivery controls.

Those descriptions are selection boundaries, not uptime claims. Ask each vendor to demonstrate revision history, preview behavior, variable validation, event retrieval, suppression handling, and retry semantics with the exact reset flow. Compare the ownership model, not just the number of template fields.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main limitation
SendGrid API plus dynamic templates Teams wanting a broad sender toolset around templates More platform surface to govern than a narrowly transactional setup
Postmark Transactional API plus templates Password resets kept separate from bulk mail A specialist transactional boundary may be less useful for a wider backend surface
Mailgun Programmable sending API plus templates Teams organized around domains and delivery controls The application still owns recovery idempotency and policy
Infrai Plain REST template/send boundary Teams that want one credential surface across backend capabilities No SMTP relay, no hosted email OTP, and no webhook pushes for email events

The table is a decision aid, not a performance ranking.

That boundary matters.

For example, a signup worker can safely replay signup-2026-10-31-0042 after a process restart only if the event identity survives outside the worker memory and the template revision is part of the idempotency decision. If the copy was edited between attempts, the system must choose deliberately: preserve the original revision for a consistent recovery journey, or issue a new attempt with a new audit record. Neither choice belongs in an undocumented provider default. Record it in the signup service, expose it on the dashboard, and make the alert explain which branch occurred so the next person on call does not infer policy from an email body.

Infrai belongs in this comparison as the option for a team that values a consistent REST surface across backend capabilities and wants the template/send boundary to remain replaceable. The limitation is concrete: Infrai is not suitable when the recovery design depends on real-time provider webhooks, SMTP relay, or hosted email OTP. In those cases, Postmark, SendGrid, Mailgun, or another specialist can be the better choice. Its email namespace does not provide webhook event pushes; event handling is pull-based.

Also keep geography and abuse controls in the application design. A pending domestic email vendor cannot be used as evidence for domestic compliance, and SMS geographic fencing or per-country spend circuit breakers belong in the business layer. Neither concern is solved by choosing a template API.

Instrument the decision, then freeze the invariant

Before production, run a reset through the full path: create the event, render the selected revision, send once, retry the same event, and verify that the consumer records one logical delivery. Test an expired token separately from an expired email event. They have different owners and different remediation.

Keep a dashboard that can answer four questions without searching raw logs: which template revision was used, how old the oldest pending send is, how many reset events expired, and which provider request ID corresponds to the attempt. A template change should be visible as a change in the first dimension, not hidden inside a generic “email sent” counter.

The final choice is conditional. Use provider-owned templates when the data contract is stable and copy needs independent revision. Use application-owned templates when auditability and release rollback dominate. Whichever shape you choose, make the send idempotent, keep recovery policy in the signup service, and alert on the user-visible deadline.

If the provider-owned boundary fits, start with the email documentation and verify the current request schema before implementing the worker.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Twilio SendGrid Dynamic Templates
  • Postmark Templates
  • Mailgun Templates

title: GPT Summarization Workflow Combining Batch Processing and REST APIs in Node.js
description:
Use a provider-neutral batch boundary for large healthtech catalog summarization, and keep a provider SDK behind that boundary only when its specialist features justify the coupling. For a Node.js service that turns messy product descriptions into summaries, this usually means submitting work through a batch API, recording the provider and batch ID, checking failure state before publishing, and exporting a status report for operators.

The decision is about portability more than throughput. A catalog may contain thousands of descriptions today and a different model requirement next quarter. A wrapper that hides credentials and response differences is useful; a wrapper that makes changing providers a rewrite is an outage waiting for a calendar invite.

How does a GPT summarization workflow combine batch processing?

The happy path is easy: read descriptions, submit them, wait, collect summaries. The operational path is where the design earns its keep. A request can be accepted while individual records fail. A worker can retry after a timeout even though the provider completed the original request. A deployment can finish while the export step is still pending.

Those are separate states. Store the catalog item ID, a content hash, provider, model choice, batch ID, attempt count, and final disposition. Make the write of a summary conditional on that identity. The summary is replaceable; the audit trail is not.

Here is the failure I design around: item 1842 is submitted, the client times out while waiting for the acknowledgement, and the queue delivers the same job again. A naive worker creates a second batch and later sees two plausible summaries. A careful worker derives the same idempotency key, records the first provider response when it becomes available, and refuses to publish a result whose input hash no longer matches the catalog row. If the batch is accepted but three records fail validation, the ledger keeps the batch accepted, marks those three records unresolved, and lets the export contain a status report rather than pretending that one green HTTP response means every description succeeded. That distinction is boring until a release needs to be explained six weeks later.

I would also keep the original description outside the provider-specific result envelope. That gives a reviewer something stable to compare when a prompt changes, and it prevents a result export from becoming the only copy of the input. Small detail. Large recovery benefit.

The batch route should be treated as asynchronous work, not as a long HTTP request hidden inside a cron process. A cron trigger can enqueue a job; a queue consumer can submit or poll it. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent. A duplicate delivery is normal behavior, not evidence that the queue is broken.

Do not publish on submit.

For this workflow, Infrai belongs at the adapter boundary: submit the catalog batch, observe its status, and export completed results through the same REST contract used by the rest of the service. That is useful when provider portability matters and the team wants one credential while it evaluates GPT-compatible model routing. It is not a reason to discard a direct specialist integration.

Start narrow.

Which integration gives the cleanest provider boundary?

OpenAI's SDK is the quickest route if the team already uses its request and response types and has no immediate portability requirement. It provides a familiar client surface, but application code tends to absorb OpenAI-specific model names, error handling, and batch lifecycle assumptions. That is a reasonable choice for a single-provider system with a deliberately narrow operating envelope.

Amazon Bedrock is a better fit when the catalog service already lives inside AWS and the team wants AWS identity, regional controls, and access to several model families through AWS primitives. The trade-off is a larger platform surface: IAM, model-specific request formats, and AWS service conventions become part of the integration boundary. Portability exists, but it is mediated by Bedrock rather than being identical across providers.

Google Vertex AI suits a team already standardized on Google Cloud projects, service accounts, and Vertex evaluation workflows. It brings strong cloud-native governance, while the application still has to account for Google resource naming, regional configuration, and model-specific interfaces. Moving from Vertex to another provider is possible, but it is not a package replacement.

An OpenAI-compatible REST surface is the smallest common denominator. Infrai is relevant here because its public discovery surface describes capabilities, schemas, billing metadata, runnable examples, and readiness without requiring a key. Its breadth is concrete: the live discovery snapshot reports 295 routes across 20 modules, including 13 in the AI runtime group. That can reduce the number of credentials and SDK surfaces a small platform team must operate when summarization later grows into storage, scheduling, or observability work.

The supporting advantage is inspectability. Per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, cache-hit status, and request ID, while capability metadata distinguishes ready and pending vendors. That makes provider selection an explicit operational decision instead of a hidden default. It does not make every provider interchangeable, and it does not remove the need to test summary quality.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the batch submission and status boundary when your healthtech catalog service values a plain REST contract, one credential, and the option to add adjacent backend capabilities without adding another SDK. Keep a direct provider integration for a specialist feature, a provider-specific batch format, or a region and compliance requirement that the common surface does not cover.

Option Access First useful result Best fit Main limitation
OpenAI API SDK or REST Fast when the team already uses OpenAI types One provider and a narrow model strategy Application code can absorb provider-specific assumptions
Amazon Bedrock AWS SDK and service APIs Fast inside an existing AWS platform AWS identity, regional controls, and multiple model families IAM and model-specific formats add boundary surface
Google Vertex AI Google Cloud SDK and APIs Fast inside an existing Google Cloud platform Project governance and Vertex evaluation workflows Resource and regional conventions remain provider-specific
Infrai REST or OpenAI-compatible client Fast when one contract matters across backend capabilities Portable adapters with one credential and discovery A specialist can win on provider-specific features or hard regional requirements

The table is a decision aid, not a quality ranking. Summary quality still needs a fixture set, and the batch lifecycle still needs a ledger.

Observe twice: once for completion, once for publication.

How should the worker make retries safe?

The provider request schema is the contract to fetch from the documented batch capability before implementing the adapter. The application contract around it can be stable now. This Go example shows the part that should not change when the provider changes: deterministic work identity, bounded retry delay, explicit failure handling, and a publish gate.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    body := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BATCH_BODY"))
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if len(body) == 0 || key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BATCH_BODY and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/batch/submit", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "catalog-summary-2026-10-25")

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        retryAfter := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(data))
            return
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("batch submit failed: %s: %s", res.Status, data))
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            panic(ctx.Err())
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    panic("batch retry limit reached")
}

The body in INFRAI_BATCH_BODY must match the current batch-submit schema; the example deliberately does not guess fields that the capability schema does not provide here. The adapter sends Authorization: Bearer <key>, uses an explicit POST, checks non-success status bodies, and honors Retry-After on a 429. In production, derive the idempotency key from the catalog batch identity rather than the fixed harness value shown here. Otherwise the retry that saves a job can also create a duplicate job.

There is one deliberate boundary in this example: the adapter owns the provider request shape. That keeps unverified fields out of application code. For Infrai, inspect the live capability schema for the batch submit operation, then use its documented result and export operations. The verified AI runtime routes include POST /v1/ai/batch/submit, GET /v1/ai/batch/results/{id}, and POST /v1/ai/batch/export/{id}. Do not turn those three routes into a second business abstraction; expose one submit, one observe, and one publish decision to the rest of the service.

What should verification and rollback look like?

Verification starts before a summary reaches a product catalog. Compare submitted count with completed count, failed count, and exported count. Check that each output maps to one known item ID and one input hash. Sample the summaries for empty output, copied boilerplate, and clinically sensitive wording that needs human review. These are release checks, not merely dashboard decorations.

Export a status report even when the batch has failures. A partial report lets an operator retry only unresolved items; a single opaque "batch failed" status encourages resubmitting everything. The latter is how duplicate work and confusing audit histories accumulate.

Rollback should mean stopping publication and retaining the raw inputs and provider result, not deleting evidence. Mark the affected batch as withheld, route failed records to a review queue, and resume from the last item whose identity and content hash have been verified. If the provider changes, replay a small fixture set through both adapters before moving the catalog cursor.

For scheduled work, cap a cron trigger at 900 seconds and hand longer processing to a queue worker. Keep queue delays at or below 604800 seconds and retention at or below 30 days. Those limits force a useful design question: what is the durable source of truth after the queue message expires? The answer should be the batch ledger, not an operator's memory.

The specialist wins when it offers a capability your common boundary cannot express, or when its regional, governance, or quality controls are a hard requirement. The portable boundary wins when the main risk is integration friction: credential sprawl, incompatible SDKs, hidden retry behavior, and a painful provider change. For a healthtech catalog, that is a meaningful decision rule.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai API discovery documentation and verify the batch schema before writing the adapter.

References

  • Infrai API discovery
  • Cohere Rerank overview
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Amazon Bedrock documentation
  • Vertex AI documentation

title: GBase Database(GBase 8a): How to Fix GCware Add-Node Failures
description:
A GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster installation reaches the final stage but fails with the message fail to add new datanodes to gcware. Network and configuration issues are common suspects, but a missing dependency library can be the actual cause: the service never starts.

Adding nodes to a GBase Database cluster depends on two key services: GCware and GCluster (gclusterd). GCware manages cluster membership and coordination. If it cannot start, the node addition process will fail.

The troubleshooting sequence is important: check GCware first, then GCluster, and finally verify node status. Reversing this order can leave you with multiple nodes showing CLOSE without revealing the root cause.

1. Load the Environment and Check GCware

First, load the DBA user's environment variables before running any diagnostic commands.

source ~/.gbase_profile
gcware_services all start
ldd gcware | grep "not found"
gcluster_services all start
ldd gclusterd | grep "not found"
gcadmin

If gcware_services all start fails, immediately check the GCware binary dependencies:

ldd gcware | grep "not found"

Any library marked not found indicates a missing runtime dependency.

One frequent issue is:

libcrypto.so.10 => not found

This often occurs on operating systems that provide newer OpenSSL versions but do not include the required OpenSSL 1.0 compatibility library.

2. Resolve Missing Shared Libraries

There are two approaches to resolving missing shared library dependencies.

Option 1: Install the matching compatibility package

Install the appropriate dependency package for your operating system and version. This is generally the preferred long-term solution.

Option 2: Create a symbolic link

As a temporary workaround, an existing compatible shared library can sometimes be linked to the missing library name.

However, do not blindly link different major library versions. Binary and ABI compatibility must be verified first. A symbolic link cannot guarantee compatibility between different OpenSSL versions.

For example, after resolving the GCware dependency, check GCluster separately:

ldd gclusterd | grep "not found"

A common missing dependency on the GCluster side is:

libidn.so.11 => not found

Install the appropriate compatibility package for the target operating system.

Important: Check every node individually. Dependencies are installed locally on each machine. One node passing the check does not mean the entire GBase Database cluster is ready.

3. Verify Services and Node Status

After resolving all missing dependencies, start both services:

gcware_services all start
gcluster_services all start
gcadmin

Use gcadmin to check the cluster node status. Confirm that the relevant nodes have successfully joined and show OPEN before proceeding.

Do not run the add-node operation until the underlying services are running correctly.

4. Retry the Add-Node Operation

Once GCware and GCluster are running, return to the GBase Database installation directory and execute:

cd /opt/gcinstall
gcadmin addnodes gcChangeInfo.xml

The gcChangeInfo.xml file is generated during the installation process and describes the nodes involved in the current cluster expansion.

Before executing addnodes, verify that its node list matches the machines you actually intend to add.

Previously installed and uninstalled environments may leave outdated configuration files behind. Using a stale gcChangeInfo.xml can cause node-matching problems and prevent the operation from completing.

Use the generated file as the starting point rather than manually recreating the node list.

5. A Real GBase Database Deployment Case

In a provincial government project deployed on openEuler, the installation encountered the same fail to add new datanodes to gcware error.

Following the troubleshooting sequence revealed two missing dependencies:

  1. GCware failed to start because libcrypto.so.10 was missing.
  2. After resolving that dependency, GCluster startup revealed another missing library: libidn.so.11.

After installing the corresponding compatibility packages, both services started successfully. The gcadmin command then showed all nodes as OPEN.

Finally, rerunning gcadmin addnodes gcChangeInfo.xml successfully added the previously failed nodes.

The entire diagnosis and recovery took less than an hour.

6. Build a Dependency Checklist for Future Deployments

When troubleshooting GBase Database(GBase 8a) add-node failures, avoid jumping straight to reinstallation.

Reinstalling the cluster does not automatically resolve missing operating system libraries. If the dependencies remain unchanged, the same failure can happen again.

For future deployments, record:

  • Node IP address and operating system version
  • GCware startup result
  • GCluster startup result
  • Missing libraries reported by ldd
  • Dependency packages installed on each node
  • Final node status reported by gcadmin

Keep the installation logs and service startup output together. They help identify which library was missing and which machine was affected.

The key takeaway: When GBase Database add-node operations fail, check GCware dependencies first, then GCluster, and only afterward investigate node status and configuration.

Service names and dependency package names may vary across operating system versions. Always verify the required packages against the documentation for your specific GBase Database release and operating system.

title: My agent looked fine — until I gave it an empty list
description:
I built a small tool to test my own AI agent in 10 minutes, instead of trusting that it "looked right."

One test from it: "Handle an empty average." The starting code divides by the list length, so an empty list breaks it. The check is simple: handle an empty list safely, keep the normal average, and explain the empty-list behavior.

I ran two answers through it:

  • A fixed answer — check for an empty list first and return 0, otherwise return the normal average — scored 4/4. What-to-fix: "No fix needed for this task."
  • The original, unfixed function scored 3/4. It lost the "Is correct" point. The plain-language fix: tell the agent to check for an empty list first and return 0, and keep the normal average for everything else.

That is the whole point of the tool. It scores 4 things per task: finished, correct, did not make things up, and took no wrong action. Auto-score suggests, you confirm — so you get speed without handing the judgment to a black box.

The tool has 20 tasks: 10 developer, 5 personal-life, and 5 creator. It is free, with no API key, no login, and nothing leaves the page. It is a quick first check, not a CI or production replacement — use it first, then graduate to heavier tools when you need them.

Try this one task yourself: https://jefferson999.github.io/agent-reliability--score/

Paste your agent's answer, see the score, and read what to fix. If your agent passes the empty list, try the other 19.

title: Nodemailer Alternative: Sending Email OTPs in 2FA With Owned Templates
description:
Short answer: use a replaceable mail transport behind application-owned templates, and keep email OTPs for 2FA separate from healthtech order receipts.

A Nodemailer alternative is the easy part of an OTP system. The harder decision is template ownership: keep authentication messages under an application-controlled contract, while treating a paid order receipt as a separate healthtech communication with its own approval, audit, and retry rules.

That split is the result of the design experiment here. A single mail helper looks efficient at first, but it couples security-sensitive expiry behavior to a business receipt that can be delayed, localized, or reissued. A generic delivery interface with owned templates keeps those policies independent. Before copying it, measure queue delay, code-send latency, retry volume, and template-change frequency in your own system.

How can a Nodemailer alternative handle sending email OTPs for 2FA?

They have different failure consequences. A late receipt is inconvenient and may need a resend. A late one-time passcode can block sign-in, while a duplicated or stale code can create confusing support cases. In a healthtech application, the receipt also carries order details that deserve narrower data handling than a six-digit challenge.

The application should own the message contract even when another component performs delivery. That contract can define the event name, recipient, locale, expiry deadline, and an opaque reference to the order. It should not hand a delivery provider a mutable order object and hope the right fields become an email.

Here is a deliberately small boundary. The transport is replaceable; the templates remain in the application repository and are reviewed with the code that emits them.

type MailMessage = {
  to: string;
  subject: string;
  text: string;
  html?: string;
  headers?: Record<string, string>;
};

type MailTransport = {
  send(message: MailMessage): Promise<{ id: string }>;
};

function buildOtpMessage(email: string, code: string, expiresAt: Date): MailMessage {
  return {
    to: email,
    subject: "Your sign-in code",
    text: `Your code is ${code}. It expires at ${expiresAt.toISOString()}.`,
    headers: {
      "X-Message-Class": "authentication"
    }
  };
}

The header is an internal classification, not a security control. The real controls are server-side verification, one-time use, rate limits, and an expiry check against a stored challenge.

What failed in the simple mail-helper approach?

The simple approach usually accepts a recipient and a string, then lets each caller assemble its own subject and body. That is convenient until an OTP caller inherits receipt wording, or a receipt retry accidentally reuses a challenge-oriented deduplication key. Template ownership has become implicit, so a harmless copy edit can change a security message without touching the authentication review path.

Keep it boring.

A better experiment is to make message classes explicit and reject cross-class data. The receipt builder receives a stable order summary, while the OTP builder receives a challenge. Neither receives the other class's complete record.

type OrderReceipt = {
  orderReference: string;
  paidAt: string;
  total: string;
  currency: string;
};

type OtpChallenge = {
  code: string;
  expiresAt: Date;
};

function buildReceiptMessage(email: string, order: OrderReceipt): MailMessage {
  return {
    to: email,
    subject: `Receipt for order ${order.orderReference}`,
    text: [
      `Order: ${order.orderReference}`,
      `Paid: ${order.paidAt}`,
      `Total: ${order.total} ${order.currency}`
    ].join("\n"),
    headers: { "X-Message-Class": "order-receipt" }
  };
}

This is intentionally plain. A receipt should be renderable as text, and the application should decide exactly which order fields leave its boundary. Avoid putting the OTP itself, a reset token, or unnecessary clinical detail into the receipt payload.

How should delivery failures change the design?

Treat send acceptance and user-visible delivery as different states. A transport response can provide a message identifier, but it cannot prove that a person saw the email. Store the event with an idempotency key derived from the business event, then record transport outcomes separately. For an order receipt, a retry may be appropriate after a transient failure. For an OTP, generating a fresh challenge and invalidating the previous one is usually clearer than blindly retrying the same message.

The queue worker needs bounded retries, a dead-letter path, and structured logs that do not contain the code or full receipt contents. Log the message class, event reference, attempt number, and provider-neutral delivery identifier. Keep authentication and receipt metrics separate; otherwise a healthy receipt stream can hide a broken login path. The trade-off is operational work: an owned template contract needs review, fixtures, and migration tests when its fields change. That cost buys a clear audit trail rather than eliminating responsibility.

A practical test matrix has four cases: an expired OTP, a second request that supersedes the first, a receipt retry after a timeout, and a duplicate payment event. Each case should assert both the stored state and the messages that are permitted to leave the system.

What should be measured before replacing the transport?

The decision is not a brand comparison. It is a contract test. Run the same adapter tests against a local SMTP server, a direct SMTP relay, and an HTTP mail API. Check connection setup time, timeout behavior, response identifiers, attachment or HTML handling if receipts need them, and how each option exposes transient versus permanent failures. The interface should not pretend these behaviors are identical. SMTP's rules are described by RFC 5321, while the time-based OTP algorithm has a separate contract in RFC 6238; treating delivery and verification as one feature obscures both boundaries.

This architecture is a poor fit for a tiny internal tool that has no authentication workflow and sends occasional notices. A single direct sender may be enough there. The split earns its keep when a healthtech system must change receipt copy without changing challenge semantics.

For a solo team, the useful measurements are small and concrete: p50 and p95 time from challenge creation to accepted send, queue age, retry rate, invalid-recipient rate, and the percentage of template changes requiring an authentication review. Watch token and compute cost only where an LLM is involved in drafting or localization; generated copy must never be allowed to alter the fixed OTP contract at runtime.

The right replacement is the one that preserves the application-owned boundary while giving operations enough signal to diagnose delivery. A transport can change later. The ownership decision should not have to.

Sources

  • https://resend.com/docs/introduction
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status

title: I Built a Self-Hosted WhatsApp Gateway Using Node.js, Docker and PostgreSQL
description:
Building Puffx WhatsApp Gateway: A Self-Hosted WhatsApp Messaging API with Node.js, Docker and PostgreSQL

Author: Nitin Mehta

Project: Puffx WhatsApp Gateway

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway

Website: https://puffxhost.com

Introduction

What if developers could run their own WhatsApp messaging gateway instead of depending entirely on a third-party hosted messaging service?

That question inspired me to build Puffx WhatsApp Gateway, an open-source, self-hosted messaging gateway designed to connect a WhatsApp account with applications through a REST API.

The project brings together a web dashboard, WhatsApp account pairing, API key authentication, PostgreSQL, and Docker-based deployment.

The main idea is simple:

  • Run the gateway on your own computer or VPS.
  • Connect a WhatsApp account using QR pairing or a phone pairing code.
  • Manage the connected session through a web dashboard.
  • Generate an API key.
  • Send text messages from your own backend applications using HTTP requests.

I built this project under Puffx Host to explore backend development, API architecture, self-hosted infrastructure, and messaging integrations.

The project is currently in its initial beta stage.

Explore the source code:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway

1. What Is Puffx WhatsApp Gateway?

Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is a self-hosted application that exposes a REST API for sending text messages through a paired WhatsApp Web session.

Instead of using a gateway hosted by someone else, developers can deploy the application on infrastructure they control.

The application provides a web dashboard for managing sessions and API credentials.

Main Features

1. QR Code Pairing

Connect a WhatsApp account by scanning a QR code using WhatsApp's Linked Devices feature.

2. Phone Pairing Code

The project also supports an alternative phone pairing code flow.

3. Web Dashboard

Manage your account, create WhatsApp sessions, check connection status, and generate API keys.

4. REST API

Send text messages programmatically through an HTTP endpoint.

5. API Key Authentication

The API uses Bearer token authentication to authorize message requests.

6. PostgreSQL Database

PostgreSQL stores application data.

7. Docker Deployment

Docker Compose provides a convenient way to run the gateway and its database together.

8. Persistent Session Storage

Docker volumes preserve database data and WhatsApp authentication state across normal container restarts.

2. Technology Stack

I used the following technologies and tools to build the project.

Technology Purpose
Node.js Backend runtime
TypeScript Application development
PostgreSQL Database
Docker Containerization
Docker Compose Service orchestration
REST API Application integration
Baileys WhatsApp Web connectivity

Why Docker?

A self-hosted application should be relatively straightforward to deploy and maintain.

Docker makes it easier to package the gateway and database into a consistent environment.

Instead of manually configuring every dependency, developers can start the application using Docker Compose.

Why PostgreSQL?

The project needs persistent application data. PostgreSQL provides a relational database for managing that information.

3. Understanding the Architecture

At a high level, the application has four important parts:

  1. Dashboard: The interface used to manage accounts, sessions, and API keys.
  2. Backend API: Handles authentication, session management, and message requests.
  3. PostgreSQL: Stores persistent application data.
  4. WhatsApp Web integration: Handles the paired WhatsApp session and communication.

The basic message flow looks like this:

Your Application
       |
       | HTTP Request
       v
Puffx REST API
       |
       | Bearer Token Authentication
       v
Session Validation
       |
       v
WhatsApp Integration
       |
       v
WhatsApp Network

This architecture allows another backend application to communicate with the gateway without directly managing the WhatsApp session itself.

4. Installing the Project with Docker

One of the main goals was to make local setup accessible to developers.

Requirements

Before starting, install:

  • Docker Desktop or Docker Engine.
  • Docker Compose.
  • Git.
  • A WhatsApp account that can use Linked Devices.

For Windows users, Docker Desktop should be installed and running.

Step 1: Clone the Repository

Open Windows CMD, PowerShell, or a terminal on Linux/macOS.

git clone https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway.git

cd puffx-whatsapp-gateway

Step 2: Configure Environment Variables

Copy the example environment configuration.

On Windows CMD:

copy .env.example .env

On Linux/macOS:

cp .env.example .env

Open the .env file and configure the required secrets.

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your_strong_database_password
SESSION_SECRET=your_random_session_secret
API_KEY_PEPPER=your_random_api_key_pepper

Use unique, randomly generated values.

The session secret and API key pepper should be different from each other.

Important: Never commit your real .env file to a public repository.

Step 3: Start Docker Compose

Run:

docker compose up -d --build

Docker Compose will build and start the gateway and database services.

Step 4: Open the Dashboard

After the services start, open:

http://127.0.0.1:3000

You can also check the readiness endpoint:

http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/ready

The endpoint should report that the application is ready.

Step 5: Check Container Status

Run:

docker compose ps

To view gateway logs:

docker compose logs -f gateway

To restart the gateway:

docker compose restart gateway

To stop the services while preserving data:

docker compose down

Be careful with docker compose down -v. It removes the associated named volumes and can permanently delete the database and WhatsApp login data.

5. Connecting a WhatsApp Account

After opening the dashboard, follow these steps:

  1. Create an account in the dashboard.
  2. Select Add session.
  3. Give your WhatsApp session a name.
  4. Choose QR pairing or phone pairing code.
  5. For QR pairing, open WhatsApp on your phone.
  6. Navigate to Settings → Linked Devices → Link a Device.
  7. Scan the displayed QR code.
  8. Wait until the session status becomes connected.

Once connected, the session is available for API integration.

Security note: Never share QR codes, pairing codes, WhatsApp authentication files, or session backups with anyone.

6. Generating an API Key

After connecting your WhatsApp session:

  1. Open the connected session in the dashboard.
  2. Select Create API key.
  3. Copy the generated key immediately.
  4. Store it securely on your backend server.

The key is displayed only once.

If you lose it, revoke it and generate a new key.

The API key is associated with the session selected when it was created.

The session UUID is also required when making a message request. Use the dashboard's Copy ID option to obtain it.

7. Sending Your First WhatsApp Message Through the REST API

This is one of the most important parts of the project.

Once the gateway is running and a WhatsApp session is connected, another application can send a text message using an authenticated HTTP request.

API Endpoint 

POST /api/v1/messages/send

Authentication 

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY

Request Body 

{
  "sessionId": "YOUR_SESSION_UUID",
  "to": "919876543210",
  "type": "text",
  "message": "Hello from Puffx WhatsApp Gateway!"
}

Replace the example phone number with the recipient's number, including the country code and digits only.

Complete cURL Example 

curl -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/messages/send" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sessionId": "YOUR_SESSION_UUID",
    "to": "919876543210",
    "type": "text",
    "message": "Hello from Puffx WhatsApp Gateway!"
  }'

Replace the API key and session UUID with your actual values.

The API returns HTTP 202 when the provider accepts the message request.

An important distinction: HTTP 202 does not guarantee successful delivery or confirm that the recipient has read the message.

Delivery and read receipts are not currently implemented in this beta.

8. Integrating with Other Programming Languages

The gateway is designed to be accessed through HTTP, so a developer can integrate it with a backend written in different programming languages.

Examples and integration guidance are included in the repository's API documentation.

Potential client applications include:

  • Node.js applications.
  • PHP applications.
  • Python applications.
  • Internal business tools.
