  • Backend automation systems.

For example, a PHP application could make an HTTP POST request to the gateway with its API key stored in a server-side environment variable.

Never expose an API key in frontend JavaScript, a public GitHub repository, or a mobile application's publicly accessible configuration.

For detailed examples, refer to:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/api-reference.md

9. Can It Run on a VPS?

Yes. The application is designed for self-hosted deployment on a Linux VPS or cloud virtual machine.

A typical deployment needs:

  • Linux server.
  • Docker Engine.
  • Docker Compose.
  • PostgreSQL.
  • Persistent storage.
  • Domain name.
  • HTTPS reverse proxy.
  • Outbound WebSocket connectivity.

For public deployments, the gateway should run behind an HTTPS reverse proxy such as Nginx.

The repository includes deployment documentation and an example Nginx configuration.

A typical deployment workflow:

Domain
  |
  v
HTTPS Reverse Proxy
  |
  v
Puffx WhatsApp Gateway
  |
  +------ PostgreSQL
  |
  +------ Persistent WhatsApp Session Data

The Docker Compose configuration binds the gateway to localhost on port 3000. The reverse proxy forwards HTTPS requests to that local service.

Ordinary shared hosting and static website hosting are generally unsuitable because the application requires continuously running services and persistent writable storage.

For additional information:

  • Docker deployment: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/docker-deployment.md
  • VPS deployment: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/vps-deployment.md
  • Installation guide: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/installation.md

10. Security Considerations

Self-hosting gives developers control over their infrastructure, but it also means they are responsible for securing it.

Some important considerations:

Environment Secrets

Use strong, unique secrets for the database password, session secret, and API key pepper.

HTTPS

Never expose a public dashboard or API over unencrypted HTTP. Configure a valid TLS certificate.

API Key Protection

Keep API keys in backend environment variables or a secret manager.

Session Data

WhatsApp authentication state is stored on disk and is not encrypted by the application. Protect the Docker volume and its backups.

Database Backups

Back up PostgreSQL and the WhatsApp authentication volume. Treat both as sensitive data.

Access Restrictions

Do not expose internal database ports or unnecessary services to the public internet.

Read the full security documentation before deploying publicly:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/security.md

11. Current Beta Status and Limitations

I want to be transparent about the current state of the project.

Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is an initial beta implementation.

Currently supported functionality:

  • WhatsApp QR pairing.
  • Phone pairing code.
  • Web dashboard.
  • Session management.
  • API key creation.
  • REST API authentication.
  • Text message sending.
  • Docker Compose deployment.

Current limitations:

  • Only text messages are supported.
  • Media messaging is not implemented.
  • Webhooks are not implemented.
  • Message queues are not implemented.
  • Delivery and read receipts are not implemented.
  • There is no separate admin console.
  • Real WhatsApp pairing and delivery behavior have not been verified by automated tests.

These limitations are important. The project should not be treated as a fully production-ready messaging platform.

12. Why I Started This Project

I enjoy exploring how software systems work beyond the frontend.

Working on this project has given me an opportunity to explore:

  • Backend architecture.
  • REST API design.
  • Database integration.
  • Docker-based deployment.
  • Authentication and secrets management.
  • Persistent application data.
  • VPS infrastructure.
  • WhatsApp Web connectivity.

I also wanted to build a practical tool that other developers could inspect, run, and experiment with.

This is an ongoing learning and development project under Puffx Host.

13. Open Source and Community Feedback

The project is publicly available on GitHub.

I welcome feedback from developers who work with:

  • Node.js.
  • TypeScript.
  • PostgreSQL.
  • Docker.
  • REST APIs.
  • Backend development.
  • Self-hosted infrastructure.

You can explore the source code, read the documentation, report issues, and contribute improvements.

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway

If you find a bug or have a technical suggestion, please open an issue in the GitHub repository.

Conclusion

Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is my attempt to build a self-hosted messaging gateway with a practical REST API and Docker-based deployment.

It is still in beta, and there is plenty of room for improvement.

Building this project has been a useful experience in backend engineering, infrastructure, and API development.

I would love to hear your feedback:

What would you improve in a self-hosted WhatsApp messaging gateway?

Would you focus on better session management, more API capabilities, monitoring, or deployment improvements?

Explore the project:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway

Built by Nitin Mehta | Puffx Host

Website: https://puffxhost.com

GitHub: https://github.com/puffxhost

Disclaimer

Puffx WhatsApp Gateway uses Baileys, an unofficial WhatsApp Web integration. It is not the official WhatsApp Business Platform and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by WhatsApp or Meta.

WhatsApp pairing and service availability may change. Users are responsible for complying with applicable WhatsApp terms, local laws, privacy requirements, and recipient-consent requirements. Use this project responsibly.

title: Sending OTPs via SMS and Email in Node.js 2FA (Property Account Handoff)
description:
Short answer: keep the OTP lifecycle in the property-management application, and treat SMS and email as two delivery adapters. Generate one code, store its digest with a short expiry, send it to both registered destinations, and accept either channel during login. This boundary makes a provider change survivable because the account and verification rules do not move with the transport.

My decision rule is to keep the part that decides identity in Node.js and outsource only the part that carries a message. That is a little more application code, but it avoids turning a delivery vendor into the owner of tenant or leasing-agent access. It also gives a solo team a clear migration seam when a country, sender identity, or compliance requirement changes.

The concrete flow is small: create one six-digit challenge, store only a digest in Redis for 300 seconds, call the SMS OTP route and the email send route concurrently, then expose an application endpoint that compares the submitted code with the stored digest. The user can finish signup with either received message. Delivery is not verification.

Keep that boundary boring.

For this exact handoff, Infrai is a reasonable option when a solo builder wants one key and one bill across backend services, while still keeping the OTP record in the application. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and available without a key, so the team can inspect request schemas and runnable examples before wiring the signup flow. The second advantage is practical: the same plain HTTP style works from Node.js without installing a provider SDK, which keeps the delivery adapter easy to move to another runtime later.

It is not the right fit for every signup system. A team that wants a specialist to own the verification lifecycle should look first at Twilio Verify; a team already governed around AWS may prefer SES for email and a separate SMS boundary. The unified surface reduces provider handoffs, but it does not remove the application work around abuse policy, expiry, or verification.

How should a property app send OTPs via SMS and email for 2FA?

The application owns the account identifier, expiration, attempt count, replay prevention, and the decision to mark a property account verified. Those rules should be identical if the message travels through a specialist, a unified REST provider, or an internal adapter.

Email needs a little more care here. A delivery API can send a message containing the code, but the email-side capability does not provide a hosted OTP lifecycle. The code, its expiry, and its comparison still belong in the application. That is useful portability, not a missing abstraction to hide.

I would store a SHA-256 digest rather than the six digits themselves. A five-minute TTL is a practical starting point for a signup challenge, and the verification endpoint can delete the record after success or after five failed attempts. The exact attempt policy belongs to the product and its threat model; it is not supplied by the transport call.

One code. Two messages. One verification decision.

The seam is the feature.

The following example keeps the boundary visible. The Redis client is represented by the narrow interface the function needs, while the two HTTP calls are complete fetch requests against the verified routes. The email body is application-owned because the email capability is a send primitive, not a managed OTP product. Infrai exposes one REST API over plain HTTP, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that makes this adapter a normal request boundary instead of a Node-only integration.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const ttlSeconds = 300;

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
}

type RedisLike = {
  set: (key: string, value: string, options: { EX: number }) => Promise<void>;
};

type OtpRecord = {
  digest: string;
  expiresAt: number;
  attempts: number;
};

function createOtp(): string {
  return crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000).toString();
}

function digestOtp(otp: string): string {
  return crypto.createHash("sha256").update(otp).digest("hex");
}

async function postJson(
  request: () => Promise<Response>,
  label: string,
): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await request();

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      const detail = await response.text();
      throw new Error(`${label} failed with ${response.status}: ${detail}`);
    }

    return response.json();
  }

  throw new Error(`${label} remained rate-limited after four attempts`);
}

export async function issuePropertySignupOtp(
  userId: string,
  phone: string,
  email: string,
  redis: RedisLike,
): Promise<void> {
  const otp = createOtp();
  const record: OtpRecord = {
    digest: digestOtp(otp),
    expiresAt: Date.now() + ttlSeconds * 1000,
    attempts: 0,
  };

  await redis.set(`property-signup-otp:${userId}`, JSON.stringify(record), {
    EX: ttlSeconds,
  });

  const requestId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const results = await Promise.allSettled([
    postJson(
      () => fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": `property-signup-sms-${requestId}`,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ phone, otp }),
      }),
      "SMS OTP delivery",
    ),
    postJson(
      () => fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": `property-signup-email-${requestId}`,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
          to: email,
          subject: "Your property account verification code",
          text: `Your verification code is ${otp}. It expires in five minutes.`,
        }),
      }),
      "Email OTP delivery",
    ),
  ]);

  if (results.every((result) => result.status === "rejected")) {
    throw new Error("Both OTP delivery attempts failed");
  }
}

The retry behavior matters more than the concurrency syntax. A 429 gets exponential backoff and honors Retry-After; a different 4xx or 5xx surfaces its response body. Each write has its own idempotency key, so a retry does not intentionally create a second delivery operation. In production, persist the delivery request IDs and outcome alongside the challenge, and do not generate a replacement OTP merely because one channel is slower.

The sample does not pretend that an accepted HTTP request proves inbox or handset receipt. The verification endpoint should load the Redis record, reject an expired or exhausted record, compare the submitted digest, and delete the record after success. It should also rate-limit issuance by account, IP address, and destination. A property signup form is an abuse surface before it is a messaging demo.

Where does provider portability actually fail?

Portability is strongest at the application boundary and weakest at channel operations. SMS and email have different sender rules, suppression behavior, and delivery signals. A common function signature can hide that difference from the signup handler, but it cannot make the underlying policies identical.

For example, both communication namespaces expose events through pull-oriented surfaces rather than webhook pushes. That means an operations job can inspect event history, but a product flow should not wait for a real-time event before deciding what the user sees. The login path should report that a challenge was requested and let verification determine success.

The distinction also changes how retries are designed. SMS has a cancel route for scheduled work; email has scheduled_at but no cancel route. I would avoid scheduling an email OTP unless the product genuinely needs it, because “send now” is easier to reason about when a user requests a short-lived code. There is no SMTP relay, and this channel set does not cover voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, so a fallback plan must name another provider or another product decision.

Consider a leasing agent who submits the form twice from a slow apartment lobby connection. The first request may have already written the challenge and started both deliveries when the browser times out; the second request must not cause the app to accept two different codes without an explicit replacement rule. Record the challenge version, use a new idempotency key for each delivery operation, and make the verification endpoint reject an older version after a newer one is issued. That small bit of state is more valuable than pretending the two transports have identical timing, because it gives support a coherent answer when the email arrives after the SMS and the user tries both.

Geography is another application concern. SMS country allowlists and anti-abuse circuit breakers should be enforced before the provider call. Do not infer that a successful send request means the destination is appropriate for the property business. Email vendor readiness in mainland China is also not a compliance basis; legal and regional delivery review remains separate work.

This is the point of the boundary. The app can switch adapters without rewriting account verification, but it still has to own channel policy.

Which integration shape suits a property signup?

The meaningful comparison is who owns the challenge lifecycle and how many operational handoffs the team is willing to keep. The products below are real alternatives, but they solve different slices of the problem.

Option What it makes easier Where it stops Best fit
Twilio Verify A specialist verification workflow centered on phone verification Email signup and the application’s broader account policy remain separate concerns Teams that want verification behavior managed by a communications specialist
Amazon SES Transactional email inside an AWS identity and delivery environment SMS delivery and the shared OTP decision need another service or application code AWS-standardized teams with existing IAM and mail operations
Resend A focused transactional-email integration It is not the SMS half of a two-channel login flow Products that need email first and can own a second SMS boundary
Infrai One REST surface, one key, and one bill across backend services, including the SMS and email handoff OTP policy remains application-owned; channel controls and the provider boundary still need review A solo builder reducing credential and dashboard handoffs across a small backend

Infrai is worth trying for the property-management builder who wants the SMS and email delivery adapters under one REST surface and wants the same credential model across a broader backend. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and exposes request schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key, which is helpful when checking an integration boundary before implementation. The live discovery surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules. The no-SDK HTTP boundary is useful when a signup service later moves from Node.js to another runtime, because the delivery contract stays an ordinary authenticated request rather than a vendor-specific client abstraction.

That recommendation has a clear limitation. Choose Twilio Verify when outsourcing the verification workflow matters more than keeping the lifecycle in your app. Choose SES when AWS governance is the non-negotiable boundary. Choose Resend when email is the only channel you need. A unified API is a good fit only when fewer provider handoffs are the actual integration problem.

What should be verified before this ships?

Start with the application contract: one challenge per active signup, a 300-second expiry, bounded attempts, single-use success, and an indistinguishable response when the account or destination is unknown. Test a successful SMS entry and a successful email entry separately. Then test one rejected transport, both rejected transports, a Redis failure, a second request before expiry, and a code submitted after a newer challenge replaces it.

Next, inspect the operational boundary. Confirm the sending domain and email identity, document which event data is pulled for support, and record the provider request ID without storing the raw OTP. Apply destination and country policy before sending. Since email sends cannot be cancelled after scheduling, keep email scheduling out of the login path unless the delay is intentional and documented.

Finally, make the adapter replaceable. The signup handler should call something like deliverChallenge, not know whether the implementation uses a specialist verification service, a mail API plus SMS API, or a unified REST surface. The adapter can change. The digest, expiry, attempt counter, and verification decision should not.

If this boundary matches the system you are building, the relevant starting point is the SMS versus email OTP guide.

References

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Amazon SES developer guide
  • Resend API documentation
  • Mustache template syntax manual
  • Infrai email event discovery

title: Tired of uploading 40MB PNGs to your server and then slicing them (React + Canvas)
description:
As a digital comic artists, we all know , we love exporting massive files.

I run a small indie comic platform called ZealPlane and we were putting together chapters for our original series KARMA, G.O.D (unpublished) We’d often send over single vertical strips that were 1600px wide and 30,000px tall from Clip Studio Paint. even upto 45MB, just for a sinlge image.

You obviously, can't serve a 30,000px tall PNG directly to a mobile browser unless you want your reader's phone to catch fire. Webtoons and Tapas make you chop up long vertical strips into 800x1280 pieces so they lazy-load cleanly as the user scrolls down.

At first, Like many backend devs, I upload the file to a Node server, pipe it through sharp, zip up the slices, and send it back.

turned out to be not a great idea.

When you decode an uncompressed 1600x30000 RGBA image into memory on the server, it eats almost 200MB of raw RAM per request. It took was three or four people slicing chapters at the same time to spike our VPS memory and stall Nginx. Additionally, waiting 40 seconds just to upload a file on a slow connection and download the exact same pixels back felt super dumb.

So a few weeks ago, I ripped out the backend endpoint and rewrote our Webtoon Slicer to run 100% in the browser. Zero uploads, zero server costs, and it finishes in like 300ms.

Here are a few weird browser quirks I ran into while building it, in case anyone else is messing with huge images in React.

Don't use FileReader.readAsDataURL()

My first instinct was to read the uploaded file as a base64 string, stick it into an tag, and draw it onto a .

Don't do this with 40MB files. Base64 inflates the string size by ~33%, and decoding a massive image on the main thread completely freezes the React UI for two seconds.

Use createImageBitmap(file) instead. It takes the raw File or Blob directly from the file input and decodes it off the main thread.

export async function sliceStrip(file, targetWidth = 800, sliceHeight = 1280) {
// Decodes off-thread without base64 bloat
const bitmap = await createImageBitmap(file);

const scale = targetWidth / bitmap.width;
const totalScaledHeight = Math.round(bitmap.height scale);
const count = Math.ceil(totalScaledHeight / sliceHeight);

const results = [];

for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
const currentY = i sliceHeight;
const h = Math.min(sliceHeight, totalScaledHeight - currentY);

// Map back to the original unscaled image coordinates
const srcY = currentY / scale;
const srcH = h / scale;

const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
canvas.width = targetWidth;
canvas.height = h;

const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = true;
ctx.imageSmoothingQuality = 'high';

ctx.drawImage(
  bitmap,
  0, srcY, bitmap.width, srcH,
  0, 0, targetWidth, h
);

const blob = await new Promise((res) => canvas.toBlob(res, 'image/png'));

results.push({
  name: `slice_${String(i + 1).padStart(3, '0')}.png`,
  blob,
  url: URL.createObjectURL(blob),
});

}

// Crucial: free the GPU texture immediately!
bitmap.close();
return results;
}

The 1px white line bug drove me crazy

Once we got this working, our artists noticed something super annoying. On dark fantasy panels—especially stuff with heavy black/purple gradients like you see in Solo Leveling: Ragnarok's vertical fight scenes—there was occasionally a tiny 1-pixel horizontal grey seam where two sliced images met on mobile screens.

Turns out, if an artist uploads an odd-width image (say 1240px wide) and you scale it down to 800px, srcY and srcH end up as floating-point decimals like 1984.3333px. When the HTML5 canvas samples sub-pixels along the very bottom edge of a crop, it blends the edge with empty transparent pixels, creating a faint semi-transparent border.

Forcing integer math on the source crop coordinates (or keeping the artist's source canvas at an exact multiple like 1600px -> 800px) killed the seam lines immediately.

Clean up your Object URLs or Safari will crash

One thing you forget when working in a React SPA: URL.createObjectURL(blob) stays pinned in browser RAM until the document unloads or you manually revoke it.

If an artist slices a 25-panel chapter, realizes they made a typo in a speech bubble, fixes it, and drops the file in again 4 times in a row, your tab is suddenly holding onto 100 uncompressed PNG blobs in memory. Mobile Safari will just hard-reload the tab without warning.

Whenever the user resets the tool or drops a new file, loop through the old state first:

useEffect(() => {
return () => {
slices.forEach((s) => URL.revokeObjectURL(s.url));
};
}, [slices]);

And don't forget bitmap.close() at the end of your slicing function. Garbage collection on ImageBitmap is notoriously lazy in Chromium.

Anyway, if you draw webcomics or just want to poke around with how it works in the browser, the tool is live here (no login or paywall or anything, it literally just runs in your tab): zealplane.com/tools/webtoon-slicer.

How are you guys handling large client-side image jobs? Has anyone played around with OffscreenCanvas inside a Web Worker for this yet, or is standard createImageBitmap fast enough for your use cases?

If you've ever worked with digital comic artists, you know they love exporting massive files.

I run a small indie comic platform called ZealPlane, and when we were putting together chapters for our original series KARMA, our artists would regularly hand over single vertical strips from Clip Studio Paint that were 1600px wide and 30,000px tall. Sometimes a single image was 45MB.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8a) Installation: 4 Ways to Troubleshoot SSH Login Failures
description:
When a distributed GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation stops at the file distribution stage with an error like Fail to login xxx errno:-1 Permission denied (publickey...), the message tells you that SSH authentication failed, but not why.

GBase Database multi-node deployment depends on the DBA user being able to connect to every node and distribute installation files. A single broken SSH connection can interrupt the entire installation.

Here are four layers to check, usually enough to pinpoint the problem within ten minutes.

1. Verify SSH Login Manually

Before changing configuration, test the connection manually from the first node to the target node using the DBA user.

su - gbase
ssh -p 22 172.27.237.164
ssh -v -p 22 172.27.237.164

Two situations help narrow down the cause:

  • Manual login works, but the installation script fails: check the installation configuration.
  • Manual login also fails: investigate the SSH service, network, authentication, or system settings.

Use ssh -v to inspect the authentication process. If publickey appears in the authentication methods but is rejected, focus on SSH key configuration.

2. Check the SSH Port

If the cluster uses a non-default SSH port, make sure sshPort in demo.options matches the actual port.

For example:

sshPort = 2222
dbaUser = gbase
dbaPwd = gbase

A port mismatch can produce the same login failure during GBase Database installation.

3. Check Password Configuration

Special characters in passwords may cause parsing problems in some installation scripts.

In a controlled test environment, you can temporarily use simple test passwords to determine whether password parsing is the cause. Restore the required strong passwords before production deployment.

Check both dbaPwd and rootPwd where applicable, and follow the configuration requirements in your GBase Database version-specific manual.

4. Check SSH Key Permissions

For passwordless SSH authentication, verify that the public keys are correctly configured and that file permissions are not too permissive.

Typical permissions are:

  • .ssh directory: 700
  • authorized_keys file: 600

Check them with:

ls -ld ~/.ssh
ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Also verify file ownership and confirm that the correct public key has been copied to every target node. In multi-node environments, it is easy to overlook one machine during key distribution.

Check SSH Logs Before Retrying

If all four checks look correct, inspect the target node's SSH service logs and the GBase Database installation logs. They can provide the exact authentication rejection reason.

One important rule: fix SSH login first, then rerun the installation.

Avoid changing passwords or SSH settings while reinstalling. Otherwise, the failure conditions keep changing, making troubleshooting much harder.

Build an SSH Pre-Installation Checklist

Before starting a multi-node GBase Database deployment, verify these items on every node:

  • Node IP address and SSH port
  • Manual login result using the DBA account
  • Password configuration and special characters
  • SSH key availability, ownership, and permissions

SSH connectivity is the foundation of GBase Database distributed installation. Spending ten minutes verifying every node before file distribution can save much more time troubleshooting a failed deployment.

For SSH port settings and parameter syntax, always refer to the manual for your specific GBase Database version.

title: Managed Services vs Portability: When Cloud Lock-In Is Worth It and How to Stay Cloud-Agnostic
description:
Lock-in is worth accepting when a managed service saves more engineering time than it will cost to leave, and it is not worth it for the core compute runtime that every workload depends on. The runtime is the layer you should keep portable. Control Plane keeps the runtime portable across AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own servers, including on premises, while still letting workloads use each cloud’s managed services through Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s credential-free access to AWS, GCP, and Azure services. This guide offers an honest framework for deciding when lock-in is a fair price, a service-by-service map of proprietary services to portable alternatives, and a practical exit plan you can act on today.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Lock-in becomes a problem when it is accidental, unmeasured, or applied to the wrong layer.

  • When lock-in is worth it: A managed service materially reduces staffing, improves reliability, or accelerates delivery, and you have documented the exit cost.
  • When it is not: The service is your core compute runtime or your identity plane, where switching costs compound across every workload. Managed Kubernetes is fine when workload definitions stay in standard manifests.
  • The portable layer to protect: Application code, container images, deployment pipelines, data formats, and the runtime itself.
  • The exit plan: Maintain a service-dependency register, test data exports quarterly, keep infrastructure as code, and budget for egress.
  • How Control Plane fits: Control Plane runs workloads on AWS, GCP, Azure, your own Kubernetes clusters through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and your own machines, from bare metal to on-premises servers, joined as locations with Control Plane Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), all mixed in one environment. Universal Cloud Identity lets those workloads call AWS, GCP, and Azure managed services without long-lived cloud keys in your code. You get managed-service benefits without surrendering runtime portability.

For a deeper look at the full lock-in landscape, see our companion piece on how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

When Do Managed Platform Services Increase Vendor Lock-In?

Managed services create lock-in in five ways, and they differ in how hard they are to undo.

Proprietary APIs

When your application code calls a vendor-specific API, every call is a line of migration debt. The more deeply integrated the API, the more refactoring a move requires. This is the most visible form of lock-in and the one engineers think of first.

Data Gravity and Egress Costs

Large datasets are expensive to move. Cloud providers charge for data leaving their network, and the sheer time to transfer terabytes or petabytes creates inertia. Transfer time and egress fees grow with data volume, so the cost of leaving rises the longer you stay.

Proprietary Identity and Permissions

IAM systems differ significantly between AWS, GCP, and Azure. Policies, roles, and service accounts written for one cloud do not translate to another. Migrating identity is tedious, error-prone, and security-sensitive.

Proprietary Serverless Runtimes

Functions tied to a specific serverless platform carry implicit dependencies on the platform’s event model, scaling behavior, timeout limits, and deployment tooling. These are difficult to replicate elsewhere.

Contract Terms

Committed-use discounts, enterprise agreements, and reserved capacity create financial lock-in. Breaking a contract early can mean forfeiting discounts or paying penalties.

Data gravity and proprietary identity are the hardest to undo. Moving data is a large but bounded transfer project, while identity must be redesigned and re-audited for every workload. Proprietary APIs come next, then serverless runtimes, then contract terms, which have a defined end date.

Decision Framework: When Is the Managed Option Worth It?

Use this table to evaluate each service category.

Service Category Lock-In Level Switching Cost Drivers When the Managed Option Is Worth It
Compute runtime High Every workload depends on it; migration touches everything Rarely worth locking in. Keep this portable.
Kubernetes Medium Storage classes, load balancer and ingress annotations, CNI plugins, and the link between pods and cloud IAM (EKS Pod Identity, Workload Identity Federation for GKE, Microsoft Entra Workload ID) are cloud-specific Use managed Kubernetes for convenience, but keep workload definitions portable via standard manifests.
Relational databases Medium Schema compatibility is high (PostgreSQL, MySQL), but managed features (replication, backups) differ Worth it when the managed service handles HA, patching, and backups you would otherwise staff for.
NoSQL databases High Proprietary query languages, data models, and SDKs (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB) Worth it for rapid prototyping or when throughput requirements match the service exactly. Document the exit path.
Object storage Low (API), Medium (large datasets) S3-compatible APIs are a de facto standard, though Azure Blob Storage uses its own API. Egress fees and transfer time scale with data volume. Lifecycle rules, storage classes, and event notifications differ by provider. Almost always worth it. For large buckets, budget for egress and keep an export or replication path.
Queues and streaming Medium Client SDKs, delivery semantics, ordering, and retention differ across SQS, Pub/Sub, Event Hubs, and Kinesis Worth it for most workloads. Wrap producers and consumers behind an interface, or use a Kafka- or AMQP-compatible managed service so client code stays portable.
Serverless functions High Event sources, cold-start behavior, and runtime constraints are proprietary Worth it for event-driven glue code, spiky traffic, and low-traffic endpoints. For core business logic, keep handlers thin and put the logic in plain libraries that can also run in a container.
Identity High Policies, roles, and trust relationships are cloud-specific Abstract identity where possible. Use workload identity federation over long-lived keys.
Observability Medium Proprietary query languages and dashboards; data export is usually feasible Worth it when the team is small. Adopt OpenTelemetry for instrumentation to keep the data portable.
Managed AI / model APIs Medium-High Model-specific prompt tuning, fine-tuning artifacts, and pricing models Worth it for speed to market. Use an abstraction layer for model calls.

Which Open-Source Alternatives to Managed Databases Best Support Portability?

When a managed service’s lock-in level is too high for your risk tolerance, open-source alternatives can restore portability. The table below maps common managed services to their portable counterparts.

Managed Service Portable Alternative Notes
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL PostgreSQL Schema-level compatibility is strong. Run it on any cloud or on premises.
Amazon RDS for MySQL, Cloud SQL for MySQL MySQL or MariaDB Widely supported. MariaDB began as a MySQL fork and is compatible with many MySQL workloads, though the two have diverged in newer versions.
DynamoDB, Cosmos DB ScyllaDB or Apache Cassandra Both are wide-column databases. Apache Cassandra is open source. ScyllaDB is source-available since 2025 and offers Alternator, a DynamoDB-compatible API. Cosmos DB also offers a Cassandra-compatible API, which eases moves in either direction.
Amazon SQS, Google Pub/Sub Apache Kafka, NATS, or RabbitMQ Kafka excels at high-throughput streaming and is the closer match for Pub/Sub. RabbitMQ is mature for task queues and is the closer match for SQS. NATS is lightweight and supports both patterns.
AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions, Azure Functions Standard containers Package functions as containers to decouple from the serverless runtime. Any container platform can run them.
Amazon ElastiCache Redis or Valkey Redis is widely deployed and, from Redis 8, is available under AGPLv3 as well as source-available licenses. Valkey is a BSD-licensed Linux Foundation fork of Redis 7.2.4. ElastiCache supports both engines, so the move is usually low-friction.

The right choice depends on your team’s operational capacity and workload requirements, not on a blanket recommendation.

When Is It Worth Accepting Platform Lock-In for Managed AI Services?

AI services are the newest and fastest-moving category of managed cloud offerings. The lock-in calculus here is different because the field changes so quickly that today’s best model may not be tomorrow’s.

Evaluate Five Factors

  1. Speed to market. Managed AI APIs remove the work of hosting, scaling, and updating models, so you can ship a first version without building GPU infrastructure. If time-to-market is critical, the lock-in trade-off is often favorable.
  2. Model quality. Some proprietary models outperform open alternatives on specific tasks. Benchmark on your data before committing.
  3. Data sensitivity. Sending data to a third-party model API may conflict with compliance requirements. On-premises or private inference may be necessary.
  4. Cost at scale. API pricing that looks cheap at prototype volume can become prohibitive at production scale. Model the cost curve before you commit.
  5. Ability to swap models behind an abstraction. If your application calls models through a thin abstraction layer, switching providers is mostly a configuration change. You still need to re-test prompts and tool calls, re-run evaluations, and re-embed stored vectors if the embedding model changes.

Use managed AI APIs for experimentation and initial deployment, and build an abstraction layer for model calls from day one. For production inference at scale, portable containers running on GPU infrastructure give you the flexibility to move between clouds or neoclouds as pricing and performance shift. On Control Plane, workloads can attach NVIDIA GPUs, and MK8s lets you join GPU servers from other providers as locations. See our guide on running AI inference across multiple GPU clouds.

What Multi-Cloud Infrastructure Patterns Reduce Dependence on Proprietary Managed Services?

Six engineering patterns reduce dependence on proprietary managed services when applied across the stack.

Containerize the Runtime

Package every workload as a standard container image that follows the OCI image spec. An image packages application code and dependencies so any runtime that supports the OCI image spec can run it. Portability still has limits. Build multi-architecture images if you may run on both x86 and Arm nodes, keep configuration in environment variables or secrets rather than the image, and treat kernel features and GPU drivers as host dependencies.

Infrastructure as Code

Define all infrastructure in code with tools such as Terraform, OpenTofu, or Pulumi. Infrastructure as code makes environments reproducible and auditable. On Control Plane, the CLI, console, and Control Plane’s own Terraform and Pulumi providers all work through the same Control Plane API, so your definitions stay consistent.

Open Protocols and Formats

Prefer open standards: OpenTelemetry for observability, S3-compatible APIs for object storage, SQL for relational data, AMQP or NATS for messaging. Open protocols reduce the surface area of proprietary dependency.

Isolate Provider-Specific Code Behind Interfaces

When you do use a managed service, wrap it behind a well-defined interface in your application code. A storage interface, a queue interface, or a model-call interface means you can swap implementations without touching business logic.

Scheduled Data Replication

For critical datasets, replicate data to a second cloud or to your own infrastructure on a schedule. This keeps a current copy outside the primary provider for migration or disaster recovery. Replication adds ongoing egress and storage costs, so limit it to data you cannot rebuild.

Workload Identity Instead of Long-Lived Keys

Long-lived API keys and service account credentials are both a security risk and a portability obstacle. Use workload identity federation to grant short-lived credentials scoped to the current task. On Control Plane, Universal Cloud Identity does this for AWS, GCP, and Azure services.

For a broader look at cloud-native design principles that support portability, see our guide on cloud-native architecture principles, patterns, and building portable systems.

Should I Choose PaaS or SaaS for Vendor Lock-In and Portability?

Choose a PaaS when portability matters. A PaaS runs your application, so you keep the code, images, and data. A SaaS product replaces the application, so only your data can move.

The platform provides the runtime, networking, and operational tooling. If the PaaS uses standard container images and open APIs, your application is portable even if the platform itself is not.

With SaaS, the contract usually says you own your data, but the export format and completeness depend on the vendor. You do not control the application logic, the runtime, or the operational model. Portability depends entirely on the vendor’s data export capabilities and API compatibility. Switching SaaS providers often means rebuilding workflows from scratch.

A PaaS keeps these advantages only if it runs standard containers and does not impose a proprietary build or deployment format. For a detailed comparison of PaaS options, see our guide to the best PaaS providers in 2026.

What Contract Clauses Should I Require for Data Portability and Service Exit?

Before signing a cloud or managed-service agreement, negotiate terms that protect your ability to leave. The following checklist covers the essentials.

This is general guidance, not legal advice. Consult qualified counsel for your specific situation.

  • Data export format and timeline. The provider must export your data in a standard, documented format within a defined number of days after termination.
  • Exit assistance. The contract should include a transition period during which the provider supports migration activities.
  • Egress fee terms. Cap or waive egress fees during the transition period. At minimum, get clarity on per-GB costs.
  • Notice periods. Ensure notice periods for termination are reasonable and symmetric. You should not need 12 months’ notice to leave.
  • Termination for convenience. You should be able to terminate without cause, subject to reasonable notice and payment for services consumed.
  • Price change caps. Limit annual price increases to a defined percentage, or require advance notice that gives you time to evaluate alternatives.
  • Data deletion certification. After migration, the provider must certify in writing that your data has been deleted from their systems, including backups, within a specified timeframe.

Maintain a service-dependency register that tracks each provider-specific component, its owner, data location, export procedure, portable alternative, and estimated exit cost. Review it quarterly.

How Control Plane Approaches Portability

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into what Control Plane calls a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a set of locations a workload runs across.

On Control Plane, a workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so you get failover without paying for idle standby capacity. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers.

During the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, which lasted about 15 hours, Control Plane customers with us-east-1 in their GVC had no downtime, and their workloads were “active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds,” according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry. See designing systems that survive the inevitable.

Control Plane runs serverless, standard, stateful, cron, and VM workloads on AWS, GCP, and Azure, on clusters you already run through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), on your own machines (bare metal or VMs) turned into managed locations with Control Plane Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), and on premises. On Control Plane-provided compute, there is no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate, and Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, Capacity AI (Control Plane’s right-sizing of CPU and memory based on historical usage), built-in observability, and security. You pay for the CPU and memory you reserve, by the millicore and the megabyte, with no contracts or minimums. Egress, storage, observability, dedicated load balancers, and GPUs are billed separately.

On Control Plane, the template catalog deploys open-source data services such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Cassandra, Kafka, NATS, RabbitMQ, and Redis or Valkey into a GVC, so the portable alternatives above run on the same platform as your workloads.

Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. The Control Plane MCP server uses the same API as the CLI, console, and Terraform and Pulumi providers, so Control Plane complements the infrastructure as code you already run.

Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

You use each cloud’s managed services where they earn their place, and your runtime stays free to move. For a walkthrough of deploying the same application across AWS, GCP, and Azure, see how to run the same app on AWS, GCP, and Azure.

FAQ

When do managed platform services increase vendor lock-in?

Managed services increase lock-in when they expose proprietary APIs, store large volumes of data subject to egress fees, impose proprietary identity models, or use non-standard event systems. The more deeply your application integrates with these surfaces, the higher the switching cost.

Which open-source alternatives to managed databases best support portability?

PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Apache Cassandra, Redis, and Valkey are widely adopted portable alternatives. ScyllaDB is a source-available option with a DynamoDB-compatible API. For queues and streaming, Apache Kafka, NATS, and RabbitMQ replace proprietary offerings.

When is it worth accepting platform lock-in for managed AI services?

It is worth it when speed to market is critical and you build an abstraction layer over model calls from day one. Avoid deep lock-in for production inference at scale; portable containers on GPU infrastructure give you pricing and performance flexibility.

What multi-cloud infrastructure patterns reduce dependence on proprietary managed services?

Containerize workloads, define infrastructure as code, use open protocols (OpenTelemetry, S3-compatible APIs, SQL), isolate provider-specific code behind interfaces, replicate critical data on a schedule, and use workload identity instead of long-lived keys.

Should I choose PaaS or SaaS for vendor lock-in and portability?

Choose PaaS when portability is a priority, because you keep control of your application code, container images, and data. SaaS portability depends almost entirely on the vendor’s data export capabilities.

What contract clauses should I require for data portability and service exit?

Require data export in standard formats within a defined timeline, exit assistance during a transition period, capped or waived egress fees, reasonable notice periods, termination for convenience, price change caps, and written data deletion certification.

How does Control Plane keep the runtime portable while using managed services?

On Control Plane, workloads (containers or VMs) run on a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s set of locations that can span AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes clusters you bring through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and your own servers on premises. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity lets those workloads use AWS, GCP, and Azure managed services without long-lived cloud keys in your code.

Is multi-cloud the same as cloud-agnostic?

No. Multi-cloud means using more than one cloud provider. Cloud-agnostic means your workloads can move between providers with minimal effort. You can be multi-cloud and still deeply locked in to each provider’s proprietary services. True cloud-agnostic architecture requires portable runtimes, open standards, and abstraction layers.

Does containerization solve cloud portability?

Only partly. Containers make application code and dependencies portable, as long as images are built for the CPU architectures you target. They do not solve portability for databases, storage, identity, networking, or observability, which often remain cloud-specific. You need additional patterns, such as open protocols and interface abstraction, to address those layers.

How often should I test my cloud exit plan?

Test your cloud exit plan on a fixed schedule set by how critical the system is, such as quarterly for revenue-critical workloads, and after any major architecture change. Each test should export real data and deploy a representative workload on an alternative cloud.

title: Modelling Environmental Monitoring in a Food ERP: Sampling Sites, Swab Results and the Workflow a Positive Should Trigger
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

A swab result looks like the simplest record in a food factory: a site, a date, a pass or a fail. In practice it is one of the hardest to model well. The same "fail" can mean "re-clean the bench" or "hold three days of product", depending on where the sample was taken, what it was tested for, when it was taken relative to cleaning, and what has been produced since the last clear result. If the data model can't express that, the result ends up in a PDF from the lab and nobody can trend it.

This post walks through how we think about modelling environmental monitoring in an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa. The operational checklist behind it is in the original article.

What the domain rules say

The requirements read like a spec:

  • Codex CXG 61-2007 (Annex I) lists what a Listeria environmental monitoring programme must define: type of samples (food contact and non-food contact), target organisms, sampling locations and number of samples, frequency, tools, analytical methods, "a system to record the data and their evaluation, e.g. performing trend analyses", and actions on positive results. Source
  • EAS 39:2001: environmental sampling "at a level commensurate with identifying the risk" (4.3.4), timely action when results exceed action limits (4.3.7), a per-line tracking system "to track the location of possible sources of contamination" (4.6.2), and "records of environmental tests" (14.3.4). Source
  • 21 CFR 117.165(b)(3) (a US benchmark, not Kenyan law): the written procedure must identify the test microorganisms, "the locations from which samples will be collected and the number of sites", the timing and frequency, the tests and methods, the laboratory, and the corrective action procedures. Source

Translated into engineering terms: a sampling plan is configuration, a sample is an event against a site, a result is a measurement against a limit, and a positive is the start of a workflow, not the end of a record.

Sites are first-class entities

The most common mistake is storing the location as free text on the sample. "Filler", "filler area", "near filler" and "Filler 2" become four sites and the trend disappears.

EmSite      (id, code, area_id, zone, surface_type, food_contact bool, active_from, active_to)
            zone IN (1,2,3,4)
EmPlanItem  (id, site_id, target, method, frequency, timing, action_limit, owner_id)
            timing IN ('in_production','pre_startup','post_clean')

Sites get stable codes that match the plant map (RTE-Z1-03), a zone, and validity dates so the history survives a layout change. The plan item says what to test at that site, how often and when relative to cleaning. Timing matters: a post-clean swab verifies the sanitiser, a mid-shift swab looks for harbourage. Mixing them in one trend hides both signals.

Samples and results 

EmSample (id, site_id, plan_item_id, collected_at, collected_by, timing, pooled_group_id, lab_id, received_at)
EmResult (id, sample_id, target, method, value, unit, result_text, status, tested_at)
         status IN ('pass','fail','pending')

Two details come straight from the guidance. First, pooling: Codex allows compositing samples where sensitivity allows, but "in the case of positive findings additional testing will be necessary to determine the location". A pooled_group_id lets a positive pool fan out into follow-up samples for each member site. Second, received_at: if the lab can't show when a sample arrived, a transport problem looks like a clean result.

In FactoraERP today, the laboratory module stores samples with a type (including environmental and water), a collection point, date, time and collector, and test results with spec min/max and a pass/fail status. Non-conformances with root cause and CAPA live in the same quality module.

A positive opens a workflow

The response is where most systems stop. Codex describes a range: "no action (no risk of recontamination), to intensified cleaning, to source tracing (increased environmental testing), to review of hygienic practices up to holding and testing of product". That's a rule table keyed on zone and target:

EmResponseRule (zone, target, actions[])
  (1, 'Listeria spp.') -> [hold_product_since_last_negative, intensified_clean, vector_sampling, ncr]
  (3, 'Listeria spp.') -> [intensified_clean, vector_sampling, increase_frequency]

"Hold product since last negative" is the expensive one, and it is only possible if the system can answer a query like this:

-- batches produced on lines served by a site since its last clear result
SELECT b.id, b.batch_code, b.produced_at
FROM batch b
JOIN em_site s ON s.area_id = b.area_id
WHERE s.code = :site_code
  AND b.produced_at > (
    SELECT max(es.collected_at) FROM em_sample es
    JOIN em_result er ON er.sample_id = es.id
    WHERE es.site_id = s.id AND er.status = 'pass'
  );

"Vector sampling" means automatically creating follow-up samples at the positive site and its neighbours. Neighbours can be modelled as an adjacency list on the site map, so the plan grows around a problem and shrinks back when it's fixed, which is what EAS 39 4.6.2 asks for.

Trending is the point

CXG 61 says long-term review "can also reveal low level, intermittent contamination that may otherwise go unnoticed". The useful view isn't a pass rate; it is positives per site over time:

SELECT s.code, s.zone, date_trunc('month', es.collected_at) AS month,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE er.status = 'fail') AS positives,
       count(*) AS samples
FROM em_sample es
JOIN em_site s ON s.id = es.site_id
JOIN em_result er ON er.sample_id = es.id
WHERE es.timing = 'in_production'
GROUP BY s.code, s.zone, month
ORDER BY positives DESC, month;

One positive is an event. The same drain showing up three months in a row is a harbourage site.

Takeaways

  • Make sampling sites first-class entities with stable codes and zones.
  • Record timing relative to cleaning, and don't trend post-clean and mid-shift swabs together.
  • Support pooled samples with fan-out on positives.
  • Treat a positive as the start of a workflow keyed on zone and target.
  • Be able to query the product made since a site's last clear result.

The full 10-step operational checklist, with references to Codex CXC 1 and CXG 61, EAS 39 and Kenya's food hygiene regulations, is on the FactoraERP blog.

title: Configuring Software to a Business, Not the Reverse
description:
Every piece of business software encodes an opinion. It has a model of what a customer is, what an order is, which fields are required, and in what sequence work happens.

Where that model matches your operation, the software is invisible and helpful. Where it does not, something has to give — and it is never the software. The business adapts, and the adaptation is paid for daily by the people using it, most of whom had no say in the purchase.

This article is about what configuration actually means, where its limits are, and why the distinction between configuring and adapting decides whether a system gets used or worked around.

Three things get called configuration

The word covers work of very different depth, and vendors are rarely precise about which they mean.

Cosmetic configuration. Your logo, your colours, renaming a field label. Real, and it changes nothing structural.

Behavioural configuration. Which modules exist, what a workflow's steps are, what is mandatory, who can approve what, what the pricing rules are. This is where fit is actually decided.

Structural configuration. Whether the system's underlying model can express your reality — a transaction that behaves differently, a relationship the data model does not anticipate, a unit conversion running through everything.

Most products offer the first generously, the second partially, and the third not at all. The important question in an evaluation is not "is it configurable" — everything claims to be. It is "can it express the specific thing my operation does that is unusual".

Vocabulary is not cosmetic

Renaming fields sounds like the shallowest kind of configuration. In practice it has an outsized effect on whether a system is adopted.

If your team says consignment and the software says shipment, every user performs a small translation on every interaction, permanently. Individually trivial. Repeated hundreds of times a day, it is a tax on attention that shows up as slower work and more errors — and it makes training longer, because new staff must learn two vocabularies.

It also has a subtler cost. When software uses different words than the business, staff describe their work in the software's terms when talking to the system and in their own terms when talking to each other. The two descriptions drift, and eventually nobody is confident they mean the same thing.

Using the terms the business already uses is one of the cheapest things a system can do and one of the most consistently skipped.

Where configuration genuinely stops

Being honest about limits matters, because over-configured software is its own failure.

When the data model cannot express it. If the system assumes one price per product and your reality is customer-specific pricing with volume breaks and retrospective rebates, no amount of configuration produces that. This is a structural mismatch, and the honest conclusion is a different system.

When configuration becomes programming without the discipline. Products with deep customisation can be pushed into becoming bespoke systems — with no tests, no documentation, and no one who understands the accumulated rules. The result has the constraints of a product and the obligations of custom software. It is the worst position of the three in off-the-shelf or custom.

When you are configuring around a process that should change. Sometimes the operation's workflow is habit rather than advantage, and a well-designed product's default is simply better. Encoding a bad process into a new system is a common and expensive way to preserve it.

That last one requires honesty that is difficult to apply to yourself, and it is the main reason our first phase is watching the work rather than collecting requirements.

How we decide what to configure

Our position, from how Truffaire builds software: document the operation as performed, then configure to it — but not indiscriminately.

Three tests we apply to any difference before encoding it:

Is it structural or vocabulary? Vocabulary gets matched, always — it is cheap and it decides adoption. Structural differences get examined properly, because they are what determines whether the architecture fits at all. The four categories that mark a genuine structural difference are in choosing technology for your sector.

Does it exist for a reason anyone can state? Many process steps exist because of a constraint that was removed years ago. If nobody can say why, that is a candidate for deletion rather than configuration.

Would a new employee find it sensible? Long-serving staff stop noticing the strange parts of a process. Someone new is a useful instrument for identifying them.

The aim is not to preserve the operation exactly. It is to preserve what is deliberate and remove what is residue.

Why this produces different systems each time

Truffaire has delivered ten systems on the same underlying architecture — a multi-outlet retail ERP, clinic management, inventory, warehouse, delivery, logistics, production monitoring, factory operations, and billing and operations management.

They are genuinely different systems, and what varied between them was rarely the structure. It was language, which modules existed at all, reporting, and the specific regulatory obligations. Same architecture, ten shapes.

That is the practical argument for the configured middle option: the shared foundation carries the parts every business needs identically, and the configuration carries the parts that are actually specific. Building all of it bespoke pays for the shared parts repeatedly; buying a fixed product pays for the specific parts in daily friction.

Frequently asked questions

How do we know if a product can be configured enough?

Ask the vendor to demonstrate your three most unusual processes on your own data, not the demo set. If they configure it live, you have your answer. If they describe how it could be done, you do not.

Does configuration make upgrades harder?

Behavioural configuration usually survives upgrades. Deep customisation frequently does not, which is one of the strongest arguments for staying within a product's intended configuration surface.

Should we change our process to fit good software?

Sometimes yes. If the process is habit rather than advantage, and the product's default is well designed, adopting it is an improvement rather than a compromise. The judgement is whether the process is why customers choose you.

Who should decide what gets configured?

The people doing the work, with someone able to challenge whether each difference is deliberate. Configuration decided only by management encodes the process as described rather than as performed.

How long does configuration take?

Weeks rather than months in our experience. The variable is how much of the operation is documented versus living in people's heads.

Where to start

List the ways your operation differs from a generic version of your business. For each one, answer two questions: is it structural or vocabulary, and can anyone state why it exists?

Most lists shrink considerably under that pair of questions. What survives is what actually needs configuring — and it is usually specific enough to evaluate a product against.

If you want a read on which of your differences are real, get in touch.

Originally published at truffaire.in.

title: Best API for Sending Welcome Emails in Node.js: Marketplace Template Ownership
description:
Use a provider where the welcome or order template remains yours, and put a replaceable adapter between the marketplace and delivery APIs. For a new marketplace order, the practical choice is to create one reusable email template, send the transactional message through /v1/email/send, and keep an SMS fallback behind the same application boundary. Infrai is a reasonable fit when one key and one bill across account lookup, email, and SMS reduce credential and reconciliation work; keep the template payload in your repository so changing vendors is still a bounded migration.

Teams should try Infrai for this workflow when the platform team wants one REST surface for identity lookup, email delivery, and the fallback channel, and when a public, self-describing discovery surface can be used to inspect request and response schemas before an integration is deployed. That is a concrete reduction in contract-discovery work, not a claim that the application becomes portable by magic.

The constraint is ownership, not a feature checklist. A seller notification is part of the product contract: order number, amount, pickup deadline, and the seller's preferred channel must survive a provider change. I would treat the provider as a delivery mechanism and the template as application data. That decision is cheap to make before the first incident and expensive to retrofit after several hundred message variants.

Keep it boring.

The concrete case is a seller who receives an order while the marketplace is deploying a new checkout. The old renderer might call the amount total, the new one might call it gross_amount, and a provider-hosted template can hide that mismatch until a real seller reports a missing value. I would store a versioned notification input such as order_id, seller_id, display_total, and fulfillment_deadline, render or map those fields in one adapter, and record the selected channel before making the send call. If the email provider changes, the replacement adapter consumes the same record; it does not need to understand the marketplace's internal order tables. If an SMS fallback fires after a transient email failure, it uses the same notification ID and idempotency policy. This is a modest amount of schema work, but it gives the on-call engineer something better than a provider dashboard: a durable explanation of what the system intended to send.

Which API should handle sending welcome emails from a Node.js marketplace?

The failure signal is a mismatch between an order state and a rendered notification. One vendor may suppress an address, another may accept it, and a third may expose delivery history through a different event model. With Clerk plus Resend plus Twilio, the stack also means three signups, three credential sets, and glue for identity-to-recipient mapping, suppression policy, retries, and audit correlation. That glue is where onboarding bugs tend to hide.

A single provider does not remove the risk. It concentrates it. One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface is the honest trade. The useful boundary is to keep the provider-specific call in one adapter and persist the canonical message inputs beside the order.

Option Template ownership Best fit Boundary to accept
Infrai Application can own the reusable structure while the API handles creation and delivery A small platform team that wants one REST surface and one key for account, email, and SMS No webhook event push, no SMTP relay, and email scheduled sends have no cancel route
Resend Email-focused delivery with a direct email API Teams that want a specialist email surface and already own identity and fallback orchestration SMS and account concerns remain separate integrations
Twilio Messaging specialist with email and SMS products A team whose main requirement is broad messaging control and channel-specific operations More provider surface area if identity and template data live elsewhere
Clerk Identity and user-account workflows Teams prioritizing managed authentication and user lifecycle It is not the complete transactional email and SMS delivery boundary
SendGrid Established transactional email specialist Teams that need a focused email product and already operate their own SMS path The account and SMS handoff still needs application glue

That comparison is intentionally unglamorous. Resend is a better fit when email is the only delivery problem. SendGrid is a better fit when a mature email-only operating model matters more than a unified backend surface. Twilio is a better fit when channel-specific messaging controls outweigh consolidation. Clerk is the identity choice, not a reason to outsource the order message contract.

Infrai is not the right choice for a team that requires webhook-driven orchestration, an SMTP relay, managed email OTP, or a domestic compliance decision for the pending Tencent email vendor. Pick a specialist instead when one of those constraints is more important than a shared key and unified REST conventions.

How should the handoff stay replaceable?

Make the seam explicit: resolve the seller account, transform the result into your own Notification, then hand that value to an email or SMS adapter. The same bearer key and base URL can cover the account lookup and the delivery call in a consolidated setup; the application still owns the intermediate value. The example uses the exact account route and the verified email routes, while the local Account type is the boundary you would preserve during migration.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Account struct { Email string `json:"email"` }
type Notification struct { To string; Subject string; HTML string }

func request(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, path string, body io.Reader, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"+path, body)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    data, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests { return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after %s", resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")) }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("request failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, data) }
    return data, nil
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{}
    accountPath := "/auth/user/get/" + url.PathEscape(os.Getenv("SELLER_USER_ID"))
    accountBytes, err := request(ctx, client, http.MethodGet, accountPath, nil, key)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    var account Account
    if err := json.Unmarshal(accountBytes, &account); err != nil { panic(err) }
    n := Notification{To: account.Email, Subject: "New marketplace order", HTML: "Order ORD-4821 is ready for fulfillment."}
    body := strings.NewReader(fmt.Sprintf(`{"to":"%s","subject":"%s","html":"%s"}`, n.To, n.Subject, n.HTML))
    sendReq, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", body)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    sendReq.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    sendReq.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    sendResp, err := client.Do(sendReq)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    defer sendResp.Body.Close()
    if sendResp.StatusCode < 200 || sendResp.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Sprintf("email send failed: %s", sendResp.Status)) }
}

The important property is not the HTTP client. It is that Notification has no provider identifier, template dashboard ID, or vendor-specific status. Add an idempotency key derived from the order ID in the production adapter, and implement exponential backoff that honors Retry-After for 429 responses; a retry must not create two seller alerts. The example keeps that policy visible without pretending that an unknown response envelope is a stable application model.

Create the reusable structure with /v1/email/template/create, then send the order-specific values with /v1/email/send. Keep the template source under version control, and treat the remote template as a deployed copy. Suppression checks belong before delivery, but they are not a complete bounce strategy: the service has suppression-list operations, while provider events are pull-based and neither namespace pushes webhooks.

Is the boundary safe to operate and roll back?

Verification should answer three separate questions. First, did the account lookup resolve the seller that owns the order? Second, did the send request return a successful status and a request identifier you can correlate? Third, does a replay of the same order leave one notification rather than two? Those checks belong in the order-notification record, not only in provider logs.

For capacity planning, size the worker from peak new orders and the provider's accepted rate, then reserve headroom for retries. An SLO such as 99.9% of eligible order notifications accepted within five minutes is more useful than a promise of instant delivery, because delivery itself is outside the order service's control. Track queue age, retry count, suppression decisions, and the age of the oldest unprocessed order.

Rollback is a configuration change: stop new sends through the adapter, drain or quarantine pending jobs, and replay canonical Notification records through the replacement adapter. Do not attempt to cancel a scheduled email as part of the rollback plan; the email side has no cancel route. SMS does have cancellation, but that asymmetry is precisely why the application needs a delivery-state model rather than a provider-shaped one.

The rollback must be boring.

For a platform team that owns several backend integrations and wants the account, order email, and SMS fallback under one key, Infrai is the option I would trial first; its one REST API and public discovery surface remove concrete integration friction, while the limitations above remain deal-breakers for some teams. If this boundary fits your system, the email capability documentation is the right place to verify the current request contract before wiring the adapter.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • Clerk documentation
  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio Messaging documentation
  • SendGrid documentation

title: Implement SMS OTP-Based 2FA in Node.js: 2026 API Integration for Property Support
description:
A property-management contact form should not decide support ownership by guessing from a phone number, and an SMS OTP should not become a second, unrelated login flow. The practical trade-off is to keep identity verification in the authentication boundary while keeping queue selection in a versioned template owned by the support team. That separation makes it possible to implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in a Node.js API without letting authentication logic choose a business queue: the OTP proves control of a phone number for a short transaction, while the verified form payload selects maintenance, leasing, or resident-account support.

The implementation below uses the same backend shape I use for communication systems: a short-lived challenge record, a single-use verification transition, and an explicit routing policy. The example uses Python only to keep the protocol mechanics visible; the HTTP calls map directly to a Node.js client. No provider-specific SDK is required.

The five-minute expiry and five-attempt ceiling are policy inputs, not magic security constants.

How can I implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in a Node.js API?

An SMS OTP proves possession of a destination at one point in time. It does not prove that the sender is a tenant, that the unit number is valid, or that the message belongs in a particular queue. Those claims need separate checks. Treating the code as a general identity token is the first design mistake.

For a contact form, I would persist a challenge with a random identifier, a hash of the code, an expiry, an attempt counter, and the normalized destination. The plaintext code belongs in neither logs nor the form record. The form submission references the challenge ID and receives a server-side status such as verified; it does not send the code through the queueing path again.

The challenge lifecycle is deliberately boring:

  1. Normalize the phone number to an accepted international representation and apply a per-destination and per-IP rate limit.
  2. Generate a cryptographically random code and store only its hash, with a narrow expiry such as 5 minutes chosen by policy.
  3. Send the message through the communication API, but do not treat an accepted request as proof of delivery.
  4. Compare a submitted code against the stored hash, atomically consume the challenge, and record the result.
  5. Route the contact form using the verified state and a template revision.

The atomically consumed transition matters. A correct code accepted twice can produce duplicate tickets, duplicate callbacks, or a second privileged action.

Keep the state transition one-time.

Here is the core shape, with provider calls represented by an interface rather than a product SDK.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
import hashlib
import hmac
import secrets


@dataclass
class Challenge:
    id: str
    destination: str
    code_digest: str
    expires_at: datetime
    attempts: int = 0
    consumed: bool = False


def create_challenge(destination: str, now: datetime) -> tuple[Challenge, str]:
    code = f"{secrets.randbelow(1_000_000):06d}"
    digest = hashlib.sha256(code.encode("ascii")).hexdigest()
    challenge = Challenge(
        id=secrets.token_urlsafe(18),
        destination=destination,
        code_digest=digest,
        expires_at=now + timedelta(minutes=5),
    )
    return challenge, code


def verify_challenge(challenge: Challenge, submitted: str, now: datetime) -> bool:
    if challenge.consumed or now >= challenge.expires_at or challenge.attempts >= 5:
        return False
    challenge.attempts += 1
    digest = hashlib.sha256(submitted.encode("ascii")).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(digest, challenge.code_digest):
        return False
    challenge.consumed = True
    return True

In production, the read, attempt increment, expiry check, and consume operation need one transactional boundary. An in-memory object demonstrates the state machine; it is not a multi-instance store. The send operation should also carry an idempotency key derived from the challenge ID when the communication API supports one. That key protects retries at the application boundary, while the consumed flag protects the verification boundary. They solve different duplicate problems.

How does template ownership change the routing design?

The support queue should be selected from a small, reviewable template rather than from free-form model output or a pile of controller conditionals.
