Abstract: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection.

title: From Natural Language to Real Schematics: An Automated Workflow for Power Electronics Schematic Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.38201v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Designing power electronics converters traditionally requires intensive human expertise across topology sizing, commercial component selection, circuit simulation verification, and schematic drafting. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in electronic design automation (EDA), applying standalone LLMs directly to board-level power electronics schematic synthesis suffers from severe engineering hallucinations, including inaccurate analytical sizing, fabricated or mismatched component part numbers, violated voltage derating margins, and broken topological connectivity. In this paper, we propose a Bounded Dual-Loop Automated Schematic Synthesis Framework that translates natural language specifications into verified, editable KiCad schematics and manufacturing deliverables. Our workflow integrates six stages across three functional columns: (1) requirement parsing and knowledge-driven power stage synthesis covering non-isolated (Buck, Boost) and isolated/resonant (Flyback, DAB, half-bridge LLC) topologies; (2) contract- and evidence-coordinated component selection grounded in distributor APIs and OEM datasheets, coupled with closed-loop ngspice transient verification and stress feedback; and (3) modular control hardware integration and multi-format deliverable generation featuring native KiCad netlist round-trip verification. End-to-end case studies on a 24-36V to 12V,2A Buck converter (29 positions, 83 verified terminals) and an isolated 48V to 24V, 0.5A, Dual-Active Bridge (DAB) converter (87 positions, 341 verified terminals), alongside comparative evaluations against a Vanilla LLM baseline, demonstrate that our framework improves component verification coverage from 22.2 to 98.6, nominal value consistency from 0 to 97.7, and SPICE simulation pass rates from 0 to 100.

title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
description:
arXiv:2610.38210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

title: Disparity Laundering: Consensus Without Fairness in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.38215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical large language models are increasingly fielded as multi-agent teams, on the assumption that deliberation averages out individual error. It does not average out bias. Across a full factorial of five model families and four aggregation topologies on 120 real MIMIC-IV emergency cases under counterfactual demographic swaps, no configuration neutralizes the disparity: all 20 cells commit the direction of their agents' independent answers, giving Black patients more acute triage. Every model has a topology that amplifies its baseline gap, but which one varies by model, so no design is reliably safe or reliably amplifying: the disparity is relocated, never removed. Late-stage fixes fail: fairness instructions and demographic masking leave the gap untouched, and per-agent self-debiasing widens it, because the bias is already encoded in the agents' ordinary clinical numbers. We call this disparity laundering; the audits now applied to clinical AI, per model, per output, per version, can certify the parts but never the committed decision. Interventions close the gap exactly when they make counterfactual versions visible inside the system and pool them, through deliberation, into the committed decision. A diverse-perspective ensemble does both while keeping the team, with no retraining or architectural change: the disparity falls by 67 to 94% where all five perspectives pool at every round, and the one topology that never pools them is the one it cannot reliably repair. Medical multi-agent systems do not filter demographic bias; they launder it into plausible decisions no single-version audit can catch, and the only defense is to make the bias visible.

title: Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training
description:
arXiv:2610.38220v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rubrics enable reward assignment on tasks without verifiable answers, but are expensive to manually produce from scratch. We present Rubricon, a pipeline that generates discriminative rubrics without requiring human preference labels, rubric annotation, or generator-model training. Using any LLM, Rubricon samples multiple rubrics, selects the most discriminative candidate, adds criteria to capture overlooked requirements or response flaws, and prunes criteria that are misaligned or shallow. Alongside LLM self-critique and test-time scaling, Rubricon uses observed criterion pass rates on example model responses to guide refinement. Across five professional, consumer, clinical, and general-use LLM benchmarks, Rubricon produces rubrics whose scores of frontier LLM responses exhibit 9% greater alignment with labor-intensive expert-authored rubrics, compared to the best alternative synthetic rubric generation method among RRD, QSRG, OpenRubrics, and agentic generation via harnesses like Codex. On HealthBench, post-training a Qwen3.5-9B model with Rubricon rubrics yields 4.5% better performance than training with rubrics from the strongest alternative synthetic rubric generator, RRD.

title: FACTS-MAS: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Adaptive Forecasting from Heterogeneous Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.38225v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world forecasting often requires integrating heterogeneous evidence whose predictive value varies across horizons, operating regimes, and domains. We introduce FACTS-MAS, a domain-agnostic multi-agent forecasting framework that decomposes evidence into specialized channels for temporal dynamics, exogenous context, seasonality, structural information, and discrete events. Each agent generates an independently testable forecast through a common interface, while leakage-safe historical validation measures its predictive skill relative to a naive reference. These skill estimates are used to weight and combine agent forecasts, so that uninformative evidence is either removed or downweighted rather than forced to participate. A calibration procedure selects domain-specific constant means based on historical validation folds. We evaluate FACTS-MAS on weekly for-sale housing inventory from Zillow and weekly unemployment insurance claims from FRED, for 15 U.S. metropolitan areas at 4-, 8-, and 13-week forecasting horizons. Our method outperforms both a naive last-value forecast method and the TimesFM foundation model. However, a factor-adjusted exponential smoothing model performs as well as the fused forecast. The evidence therefore supports FACTS-MAS as a systematic protocol for testing, calibrating, and recomposing evidence channels before assembling them into the strongest single model for a specific application domain. Code, data, and results are available at https://github.com/Madumita24/FACTS-MAS.

title: Verification-Guided Retrosynthesis: Reaction Feedback and Evidence Timing
description:
arXiv:2610.38245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrosynthesis planning seeks synthesis routes from purchasable starting materials to a target molecule. Search over predicted reactions can connect a target to available materials, yet an infeasible reaction can invalidate the resulting route. Evaluating route quality only after search has finished cannot correct errors made during search. We introduce Verification-Guided Reflow (VGR), incorporating reaction verification as a decision action in AND/OR search. Verification results are represented as binary verdicts; queries are scheduled from the search structure, and acquired verdicts exclude reactions or adjust search priorities. We define verified solvability as the fraction of targets for which a complete route accepted stepwise by the verifier is found. On Retro190, feeding verification results into search increases verified solvability from 51.1% to 62.6% relative to route evaluation without feedback. Further controlled experiments show that earlier verification and immediate prioritization of accepted reactions each improve route discovery, yet combining them performs worse than either change alone. We therefore propose early pruning and delayed guidance: rejected reactions are pruned immediately, while accepted reactions gain search priority when processed as part of a complete candidate route. In a separate comparison with the verification scheduling rule fixed, this strategy increases verified solvability from 61.1% with immediate guidance to 71.1%, using fewer proposal calls and unique verifier queries.

title: Inner-Learning: From Hand-Coded Beliefs to Declarative Knowledge in Trick-Taking Games
description:
arXiv:2610.38304v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a declarative approach to belief-state modeling in trick-taking card games. Starting from a state-of-the-art Skat player, we automatically extract its hand-coded inference rules into a domain-specific language built on the primitive $\neg\mathsf{holds}(P,C)$, denoting that player $P$ cannot hold any card in set $C$. Round-trip code generation verifies that the extracted rules reproduce the original engine's intended behavior, up to three audited bugs in the original that the declarative engine corrects. We then grow the rule base through symmetric derivation and annotation of an expert strategy document---unifying code, symmetry, and expertise in one representation. We extend the knowledge representation with \emph{cardinality constraints}: at-most-$k$ and at-least-$k$ bounds on the cards a player holds from a named group, expressed in the same declarative language and enforced at world-generation time. Confidence parameters connect symbolic rules to probabilistic belief updates. Self-play evaluation shows the declarative engine measurably improving winning percentage and score over the original hand-coded engine, with the extracted rules, the human-annotated rules, and the cardinality constraints each contributing to the effect.

title: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics
description:
arXiv:2610.38313v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bisimulation metrics offer a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions and methods are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments ensure well-defined fixed points and downstream guarantees. We develop a unified foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted settings, that is total- and average-reward problems, by replacing the standard operator-centric view with a game-centric one: we interpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define metrics as the corresponding game value functions, yielding unique definitions even when $\gamma=1$. This game-theoretic foundation facilitates transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. We also use this game-centric perspective to characterize how metric finiteness depends on structural properties of the underlying MDP and motivate certain directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. We further introduce an abstract framework for modifying the games' action spaces, allowing general transition coupling sets, that recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions. Finally, we prove that these metrics bound total-reward and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. We also provide error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.

title: CHORD: Cross-Model Hallucination Detection via Relational Graph Discrimination
description:
arXiv:2610.38314v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination detection is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. Due to strong empirical performance, internal representation-based methods have emerged as the prevailing direction for detecting hallucinations, yet they remain largely model-specific and often fail to generalize to unseen LLMs. In this paper, we study an important yet underexplored problem, termed cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD), which aims to train hallucination detectors on source LLMs while ensuring performance on unseen target LLMs. The core challenge of CMHD lies in cross-model representation heterogeneity: hidden states from different LLMs exhibit severe semantic inconsistency, which limits the transferability of classical representation-based detectors. Through analysis and empirical validation, we show that relational structures over layers, tokens, and features capture transferable detection signals despite semantic inconsistency. Based on this observation, we propose cross-model hallucination detection via heterogeneity-oriented relational discrimination (CHORD), a relational graph discrimination framework that represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features. It feeds these graphs into relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape these features toward transferable detection signals. Extensive experiments show that CHORD outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/MiracleworkerD/CHORD.

title: Can LLMs Faithfully Solve Ontology Engineering Tasks? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study
description:
arXiv:2610.38326v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ontological knowledge underpins large language model (LLM) performance on knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing evaluations of LLMs' ontological understanding largely rely on behavioral correctness, leaving the underlying mechanisms unexplained. Existing mechanistic interpretability work has largely focused on instance-level factual knowledge, leaving ontological knowledge under-explored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MIOE, a causal-abstraction benchmark that evaluates interchange interventions for two ontology engineering tasks: entity typing and subsumption prediction. MIOE tests whether learned internal intervention targets can change an ontology-level target answer while preserving class-specific auxiliary information. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B, we evaluate SAE-, DBM-, and DAS-based methods, including multi-task and multi-layer variants. Distributed subspace methods give the strongest results and generalize across prompt settings, but the induced changes remain only partially separated from auxiliary class-specific information. Multi-task objectives and contiguous layer-window interventions improve this balance, while class-level analyses reveal substantial variation across ontology classes. These results suggest that ontological predictions are mechanistically accessible in LLMs, although current methods do not yet isolate a cleanly disentangled causal mechanism for ontological knowledge.

title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?
description:
arXiv:2610.38342v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial agents must form forecasts and investment judgments from decision-time evidence, with predictions evaluated against subsequent outcomes. Existing benchmarks assess financial knowledge, research workflows, or forecasting, but evaluating the full research process requires a strictly frozen information set and professional evaluation criteria. We introduce Investor's Last Exam (ILE), an equity-research benchmark led by experienced buy-side investors and fund managers. Its three components are a versioned financial database spanning 3.43 million document versions and nine source categories, supplemented by structured market data, with validated timestamps governing retrieval and computation; a task taxonomy organized around professional analyst deliverables; and an expert-led framework linking scoring criteria to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs. Evaluation spans 86 assignments and jointly assesses research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment performance. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead overall at 68.1 and 66.9 out of 100, yet even Astra scores only 52.5 on Forecast & Model. Our results show that even state-of-the-art models fail to translate overall research capability into predictive performance. ILE shifts the evaluation unit from isolated capabilities to the evidence--assumption--judgment chain, allowing researchers to locate where analytical advantages fail to translate into forecasts and investment judgments, and providing a traceable, diagnostic foundation for training and evaluating financial agents.

title: Encode Once, Answer Many: Internalizing Context via Parametric Flow
description:
arXiv:2610.38356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to a task either by placing knowledge in the input context, which keeps it external and re-encodes it on every call, or by fine-tuning, which internalizes it but demands a costly round of optimization per task. We aim to internalize the knowledge carried by a context directly into model parameters, without per-task optimization and without keeping the context in the input at inference time. To this end, we propose CLIK, a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a given context to LoRA parameters for internalizing knowledge in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, requiring no test-time gradient updates. Once the generated LoRA is inserted into a frozen base model, the model answers downstream queries from the query alone, having internalized the context into its weights rather than re-reading it. Because the adapter depends only on the context, it is generated once and reused for every query on the same document, so the cost of reading that document is amortized across queries. On document question answering, CLIK substantially improves over the no-context base model and outperforms existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without any multi-turn-specific training. Analysis further shows that the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.

title: Compute Has Shape: Self-Morphing the Internal Computation of Frozen LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.38382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time scaling improves large language models through additional computation, but how to adapt the topology of internal computation to individual inputs remains underexplored. Existing approaches largely fix recurrent or parallel architectures during training, or reconfigure frozen models along a single structural axis. We introduce SelfMorph, which makes computational shape an input-dependent inference-time decision. It unifies the original forward path (BASE), serial reuse of a layer span (REPEAT), and local branching and merging of perturbed hidden states (BRANCH) in a unified space parameterized by type, location, and intensity. Since they offer complementary benefits rather than uniform dominance, we use a lightweight selector that reads the backbone's depth-wise hidden state trajectory on the prompt to choose a morphology before response generation. We train the selector by distilling utility-based distribution from offline morphing that jointly account for task performance and computational cost. Evaluated on three LLMs spanning 4B-27B, SelfMorph achieves a 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks. It achieves the strongest performance in 24 of 27 settings. These findings identify input-adaptive computational topology as a complementary axis of test-time scaling beyond generating more tokens. Our code is available at https://github.com/creator-xi/SelfMorph.

title: SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.38391v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides coarse supervision for long-horizon LLM agents: failed trajectories may contain correct steps, while successful trajectories can contain errors. Trajectory-level skills can also shift teacher preferences at unrelated steps, introducing off-target distillation signals. We introduce SCOPE, a framework for Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation. After a supervised warm-up, the policy analyzes its own trajectories, generates step-specific hindsight skills, and distills their guidance only at selected error steps. A bounded signed teacher-student coefficient stabilizes auxiliary updates while preserving positive reinforcement and negative correction. A success-relative pairwise length reward further encourages efficient task completion. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple model backbones. With Qwen2.5-3B, SCOPE achieves 97.7% success on ALFWorld and 85.2% on WebShop, outperforming SEED by 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE reaches 89.6% success, improving over GRPO by 23.2 percentage points with 46.7% fewer interactions. Scaling to Qwen3-32B, SCOPE achieves 99.2% success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 94.0% on unseen tasks.

title: Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.38392v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents edit their own harness, the prompts and rules around a fixed model, and keep an edit only if an acceptance gate scores it higher on a batch of tasks. Such a gate sees what the harness does under the current model, not what it would still prevent if one safeguard failed. When safeguards overlap, deleting one is masked: the others still block the harm, so the gate decides on task success alone and redundancy erodes unseen. We measure harm for every subset of four written safeguards in two agent environments and run 411 improvement loops under ten gate rules, mostly as controlled deletion experiments, plus three runs of the GEPA optimizer. A deletion behind another working safeguard adds almost no observable harm. A paired significance test blocks deletions that pass by chance but not deletions that genuinely raise task success, and a larger evaluation batch lets it delete cheaper safeguards: at the same cost, 20-task batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six. Large harm audits prevent exposure but not the loss of depth, which turns into harm when the harness is reused with a weaker model. GEPA kept every safety rule verbatim, yet two of its three final harnesses misused credentials under a weaker model. A statistical model frozen before the runs predicts where each gate's protection breaks as safeguard cost and batch size change, and freezing safety text or auditing one-layer ablations preserves depth.

title: Agent Transfer Protocol: Server-Mediated Agent-to-Agent Communication Architecture for the Agentic Web
description:
arXiv:2610.38398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Agentic Web needs to support continuous collaboration among agents from different organizations. These collaborative relationships may span multiple tasks, network connections and execution instances. Such interactions require stable communication entries, message reception when instances are offline, and source verification after delayed reading. How to organize these responsibilities so that cross domain communication does not depend on specific execution instances being continuously online is a key issue for building long term agent interaction infrastructure. We propose ATP (Agent Transfer Protocol), a cross organization agent communication protocol adopting a domain mediated architecture. In this architecture, administrative domains maintain stable addresses and receiving entries for logical agents. The domain servers of both parties continuously undertake cross domain transmission. The receiving domain verifies and saves messages for execution instances to read later. The sending domain signs the complete message envelope. This allows the receiving instance to independently reverify the domain source and content integrity after the original connection ends, provided the original verification public key is still trusted and obtainable. We implemented an ATP prototype and evaluated it through a controlled cross organization LLM agent workflow, mechanism checks and latency measurements. The workflow completed subsequent business processing after instances went offline or were replaced. The independent verifier successfully verified the domain source and content integrity of saved messages. Latency measurements further quantified the communication and processing overhead introduced by the continuous mediation of domain servers.

title: Governance-Aware Federated Learning for Multi-Agent AI Systems: A Policy-Driven Framework for Trustworthy Collaborative AI
description:
arXiv:2610.38411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without exchanging raw data, but conventional FL provides limited runtime governance, evidence verification, fairness assessment, explainability monitoring, and auditability. This paper proposes Governance-Aware Federated Learning (GAFL), which combines independent governance-evidence verification, temporal trust, fairness and explanation assessment, anomaly detection, policy enforcement, normalized aggregation, and tamper-evident audit logging. Client-reported governance values are authenticated, bound to their submitted model updates, and independently recomputed before aggregation. A cross-silo prototype with 10 participants was evaluated on the Adult Income dataset under honest, benign non-IID, biased-data, malicious-update, non-compliant, falsified-evidence, and mixed-threat scenarios. Four methods were compared across five random seeds: FedAvg, FedAvg with anomaly filtering, GAFL without independent verification, and complete GAFL. Complete GAFL intervened on all affected participants at the final round across the evaluated risk scenarios, including identifying 100% of falsified-evidence participants, whereas GAFL without verification identified none of the falsified-evidence participants. Final macro-F1 ranged from 0.7520 to 0.7733 across GAFL scenarios. Complete GAFL required 173.67 plus or minus 26.94 ms of governance processing per round, compared with 3.82 plus or minus 0.79 ms for FedAvg. A strict demographic-parity threshold also caused frequent interventions for honest participants, demonstrating a significant fairness-policy and utility trade-off.

title: Stop Modeling State With Booleans: Make Impossible States Impossible in TypeScript
description:
Here is a type you have probably written:

type UserState = {
  isLoading: boolean;
  error?: string;
  data?: User;
};

It looks reasonable. Then one day your UI shows a spinner on top of an error message, and a user stares at a screen that says both "Loading..." and "Something went wrong".

The bug is not in your rendering code. It is in the type, which allows states that should never exist.

Count the States You Actually Allow

That type has three fields. How many combinations can it represent?

  • isLoading can be true or false: 2
  • error can be a string or missing: 2
  • data can be a user or missing: 2

That is 8 combinations, and your app has 4 real states: not started, loading, failed, succeeded. Four of the eight are nonsense:

{ isLoading: true,  error: 'Failed', data: user }   // loading AND failed AND loaded?
{ isLoading: false, error: undefined, data: undefined } // finished, but with nothing?

Every one of those is a bug waiting for a code path that forgets to reset a flag. Your components have to guess which flag wins, and different components guess differently.

The Fix: One Field That Decides Everything

A discriminated union is a type where one shared field, the discriminant, tells you which shape you have.

type UserState =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'error'; error: string }
  | { status: 'success'; data: User };

Now there are exactly four states, and each carries only the data that makes sense for it. A loading state has no data field to forget. A success state always has data, with no ? and no undefined to check.

TypeScript Narrows It for You 

function UserCard({ state }: { state: UserState }) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':
      return null;
    case 'loading':
      return <Spinner />;
    case 'error':
      return <p>{state.error}</p>;       // error exists here
    case 'success':
      return <h2>{state.data.name}</h2>; // data exists here
  }
}

Inside each case, TypeScript knows exactly which variant you are in. Write state.data inside the error branch and you get a compile error, not a runtime crash.

Using It in React 

const [state, setState] = useState<UserState>({ status: 'idle' });

async function load(id: string) {
  setState({ status: 'loading' });
  try {
    const user = await fetchUser(id);
    setState({ status: 'success', data: user });
  } catch (e) {
    setState({
      status: 'error',
      error: e instanceof Error ? e.message : 'Unknown error',
    });
  }
}

Notice what you no longer do: you never reset error before a retry, and you never clear data on failure. Each setState replaces the whole object, so stale fields cannot survive. That is the entire class of bug that booleans create, gone.

Make the Compiler Tell You When You Forgot a Case

Add a new state later, say 'refreshing', and every switch that does not handle it should complain. You can force that with a never check:

function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled state: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

switch (state.status) {
  case 'idle':
    return null;
  case 'loading':
    return <Spinner />;
  case 'error':
    return <p>{state.error}</p>;
  case 'success':
    return <h2>{state.data.name}</h2>;
  default:
    return assertNever(state);
}

If a case is missing, state is no longer never in default, and TypeScript reports an error at that exact line. Adding a state turns into a to-do list generated by the compiler.

The Same Trick for API Responses

Functions that can fail are another place where optional fields hide bugs:

// Allows { data: undefined, error: undefined } and { data: x, error: y }
type Result<T> = { data?: T; error?: string };

Replace it with a union:

type Result<T> =
  | { ok: true; data: T }
  | { ok: false; error: string };

const result = await createOrder(input);

if (!result.ok) {
  showToast(result.error); // error is a string here
  return;
}

redirectTo(`/orders/${result.data.id}`); // data is defined here

The caller cannot touch data without first checking ok. You cannot forget the error path, because the types will not let you reach the success value until you have handled it. This pattern works nicely for Server Actions and API handlers.

Two Gotchas

1. Use a literal for the discriminant. status: string will not work. The field must be a literal type like 'loading' or true, so TypeScript can tell the variants apart.

2. Data from outside still needs checking. A union describes what your code produces. If you receive JSON from a network, TypeScript cannot know it matches. Validate it with a schema library at the boundary, then trust the type inside.

When Not to Bother

Not everything needs a union. A form field with an optional middle name is fine as middleName?: string. Use unions when several fields depend on each other, meaning some combinations are valid and others are not. If you catch yourself writing a comment like "error is only set when status is failed", that comment belongs in the type.

The Rule

If a combination of fields should never happen, make it impossible to write down. Replace booleans and optional fields with one discriminant, let TypeScript narrow it, and add a never check so new states cannot be forgotten.

Quick audit: search your project for isLoading, isError and ?: in state types. Wherever two or more of them appear together, ask which combinations are real. The gap between the number you allow and the number you need is a list of bugs you have not met yet.

If you work with TypeScript and Next.js, you can browse my templates on pixelanas.com for a typed starting point.

Get the templates: https://pixelanas.gumroad.com

What is the strangest impossible state you have ever seen on a screen? Tell me in the comments.

Anas, full-stack Next.js developer building SaaS products and premium templates. X: @ASheikh69751

title: Rate-Limiting OTP Requests for SMS-Based 2FA in Node.js: Identity Handoffs
description:
Short answer: rate-limit the request before sending anything. Keep a counter keyed by the normalized phone number and the login session, store the timestamp in Redis or your database, and apply a configurable per-minute ceiling plus progressive backoff. Only after that check should the service call POST /v1/sms/otp.

This matters more in a developer tool than it first appears. A failed invitation, a stale test account, and a real login attempt can all look like “send another code” to the SMS provider. The useful unit of control is the recipient and the session, not the HTTP request. I would also keep a suppression check for known-invalid recipients so a bounce does not become a recurring bill or a noisy support ticket.

For a small team, Infrai is a plausible fit when the identity lookup and SMS send should live behind one self-describing REST surface. Discovery exposes schemas and runnable examples, so the integration starts with the capability you need rather than a second SDK’s conventions. That is an integration-effort argument, not a claim that it is the best SMS specialist.

How should Node.js rate-limit OTP requests for SMS-based 2FA?

The counter needs two keys. The phone number catches abuse spread across login sessions; the session key prevents one legitimate user from clicking Resend repeatedly while waiting for delivery. Store the last request time and the count for the current window. A practical starting policy is configurable rather than hard-coded: a small fixed limit per phone number per minute, a separate session limit, and a longer lockout after repeated violations.

The exact threshold belongs to the application. Geography, login risk, and the cost of a failed verification change the answer. A developer tool used by a small team can tolerate a different ceiling from a public signup flow. I would record the reason for every rejection, return a stable retry hint, and avoid revealing whether a phone number is registered.

The counter is not a dashboard. It is a gate.

The SMS call should be the final side effect of the decision. In a Node.js service, the order is easier to audit when the rate decision is a separate function from delivery:

type RateDecision = {
  allowed: boolean;
  retryAfterSeconds: number;
  reason: "allowed" | "phone_limit" | "session_limit" | "backoff";
};

async function requestOtp(
  phoneNumber: string,
  sessionId: string,
  now: number,
): Promise<RateDecision> {
  const phoneKey = `otp:phone:${phoneNumber}`;
  const sessionKey = `otp:session:${sessionId}`;

  const phone = await rateStore.checkAndIncrement(phoneKey, now);
  const session = await rateStore.checkAndIncrement(sessionKey, now);

  if (!phone.allowed) {
    return { allowed: false, retryAfterSeconds: phone.retryAfterSeconds, reason: "phone_limit" };
  }
  if (!session.allowed) {
    return { allowed: false, retryAfterSeconds: session.retryAfterSeconds, reason: "session_limit" };
  }

  await sendSmsOtp(phoneNumber);
  return { allowed: true, retryAfterSeconds: 0, reason: "allowed" };
}

rateStore is deliberately an application boundary here. Its increment must be atomic in Redis or in the database; a read followed by a write lets concurrent requests pass the limit. The SMS provider call also needs an idempotency strategy in the surrounding service so a client retry cannot turn one button click into two messages. When the decision is denied, return a throttled response with Retry-After and a plain message such as “Too many requests. Try again later.”

The retry path deserves a concrete rule. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when it is present; otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter and a small maximum attempt count. For a write, send an idempotency key derived from the login session and OTP issuance attempt. The platform convention documents a 24-hour default deduplication window, but your application still has to decide when a new code is a new issuance rather than a retry.

That distinction prevents a subtle accounting error. Suppose the user taps Resend, the client times out, and the client retries the same request. The first attempt may have reached the sender even though the browser saw no response. A new random key would make the second attempt look new; a key tied to the issuance attempt lets the server deduplicate it. Once the user deliberately asks for a fresh code after the backoff window, create a new issuance key and increment the policy counter. This is also why the rate check, the key choice, and the send decision belong in one small service boundary instead of three unrelated handlers.

That is the boundary.

How Do Identity and Delivery Meet?

The awkward handoff is not the counter. It is deciding which phone number is eligible to receive the code, then passing that value into the sender without maintaining a second identity integration. An identity lookup can supply the phone identity; the same authenticated client can then send the OTP:

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const userId = process.env.USER_ID;

if (!apiKey || !userId) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and USER_ID are required");
}

const headers = {
  Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
};

const identityResponse = await fetch(
  `${baseUrl}/auth/identity/list/${encodeURIComponent(userId)}`,
  { method: "GET", headers },
);

if (!identityResponse.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Identity lookup failed: ${identityResponse.status}`);
}

const identityResult: unknown = await identityResponse.json();
const phoneNumber = selectVerifiedPhone(identityResult);

const otpResponse = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/sms/otp`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers,
  body: JSON.stringify({ phone_number: phoneNumber }),
});

if (!otpResponse.ok) {
  const detail = await otpResponse.text();
  throw new Error(`OTP request failed: ${otpResponse.status} ${detail}`);
}

The important property is architectural: the identity lookup and the SMS request use the same base URL and bearer key. selectVerifiedPhone is an application-owned policy boundary because verification fields and the choice of identity are part of the product’s account model. Keep the rate check immediately before the second call, and make that check use the selected normalized number.

There is a cost to this consolidation. You trust one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface. The alternative stack of Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify means two signups, two credential sets, and glue code to reconcile the identity record, phone verification state, throttling decisions, and delivery status. That can be the right trade when your organization already standardizes on one of those services, but the glue is still an operating cost even when the APIs are individually familiar.

For invalid recipients, keep suppression in the same workflow. A failed delivery should update the application’s recipient state, and a future OTP request should consult that state before attempting delivery. SMS suppression operations are available in the communication surface, but a geographic fence or country-based spending circuit breaker is still business logic you must build yourself. There is also no webhook event push here, so a design that needs immediate cross-channel reaction should account for polling.

Which Option Fits the Workload?

The comparison is less about a leaderboard than about where integration effort lands.

Option Where it helps Integration boundary to own
Infrai identity plus SMS One REST surface can connect the identity lookup and OTP send with one key; public discovery documents request schemas and runnable examples. Your counter, verified-phone selection, suppression policy, and polling model remain application work.
Auth0 plus Twilio Verify A strong fit when both products are already approved and your team wants their established operational boundaries. Two accounts and credential sets, plus the identity-to-message handoff and shared throttling state.
Clerk plus Twilio Verify Useful when Clerk already owns the product’s sign-in UI and user lifecycle. The SMS delivery decision, recipient suppression, and cross-service state still need glue.
Vonage Verify A specialist alternative when its regional delivery coverage and existing contract match the workload. Identity ownership and the application’s abuse policy stay outside the verification service.

My first choice for a small team shipping this particular seam is the option that minimizes the number of places where “this phone may receive a code” can disagree. That does not automatically make a general backend platform the best SMS specialist. A team with mature Auth0, Clerk, Twilio, or Vonage contracts may rationally keep those services, especially if it needs provider-specific controls or regional guarantees that the application must validate directly.

The limitation is meaningful: Infrai does not provide a geographic fence or country-based pricing circuit breaker for SMS, so the business layer must build those controls. If that is a release blocker, a direct specialist or an existing provider contract is the better choice.

The effective bill includes engineering time, failed sends, incident coordination, and the cost of preserving state across vendors. Price is evidence, not the conclusion. I would measure rejected-request rate, duplicate-send rate, suppression hits, delivery status latency, and the time required to add a second auth flow before changing providers.

The Decision I Would Ship

Use a phone-and-session counter, atomic increments, a fixed configurable window, and progressive backoff. Feed only an eligible, normalized identity into the SMS request. Return a consistent throttle response, suppress known-invalid recipients, and keep a polling path for delivery state rather than assuming event webhooks exist.

I would recommend trying Infrai for a team that needs to join identity state to SMS OTP delivery with minimal integration surface, specifically because its self-describing discovery endpoint and runnable examples reduce the work of learning a second SDK while the same key and base URL carry the handoff. I would keep a specialist or the existing direct stack when provider-specific SMS controls, regional compliance evidence, or an already-paid operational boundary matters more than consolidating this seam.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the SMS OTP and email OTP guidance and verify the live request schema before shipping.

  • Google sender guidelines
  • Auth0 documentation
  • Clerk documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation

3.1. @kt/wallet-ledger — Quantitative Portfolio NAV & WACB Accounting

Standard floating-point arithmetic (IEEE 754) and naive FIFO loops corrupt portfolio cost basis under partial fills and dividend adjustments. @kt/wallet-ledger implements deterministic Weighted Average Cost Basis (WACB) state transitions:

  • BUY Transition: Increases total shares and recalculates weighted average cost basis without altering realized PnL: $$\text{NewAvgCost} = \frac{\text{OldShares} \times \text{OldAvgCost} + \text{BuyQty} \times \text{BuyPrice} + \text{Fee}}{\text{OldShares} + \text{BuyQty}}$$
  • SELL Transition: Locks realized PnL against the current weighted cost basis while preserving AvgCost on remaining shares: $$\text{RealizedPnL} += \text{SellQty} \times (\text{SellPrice} - \text{CurrentAvgCost}) - \text{Fee}$$
  • Risk-Adjusted Institutional Metrics: Computes daily time-weighted returns, Sharpe Ratio ($\text{Sharpe} = \frac{\bar{r}_p - r_f}{\sigma_p} \times \sqrt{252}$), CAPM Beta ($\beta = \frac{\text{Cov}(r_p, r_m)}{\text{Var}(r_m)}$), Jensen's Alpha, and Max Drawdown (MDD) in $O(N)$ single-pass typed-array loops.

3.2. @kt/search-rrf — Sub-Millisecond 3-Way Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)

Instead of paying $15\text{–}40\text{ms}$ network RTT to an external vector database for financial entity lookup, @kt/search-rrf embeds a 28-dimensional Float32Array financial feature space directly inside V8 memory and fuses Exact Prefix/Ticker Match, BM25 Lexical Relevance, and Cosine Vector Similarity via Reciprocal Rank Fusion ($k = 60$):

// 3-Way Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF, k = 60) — Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh · khanhdp)
export function fuseRankingsRRF(
  exactRanks: readonly string[],
  bm25Ranks: readonly string[],
  vectorRanks: readonly string[],
  k = 60
): Map<string, number> {
  const scores = new Map<string, number>();
  const accumulate = (list: readonly string[], weight: number) => {
    for (let i = 0; i < list.length; i++) {
      const id = list[i];
      scores.set(id, (scores.get(id) ?? 0) + weight / (k + i + 1));
    }
  };
  accumulate(exactRanks, 1.5);
  accumulate(bm25Ranks, 1.0);
  accumulate(vectorRanks, 1.0);
  return scores;
}

3.3. Valkey/Redis Bitmaps (46 Bytes/User/Year) & PostgreSQL 17 Base32 Materialized Paths

title: Testing Webhook & Transactional Email Flows with Ephemeral Inboxes: A Practical Guide
description:
Testing Webhook & Transactional Email Flows with Ephemeral Inboxes: A Practical Guide

When developing features that trigger transactional emails—such as password reset tokens, purchase receipts, or magic login links—validating that emails actually reach inboxes and parse correctly is one of the most frustrating parts of testing.

Relying on staging trap systems like MailHog or Mailpit works inside local Docker networks, but falls short when third-party SaaS services (Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, Auth0) need to deliver real webhooks and real SMTP messages to public internet domains.

Here is how modern engineering teams architect frictionless transactional testing using public ephemeral inboxes.

The Problem with Traditional Email QA

  1. Shared Team Inboxes: Testing with team-qa@mycompany.com causes test runs to overwrite each other. When two engineers trigger a reset flow simultaneously, race conditions occur.
  2. Plus-Addressing Limitations: While qa+user123@gmail.com routes to your personal inbox, many third-party auth platforms and payment gateways strip or reject plus tags.
  3. Domain Blocking in Staging: Mock mail servers running on localhost cannot receive emails sent by external third-party production webhooks.

Architecture: Ephemeral Inbound Webhook Pipelines

The optimal setup requires:

  • An internet-accessible domain with valid MX, SPF, and DKIM records.
  • High-concurrency edge ingestion that converts inbound SMTP to WebSocket / JSON streams.
  • Ephemeral mailboxes generated per test execution. 
[External SaaS / Auth0 / Stripe]
               │ (Real SMTP Delivery)
               ▼
[Edge MX Router (@mailfo.site)]
               │ (Sub-second Parse)
               ▼
[Real-Time WebSocket / In-Memory Queue]
               │
               ▼
[Test Runner / Mobile App / Web Client]

Key Verification Metrics

When running automated integration tests, your assertion library should verify:

  • Time-to-Delivery: Ensure transactional emails arrive in < 5 seconds.
  • Regex Extraction: Pull verification codes (/\b\d{6}\b/) immediately from HTML/plaintext payloads.
  • Header Integrity: Verify SPF and DKIM pass indicators to confirm delivery hygiene.

Instant Ephemeral Testing with Mailfo

title: SQL EXISTS vs JOIN: Find Customers Who Have Placed an Order
description:
SQL EXISTS vs JOIN: Find Customers Who Have Placed an Order


Imagine your manager asks you to find all customers who have placed at least one order.

You have two tables. Some customers have placed multiple orders, while others haven't placed any.

How would you write this query?

Let's look at the data.

  1. Sample Tables

customers

cust_id| name| city
101| Amit| Pune
102| Neha| Mumbai
103| Rahul| Pune
104| Priya| Delhi

orders

order_id| cust_id| amount
501| 101| 5000
502| 101| 3000
503| 103| 7000
504| 103| 2000

Notice that Amit and Rahul have placed two orders each. Neha and Priya haven't placed any orders.

  1. Find Customers Who Have Placed an Order

One way to solve this problem is by using the "EXISTS" operator.

SELECT c.cust_id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
SELECT 1
FROM orders o
WHERE o.cust_id = c.cust_id
);

  1. Output

cust_id| name
101| Amit
103| Rahul

Only Amit and Rahul are returned.

  1. How Does EXISTS Work?

The database checks each customer against the orders table.

  • Amit: A matching order exists, so he is included.
  • Neha: No matching order exists, so she is excluded.
  • Rahul: A matching order exists, so he is included.
  • Priya: No matching order exists, so she is excluded.

Even though Amit and Rahul have multiple orders, each customer appears only once.

That's because "EXISTS" checks whether at least one matching record is available. It doesn't return the matching order records.

  1. What Happens If We Use JOIN?

We can also write the query using an INNER JOIN.

SELECT c.cust_id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
ON c.cust_id = o.cust_id;

The result will be:

cust_id| name
101| Amit
101| Amit
103| Rahul
103| Rahul

Why do we get four rows?

Because each matching order produces a row in the JOIN result.

If a customer has 10 orders, that customer can appear 10 times.

We could use "DISTINCT" to remove duplicate customers:

SELECT DISTINCT c.cust_id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
ON c.cust_id = o.cust_id;

This returns the same two customers as the EXISTS query.

  1. EXISTS vs JOIN: Which One Should You Use?

Use "EXISTS" when you only need to check whether a matching record is available.

Use "JOIN" when you need columns from both tables or want to combine related records.

Both approaches are useful. The right choice depends on what information you need from the query.

  1. Want to Learn More About SQL Subqueries?

If you want to understand SQL subqueries better, including "EXISTS", "NOT EXISTS", and "IN", have a look at this practical guide:

"SQL Subqueries Explained with Examples – Sankalan Data Tech" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/subqueries-solve-queries-sql-faq.html)

It covers useful subquery concepts with practical SQL examples.

You can also explore more SQL and PL/SQL tutorials at "Sankalan Data Tech" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/).

  1. One Question for You

What would happen if Amit placed 10 more orders?

Would he appear 11 times in the output when using "EXISTS"?

Think about it before checking your answer.

Answer: No. Amit would still appear only once.

Follow Sankalan Data Tech for more practical SQL examples, database concepts, and interview challenges.

title: Converting Web Applications to Native iOS & Android Apps: Modern WebView Architectures, PWA, and Native Shell Engineering
description:
Converting Web Applications to Native iOS & Android Apps: Modern WebView Architectures, PWA, and Native Shell Engineering

One of the most frequent dilemmas for modern product teams and startups is choosing between a costly, multi-codebase native mobile development cycle (Swift/Kotlin) and delivering a cross-platform mobile experience from an existing responsive web application.

While modern Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) deliver near-native performance, businesses still require App Store and Google Play distribution for push notifications, in-app purchases, camera integration, and brand discoverability.

However, simply wrapping a web URL inside a standard webview almost always leads to Apple App Store rejection under Guideline 4.2 (Minimum Functionality), sluggish touch response times, and broken offline states.

In this technical case study, the engineering team at UCDREAMS breaks down how we architect native-shell applications that pass App Store review, achieve 60fps scrolling, and integrate native hardware bridges.

1. Why Naive "URL Wrappers" Fail App Store Review

Apple Guideline 4.2 explicitly states:

"Your app should include features, content, and UI that elevate it beyond a repackaged website. If your app is not particularly useful, unique, or 'app-like', it doesn't belong on the App Store."

Common failure modes of naive web wrappers include:

  1. White Flash on Cold Boot: Loading remote web pages causes a 1-3 second blank viewport before CSS renders.
  2. Missing Native Navigation: Hardware back buttons on Android break or exit the app unexpectedly.
  3. Viewport Bounce & Text Selection: Default Safari/WebKit bounce physics make the UI feel like a webpage rather than a compiled app.
  4. Zero Offline Capability: When connectivity drops, users see the browser's default "No Internet Connection" error.

2. The Modern Native Shell Architecture (Capacitor & WKWebView)

To deliver an authentic native experience, the web application assets (HTML, CSS, JS, WASM) must be bundled locally inside the application bundle or served through an asset bridge (capacitor://localhost or http://localhost:8080), eliminating remote HTTP latency.

// capacitor.config.ts - Enterprise Shell Configuration
import { CapacitorConfig } from '@capacitor/cli';

const config: CapacitorConfig = {
  appId: 'com.ucdreams.webapp',
  appName: 'UCDreams Mobile App',
  webDir: 'dist',
  bundledWebRuntime: false,
  server: {
    androidScheme: 'https',
    cleartext: false,
    allowNavigation: ['ucdreams.com', '*.ucdreams.com']
  },
  plugins: {
    SplashScreen: {
      launchShowDuration: 1800,
      launchAutoHide: true,
      backgroundColor: '#0F172A',
      androidSplashResourceName: 'splash',
      showSpinner: true,
      spinnerColor: '#2563EB'
    },
    PushNotifications: {
      presentationOptions: ['badge', 'sound', 'alert']
    }
  }
};

export default config;

3. High-Performance Bridge & Hardware Acceleration

Eliminating Webview Clutter

In CSS, lock down mobile browser physics to ensure native tactile response:

/* Native App CSS Normalization */
html, body {
  overscroll-behavior-y: none;
  -webkit-touch-callout: none;
  -webkit-user-select: none;
  user-select: none;
  -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent;
  touch-action: pan-x pan-y;
}

/* Enable hardware-accelerated GPU layer compositing */
.mobile-view-container {
  transform: translateZ(0);
  will-change: transform, opacity;
  overflow-y: auto;
  -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
}

Bi-directional Native Bridge (WKScriptMessageHandler)

In iOS (Swift), establish secure, zero-overhead asynchronous bridge communication between JavaScript and the native runtime:

// Swift WKScriptMessageHandler Implementation
import WebKit

class BridgeController: NSObject, WKScriptMessageHandler {
    func userContentController(_ userContentController: WKUserContentController, didReceive message: WKScriptMessage) {
        guard let dict = message.body as? [String: Any],
              let action = dict["action"] as? String else { return }

        switch action {
        case "hapticFeedback":
            let impact = UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(style: .medium)
            impact.impactOccurred()
        case "biometricAuth":
            authenticateUser()
        default:
            break
        }
    }
}

While automated shells work great for basic web utilities, high-traffic SaaS platforms and enterprise applications require custom native bridge engineering, background geolocation, offline SQLite synchronization, and dedicated App Store review consulting.

title: Why Modern Android Apps Need Disposable Inboxes for QA & Anti-Spam Testing in 2026
description:
Why Modern Android Apps Need Disposable Inboxes for QA & Anti-Spam Testing in 2026

Testing authentication and user onboarding flows on mobile is notoriously tricky. Every time you run a test on Android emulator or physical device, you need a clean email address to test account creation, magic links, and OTP codes.

Using real personal emails or even standard alias tricks (user+test@example.com) leads to inbox pollution, carrier rate limits, and linked personal data.

The Core Challenge: Mobile QA and Ephemeral Verification

When testing mobile applications, QA engineers face specific hurdles:

title: Automating OTP & Email Verification in Mobile App Testing (Without Burner SIMs)
description:
Automating OTP & Email Verification in Mobile App Testing (Without Burner SIMs)

End-to-end (E2E) automated testing of user authentication flows is one of the biggest headaches in modern mobile QA. Every time a test suite creates a new staging user, it inevitably triggers a one-time password (OTP) or magic link verification email.

If you have ever had test suites blocked because of rate limits on test email addresses or shared mailbox chaos, you know the frustration.

The Flaws of Common Workarounds

  1. Static Test Mailboxes (qa_test@company.com):

    • Concurrent test runs overwrite or conflict with the latest OTP.
    • Mailbox spam filters frequently block rapid-fire incoming test codes.
    • Manual cleanup scripts break constantly.

  2. Google/Outlook Alias Hacks (user+staging12@gmail.com):

    • Many sign-up validators aggressively reject + aliasing.
    • Google account rate limits kick in during CI/CD batch runs.

  3. Heavy Web-Only Burner Portals:

    • Ad-heavy web temp mails lack fast API access and real-time push.
    • Inboxes expire mid-run if browser tabs are cycled.

Modern Best Practice: Webhook-Driven Ephemeral Inboxes

In 2026, mobile QA engineering teams are shifting to dedicated ephemeral inbox clients with real-time webhooks.

Tools like Mailfo (available on Google Play) solve this by:

  • Zero Registration: Generate clean, isolated mailboxes per test run across diverse domain pools (.site, .cfd, .xyz).
  • Sub-3s Delivery Latency: Webhook routing ensures verification OTPs land instantly without sluggish IMAP/POP3 polling delays.
  • Smart OTP Extraction: Regex engines parse the email body directly to surface 4-to-8-digit PINs, drastically reducing token-parsing complexity in automation scripts.
  • Offline Persistence: Received tokens are stored locally on SQLite so app process kills in Android UI testing never lose the received OTP payload.

Example: Programmatic Test Flow Pattern 

// Example pseudo-code for mobile UI testing with ephemeral inboxes
class RegistrationFlowTest {

    @Test
    fun testUserRegistrationWithOtp() {
        // 1. Generate unique isolated burner address
        val testEmail = TempMailClient.generateRandomInbox()

        // 2. Perform app registration via Espresso / Compose UI
        onView(withId(R.id.email_input)).perform(typeText(testEmail))
        onView(withId(R.id.submit_button)).perform(click())

        // 3. Await instant OTP delivery
        val otpCode = TempMailClient.waitForOtp(testEmail, timeoutSeconds = 10)
        assertNotNull(otpCode)

        // 4. Enter verification PIN
        onView(withId(R.id.otp_input)).perform(typeText(otpCode))
        onView(withId(R.id.verify_button)).perform(click())

        // Verify successful onboarding
        onView(withId(R.id.home_dashboard)).check(matches(isDisplayed()))
    }
}

Summary

Automating user registration should not depend on fragile personal mailboxes or manual OTP entry. Adopting instant ephemeral inboxes makes your CI/CD test pipelines deterministic, parallelizable, and completely isolated.

title: My open-source text-to-SQL layer is #1 on BIRD Mini-Dev in all three dialects
description:
BIRD Mini-Dev is 500 text-to-SQL questions over 11 databases, in SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL versions, scored by whether the query returns the right rows. BIRD keeps the leaderboard and checks the submissions.

schemagate, the Apache-2.0 library I maintain, is now first in all three columns:

schemagate Next entry
SQLite 81.0 75.6
PostgreSQL 72.6 69.0
MySQL 72.4 49.2

The setup is plain: schemagate picks the tables a question needs, the prompt carries only those plus BIRD's column notes, and Claude Opus 5.5 writes one query. No candidate voting and no agent loop. If the query errors, the model sees the error and tries again.

schemagate's main job is access control. It removes the tables the caller may not read before the model sees the schema. A benchmark doesn't test that part, but it shows the filtering doesn't cost accuracy.

What it isn't: the main BIRD board, which uses a hidden test set. Our first test result there was 72.11, and a rerun is pending.
