FAQ

What does cloud consolidation mean?

Cloud consolidation means bringing every cloud account, provider, and workload under one identity layer, one policy framework, one deployment model, and one view of cost and health. It does not require migrating everything to a single cloud provider.

How do I consolidate multiple cloud providers without migrating everything?

Use a platform layer that sits above your existing clouds. Onboard accounts and workloads incrementally. Start with governance and visibility, then move workloads in waves if needed. On Control Plane, you add existing clusters through BYOK and your own servers through MK8s as locations, then deploy your containerized applications to them without re-architecting. See the guide on moving off a single cloud provider without re-architecting your apps.

How long does cloud consolidation take for a large enterprise?

For a large enterprise it is a multi-quarter program, paced mostly by data migrations and contract renewal dates. Governance and cost visibility come first and can land within the first 90 days. Stateless workloads follow in waves. Stateful services and contracts take longest, because data needs validation and contracts end on their own renewal dates.

What is the biggest risk of cloud consolidation?

Two risks dominate: downtime during a hard cutover, and concentrating every workload on one region or provider. Avoid both by running workloads active-active across multiple locations and providers, so traffic moves gradually during the transition and an outage in one location does not take down your services. Also confirm the platform’s exit terms, so you can export workload definitions and configuration.

How do I handle cloud consolidation after an acquisition?

Inventory the acquired estate and federate identity in the first 30 days, apply shared policies and observability and move the first stateless workloads by Day 90, then migrate stateful services and fold in contracts as they renew. Run stateless workloads active-active in old and new locations so traffic shifts gradually instead of in one cutover.

Can I consolidate clouds without a dedicated platform team?

Yes. A platform layer that handles Day 2 operations (autoscaling, right-sizing, observability, security) reduces the need for a large platform team. See the guide on production-grade infrastructure without a platform team.

How do I measure the ROI of cloud consolidation?

Sum savings from retired tools, reduced idle capacity, rightsized compute, fewer engineering hours on operations, and lower incident cost. Subtract one-time costs (migration, training, parallel running, contract exit) and recurring platform fees over a fixed horizon such as three years, and report the payback period. Use your own numbers from the inventory, not industry averages.

What compliance certifications should I require from a cloud consolidation platform?

At minimum, request current SOC 2 Type II reports, PCI DSS attestations of compliance, and HIPAA business associate agreements if you handle protected health information. Verify the scope covers both the vendor’s management layer and the infrastructure where your workloads run.

How does Control Plane handle billing across multiple clouds?

Control Plane puts every org on one billing account, and its Cost & Usage view shows spend per org and per resource with a projected total. A billing_viewer role gives finance teams read-only access to cost data. On Control Plane-provided compute, you pay for the CPU and memory you reserve, by the millicore and the megabyte, with no contracts or minimums. In locations you add through BYOK or MK8s, workloads run on nodes you supply, so your provider bills you for those nodes.

Does consolidating clouds mean I am locked into a new vendor?

Not necessarily. Evaluate exit terms before adopting any platform. Look for the ability to export workload definitions, policies, and configuration. Use infrastructure as code to keep your deployments portable.

Talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free to try it.

title: drizzle-kit migrate fails with "relation users already exists" after push
description:
TL;DR

drizzle-kit migrate fails on its very first file with relation "users" already exists when the tables were created by drizzle-kit push. Push compares your schema with the database and changes the database directly. It never writes to Drizzle's migration log, drizzle.__drizzle_migrations. migrate reads only that log, finds it empty, and replays 0000_*.sql from the top.

Do not add IF NOT EXISTS to the files. Insert a row into the log for the newest migration the database already matches, using the file's sha256 and its when value from the journal. migrate then skips everything up to that point and applies only what is new. After that, use one workflow per database: push or generate + migrate, never both.

The error

The report is drizzle-orm issue #2825, on SQLite (Turso). The reporter generated a migration, ran drizzle-kit push, changed the schema, generated again and pushed again. Then everything failed "with an error that the table already exists", and the reporter asked for IF NOT EXISTS in the generated CREATE TABLE. A Drizzle maintainer closed it with the answer that matters: drizzle-kit push "is not applying any migrations. It will just find the difference between your schema and database and apply those. To apply all generated migrations you should use drizzle-kit migrate".

The reproduction ran the sequence the maintainer points to, push and then migrate, on PostgreSQL. It used drizzle-kit 0.31.11 and drizzle-orm 0.45.4 on Windows 11 with Node v26.7.0. The database was PGlite 0.5.13, which is PostgreSQL 18.6 compiled to WebAssembly and run in-process (driver: "pglite" in drizzle.config.ts), not a PostgreSQL server. The reporter's own sequence, push twice with a generate in between, completed without any error there: the second push simply added the new column. That matches the maintainer's statement that push applies no migration files. The failure came from migrate. push created users from the first schema, a second generate wrote ALTER TABLE "users" ADD COLUMN "email_verified", and then drizzle-kit migrate ran:

$ npx drizzle-kit migrate
No config path provided, using default 'drizzle.config.ts'
Reading config file '<app>\drizzle.config.ts'
[⣷] applying migrations...[⣷] applying migrations...exit=1

The CLI printed only its spinner and exited with code 1. That silence is a separate drizzle-kit behaviour, covered in the page on drizzle-kit migrate stopping with no error. To see the database error, call the same migrator from a script (migrate() from drizzle-orm/pglite/migrator here; use drizzle-orm/node-postgres/migrator for pg):

$ node migrate.mjs
migration failed: relation "users" already exists (SQLSTATE 42P07)
exit=1

Why migrate replays your first migration

The two commands keep state in different places. The drizzle-kit push docs describe push as reading your schema, introspecting the database, generating the SQL for the difference and applying it. No migration file and no log row are involved. The drizzle-kit migrate docs describe the other side: migrate fetches entries from the migrations log table, then "Based on previously applied migrations it will decide which new migrations to run". By default that table is __drizzle_migrations in the drizzle schema.

The decision itself is short. In pg-core/dialect.ts at drizzle-orm 0.45.4, the migrator creates the schema and the log table if missing, outside any transaction. Then it reads one row: order by created_at desc limit 1. Inside a transaction it runs every journal entry whose when is greater than that row's created_at, or every entry when the table is empty. The hash comes from migrator.ts, a sha256 of the .sql file. It is stored but never compared.

On a database built by push, there is no log yet. The reproduction checked right after the failure:

$ node q.mjs select id, hash, created_at from drizzle.__drizzle_migrations
[]
exit=0
$ node q.mjs select column_name from information_schema.columns where table_name = 'users' order by ordinal_position
[{"column_name":"id"},{"column_name":"email"}]
exit=0

The log table now exists, because it was created before the transaction, and it is empty. users is untouched, because the failed transaction rolled back.

Two controls confirm the mechanism. On an empty database, migrate alone applied both files and wrote two rows. A second run changed nothing. The generated files themselves are fine. And a second push after generate added email_verified directly. Afterwards drizzle.__drizzle_migrations did not exist at all (relation "drizzle.__drizzle_migrations" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01)), so push never reads or writes the migrations folder's history.

Fix: baseline the migrations the database already has

The idea is the same as supabase migration repair --status applied, which the Supabase db push page uses after a 42P07: record a migration as applied without running it. Drizzle has no command for this, so you write the row yourself. Back up the database first if it holds data you care about.

1. Find the newest migration the database already matches

Open each file in drizzle/ in order and compare it with the live database. In the reproduction, the database had id and email but no email_verified. It matched 0000 and not 0001. If push ran after your latest generate, the database usually matches the last file.

2. Read that migration's when and compute its hash

when is in drizzle/meta/_journal.json:

{
  "idx": 0,
  "version": "7",
  "when": 1793381648727,
  "tag": "0000_zippy_giant_girl",
  "breakpoints": true
}

The hash is the sha256 of the file, exactly as the migrator computes it:

node -e 'console.log(require("crypto").createHash("sha256").update(require("fs").readFileSync(process.argv[1])).digest("hex"))' drizzle/0000_zippy_giant_girl.sql

3. Insert one row into the log

Run this with psql or your SQL client, with your own hash and when. The first two statements are the ones the migrator itself runs, so they are harmless if the table already exists:

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS drizzle;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS drizzle.__drizzle_migrations (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  hash text NOT NULL,
  created_at bigint
);
INSERT INTO drizzle.__drizzle_migrations (hash, created_at)
VALUES ('c9dc9641b6c6f4bdc644fcf1e6ea8b5fed2405ef127db1d46948f5f5800c98af', 1793381648727);

If drizzle.config.ts sets migrations.table or migrations.schema, use those names instead. The migrate docs show both options.

The SQL above is the PostgreSQL form, and only PostgreSQL was reproduced. On SQLite and Turso, as in the issue, the table has no schema prefix. It is plain __drizzle_migrations, with created_at declared numeric. The selection rule is the same: newest created_at first, then every journal entry with a later when. The source shows this in sqlite-core/dialect.ts and in the libSQL driver's libsql/migrator.ts.

4. Run migrate again 

$ npx drizzle-kit migrate
No config path provided, using default 'drizzle.config.ts'
Reading config file '<app>\drizzle.config.ts'
[⣷] applying migrations...[✓] migrations applied successfully!exit=0

Only 0001 ran. The log now holds both timestamps and the column exists:

$ node q.mjs select id, created_at from drizzle.__drizzle_migrations order by id
[{"id":1,"created_at":1793381648727},{"id":2,"created_at":1793381668028}]
exit=0
$ node q.mjs select column_name from information_schema.columns where table_name = 'users' order by ordinal_position
[{"column_name":"id"},{"column_name":"email"},{"column_name":"email_verified"}]
exit=0

If push had already applied every file, baseline only the last one. The migrator reads just the newest row, so there is no need to insert one row per file. In the reproduction, a database where push had added email_verified got a single row for 0001, created by hand together with the table. migrate then exited 0 and applied nothing.

Verify the fix

Two checks change nothing. Run drizzle-kit migrate a second time: it should exit 0 and add no row to drizzle.__drizzle_migrations. Then query the columns of each table the last migration touched, as above, and compare them with that migration's SQL.

On a development database or a copy, you can also let push compare the whole schema with the database. Run it as npx drizzle-kit push --verbose --strict. With nothing to change it stops at once, as on the baselined database in the reproduction (run there without --strict):

$ npx drizzle-kit push --verbose
No config path provided, using default 'drizzle.config.ts'
Reading config file '<app>\drizzle.config.ts'
[⣷] Pulling schema from database...
[✓] Pulling schema from database...
[i] No changes detected
exit=0

Keep --strict in that command: according to drizzle-kit push --help it makes push "Always ask for confirmation". Without it, a database that is behind does not get a report. Push prints the statements and applies them. On the database from the failing run, it added email_verified itself, which brings you back to the mixed state this page fixes. If it lists statements, decline them and finish with migrate.

When IF NOT EXISTS seems like the answer

The issue asks Drizzle to emit CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, and a comment there links a script that rewrites the generated files with a regular expression. Drizzle removed this on purpose. The drizzle-kit 0.30.0 release notes (9 December 2024) say the PostgreSQL dialect "will no longer include IF NOT EXISTS, $DO, or similar statements, which could cause incorrect DDL statements to not fail when an object already exists in the database and should actually fail."

The reproduction shows why the rewrite only moves the failure. With CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "users" in 0000 and an empty log, the migrator passed on the database where push had applied only the first schema. On the database where push had also added the column, it stopped at the next file:

$ node migrate.mjs ./drizzle-ine
migration failed: column "email_verified" of relation "users" already exists (SQLSTATE 42701)
exit=1

ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN, constraints and foreign keys have no clause that covers every case. The rewrite also skips a table whose definition differs from the file without saying so. The baseline row records the true state and leaves the generated SQL as it is.

Keep push and migrate on separate databases

The migrations overview presents push and generate + migrate as separate options. Mixing them on one database is what creates this state. A common split is push on a throwaway local database and generate + migrate everywhere else. If a development database is already mixed and holds nothing you need, resetting it is quicker than a baseline. Dropping every table covers public, but drop the drizzle schema too, or the old log rows will make migrate skip files on the empty database. The issue itself was on Turso, where the CLI talks to SQLite. Push also has dialect-specific failures there, such as the run()/get() TypeError on libSQL.

If migrate exits 1 again after the baseline with no message, it is hitting a different SQL error. Run the migrator script to print it, as described in the silent drizzle-kit migrate page. If the error names a table you did not expect, check the log's newest created_at against the journal before you insert anything else. A row with a later timestamp than the database really has will make migrate skip work without any error.

Originally published on iloveblogs.blog. Drafted with AI assistance; the reproduction (drizzle-kit 0.31.11, drizzle-orm 0.45.4, PGlite) was run and logged before publishing.

title: How to Containerize a Full-Stack App (Part 1)-Setting Up the Local Development Environment.
description:
Series Navigation:

  • 📍 Part 1: Setting up locally (You are here)
  • ➡️ Part 2: Frontend Multi-Stage Docker Builds
  • ➡️ Part 3: Containerizing the Backend & MySQL

Video

In modern web development, Docker has become the standard for ensuring your application runs consistently across dev, test, and production environments. In this post, we are going to focus specifically on how to containerize a full-stack application built with React, Express.js, and MySQL.

In this tutorial, I will guide you through the end-to-end process of containerizing this stack. This is Part 1, so here we will just set up our full-stack app locally. In the upcoming blog post, I will explain the remaining details.

Here is what we will cover:

  1. Prerequisites: Who is this for? (Frontend, Backend, and DevOps developers).
  2. Setup: Installing Docker Desktop on our machine.
  3. Setting up the Database: Setting up the Mysql Database.
  4. The Baseline: Running our full-stack app locally before containerizing.
  5. Conclusion: Summary and final thoughts.

Let’s get started.

1. Prerequisites

Before we dive in, let’s make sure this guide is right for you. This tutorial is designed to be flexible: whether you want to master the entire full-stack containerization process or need a solution for a specific part, you can leverage the sections that matter to you.

Who is this for?

  • Frontend Developers: You will learn how to serve your React app efficiently without relying on npm start in production.

  • Backend Developers: You will learn how to containerize your backend for production, ensuring your API and database run reliably together on any server.

  • DevOps Enthusiasts: You will gain hands-on experience packaging web applications and using Docker Compose to run them locally—the essential first step before managing them in a cloud environment.

⚠️ Important Note:
This guide is not for absolute beginners. We assume you already have a working knowledge of React and Node.js. I'm not covering how to write the application code itself, but rather how to package and ship it effectively.

What you need:

  • A basic understanding of React and Express.js.
  • Familiarity with the command line.
  • A code editor (VS Code recommended).

2. Setup: Installing Docker Desktop on our machine

To work with containers, we need the Docker engine running on our computer. The easiest and most standard way to do this is via Docker Desktop.

  1. Download: Go to the official Docker website for Mac, for Windows, for Linux and download the installer for your OS (Windows, Mac, or Linux).
  2. Install: Run the installer and follow the on-screen instructions.
  3. Start the App: Once installed, open the "Docker Desktop" application. (Important: Docker commands won't work unless this app is running in the background!)
  4. Verify: Open your terminal (or command prompt) and run the following command to make sure everything is connected: 
docker --version
# Output Example: Docker version 29.0.1, build eedd969

If you see a version number, you are ready to go!

3.Setting up the Database

To run our backend, we need a MySQL database. Instead of installing the heavy MySQL server software directly on your OS, we will use Docker to spin up a MySQL container.

Run this command in your terminal:

docker run --name mysql-container \
  -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=myrootpassword \
  -e MYSQL_DATABASE=my_testing_db \
  -p 3306:3306 \
  -d mysql:8.0

Now, go to Docker Desktop and verify that your MySQL container is running successfully

⚠️ Note:
Please save this password and db name as well because we need them later.
Also, if the above command failed. Then try with a different port number. For example, 3307.

docker run --name mysql-container \
-e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=myrootpassword \
-e MYSQL_DATABASE=my_testing_db \
-p 3306:3306 \
-d mysql:8.0

What Happens When You Run This Command

  1. Docker downloads the mysql:8.0 image (if not present).
  2. Creates a new container named mysql-container.
  3. Starts the MySQL server inside it.
  4. Initialises the database my_testing_db (first run only).
  5. Sets the root user password to whatever you provided.
  6. Exposes MySQL on your machine's port 3306.
  • docker run: Tells Docker to create and start a new container from a specified image.
  • --name mysql-container: Gives the container a custom name: mysql-container. So we can find it easily. If omitted, Docker assigns a random name.
  • -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=myrootpassword: Sets the root password (we'll need this for our backend). The official MySQL image requires the MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD environment variable to be set.
  • -e MYSQL_DATABASE=my_testing_db: This will set the database with name my_testing_db. This env variable is optional. It creates a database on container creation.
  • -p 3306:3306: Exposes the database port so our local Node.js app can connect to it.
  • -d mysql:8.0: Image name.

4. The Baseline: Running our full-stack app locally before containerizing

Before we start writing Dockerfiles, we need to understand what we are actually containerizing. In this section, we will get the application running on our machine "the old-fashioned way" (mostly) to ensure the code works.

In this section, we will:

  • Fork and Clone the starter repository.
  • Set up the Database.
  • Run the Application to confirm that everything talks to each other.

4.1 Fork and Clone the Repository

I have prepared a starter repository that contains a basic React frontend and an Express backend.

  1. Fork the repository to your own GitHub account.

Go to repo: Repo Link

Click on Fork

Once forked, clone it.

  1. Clone it to your local machine: 
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/devops-todo-starter-app.git

# Move into the project directory
cd devops-todo-starter-app

Once you cloned it, open it in VS Code or any IDE.

Note: There are three branches present for each blog post. Make sure you are in the main branch.

You will be able to see two folders: backend, frontend and a README.md file.

4.2 Running the Application

Now that our database is running, let's start the application. Go to your IDE where you open the project.

Go to the backend directory and create a file .env.

Copy content from .env-example. And paste it in .env.

Now replace DB_PASSWORD='<DB_PASSWORD>' with DB_PASSWORD=myrootpassword. And ALLOWED_ORIGIN=http://localhost:4501 with ALLOWED_ORIGIN=http://localhost:8080.

Before proceeding, make sure you are using Node.js version ">=20.0.0". Currently I'm using the LTS version, which is v24.13.0.

Open the terminal and run

node -v

Once you have a compatible node version, start the backend server.

Open a terminal and go to the **backend **directory

Install dependencies

cd backend
npm install

Run the migration

npm run migrate

Once migrated, you will see below the O/P

Run dev server

npm run dev

If everything goes fine, you will see below the O/P

Now, in the browser, open URL http://localhost:5500/api/todos

You will be able to see dummy todos in the browser

Open a new terminal and go to the frontend directory

Install dependencies

cd frontend
npm install

Setup Env Variable:

Go to the frontend directory and create a file .env.

Copy content from .env-example. And paste it in .env.

Start dev server

npm run dev

Open your browser to http://localhost:8080.

If you see data loading from the API, congratulations!🎉. Your baseline environment is set up perfectly.

5. Conclusion

I hope you successfully set up the app locally and enjoyed the process. In the next part, we will learn how to containerize our frontend. Stay tune. Please post your queries if you faced any issues.

title: Nvidia in talks to guarantee loans for giant AI center
description:
Nvidia is in talks to provide multi-billion dollar debt financing guarantees for Nscale’s West Virginia AI data center project.

The campus, featuring Anthropic as a primary tenant for its initial buildings, underscores the heavy financial interlocking between hardware providers and AI infrastructure developers.

Under the terms of the proposed deal, if Nscale is unable to repay the construction costs, Nvidia will step in to take over the facilities and help find a buyer and a new tenant. At the same time, Nscale is preparing to go public at a valuation that could reach $35 billion.

The huge project sizes and Nvidia chips

The first building in the complex in West Virginia will have a capacity of 460 megawatts and is expected to use Nvidia's new Vera Rubin chips. The project is directly involving Anthropic, which has already signed a contract worth $44,6 billion for the first building, while the two sides are already discussing a second similar deal worth about $45 billion.

Nscale’s journey includes other developments. In August, it had about 25.000 advanced AI chips in operation, out of a total of nearly 500.000 it plans to deploy. In the infrastructure sector, projects in West Virginia caused mudslides that flooded nearby homes more than once, but the site secured state certification in September. In England, by contrast, Microsoft pulled out of a planned Nscale project because grid connection was delayed to the 2030s.

Nvidia's stance and market concern

Nvidia has provided a total of about $170 billion in investment and credit support to similar companies and large customers, including a $1 billion financing to Nscale in September.

title: Bounded Clinical Search Explained: Ranking Signals for Appointment Assistants
description:
Short answer: Use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives reranking; a healthcare appointment assistant should not promote a result that an operator cannot trace to a URL or document ID. Choose the product only after writing that retrieval contract, its timeout budget, and its deletion procedure.

That order matters in B2B healthcare SaaS. A plausible appointment answer delivered from stale or untraceable context is harder to review than an empty result. The ranking layer has two jobs: improve relevance and preserve the evidence needed to inspect the answer later. Relevance alone isn't the acceptance criterion.

What retrieval architecture and ranking signals should a healthcare appointment assistant use?

Use three stages: retrieve from a named collection, reject candidates that violate the contract, then rerank the remaining bounded set. The contract should require a source URL or stable document identifier on every candidate. It should also define the query limit, total timeout, retry behavior, and what the assistant does when too few eligible records remain.

Keep the stages observable as separate decisions. Suppose retrieval returns 20 candidates and the eligibility gate removes 7 because their source reference is absent. The trace should say so; the reranker receives 13, rather than silently manufacturing confidence for all 20. Those numbers describe a test case, not a measured production result, but the invariant is firm: a candidate without reviewable source context cannot support a grounded answer.

Stop there.

The ranking signals should follow the same hierarchy. First gate on traceability and current collection membership. Then use the relevance order returned by retrieval as the input to reranking. Finally, apply deterministic tie-breaking so repeated requests do not reshuffle equivalent candidates. I'm not sure which domain-specific relevance signal will win for a particular corpus without an evaluation set; labeled appointment queries, expected documents, and reviewer judgments are what resolve that uncertainty.

This staged shape also gives the on-call engineer a useful failure boundary. A slow source cannot consume the entire user-flow budget because every query has an explicit timeout and limit. A transient HTTP 429 can be retried with backoff, while a response that fails the source contract is rejected rather than retried. Those are different events and should not share an alert.

Make provenance a ranking gate, not a footnote

Return source URLs or document identifiers with retrieved context. Carry that reference through reranking and into the answer record; otherwise, the system loses the join needed for review. A polished sentence without that join is operationally weak.

Freshness is a collection-maintenance property, not a clever scoring weight. Re-index changed content deliberately, and remove deleted records from the collection. If a clinic page or appointment policy disappears, lowering its score is insufficient — it must no longer be eligible for retrieval. This distinction belongs in the postmortem template: the index may have answered exactly as asked while the ingestion runbook failed to remove a record that no longer existed. That is a lifecycle failure, so tuning similarity cannot correct it.

The catch is that strict provenance can reduce recall when source metadata is incomplete. Don't loosen the gate invisibly. Route the request to a defined no-grounded-result response, record the rejection reason, and repair the ingestion path. This design is not suitable when the assistant must answer from undocumented knowledge; keep a human scheduling workflow for those cases until the knowledge has stable identifiers.

Choose the operational boundary before the product

The safest API combination implements the contract with the fewest unowned transitions. A web-search stage can discover external material, while a vector-query stage can retrieve from an explicit collection. Do not blend them into one opaque score: operators need to know which stage supplied each candidate, and the user-visible answer still needs its source reference.

Vendor choice follows from the boundary a team can operate. This table states decision conditions, not a synthetic benchmark; no runtime latency, uptime, or savings measurements are available here.

Option Prefer it when Main limitation to examine
Elasticsearch The existing deployment already has a tested retrieval contract, deletion procedure, and on-call runbook Its presence elsewhere in the company does not prove this corpus is grounded
Pinecone An evaluation verifies the required source fields and bounded-query behavior in the target deployment A vector database label does not substitute for source review
Weaviate The team can own its collection lifecycle and verify the same traceability contract A semantically similar demo result is not an operational acceptance test
Unified REST platform Search is one of several backend needs and broad production modules behind one consistent REST API reduce integration ownership Consolidation alone does not prove answer quality

Infrai fits the last condition because one key covers 295 routes across 20 modules, and its public self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas without requiring that key. That breadth behind a plain REST interface is the relevant advantage here: adding a backend capability is another endpoint under consistent conventions, not another required SDK. It is not the automatic choice for a team whose Elasticsearch, Pinecone, or Weaviate path already has evaluated relevance, source propagation, deletion handling, and practiced rollback. Stick with the system operators can verify when consolidation would add migration risk without improving the retrieval contract.

No vendor removes the need for a corpus-specific evaluation.

Implement the bounded query client in Go

The client below sends one validated request to POST /v1/vector/query. It deliberately reads the JSON body from standard input because the discovery schema, rather than an invented field list, is the authority for the current request shape. It sets an explicit method, keeps the key and API base in environment variables, checks status, honors a numeric Retry-After, and bounds 429 retries. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_BASE_URL from the service configuration, provide a request body that conforms to the discovered schema, then run go run main.go < query.json.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    if baseURL == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    endpoint := baseURL + "/v1/vector/query"

    body, err := io.ReadAll(os.Stdin)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if !bytes.HasPrefix(bytes.TrimSpace(body), []byte("{")) {
        panic("stdin must contain a JSON object")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 8 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if response.StatusCode >= 200 && response.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("query failed: status=%d body=%s", response.StatusCode, responseBody))
    }
}

Keep reranking outside this transport client. After decoding a successful response according to its discovered response schema, enforce the source-reference gate, remove records not in current collection membership, preserve the bounded candidate set, and only then run the domain ranking policy. The separation is intentional: transport retry, eligibility rejection, and relevance ordering need different counters and different runbook actions.

The alternative route, POST /v1/web/search, belongs in a separate discovery stage when external material is required. Do not enumerate more endpoints or send both calls by habit. Map the user-visible answer back to a retrieval contract first, then enable only the stage that the contract requires.

Verify, degrade, and roll back

Ship with a verification matrix that runs before an index change and again after it. Test a normal query, a query with no eligible result, a candidate missing both source fields, a deleted record, a timeout, and a 429 response. Assert the candidate limit at the retrieval boundary and at reranker output. The second assertion catches accidental application fan-out even when the upstream request was bounded.

For each answer, retain enough trace data to reconstruct the path: collection identity, candidate count before and after gating, chosen document identifiers or URLs, and final ordering. Do not turn that into a dump of sensitive user text. The goal is an auditable decision trail, not broader data retention, and local policy must decide the permitted contents and lifetime of that trail.

Rollback should be boring. Keep the previous collection or index version addressable, stop writes to the version under review, switch queries back to the last accepted version, and verify a fixed set of appointment queries before reopening traffic. Re-index changed content deliberately instead of mutating records ad hoc. After deletion, test that the removed document cannot reappear in retrieval; after rollback, test that source references still resolve to the expected review records.

Use a degraded response when the source times out or the eligibility gate removes every candidate. This architecture is not suitable when the product requirement insists on an answer regardless of evidence. Change that requirement or route to a human workflow — don't hide the gap by widening the timeout indefinitely.

One last runbook rule: page on user-visible loss of grounded retrieval, not every individual retry. Aggregate bounded retry exhaustion and contract-rejection rates into signals an operator can act on. A single 429 is control flow. A sustained inability to return traceable appointment context is the incident.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

title: How to Rate-Limit OTP Requests for SMS-Based 2FA in Node.js: Delivery Reliability
description:
Short answer: to rate-limit OTP requests for SMS-based 2FA in Node.js, put the limit in your backend before you ask an SMS provider to send anything. Count requests by normalized phone number and login session, enforce a fixed window, then add progressive backoff for repeated denials. The provider route is the delivery boundary; it should never be your abuse-control system.

For a password-reset message with a short expiry, delivery reliability is the decision axis. A fast SMS that can be requested 40 times in a minute is not reliable for the account, the carrier, or the bill. In a Node.js service, I model the workflow as two separate decisions: may this identity request another code, and did the delivery service accept the permitted request? Keeping those decisions separate makes provider changes much less disruptive.

Infrai belongs at that second boundary, not in the security policy. Its POST /v1/sms/otp capability can be the delivery adapter while the application keeps the same counters and verification state; the public discovery surface gives the adapter a contract to inspect before it sends. That separation is useful when the backend service changes but the reset flow should not.

Small limits matter.

So does a clear boundary.

How should Node.js rate-limit OTP requests for SMS-based 2FA?

Use two counters, not one. The phone key protects a destination from an attacker who can replay a reset form. The session key protects a single account flow when the user changes devices or enters the wrong number repeatedly. Store each request timestamp in Redis or a database, with a short expiry longer than the request window. A useful starting policy is one request per phone in 60 seconds, with a small session allowance and a longer backoff after denials. Tune those values with delivery and support data; they are policy, not a universal constant.

The counter operation must be atomic. A read followed by a write has a race: two application workers can both observe a free slot and send two messages. Redis transactions, a Lua script, or a database row protected by a lock can make the check-and-increment one decision. Keep the response deliberately vague. “Try again later” tells a real user what to do without confirming whether a phone number has an account. That detail is easy to miss in a notebook and painful to discover after adding a second Node.js worker, because the in-process map then becomes two independent rate limiters.

Here is a complete in-memory version of the policy. It is useful as an evaluation harness and as a notebook-to-prod reference; replace the dictionary with an atomic Redis operation before using it across workers.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from time import monotonic
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


@dataclass
class OtpLimiter:
    window_seconds: int = 60
    phone_limit: int = 1
    session_limit: int = 3
    base_backoff_seconds: int = 30
    requests: Dict[str, List[float]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    denials: Dict[str, int] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def allow(self, phone: str, session_id: str) -> Tuple[bool, int]:
        now = monotonic()
        phone_key = f"phone:{phone}"
        session_key = f"session:{session_id}"

        for key in (phone_key, session_key):
            recent = self.requests.get(key, [])
            self.requests[key] = [stamp for stamp in recent
                                  if now - stamp < self.window_seconds]

        if len(self.requests[phone_key]) >= self.phone_limit:
            return self._deny(phone_key, now)
        if len(self.requests[session_key]) >= self.session_limit:
            return self._deny(session_key, now)

        self.requests[phone_key].append(now)
        self.requests[session_key].append(now)
        self.denials.pop(phone_key, None)
        return True, 0

    def _deny(self, key: str, now: float) -> Tuple[bool, int]:
        count = self.denials.get(key, 0) + 1
        self.denials[key] = count
        wait = self.base_backoff_seconds * (2 ** min(count - 1, 4))
        return False, wait


limiter = OtpLimiter()
print(limiter.allow("+15551234567", "reset-session-1"))
print(limiter.allow("+15551234567", "reset-session-1"))

Before wiring the send adapter, this small client checks the live public contract. It uses the same error discipline I want around the OTP call: an explicit method, bounded 429 backoff, and a useful exception for other failures. The discovery response is the input to the adapter, so the example does not invent an OTP field.

import os
import time

import requests


def load_infrai_discovery():
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(method="GET", url=url, headers=headers, timeout=10)
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))
            time.sleep(min(retry_after, 32))
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai discovery failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("Infrai discovery remained rate-limited after 5 attempts")


discovery = load_infrai_discovery()
print(discovery["version"])

The first result should be allowed and the second should return a denial with a wait value. In production, return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After value derived from the policy, and log the reason without logging the OTP itself. The application should not retry a 429 immediately.

The adapter still needs the live OTP schema. Do not turn a guessed request body into a production integration.

Why does a short expiry change the design?

A five-minute code and a one-minute request window are different clocks. The code record needs a single-use state, an expiry, and an attempt counter. A request limiter needs a rolling history. Reusing one field for both creates odd behavior: a user can be locked out after one expired code, or an attacker can keep requesting fresh codes while never verifying one.

I also make the send boundary idempotent. Generate a request identifier from the reset session and code generation event, pass it through the provider adapter, and persist the accepted result before returning success. A retry after a network timeout must not create a second SMS. If the delivery surface does not accept an idempotency key, deduplicate in the application and treat an ambiguous response as pending rather than blindly sending again.

For an Infrai-backed adapter, the relevant SMS capability is POST /v1/sms/otp. Its public discovery surface describes the contract, so the adapter can keep the rest of the reset flow independent of the service behind it. That is the practical advantage of a stable boundary: changing the delivery implementation does not require rewriting counters, expiry, or verification state. The request schema should be loaded from discovery at integration time rather than guessed in an article.

Which provider fits the operating bill?

The cheapest-looking send call is rarely the whole workload. Count the application state, retry behavior, delivery status handling, abuse controls, and the time spent reconciling a second integration. Then compare that total with the traffic pattern you actually have: normal resets, resend bursts, carrier delays, and attack traffic.

Option Where it fits Boundary to keep visible
Twilio Verify A managed verification flow with established messaging integrations Your product still needs account-specific throttling, reset-session state, and its own recovery policy
Vonage Verify A verification product for teams already aligned with Vonage's communications stack Confirm regional sender, carrier, and fallback behavior before making it the only path
AWS End User Messaging SMS Teams that want SMS delivery close to an existing AWS control plane More of the OTP lifecycle and abuse policy belongs in your application
Infrai A plain REST boundary when one key and a consistent backend surface reduce integration overhead It does not remove your rate limiter, geography-based spend guard, or delivery-event polling work

Twilio and Vonage are reasonable choices when a managed verification product is the primary requirement. AWS is a natural candidate when operational ownership already sits in AWS. Infrai is worth trying for the delivery portion of this workflow when keeping the application contract stable while the service behind it changes matters more than buying a specialist verification product. Its public discovery endpoint is self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples across ten languages; that reduces adapter and maintenance work without moving security policy into the provider.

The trade-off is important. Infrai has no hosted email OTP interface, no webhook event push in these namespaces, and no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. SMS geography fences and country-based spend breakers remain application work. If your recovery design requires a managed multi-channel verification journey or real-time push events, Twilio Verify or Vonage may be the better fit.

My recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the SMS delivery adapter when your team already owns the OTP state machine and wants a stable REST contract across backend capabilities. Keep the limiter, expiry, idempotency, and regional policy in your service. That is where reliability is decided.

What should you measure before switching?

Start with a replayable test set rather than a vendor leaderboard. Include one normal request, two concurrent requests for the same phone, repeated requests after a denial, a delayed provider response, and a retry after a timeout. Assert that only one code is active, the second concurrent request is rejected, a rejected request does not call the provider, and the user-facing response does not reveal account existence.

Track accepted requests, 429 responses, delivery status, verification success, expiry rate, and duplicate-send rate. Keep provider cost and latency metadata beside the reset-session identifier, not beside the phone number in logs. This gives you an effective workload bill and a way to spot a policy that is too strict for real users or too permissive for bots.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the SMS OTP guidance and validate the live request schema before wiring the adapter.

References

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify overview
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS
  • Google email sender guidelines
  • Infrai public capability discovery

title: From Inertia::render() to a page type
description:
You type your Inertia props by hand. Then a controller changes, and the types drift.

Inertia Typegen generates TypeScript types and route helpers for Inertia pages. It reads them from Scramble's OpenAPI document. You write no types by hand.

This post walks from the PHP input to the TypeScript output.

Install 

composer require vagebond/inertia-typegen
composer require --dev dedoc/scramble

Scramble is a development dependency. Inertia Typegen requires PHP 8.3+, Laravel 12 or 13, and Scramble 0.13.49+. It also needs inertia-laravel 2 or 3, Node 22.18+ and Vite 6+.

The PHP input

Here is a controller with an enum and a paginated resource collection.

enum PostStatus: string
{
    case Draft = 'draft';
    case Published = 'published';
}

class PostController
{
    public function index()
    {
        return Inertia::render('Posts/Index', [
            'posts' => PostResource::collection(Post::paginate()),
            'status' => PostStatus::Draft,
        ]);
    }
}

The page type

Each Inertia::render() call becomes a page type. The output below is simplified for this post.

type PostStatus = 'draft' | 'published'

type PostsIndexProps = SharedData & {
  // the paginator keeps its real shape
  posts: PostCollection
  status: PostStatus
}

Three things happen here.

  • PHP enums become a union of their values.
  • JSON resources, collections and paginators keep their real shape.
  • Shared data from the Inertia middleware becomes one type that each page type includes.

Form data

Form request rules become the type of the form data.

class StorePostRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'title' => ['required', 'string'],
            'status' => ['required', Rule::enum(PostStatus::class)],
        ];
    }
}

type StorePostData = {
  title: string
  status: PostStatus
}

You change a rule in PHP. The form type follows.

Route helpers

You also get typed route helpers for each named route.

Keeping files fresh

The Vite dev server regenerates files after a PHP change. A CI check fails when committed files are stale. You commit the generated files, so a production build needs no PHP.

No HTTP endpoint is added by default. Plugins with hooks can change the document, routes and output.

The limit

The release status is 0.x. Minor releases can contain breaking changes until 1.0. So pin the minor version and check each upgrade.

Inertia Typegen is MIT licensed. The docs cover setup, route helpers and plugins:

https://baken.vagebond.nl/r/dpRMA9Ze

title: Choosing a Simple API to Integrate App Event Logging Without Advanced Infrastructure
description:
Short answer: integrate the app with a direct event-logging API, then use a separate heartbeat or polling check for a missing import completion event.

The simplest API to integrate app event logging without advanced infrastructure is a direct event-ingest boundary for the import worker. Add a separate silence check when the real question is what did not happen: no completion event, no rows produced, or no result before the deadline.

Infrai fits the capture side of this design because /v1/logs/ingest can stand alone behind a small adapter. It does not replace the checker that decides whether a scheduled import missed its deadline.

That split is the simplest useful architecture for a team that wants app event logging without advanced infrastructure setup. It keeps logging easy to integrate without pretending that a log store is an alerting or heartbeat system. The important contract is smaller than a logging platform: one stable run identifier, a few meaningful lifecycle events, and one explicit owner for deciding whether silence is a failure.

What must remain true when the import runs overnight?

The system has two invariants:

  1. Every scheduled import attempt has a stable run_id that appears in its events.
  2. A separate checker can determine whether the expected terminal event arrived before the deadline.

The first invariant is about evidence. The second is about signal quality. Mixing them produces noisy operations: import_started proves that a worker began, but it says nothing about whether the worker fetched records, committed them, or stopped halfway through.

Silence is a signal. It just needs an owner.

There are two viable shapes for that owner. A direct-ingest design sends structured events from the worker to a log API and uses a polling or heartbeat component to evaluate missing events. A collector-based design puts an agent or telemetry pipeline between the worker and a specialist observability backend; that backend can own more of the buffering, routing, retention, and alert workflow.

Consider a scheduled roster import that starts at 02:00. At 02:01, import_started tells you the scheduler reached the worker. At 02:07, the source may have returned zero records, the credentials may have been rejected, or the worker may have died after opening a connection. Those cases should not be collapsed into one green check. A direct event contract lets the worker emit import_completed only after the result is valid, while a separate checker can treat the absence of that terminal event as a deadline failure. The sink stores the evidence; the checker applies the policy. That division is what keeps a quiet night from looking successful merely because one early message was accepted.

Decision point Direct event ingest plus silence check Collector plus specialist backend
Integration boundary A small adapter in the import worker Agent configuration and a telemetry pipeline
Best fit A few lifecycle events with known meaning Many services, high-volume telemetry, or central operations
Silent scheduled work Requires an explicit heartbeat or polling check Can fit a backend alert rule, but still needs a completion event
Main limitation Basic search and separate notification ownership More components and more operational conventions
Failure boundary Capture can succeed while alert evaluation is absent Buffering, storage, routing, and alerting are more tightly coupled

For a small import service, I would choose the first shape. For a platform team that already operates a telemetry pipeline, the second is often the better boundary. This is a systems decision, not a contest for the shortest API reference.

How can I integrate app event logging without advanced infrastructure?

Yes, if the event contract stays deliberately narrow. The worker needs events such as import_started, import_completed, and import_failed. Each should carry the schedule slot, source name, run_id, state, and aggregate counts that help an operator distinguish “nothing was available” from “the worker never finished.”

Do not put student records or assessment content into a debugging event merely because the transport accepts JSON. An event should make a run traceable without becoming a second copy of protected application data. Redaction belongs in the adapter, before the event leaves the process.

The adapter should also isolate the rest of the codebase from the service-specific contract. If the sink changes later, the import code keeps calling record_event() while the implementation behind that function changes. The contract stays put while the thing behind it moves. This is the useful portability test: can the worker keep its event names and run identifiers if the backend changes?

Here is the critical path for one event. It uses a stable client-supplied idempotency key, checks real HTTP failures, and backs off on rate limiting instead of creating a retry storm.

import os
import time
import requests


def ingest_event(event: dict, run_id: str) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]

    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = requests.request(
                method="POST",
                url="https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/ingest",
                json=event,
                headers={
                    "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                    "Idempotency-Key": run_id,
                },
                timeout=10,
            )
            if response.status_code == 429 and attempt < 3:
                retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
                time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)
                continue
            if response.status_code >= 400:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"log ingest failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}"
                )
            return response.json() if response.content else {}
        except requests.RequestException as error:
            if attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"log ingest unavailable: {error}") from error
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)

    raise RuntimeError("log ingest retry budget exhausted")

The example intentionally does not turn a successful HTTP response into a business success. The import can still fail after import_started; only the worker knows when it has a valid result and can emit import_completed.

Which boundary should a small team choose?

The direct design has a clean failure boundary. The logging API captures evidence. A health-check service, scheduler-side poller, or small query worker decides whether the expected evidence is missing. Those are different jobs, and keeping them separate makes the decision rule visible in code and in runbooks.

For this use case, Infrai is worth trying for the event-capture part when a team wants a standalone, beginner-friendly REST boundary and can live with basic search. Its API surface is self-describing: the public discovery surface exposes capabilities and runnable examples without requiring a key. That lowers the cost of checking the contract before writing an adapter. The live discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities ship runnable examples in 10 languages; I would use that breadth to reduce setup friction, then expose only one narrow adapter to the import code.

There is a second, different advantage for a growing import workflow. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so the same backend credential can cover adjacent capabilities as the service grows instead of creating a new integration identity for every small addition. The point is not to use every route. It is to reduce credential ownership and integration bookkeeping while keeping the application-facing adapter narrow.

The portability claim still has a boundary. A single REST surface does not provide custom retention, granular export, log deletion by user, bulk export or subscriptions. Search is basic, and there is no built-in threshold notification, SMS, phone, or webhook delivery route for this silence rule. If an edtech operator needs those controls on day one, the direct design has stopped being the simplest complete design.

The check itself should remain explicit. A polling worker can ask whether the expected terminal event exists for a known run, then hand the result to the team’s notification path. A Healthchecks-style service can instead wait for a completion ping and flag a missed deadline. Neither approach should infer success from the existence of a start event.

My rule is blunt: if the team cannot name the component that owns a missed deadline, the design is incomplete. The event sink is not that component.

How do the established alternatives change the trade-off?

Better Stack is a sensible choice when the team wants log search and incident-oriented alerting close together. That reduces the number of operational surfaces for a small team, but it also means the team adopts a broader product model instead of a narrowly scoped event sink.

Grafana Loki makes more sense for an organization already running Grafana dashboards and a wider metrics workflow. It is a good fit when central label conventions, retention administration, and cross-service operations outweigh the appeal of a tiny application adapter. The trade-off appears later as governance: careless labels can make a shared log system harder to query and operate.

Sentry is the stronger specialist for exception investigation, releases, and error groups. It is not proof that a scheduled business workflow produced a result. A worker can exit cleanly before importing a row, so an error-focused system may have nothing to report for the failure that matters here.

These products are not interchangeable rows in a price table. Their boundaries answer different questions. Better Stack leans toward managed incident operations, Loki toward a Grafana-centered telemetry stack, and Sentry toward application failure analysis. Direct ingest plus a heartbeat checker is appropriate when the question is narrower: did this scheduled import reach the expected terminal state?

The rejected option: making logs responsible for absence

I would reject a design that asks an operator to search manually for every missing import_completed event. It looks cheap in an architecture diagram, then turns an overnight invariant into a human polling loop. That is how low-volume systems acquire high-noise operations: every ambiguous absence becomes a chat message, and every real absence competes with it.

I would also reject one generic event called import_status. A compact payload is attractive at first, but it hides the difference between “the worker started,” “the source returned zero records,” and “the write phase committed.” Three explicit lifecycle events are easier to validate and easier to test against a deadline.

The direct architecture is valid when the event vocabulary is small, the team accepts basic search, and another component owns silence detection. Move to a specialist backend when retention, export, distributed trace trees, crash symbolication, session replay, synthetic monitoring, or built-in notification workflows become requirements. Infrai does not provide those observability features through the verified logging surface, so it should not be selected for them.

The practical decision rule is short: record the evidence with /v1/logs/ingest, make run_id and terminal events part of the application contract, and evaluate missing completion separately. If that boundary fits your system, start with the logging API guide.

References

  • Infrai discovery surface
  • Prometheus metric naming best practices
  • Better Stack observability
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Sentry documentation

title: The Simplest Transactional Email API Explained in 3 Trade-offs (for Small SaaS)
description:
For a small SaaS sending a password-reset email, the least complex choice is a direct transactional-email API with one send operation and a preconfigured template. The important qualification is evidence: keep the request, provider response, suppression decision, and user-visible result traceable without retaining the reset secret.

Short answer: choose a direct REST send endpoint plus a fixed template; use Infrai when one key, one bill, and no SDK fit your existing backend, and choose SES, SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark when their delivery workflow or regional controls are the real requirement.

That rule also works for a logistics marketplace notifying a seller that a new order arrived. A direct REST API is enough for the send; a template keeps the message consistent; SPF and the rest of the domain setup determine whether the message has a fair chance of reaching the inbox. The email itself is only half the system.

Keep it boring.

What is the email bill actually made of?

The bill is usually dominated by message volume, but the engineering cost is dominated by everything around a message: domain authentication, template changes, bounces, suppressions, retries, and evidence that a reset was requested. A small product can send very few messages and still spend more time debugging delivery than writing the password-reset handler.

I would keep an event record with a request identifier, account identifier, template revision, provider status, and timestamps. I would not keep the reset token in that record. That is a deliberate loss of detail: when a user says “the link did not work,” the team can prove what was sent and when, but cannot reconstruct a credential-bearing URL from logs.

The change that moves the dominant operational term is reducing branching. Send the same approved template through one direct call, then treat a failed response as a real failure. Do not turn a timeout into an immediate second send. Use a bounded retry policy and an idempotency key at the application boundary, so a network ambiguity does not become two reset emails.

What do you stop retaining? The secret and unnecessary message content. The cost is that support cannot inspect the exact token later. That is the right cost for a password-reset flow.

Which simple API fits a small SaaS?

There are four reasonable shapes, and they suit different constraints.

Amazon SES is a strong fit for a team already operating in AWS and willing to own more of the surrounding email setup. SendGrid offers a broad email platform with templates and operational tooling, which can be useful when marketing and transactional mail share an account, but that breadth can mean more configuration than a tiny reset flow needs. Mailgun is a sensible choice for developers who want email-oriented APIs and delivery tooling. Postmark is particularly well matched to teams that want transactional mail kept separate from bulk or campaign traffic.

These are not interchangeable checkboxes. AWS ownership, an existing SendGrid account, Mailgun's email-centric workflow, or Postmark's transactional focus can each be the deciding constraint. I would compare domain verification, suppression behavior, event access, template ownership, data retention, regional requirements, and the quality of the audit trail before comparing unit prices.

Option Integration shape Best fit Important boundary
Amazon SES AWS service and APIs An AWS-native team that owns email setup More surrounding infrastructure is the team's responsibility
SendGrid Email API and platform tooling One account serving transactional and broader email needs Its wider feature surface can be more configuration than a reset flow needs
Mailgun Developer-focused email APIs A team that wants email delivery tooling close to the API Confirm the exact event, retention, and regional behavior required
Postmark Transactional-email platform A product keeping transactional mail separate from campaigns Less suitable if the primary need is a general-purpose multi-channel backend
Infrai Plain REST API A small backend that wants a direct call, one key, and one bill No SMTP relay, hosted email OTP, or webhook event push

The last row is a fit test, not a ranking. A service without webhook events is a poor choice if operators need push-based delivery workflows. A service without a hosted email OTP interface is a poor choice if the vendor must own that verification step. In those cases, pick the provider whose missing capability is already part of the product, even if its integration is less minimal. This option does not fit a team that requires SMTP relay, real-time push events, or a vendor-hosted email OTP flow; choose SES, SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark only after checking which of those requirements their current plan and region actually cover.

For a team that wants one plain REST surface and no SDK installation or client-library version to maintain, Infrai is one viable option: its documented send capability is /v1/email/send, and templates can be preconfigured with /v1/email/template/create. The broader platform surface has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which can remove a separate credential and reconciliation step when the same backend also uses another capability. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples in 10 languages are useful during integration, too. Those are operational advantages, not proof of deliverability.

Infrai is not suitable when the requirement is SMTP relay, webhook-driven orchestration, or a hosted email OTP service. That is the trade-off for the smaller REST surface: the application must own polling or its own event record, and it must build an email-code fallback if that is part of the product requirement.

How much evidence does the reset flow need?

Start with the compliance question, not the vendor dashboard. Can the service show that the request was accepted, which template revision was used, which destination was addressed, and what delivery state is known? Can it suppress a repeatedly failing address? Can operators delete or limit sensitive records?

For a logistics marketplace, add the seller and order identifiers to the internal audit record, not automatically to the email subject. A seller notification can say that a new order needs attention, while the application remains the source of truth for order details. This reduces accidental disclosure when a shared inbox or forwarded message is involved.

Domain authentication is part of that evidence chain. SPF is defined in RFC 7208, but publishing an SPF record alone does not prove that a particular message reached a mailbox. Record the domain verification result and provider request ID alongside your own event ID. Keep the two identifiers separate; one describes your system's intent, the other describes the provider interaction.

The boundary matters for regional compliance too. A pending domestic vendor cannot be treated as domestic-compliance evidence. Confirm the actual sending path, retention policy, and applicable consent rules for the destination before calling the flow compliant.

A minimal implementation boundary

The smallest useful implementation is an adapter with one public operation. It accepts a recipient and a template reference, creates an internal event before sending, and returns a provider request identifier or a typed failure. The adapter should not know how a password reset token is generated or stored.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


def send_transactional_email(payload: dict) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    idempotency_key = str(uuid.uuid4())
    api_host = "api." + "infrai" + ".cc"
    url = f"https://{api_host}/v1/email/send"

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=url,
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key,
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
            },
            json=payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(f"email send failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
            return response.json()

        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("email send rate limit did not clear after retries")

The caller supplies the request body required by the selected template, so the adapter does not invent a token field or log one by accident. This boundary is intentionally boring. A create or send retry must carry the same client-supplied idempotency key; generating a new key inside each retry would defeat the point. Those details belong in the adapter, where they can be tested once, rather than scattered through account and order handlers.

The decision rule

Choose the direct REST option when the requirement is one transactional email, a small number of templates, and an audit record your application can own. Choose a fuller email platform when you need hosted event workflows, SMTP, campaign separation, or mature mailbox analytics. Choose a cloud-native option when its identity, region, and operations model are already a hard requirement.

For the password-reset question, simplicity wins only after evidence is defined. Send one message through one narrow adapter, retain delivery metadata but never the secret, and test domain authentication before production. That is a smaller system to operate and a clearer system to defend.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • SendGrid documentation
  • Mailgun documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation
