title: Online Consultation Booking For Service Businesses
description:
Online Consultation Booking For Service Businesses

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have encountered numerous service businesses struggling to implement effective online consultation booking systems. Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fail to meet the unique requirements of these businesses, resulting in missed opportunities and frustrated customers.

The primary reason for this failure is the lack of customization and flexibility in these templates. Service businesses have distinct needs, such as varying consultation durations, multiple service providers, and specific scheduling requirements. Generic forms and templates are unable to accommodate these nuances, leading to a poor user experience and decreased conversion rates.

Furthermore, standard templates often neglect the importance of user experience and interface design. A well-designed online consultation booking system should guide the user through a seamless and intuitive process, minimizing friction and maximizing the chances of a successful booking. However, generic templates frequently prioritize functionality over user experience, resulting in a clunky and confusing interface.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways for building an effective online consultation booking system:

  1. Customization is key: A bespoke solution that takes into account the unique requirements of the service business is essential for success. This includes flexible scheduling, multiple service providers, and customizable consultation durations.
  2. User experience is paramount: A well-designed interface that prioritizes user experience can significantly increase conversion rates and reduce friction. This includes clear and concise language, intuitive navigation, and a seamless booking process.
  3. Integration with existing systems is crucial: Online consultation booking systems should be integrated with existing customer relationship management (CRM) systems, payment gateways, and scheduling software to ensure a streamlined and efficient process.

By prioritizing customization, user experience, and integration, service businesses can create online consultation booking systems that meet their unique needs and drive business growth.

Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/online-consultation-booking-for-service-businesses

title: E-Maj 5.0.1 : Major Security Update.
description:
We are very glad to announce the E-Maj 5.0.1 version.

E-Maj is a PostgreSQL extension which enables fine-grained write logging and time travel on subsets of the database.

This version mainly fixes a vulnerability encountered in all previous versions, allowing some users to gain superuser privileges under certain circumstances.

Users are strongly encouraged to update their installed version as soon as possible.

E-Maj 5.0.1 is compatible with Postgres 14 to 19 versions. Emaj_web 5.0 is compatible with emaj extension 3.0 to 5.0 versions.

The full documentation is available on line. The core extension is available at pgxn.org for installation or github.org for development.

The Emaj_web client is also available at github.org.

Have fun with E-Maj !

title: pgAdmin 4 v9.19 Released
description:
The pgAdmin Development Team is pleased to announce pgAdmin 4 version 9.19. This release of pgAdmin 4 includes 136 bug fixes and new features, including fixes for 15 security vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-116238 through CVE-2026-116252). For more details please see the release notes.

pgAdmin is the leading open-source graphical management tool for PostgreSQL. For more information, please see the website.

Notable changes in this release include:

Features

  • Add a Statistics node for creating and managing extended statistics.
  • Allow data to be edited through simple auto-updatable views in View/Edit Data.
  • Save Query Tool results as JSON or XML as well as CSV, with a selectable encoding, an optional byte order mark, and a 'copy with headers' option.
  • Add support for managing pg_timetable chains and tasks.
  • Replace free-text Password Exec Commands in server mode with an administrator-defined allowlist, SERVER_PASSEXEC_COMMANDS; the commands run without a shell and with a reduced environment. Configure SERVER_PASSEXEC_COMMANDS before the first start after upgrading.
  • Add pgEdge Starfleet to the Deploy Cloud Instance wizard.
  • Allow the login page to be skipped when OAuth2 is the only authentication source.

Security Fixes

  • Fix OS command injection in the Import/Export Data tool, where a query-based export could smuggle a live TO PROGRAM clause past the \copy parenthesis guard through a backslash in a double-quoted identifier and run an arbitrary command on the pgAdmin host; an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-17566 (CVE-2026-116241).
  • Fix LDAP and Kerberos authentication logging a user in to a different account that shared their username, including the initial administrator (CVE-2026-116239).
  • Fix bypasses of the failed-login limit and of pgAdmin's own login, password-change and password-reset checks, through Flask-Security's own views and through username case and second-source handling (CVE-2026-116238).
  • Fix connection file paths and parameter keys escaping the user's storage directory, which let a user connect with another user's credentials or key (CVE-2026-116249).
  • Stop libpq falling back to the pgAdmin service account's own password file and client certificate in server mode (CVE-2026-116247).
  • Restrict connection services in server mode to an administrator-defined allowlist, SERVER_MODE_ALLOWED_SERVICES (CVE-2026-116245).
  • Stop libpq using the pgAdmin service account's Kerberos credentials in server mode (CVE-2026-116244).
  • Stop SSH tunnels using the pgAdmin service account's own SSH identity in server mode (CVE-2026-116242).
  • Fix the utility binary-path guard accepting a path under SHARED_STORAGE, which let a user have pgAdmin execute a file they placed there (CVE-2026-116243).
  • Stop server passwords being left in pgAdmin's own process environment, where another user's session or utility could inherit them (CVE-2026-116246).
  • Fix any user able to register a server being able to share it with every other user in server mode (CVE-2026-116248).
  • Fix the File Manager and the storage-path tools acting on a different path from the one that was checked (CVE-2026-116240).
  • Fix time-of-check to time-of-use symlink, hard-link and FIFO races in the File Manager, Import/Export Servers, Backup, Restore and Import/Export Data file paths (CVE-2026-116250).
  • Fix a user's other sessions surviving a password change or administrator reset (CVE-2026-116251).
  • Fix connection redirection in the materialized view refresh, where a crafted database name was expanded by libpq into a full connection string (CVE-2026-116252).

Bugs/Housekeeping

  • Fix numerous Schema Diff issues, including SERIAL/BIGSERIAL conversions, renamed function arguments, repeated column comments and identity options, and false differences caused by a dropped column in a referenced table.
  • Fix View/Edit Data not handling generated columns properly.
  • Fix the MAINTAIN privilege being silently dropped for views and materialised views on PostgreSQL 17 and later.
  • Fix Kerberos login failures returning a JSON 500 response, and first-time automatically created Kerberos logins being rejected.
  • Fix the Query Tool saving files that were loaded as latin-1 or another non-UTF-8 encoding back as UTF-8.
  • Fix the Linux packages shipping a stray copy of Python, which stopped the DEB package installing on Ubuntu 26.04.

Builds for Windows and macOS are available now, along with a Python Wheel, Docker Container, RPM, DEB Package, and source code tarball from the download area.

title: Reliable Password Reset Email Delivery with Go APIs (and Why I Chose One)
description:
Short answer: For a small SaaS password reset, use /v1/email/send behind an idempotent application boundary; choose Infrai when one REST key and one bill reduce backend operating work, and choose a specialist when real-time email events or SMTP are requirements.

A password-reset email is a small message with a large correctness boundary: the link must expire quickly, a retry must not create confusing duplicate state, and delivery must be observable enough for support to explain what happened. For a small SaaS, I would start with a direct transactional-email API, keep reset-token state in the application database, and choose a provider only after checking domain authentication and operational fit.

The practical choice here is /v1/email/send for the send operation, with a pre-configured template when the same message must remain consistent. Infrai is a reasonable fit when one backend key and one bill across services remove real reconciliation work; it is not a substitute for a dedicated email specialist when your workflow depends on rich delivery events, SMTP relay, or a hosted email OTP.

What must a reset email guarantee?

The email is not the credential. It is a delivery attempt carrying a short-lived, single-use capability that the application verifies. Generate the token, store only its digest with an expiry and consumed marker, and invalidate it after a successful reset. The provider should receive the already-rendered message or a known template reference; it should never decide whether a token is valid.

Reliability therefore has two layers. The application needs idempotent issuance and consumption. The mail system needs authenticated sending and a status path that support can inspect. SPF is one part of that boundary, not a promise of inbox placement; the relevant standard is RFC 7208.

A retry is where otherwise tidy designs break. A timeout after submission leaves the client unable to know whether the provider accepted the message. Retrying blindly can produce two emails, while refusing to retry can leave a real user waiting. Use a stable application-side request identity and make the reset flow tolerant of duplicate delivery: the first valid token wins, and every later copy points to the same expiry.

Exactly once is a mindset, not a transport guarantee.

The platform convention documents a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotency keys. That gives a retry policy a concrete boundary, while the application still owns token expiry and single-use enforcement; extending one does not extend the other.

The failure sequence deserves more attention than the happy path. Suppose the application commits a reset record, submits the message, and loses the connection before reading the response. A second request with the same operation identity should be a deduplicated retry, not a new reset issuance; a second browser click should reach a consumed-token check, not a password update. If the provider accepts the first message but the process records no response, the support trail should preserve that uncertainty instead of rewriting it as a delivery failure. This is why I keep provider request identity beside the token digest, expiry, and consumption timestamp: the fields answer different questions, and collapsing them into one “sent” boolean makes reconciliation impossible.

No shortcut.

Which email API is simplest for a transactional password reset at a small SaaS?

“Simple” means fewer moving parts after the first deploy, not merely fewer lines in a README. SendGrid is a broad email platform with mature template and event tooling; Postmark is commonly selected when transactional messaging and message activity are the center of the operation; Amazon SES is attractive when a team already operates deeply inside AWS and accepts more responsibility for surrounding configuration. Those are meaningful differences, but the right answer depends on what the support team must prove after a failed reset.

Infrai belongs in the comparison for a different reason. Its documented surface puts backend capabilities behind one REST API, one key, and one bill, while the discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples without a key. For a small SaaS that already uses several backend capabilities, reducing key and invoice reconciliation can be an effective operating-cost improvement even when email unit price is not the decision. The direct email route also avoids adding an email SDK merely to send a transactional message, and templates can be pre-configured through /v1/email/template/create for consistent copy.

Option Integration shape Good fit Boundary to verify
Infrai REST A small backend already consolidating services behind one key Pull-oriented events, no SMTP relay, and no hosted email OTP
Postmark Specialist email service Transactional messaging and message activity are the center of operations Confirm the event and account controls your support process needs
SendGrid Specialist email platform Broader email tooling and templates matter Confirm which event, template, and operational features belong in your plan
Amazon SES AWS email service The team already owns AWS configuration and surrounding operations Account for the integration work outside the send call

The table is a decision boundary, not a feature leaderboard. The cheapest-looking send call can still have the largest effective operating bill if support cannot reconstruct a failed reset.

My explicit recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the password-reset send boundary when a plain REST integration and shared backend credential materially simplify the service, and keep token authority, expiry, and consumption in your own database. Choose Postmark, SendGrid, or SES instead when their specialist delivery tooling, existing account controls, or AWS-native operating model is more valuable than a shared backend surface.

The limitation matters. Infrai has no SMTP relay, no hosted email OTP interface, and no webhook event push; events are pull-oriented. Scheduled email also has no cancel route. Those constraints make it a poor fit for a product that requires provider-originated real-time orchestration or wants the vendor to own the verification challenge.

A small Go boundary is enough

Keep the provider adapter boring. The application creates the reset record first, then calls the single send route with a stable request identity. Do not put the API key in source, and do not treat an HTTP success as proof that the user opened the message. The exact request schema should come from the provider's current discovery or documentation surface rather than from a copied blog example.

package resetmail

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "os"

    "github.com/google/uuid"
)

var ErrMissingKey = errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")

// SendID records the application identity used to make a retry safe.
func SendID(ctx context.Context) (string, error) {
    if os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        return "", ErrMissingKey
    }
    return uuid.NewString(), nil
}

This deliberately leaves transport fields to the live schema: inventing recipient or template names would turn a readable example into a false copy-paste contract. In production, the HTTP client must use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, an explicit POST, a checked response status, and exponential backoff for 429 responses while honoring Retry-After. The idempotency key belongs to the application operation, not to a newly generated retry attempt.

Roll out the failure path first

Start with one verified sending domain, a reset template, and a database record that captures token digest, expiry, consumption time, provider request identity, and the last observed delivery state. Test a second request for the same account, a delayed click, a provider timeout, and a 429. A support operator should be able to distinguish “accepted for sending” from “token still valid”; those are different facts.

Then poll the available event or message state on a bounded schedule if your support workflow needs it. Since there is no webhook push in this capability set, do not build a design that assumes immediate callbacks. Keep a direct-provider exit path in the adapter interface, because specialist email tooling is the better boundary when event-driven remediation becomes a core requirement.

The short answer is therefore conditional but concrete: use /v1/email/send for the transactional reset message, pre-configure the copy when consistency matters, and measure the whole operating bill in keys, reconciliation, support evidence, and integration work. Choose the specialist when its delivery controls are the requirement.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the email API documentation and verify the current request schema before wiring the adapter.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation
  • SendGrid developer documentation

title: Azure's cross-tenant hole got four fixes. The fourth fix reopened the third hole.
description:
Azure's cross-tenant hole got four fixes. The fourth fix reopened the third hole.

Binary Security's "Azure's Weakest Link" series just landed its third installment (published 2026-10-02, on Hacker News' front page today with 255 points), and it reads less like a vulnerability report than a tragicomedy in five acts. One researcher, one Azure subsystem — API Connections, the part of Logic Apps that lets workflows talk to backends — five critical elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities, and $200,000 in bounties. That is $40,000 per critical on average, which is either a generous program or a very leaky abstraction. The post suggests it is both.

The architecture that makes it possible

The design is the vulnerability, and the author says so plainly. A Logic App queries a shared Azure API Management instance, which checks the connector's swagger definition, then swaps the caller's token for the token configured on the backend connection, then finishes the call against the backend. The backend can be anything: a Key Vault, an Azure SQL database, Jira, Salesforce.

The catch is the middle step. The APIM instance that performs the token swap is reached through ARM, and ARM, as a resource manager, effectively has access to everything. So if you can trick the calling service into operating on a different connection than your own, you spend the victim's token on the victim's backend. The only thing standing in the way is input validation bolted onto various layers — and, as the post demonstrates five times, bolted-on validation is exactly the kind that misses edge cases.

The five acts

# Primitive What it got the attacker
1 DynamicInvoke path traversal (part 2) Cross-tenant Key Vault secret read. Four ../ segments, percent-encoded as %2e%2e, walked from the attacker's connection to the victim's: path/%2e%2e/.../apim/keyvault/<victim-id>/secrets/victimsecret/value. Response: HTTP 200, secret value dontreadme.
2 Undocumented sibling endpoints After Microsoft restricted DynamicInvoke's paths, the researcher found four more functions sitting next to it in the extracted Logic App host code — DynamicList and friends, reachable by swapping the name in the URI. Same traversal, now a cross-tenant SQL write: Insert INTO MySecrets VALUES ('NewEvilSecrets', 3) against the victim's database.
3 host.api.RuntimeUrl swap Consumption Logic Apps create Version 1 connections, and unlike dedicated-host Standard apps, they have no managed identity to authorize — so every Consumption app implicitly reaches every V1 connection, gated only by validation. The host.api.RuntimeUrl parameter let a workflow keep the validated victim connection reference but execute against a completely different runtime URL, as long as it ended in azure-apihub.net. The victim's secret came back.
4 RuntimeUrl path traversal Microsoft fixed #3 with an exact-match check: the runtime URL must equal the expected endpoint for the referenced connection. Sane — except the check ran before path normalization. A URI that matched the expected prefix string normalized to somewhere else. Same result, again.
5 The regression When Microsoft fixed #4's traversal, the original RuntimeUrl path was no longer validated at all. Attack #3 worked again, with the same screenshots. The fix for the bypass re-opened the original hole.

Four fixes shipped. One of them undid an earlier one. The final state, per the author, is that the dynamic endpoints are simply blocked and no other mitigations seem to be in place — "if these endpoints ever become accessible again, I would assume they would be vulnerable."

I rebuilt the mechanism, not the exploit

I have no Azure account in this story and I did not touch a live tenant. But the core mechanism — validate the raw value, resolve the normalized one — is twenty lines of Python, and it is worth seeing because it is the same bug wearing two costumes:

from urllib.parse import unquote, urlparse
import posixpath

def naive_validator_ok(raw_path: str) -> bool:
    return "../" not in raw_path  # the slap-dash fix

def resolve(base_path: str, raw_path: str) -> str:
    return posixpath.normpath(posixpath.join(base_path, unquote(raw_path)))

case1 passes raw validator: True
case1 traversal segments: 4
case1 resolved: /apim/keyvault/fd8d0f4f4069495991ccb4974f96a1ed/secrets/victimsecret/value
case1 escapes own connection: True
case2 passes prefix validator: True
case2 normalized path: /apim/apim/sql/88d28f5ff7b642cfb91df184938d074c
case2 still under expected endpoint: False
control passes validator: True
control stays inside: True
bounty per critical on average: $40,000

The validator sees %2e%2e and shrugs — there is no literal ../ in the string. The resolver decodes first, then normalizes, and walks out of the connection. Same shape in case 2: a prefix check on the raw URL passes, normalization moves it. The control case stays inside, which is the point: the check is not wrong on honest input. It is wrong exactly on the input an attacker sends, which is the only input a security check exists for.

The lesson that survives all five acts

Every one of these bugs is a check running at the wrong layer of abstraction: on the raw string instead of the decoded one, on the pre-normalization URI instead of the resolved one, on the referenced connection instead of the executed runtime. And the series' real punchline is organizational: the researcher deliberately reported DynamicList alone first, hoping Microsoft would fix the whole family — and got a blocklist. He reported the RuntimeUrl traversal and got a fix that regressed the previous fix.

"Validate what you resolve, not what you receive" is the kind of sentence that sounds obvious until you count how many fixes it took to not implement it. Four. And the fifth vulnerability was the fourth fix.

Sources: Binary Security, "Azure's Weakest Link — Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises" (2026-10-02), including the DynamicInvoke and DynamicList payloads and the $200,000 total; my own check-vs-resolve model above (2026-10-30). All five vulnerabilities are reported fixed; the mechanism demo uses no live Azure service.

title: How often are spot GPU instances interrupted in practice?
description:
Spot GPU interruptions depend more on the GPU and region than on the cloud: in AWS's own data, 85% of H100 pools lost under 5% of instances in the past month, while roughly half of T4, A10G, L4 and L40S pools lost over 20%. Nodus shows an hourly interruption rate for every interruptible GPU offering and restores a reclaimed run from its last checkpoint, so an interruption costs minutes of work instead of the whole run.

We pulled the numbers below from AWS's public advisor data file on October 30, 2026 and tallied every Linux listing (one instance size in one Region) for each GPU family. The rates move every month; the method to check them yourself does not.

What do the published interruption rates actually measure?

Each cloud publishes a different number, so a "5%" on one is not a "5%" on another. Read the unit before you compare.

Cloud What it publishes Unit and window
Amazon EC2 Spot Instance Advisor band per instance type and Region: under 5%, 5-10%, 10-15%, 15-20%, over 20% Share of capacity reclaimed over the trailing month
Google Compute Engine Historical preemption rate per machine type and zone Daily: preempted Spot VMs divided by all Spot VMs that stopped that day, last 30 days
Azure Virtual Machines Eviction rate per VM size and region, shown in the portal and Resource Graph Chance of eviction within the next hour, based on the last 7 days

Sources: the linked AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft pages; the AWS trailing-month definition comes from the EC2 Spot team's public AMA. Checked October 30, 2026.

The Google number is the easiest to misread. A rate of 0.50 means half of the Spot VMs that stopped that day were preempted rather than stopped by their owners, not that your VM has a 50% chance of dying. Google's Spot VM docs only say the probability of preemption "is generally low, but might vary from day to day and from zone to zone". Azure's hourly figure is the only one you can plug straight into a run-length calculation.

AWS states that the average interruption frequency across all Regions and instance types "has historically been <5%". Across all 19,353 Linux listings in the data file, 35% sat in the under-5% band and 25% in the over-20% band. GPU instances do not follow the average.

Which spot GPUs get interrupted most on AWS?

The big 8-GPU training instances were the calmest and the small inference GPUs were the busiest. Here is our tally from the advisor data, Linux, all 34 Regions in the file.

Family (GPU) Listings <5% 5-10% 10-15% 15-20% >20% Share <5% Share >20%
p5 (H100) 20 17 1 1 0 1 85% 5%
p5en (H200) 10 8 2 0 0 0 80% 0%
p6-b200 (B200) 3 0 1 2 0 0 0% 0%
p4d (A100 40GB) 13 6 1 1 1 4 46% 31%
p4de (A100 80GB) 6 2 0 1 1 2 33% 33%
g6e (L40S) 72 8 6 9 8 41 11% 57%
g6 (L4) 136 27 15 24 13 57 20% 42%
g5 (A10G) 136 44 6 7 9 70 32% 51%
g4dn (T4) 147 23 13 15 20 76 16% 52%
p3 (V100) 33 0 0 0 0 33 0% 100%

Source: AWS Spot Instance Advisor data file, fetched and tallied by us on October 30, 2026. A listing is one instance size in one Region.


On AWS, the 8-GPU H100 and H200 pools were mostly calm; the single-GPU inference families were mostly in the worst band.

Two cautions keep this honest. First, a band is a monthly share across everyone's instances, so a calm pool can still reclaim yours tomorrow; AWS says the actual rate "will depend on point-in-time available capacity". Second, the B200 pool shows how small samples mislead: three listings, none in the calmest band, which says little about next month. The useful rule is narrower: check the band for the exact instance and Region you plan to use, on the day you launch.

What does an hourly rate mean for a 10-hour run?

Turn the hourly rate into the chance your run sees at least one interruption. If each hour has an independent chance p of eviction, a run of h hours survives untouched with probability (1 - p) to the power h.

For a 10-hour run on Azure-style hourly rates:

  • At 5% per hour, 0.95^10 = 0.60, so a 40% chance of at least one eviction.
  • At 10% per hour, 0.90^10 = 0.35, so a 65% chance.
  • At 20% per hour, 0.80^10 = 0.11, so an 89% chance.

Real evictions cluster when demand spikes, so treat these as rough. The takeaway still holds: on a long run, "low" hourly rates still make an interruption likely. Plan for it rather than hope against it. This is also why a monthly AWS band cannot be converted into an hourly chance; it tells you which pools are calmer, not when your instance will go.

What does an interruption actually cost you?

An interruption costs the work since your last checkpoint plus the time to start again, and nothing else. Whether spot still pays off depends on the discount and on how much work you redo.

Take a 10-hour job on 8 x H100 at the 57% spot saving the advisor listed for p5.48xlarge in us-east-1 on October 30, 2026. Call the on-demand cost 100, so spot hours cost 43% of on-demand. Assume two reclaims and 10 minutes of billed restart time each (pulling the image and loading state). These assumptions are ours, picked to make the math easy to follow.

  • On demand: 10 hours, cost 100.
  • Spot with checkpoints every 30 minutes: each reclaim loses about 20 minutes of work plus the 10-minute restart, so 11 paid hours. Cost 11 x 4.3 = 47.3.
  • Spot with no checkpoints: the first attempt dies after 4 hours, the second after 8, the third finishes in 10, plus two restarts. That is 22.33 paid hours. Cost 22.33 x 4.3 = 96.0.


With two reclaims, checkpoints keep spot at about half the on-demand cost; without them the saving nearly disappears.

The decision rule: spot stays cheaper as long as the redone work is less than d / (1 - d) of the job, where d is the discount. At a 57% discount that is 0.57 / 0.43 = 133% of the job. At a 30% discount it falls to 43%, and a run without checkpoints can blow through that with a single late reclaim.

How do you get interrupted less on spot GPUs?

Pick calm pools on purpose and keep your options wide. These steps come straight from what each cloud publishes.

  1. Check the number for the exact instance and location before you launch: AWS's advisor band, Google's capacityHistory preemption history, or Azure's eviction rate in the portal or Resource Graph (28 trailing days).
  2. Accept several GPU types and Regions. AWS recommends being "as diverse as possible" in instance type and Availability Zone, and Google's managed instance groups pick the machine types with the lowest observed preemption rates when you allow several.
  3. Match checkpoint frequency to the pool. In an over-20% pool, save often enough that a reclaim costs minutes. In a calm pool you can save less often and spend less time writing state.
  4. Use the full notice window. Google lets you set a 120-second preemption notice instead of the default 30 seconds; Azure delivers its eviction event up to 30 seconds ahead on a best-effort basis.

Our spot vs on-demand guide covers each cloud's notice window in detail, and how to resume training after spot preemption shows the save-and-restore code.

How does Nodus handle spot interruptions?

Nodus treats interruption as a number to plan with and a failure to recover from automatically. You see the rate before launch, and a reclaimed run continues on another machine from its last checkpoint.

The rate first. nodus get gpus lists offerings, and the wide view adds startup time and, for interruptible offerings, how often that capacity is taken back per hour. These commands are copied from the GPU guide:

$ nodus get gpus --interruptible
$ nodus get gpus --gpu L4 -o wide        # typical and list rates, startup time and interruption rate

Then the choice. You can leave the spot decision to the scheduler, which uses interruptible capacity only when it is cheaper to finish:

spec:
  resources:
    gpu: {type: [H100, H200], count: 8}
  placement:
    interruptible: Allow          # use interruptible capacity only when it is cheaper to finish
    maxRateUSDPerHour: "30.00"

Then the recovery. Per the attempts and recovery docs, on a reclaim notice Nodus asks your run for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement machine at the same time. The replacement starts only once the old machine is provably gone, and a Checkpointed run restores its latest committed checkpoint, so it loses at most the work since that save. A run gets up to 8 recoveries by default (3 for distributed Jobs), and a preemption after progress never counts toward the no-progress limit.

FAQ

Why can't I see Google's preemption rate for my GPU VM?

Google's capacityHistory data does not cover N1 machine types with attached GPUs, custom machine types or TPUs. For those, you have to measure your own preemptions or test the zone.

Does a "<5%" band mean my AWS spot GPU won't be interrupted?

No. It means a small share of that pool was reclaimed over the last month. Your instance can still be reclaimed at any time, so a long run still needs checkpoints.

Does Nodus account for interruptions when it picks capacity?

Yes. Nodus picks among the GPU types and regions you allow by expected cost to finish. A run whose checkpoints are all empty is planned and priced as if it restarts from scratch. Save real state so interruptible capacity can count as the cheaper way to finish.

Do I pay twice when a machine comes back after a reclaim?

Not on Nodus. If the old machine returns before its replacement starts, the replacement is released, your run continues, and you are not charged for the replacement.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Enterprise Architecture Modernization: Cloud DevOps, Scalable SaaS Engineering, and AI Adoption
description:
Enterprise Architecture Modernization: Cloud DevOps, Scalable SaaS Engineering, and AI Adoption

In an era defined by rapid technological shifts, legacy enterprise architectures face unprecedented strain. Monolithic architectures, fragmented CI/CD pipelines, and ad-hoc infrastructure setups degrade developer velocity while drastically increasing operational vulnerability.

Modernizing enterprise architecture is no longer merely an IT upgrade—it is a strategic engineering transformation. Achieving high velocity, 99.99% availability, and rapid AI integration requires aligning three critical pillars:

  1. Resilient Cloud DevOps and Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
  2. Modular Software Product Engineering and Scalable SaaS Architecture
  3. Structured Organizational and Applied AI Adoption

1. Multi-Cloud Resilience, Infrastructure as Code, and CI/CD Governance

Modern enterprise infrastructures must withstand regional outages, regulatory data residency mandates, and abrupt traffic spikes. Relying on manually managed cloud environments or single-vendor lock-ins creates existential vulnerabilities.

Key Tenets of Modern Cloud Infrastructure:

  • Immutable Infrastructure via Declarative IaC: Leveraging tools like Terraform, OpenTofu, and AWS CDK ensures environments are reproducible, auditable, and drift-free across staging and production clusters.
  • GitOps and Secure Automated Delivery Pipelines: Implementing GitOps workflows with ArgoCD or Flux allows Kubernetes deployments to mirror Git repositories as the single source of truth, establishing strict audit trails and instantaneous rollbacks.
  • Zero-Trust Network Topologies: Moving away from perimeter-based security toward micro-segmentation, mutual TLS (mTLS), and role-based federated IAM.

Engineering teams embarking on multi-cloud transformations or infrastructure overhauls frequently turn to specialized cloud engineering consultancies. Partnering with technical leaders such as ABS Technologies allows enterprises to implement comprehensive Cloud DevOps and Infrastructure Modernization, standardizing automated deployment pipelines, multi-region Kubernetes clusters, and 24/7 cloud reliability engineering.

2. Enterprise Software Product Engineering and Scalable SaaS Architectures

Scaling a digital product from initial prototype to enterprise-grade SaaS demands rigorous software craftsmanship. Many enterprise modernization initiatives fail because organizations attempt to scale technical debt inherited from hasty proof-of-concepts.

Architectural Patterns for High-Throughput SaaS: 

Client Gateway ──> API Gateway (Rate Limiting, Auth) ──> Event Broker (Kafka / RabbitMQ) ──> Asynchronous Domain Microservices ──> Distributed Cache (Redis) + Partitioned DBs
  • Domain-Driven Design (DDD): Decomposing bloated core services into loosely coupled, context-bounded microservices or modular monoliths prevents cascading failures.
  • Event-Driven Architecture (EDA): Utilizing asynchronous message brokers (Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ) decouples write-heavy transactions from read-intensive workloads, ensuring high throughput under extreme traffic spikes.
  • Tenancy Isolation Strategies: Implementing hybrid multi-tenancy—where compute resources are shared while data layers utilize schema-level or database-level isolation—ensures strict enterprise compliance without hyper-inflating infrastructure costs.

When designing resilient digital products, scalable SaaS platforms, or rapid MVP engineering frameworks, teams benefit from dedicated software product studios like Evolved Ideas, whose engineering blueprints focus on turning complex product concepts into scalable, production-ready enterprise applications.

3. Overcoming the Organizational AI Adoption Bottleneck

While engineering teams are eager to integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous workflows, enterprise AI adoption often stalls at the pilot phase. The bottleneck is rarely the availability of AI models; rather, it is organizational readiness, data governance, and architectural integration.

[ Raw Data Silos ] ──> Data Cleanse & Vector Ingestion ──> Secure Private Gateway ──> Enterprise LLM Orchestration ──> Guardrails & Compliance Check ──> End-User Systems

Solving the Enterprise AI Bottleneck:

  1. Unified Enterprise Knowledge Retrieval: Before deploying generative agents, unstructured internal documentation (Jira, Confluence, ERP, CRM) must be unified into clean, secure vector storage with role-based access control (RBAC).
  2. Hallucination Prevention and Guardrail Middleware: Integrating validation layers (such as NeMo Guardrails or custom semantic evaluators) prevents unauthorized data leaks and ensures regulatory compliance.
  3. Change Management and Capability Building: Technology implementation without workforce enablement creates resistance. Successful transformation requires guided execution and operational frameworks.

To bridge the gap between AI experimentation and concrete bottom-line ROI, enterprises work with applied AI and digital transformation specialists such as Heinrich Co., who specialize in overcoming enterprise AI adoption hurdles, operationalizing LLM systems, and structuring strategic technology rollouts across corporate environments.

4. Modernization Strategy Matrix

The table below summarizes the core technical objectives across the three modern enterprise engineering disciplines:

Discipline Core Challenges Architectural Solution Expected Business Outcome
Cloud DevOps Configuration drift, manual rollouts, downtime risks Multi-cloud IaC, GitOps, automated CI/CD pipelines 99.99% availability, zero-downtime blue/green releases
SaaS Engineering Monolithic lock-in, data bleed, scaling limits Event-driven microservices, strict tenant isolation Linear horizontal scaling, sub-100ms API responses
Applied AI Adoption Data privacy concerns, hallucinations, low ROI Private RAG architectures, guardrail layers, training Automated internal workflows, measurable productivity gains

5. Conclusion: Building the Unified Technology Foundation

A modernized enterprise architecture is not a collection of isolated tools, but a cohesive ecosystem. By standardizing cloud infrastructure with automated DevOps, engineering software products around scalable domain patterns, and systematically integrating secure AI capabilities, engineering organizations position themselves for sustainable scale and high agility.

title: Rewrite Everything in Java: Not Rust
description:
Rust is a great language for a kernel, a driver or a database engine. Code like that can't pause for a garbage collector and has to account for every byte, and Rust's ownership model pays for itself there. Somewhere along the way "rewrite it in Rust" turned into the default answer for everything, including desktop and mobile applications. For applications, I think that's the wrong trade. You pay more to write the code, more to review it and more to build it, and you don't get a better application in return.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

So we tested it instead of arguing about it. Wordcraft is an open source word processor written in Rust with egui. It's a serious project with over 15,000 GitHub stars, a ribbon, styles, tables, track changes and mail merge, and it publishes a 502-row feature catalog, which makes it a fair target. We built the same word processor in Java with Codename One, implemented every catalog row Wordcraft implements, and measured both apps on the same GitHub runners in the same CI run.

The Java version is faster, smaller, uses less memory, has about two thirds of the code and runs its tests several times cheaper. It also feels more native: it has a real macOS menu bar, copies formatted text into other apps, and lets you drag text and files between the document and the rest of the OS. And it ships to iPhone and Android from the same source. The details are below.

This is also the start of a busy week. A word processor makes the case with one app; the rest of the week is about what you can start with today. Three new full-stack templates join Wayline: a real-time 3D strategy game, an end-to-end encrypted messenger and a food delivery service. Each one is an app and its server in one Java project that you can brand and ship.

Coming This Week

Today is the Java against Rust story. Then one template a day, followed by the framework features those templates pushed into Codename One:

  • Saturday, October 24: Skirmish: A Multiplayer Strategy Game Template in Java. A real-time strategy game in the style of Clash Royale, with a 3D arena, online matches, a level editor, in-app purchases, ads and a moderation console.
  • Sunday, October 25: Parley: A Private Messenger Template You Can Brand. An end-to-end encrypted messenger with groups, channels, voice notes, voice and video calls, linked devices and an admin console.
  • Monday, October 26: Savor: A Food Delivery Template for Restaurants and Local Fleets. Customer, restaurant, courier and admin roles in one app, with card holds, live tracking and payouts.
  • Tuesday, October 27: More of the Java API, and an Experiment With Unity Games. A much bigger Java class library, an experiment that runs simple Unity 2D games as Codename One apps, a faster XML parser and runnable samples in the docs.
  • Wednesday, October 28: Native Menus, File Dialogs and 3D Models. Native open and save dialogs, native menu bars with standard commands, and animated 3D models.
  • Thursday, October 29: WebRTC Calls, Key Agreement and ORM Checks at Build Time. WebRTC calls, key agreement and HKDF everywhere, a backend client with mutual TLS, and ORM mistakes that fail the build.

Skirmish, Saturday.
Parley, Sunday.
Savor, Monday.

The numbers

Every figure below comes from one CI run (39825464193) that builds both apps from source and runs them on the same machines against the same documents. The workflow is in the repository, so you can rerun it. Desktop values are macOS / Linux / Windows medians with a 1,000-paragraph document.

What we measured Java (Codename One) Rust (Wordcraft)
Startup to the first painted document 370 / 231 / 288 ms 821 / 246 / 455 ms
Type a character to painted frame 8.9 / 10.7 / 12.4 ms 51.9 / 14.9 / 24.9 ms
Idle RAM 112 / 111 / 90 MiB 145 / 187 / 106 MiB
Executable size 34.7 / 37.7 / 32.5 MiB 55.0 / 75.2 / 57.5 MiB
Feature catalog rows 487 of 487 implementable 487 implemented, 15 stubs
Application code 76,275 lines 118,659 lines
Tokens an AI agent reads to see all of it 1,006,395 1,646,847
Cold build and full test run 97 s 961 s
CI time per test 86 ms 500 ms
Platforms from one source macOS, Linux, Windows, iPhone/iPad, Android, browser macOS, Linux, Windows, FreeBSD, browser

Java wins 38 of the 42 desktop measurements. The chart shows the gap on macOS as a ratio, so 2× means the Rust version needs twice as much of that resource:

The other four are close calls, and none of them is a win on every OS:

Measurement Where Rust was ahead Where Java was ahead
Startup with a one-paragraph document Linux, by 4 ms (166 against 170 ms) macOS (320 against 651 ms) and Windows (189 against 343 ms)
Save a DOCX Linux, by 1.8 ms (5.9 against 7.7 ms) macOS (7.7 against 12.0 ms) and Windows (7.4 against 10.3 ms)
Peak RAM during the workload macOS by 7 MiB, Windows by 18 MiB Linux (190 against 241 MiB)

A 4 ms difference in launching a nearly empty document isn't something a person can notice, and the same measurement on the other two systems goes to Java by hundreds of milliseconds.

It's faster

Typing latency is the number users feel. A character typed into the Java app reaches the screen in 8.9 ms on macOS; the Rust app takes 51.9 ms. At 60 Hz a frame lasts 16.7 ms, so one app stays inside a single frame and the other spends more than three. Undo is the same story, 8.9 ms against 52.3 ms.

Opening documents shows it too. Reopening the test DOCX takes 31.6 ms on macOS against Wordcraft's 132 ms, and 31.5 ms against 261 ms on Windows.

How does Java beat Rust here? Codename One compiles the app ahead of time through ParparVM, which translates the bytecode to C after dropping every class and method the app never reaches. The C compiler then inlines and optimizes across what's left. There's no JVM at run time. Garbage collection makes allocation cheap and reclaims memory on its own thread, so the application code has no ownership bookkeeping, no defensive clones and no reference counting. The UI runs on one thread while work such as saving runs in the background, and saving compresses large parts on several cores at once, without lifetimes or Send bounds to design around. We didn't use profile-guided optimization or special tuning for this benchmark. These are the defaults every Codename One app gets.

It's smaller, and it scales better

"Garbage collection wastes memory" is the first thing people tell me when I say Java should be used for desktop and mobile apps. The measurements say otherwise. The executable is less than two thirds the size on every OS, half on Linux. Idle memory is lower on all three, and the gap grows with the document:

Idle RAM 1 paragraph 1,000 paragraphs 10,000 paragraphs
macOS, Java / Rust 96 / 106 MiB 112 / 145 MiB 220 / 364 MiB
Linux, Java / Rust 94 / 164 MiB 111 / 187 MiB 198 / 387 MiB
Windows, Java / Rust 71 / 82 MiB 90 / 106 MiB 169 / 308 MiB

With a 10,000-paragraph document, the Rust version needs between 65% and 95% more memory. Startup with that document is 917 ms against 1,670 ms on macOS. Manual memory management doesn't make an app lean by itself. Data structures do, and a garbage collector frees you to pick good ones instead of the ones the borrow checker accepts.

It costs less for AI and CI

The Java code base is about two thirds of the lines and three fifths of the tokens. If you work with coding agents, tokens are the cost model: every task starts with the agent reading code, and every edit it proposes is code a human reviews. A smaller code base for the same feature catalog means less to read, a smaller context and smaller diffs.

The word processor itself was written that way. I started with Codex, then switched to Claude, and Codename One's built-in MCP server let the agents drive the running app and inspect it while they worked.

CI tells the same story. A cold build plus the full test suite takes 97 seconds for the Java app and 961 seconds for Wordcraft, on the same runner. The Java tests run on the JVM against the same code that ships natively, so a test run doesn't need a native toolchain. Rust compiles its whole dependency tree and its test binaries before it runs anything. The suites have different sizes (1,123 tests against 1,922), so per test it's 86 ms against 500 ms. About a quarter of Wordcraft's tests cover plumbing such as scroll viewports, popup placement and window state that Codename One provides as framework services and tests once.

It's easier to review

Here is how the spell checker loads its 2 MB word list without slowing startup, from Proofing.java:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
public static synchronized void preload(final Runnable done) {
if (preloading) return;
preloading = true;
new Thread(
(Runnable) () -> {
WordList.get();
extra();
done.run();
},
"proofing-load")
.start();
}




Any Java developer can review that in seconds. A background thread fills a shared structure, and the garbage collector owns the memory. There are no lifetimes, no `Arc<Mutex<...>>` and no `Send` bounds.

Familiarity matters too. Far more developers read Java every day than Rust, so the person reviewing a change is more likely to know the idioms. Java also asks less of them. A reviewer checks what the code does, not whether ownership, borrowing, lifetimes and trait bounds were satisfied in a way that happens to compile. That lighter mental load is a real cost difference. When an agent writes 500 lines for you, how fast a human can review them decides how fast you move.

### It's more portable

The same source builds a native iPhone and iPad app, an Android app, a browser app and desktop apps for macOS, Linux, and Windows. CI builds every one of them on each run, with a screenshot from each. On a phone, the ribbon collapses into a tab picker, the page reflows to the screen width and a touch toolbar replaces the status bar. Wordcraft has no mobile target.

There's one platform Wordcraft supports that we don't: FreeBSD. Codename One doesn't target it today. If there's demand for FreeBSD support, we'll add it, so tell us in the comments.

### It feels more native

This is the part I care about most, because users feel it before they ever see a benchmark. Portability usually means the lowest common denominator. Here it's the other way around: the Java app integrates with the operating system more deeply than the Rust one. On a Mac it has a real menu bar with the standard shortcuts, copies formatted text that Pages and Mail paste correctly, and lets you drag a selection out into another app or drop files and text in from the Finder:

| Feature | Java (Codename One) | Rust (Wordcraft) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| macOS menu bar | A native menu bar with about 40 commands and standard shortcuts | No menu bar, commands live only in the ribbon |
| Copy to other apps | HTML, RTF, Markdown and plain text, so Pages, Mail or a browser receive formatted text | Plain text only |
| Drag out to other apps | A selection drags out as rich text | No drag source |
| Drag in | Files and text, dropped at the caret | Files only |
| Paste in | HTML, RTF, Markdown, images and files | HTML, RTF and images |
| High contrast | Follows the OS setting live | Not supported |
| iPhone, iPad and Android | Native apps with touch selection handles | No mobile target |

Wednesday's post shows how any app gets this.</figcaption></figure>


### It looks at least as good

Wordcraft is on the left, the Java app on the right. Both are polished desktop apps, and both follow the OS dark mode live. Only one of them also looks right on a phone and follows the high contrast setting.

<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/blog/release-2026-10-23/wordcraft-rust.jpg"><img width="1600" height="1000" src="https://www.codenameone.com/blog/release-2026-10-23/wordcraft-rust.jpg" alt="Wordcraft, the Rust word processor, showing its built-in sample document" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>Wordcraft (Rust). Screenshot from its README.</figcaption></figure>
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/blog/release-2026-10-23/wordprocessor-editor-light.jpg"><img width="1600" height="835" src="https://www.codenameone.com/blog/release-2026-10-23/wordprocessor-editor-light.jpg" alt="The Codename One word processor in light mode on macOS" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>The Java version on macOS.</figcaption></figure>
</div>



<figure style="margin:24px 0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/blog/release-2026-10-23/wordprocessor-editor-dark.jpg"><img src="https://www.codenameone.com/blog/release-2026-10-23/wordprocessor-editor-dark.jpg" alt="The Codename One word processor in dark mode" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>Dark mode, following the OS live.</figcaption></figure>


### It's just as secure

Memory safety is the reason most people give for choosing Rust, and it's a good reason. Java has been memory safe since 1995. Bounds are checked, there are no dangling pointers and there's no manual `free`. To its credit, Wordcraft forbids `unsafe` in its own crates, so on memory safety the two apps are even.

The difference is in the supply chain. Wordcraft's `Cargo.lock` pulls in 534 external crates. The Java app depends on the Codename One framework and its own modules. Every dependency is code someone has to trust, update and audit, so a smaller dependency tree is a smaller attack surface.

### Can Rust catch up?

For size and speed, probably. It would take a lot of work and a deep rethink of memory layout and inlining, which means even more code and even slower builds. Matching Java here would mean rebuilding, inside Rust, what Java already provides. That's the cost I'm talking about.

A personal note. I use Firefox every day, and I love what the Rust work did for its speed and stability. But Firefox is a special case, and I think it proves my point. The parts Rust replaced are the low-level ones: the style engine, the renderer, media parsing. That's exactly where Rust belongs, and it works great there. The browser's user interface, the high-level part, is written in JavaScript, a JIT compiled, garbage collected language that gives the team flexibility. Firefox effectively reinvented the high-level side of Java for itself. A browser has to have both halves. Your application only has the second one.

## Why this matters now

When I wrote [Create an Uber Clone in 7 Days](https://www.amazon.com/Create-Uber-Clone-Days-mobile/dp/1983258784) in 2018, building an Uber-style app was the goal. Today it should be where you start. With coding agents, one developer can take on a scope that used to need a team. Hello world isn't a label on a screen anymore. It's a full application with a backend, an admin console, payments and push notifications, and your work begins from there.

At that scale, the language's overhead compounds. Every extra line is something an agent writes, a human reviews and CI builds, on every change, for the life of the product. Java was designed for big code bases maintained by many people, and it shows. It has a huge ecosystem, readable code, a fast compiler, fast tests and a garbage collector that takes memory management off your plate. Spending that budget on lifetimes in a settings screen doesn't buy your users anything.

That's the direction Codename One is taking: complete starting points, plus everything around the code that a real product needs.

Each template is a working application and its server in one Java project. The client and server share the API types, so a REST call or a WebSocket message is type checked on both ends. Growth and monetization are built into the framework instead of bolted on: invite-a-friend links, analytics, push notifications, ads and in-app purchases are all Codename One APIs that the templates already use. Commerce is the next piece we're working on. The template source is free under [MIT-0](https://github.com/codenameone/CodenameOne/blob/master/scripts/skirmish/LICENSE), with no royalties and no revenue share.

## More This Week

### A real-time 3D strategy game, royalty free

For years I avoided pitching Codename One for games. That changed while we built these templates: a modern mobile game is mostly app. Sign-in, menus, a shop, friends, quests, push and a server, with the battle as a small part of the code. **Skirmish** is a real-time strategy game in the style of Clash Royale. Two players face each other across a 3D arena of animated glTF characters, each drawing troops and spells from a deck, and try to bring down the other's towers. Matches run online in lockstep over a WebSocket, with replays, progression, gem packs, a season pass, ads, and invites.

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}

No royalties, no per-install fees, no revenue share. Saturday's Skirmish article walks through the arena, the multiplayer model and the monetization.

A messenger your server can't read

Hospitals, companies and communities want their own messenger and can't use WhatsApp for it. Parley is that messenger: chats, groups, channels, voice notes, voice and video calls and linked devices, encrypted end to end with X3DH and the Double Ratchet, the design Signal uses. The server stores and forwards ciphertext, and calls go peer to peer.

Chats, groups and channels. An encrypted conversation. Calls, peer to peer. Moderation without reading messages.

The crypto reads like ordinary Java because the primitives are now part of Codename One:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
KeyPair ephemeral = KeyGenerator.ec(256);
PrivateKey me = Identity.privateKey();
byte[] dh1 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(me, pub(signedKey));
byte[] dh2 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(ephemeral.getPrivateKey(), pub(identity));
byte[] dh3 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(ephemeral.getPrivateKey(), pub(signedKey));

### More of Java, and a question about Unity

The class library gained 116 classes and interfaces, including `java.util.function`, streams, `Optional`, `java.time` and readers and writers. Existing Java code ports with fewer changes, and ParparVM and the obfuscator strip whatever your app doesn't call, so the overhead is minor. There's still no reflection and no class loading, on purpose.

We also tried something new to learn from what Unity does right: simple Unity 2D projects, C# scripts and all, now build and run as Codename One apps. Five open source games run unmodified. It's a proof of concept, and you can't take any Unity game and run it.

### Desktop apps that feel native

The word processor needed a real menu bar and real file dialogs to hold up next to a native app, so now every Codename One app has them. A `Command` goes into the native menu bar with one call, and standard commands land where each OS expects them, with its own shortcuts:



```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
Command settings = Command.createDesktopRole(Command.DESKTOP_ROLE_SETTINGS, e -> showSettings());
Command quit = Command.createDesktopRole(Command.DESKTOP_ROLE_QUIT, e -> quit());

That's "Settings…" with Cmd+, on a Mac, "Options" under Tools on Windows and "Preferences" under Edit on Linux. Open and save dialogs are the operating system's own, with filters, options and a preview where the platform supports them:

An open dialog with a preview and an option. Standard commands in the macOS application menu.

Wednesday's desktop article has the details, plus the animated 3D models behind Skirmish.

Calls, crypto and an ORM that fails the build

Voice and video calls are now a Codename One API, built on WebRTC on Android, iOS and the browser. Signaling stays yours, so the same code works with any server:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
WebRtc.openUserMedia(true, true, true).ready(media -> {
pc = WebRtc.createPeerConnection(config, listener);
pc.addTrack(media.getAudio());
pc.addTrack(media.getVideo());
pc.createOffer().ready(offer -> pc.setLocalDescription(offer)
.ready(done -> signalling.send(offer)));
});




Turning a key agreement into an encryption key takes two lines, and works the same on every device and on the server:



```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
byte[] shared = KeyAgreement.ecdh(mine.getPrivateKey(), theirs.getPublicKey());
byte[] key = Hkdf.derive("SHA-256", null, shared, "chat message key v1".getBytes(), 32);

On the server, a partner API that wants a client certificate and HTTP/2 is one builder:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
WebClient partner = new WebClient()
.setClientCertificate(ClientCertificate.pkcs12(archive, password))
.setRequireHttp2(true)
.setRequestTimeoutMillis(10000);




And with Hibernate and Spring, plenty of mapping mistakes compile fine and blow up when the app starts or on the first request that touches the entity. Codename One's ORM reads your entities at compile time, so these are build errors:

@temporal requires a java.util.Date field: signedUp
Persistent fields must be writable: name
@entity class com.example.Customer must declare a public no-arg constructor




Thursday's [calls and backends article](https://www.codenameone.com/blog/private-calls-and-safer-backends/) goes through each of these.

## Where is this going?

I don't want this read as "Rust is bad." If you're writing a kernel module, a codec, an embedded controller or anything with hard real-time limits, determinism matters more than throughput, and Rust is an excellent choice. A user-facing application has different constraints. It can trade determinism for throughput, for a smaller code base and for a team that moves faster.

For applications, Java is the better tool, and Codename One is turning into the place where you start with a whole product instead of a blank screen. The word processor is now on the [demos page](https://www.codenameone.com/demos/). Clone the [repository](https://github.com/shai-almog/cn1-wordprocessor), rerun the benchmark workflow and check my numbers. If you find a measurement I got wrong, open an issue there. And if you want to start a project today, the [Initializr](https://www.codenameone.com/initializr/) generates any of the templates in a minute.

title: Haunted Stack Traces: Explaining Java Errors with Gemma 4, Running Locally
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every Java developer knows the moment: the app crashes, the console fills with red, and somewhere in sixty lines of stack trace is the one line that matters.

The Haunted Stack Trace is a Spring Boot error handler possessed by the ghosts of deprecated Java APIs. When the app throws an exception, it does not return a plain 500 page. The stack trace goes to Gemma 4, running locally through Ollama, and a ghost answers: java.util.Date, Vector, Hashtable, Applet or StringTokenizer, whichever fits the crime.

The ghost tells you:

  • the exception and the culprit: the exact line in your code, copied from the trace, not invented
  • the cause, in plain English
  • the fix, practical and specific
  • and then a whisper, because it is Halloween 
{
  "ghost": "java.util.Date",
  "exception": "java.time.format.DateTimeParseException",
  "culprit": "...CursedController.halloweenDate(CursedController.java:63)",
  "cause": "LocalDate.parse expects ISO-8601 (yyyy-MM-dd), but '31/10/2026' is in a different format.",
  "fix": "Use LocalDate.parse(dateString, DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(\"dd/MM/yyyy\")).",
  "whisper": "You reach for the current moment, but you are trapped in a format of the past."
}

I took the theme literally: the ghosts in the machine are the dead APIs we all still trip over. java.util.Date was replaced by java.time, Vector by ArrayList, and they are still haunting codebases. Here, at least, they are being useful.

There are two ways to wake them:

  • Curse buttons that call endpoints which crash on purpose (NullPointerException, ConcurrentModificationException, DateTimeParseException and others)
  • The séance: paste any Java stack trace from any project, and the ghost explains it

Demo

It runs locally by design, so there is no deployed link. You can run it yourself in about five minutes (instructions in the repo), with your Wi-Fi off if you want to check my claim.

Code

Maurodc90 / haunted-stack-trace

Entry for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge (Ghost in the Machine). A Spring Boot error handler possessed by ghosts of deprecated Java APIs: explains stack traces with Gemma 4 running locally via Ollama. No API key, nothing leaves your machine.

The Haunted Stack Trace

Write-up: Haunted Stack Traces on DEV

A Spring Boot error handler possessed by the ghosts of deprecated Java APIs.

When the application throws an exception, it does not return a plain 500 page. The stack trace is sent to Gemma 4, an open-weight model running locally through Ollama, and a ghost (java.util.Date, Vector, Hashtable, Applet or StringTokenizer) answers with what broke, the exact line, why it happened and how to fix it. Then it whispers something unsettling.

Everything runs on your machine. No API key, no internet, and no stack trace ever leaves your laptop.

Built as an entry for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge (Week 4: Ghost in the Machine).

Example

GET /cursed/date calls LocalDate.parse("31/10/2026"):

{
  "ghost": "java.util.Date"
  "exception": "java.time.format.DateTimeParseException",
  "culprit": "com.maurodc90.hauntedstacktrace.controller.CursedController.halloweenDate(CursedController.java:63)",
  "cause"
…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Stack: Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1, Spring AI 2.0, Ollama, Gemma 4 (12B), plain HTML/CSS/JS, GitHub Actions.

The flow is short:

  1. A controller throws a RuntimeException.
  2. A @RestControllerAdvice catches it and turns the stack trace into text.
  3. GhostService sends the top 25 lines of the trace to Gemma through Spring AI's ChatClient.
  4. BeanOutputConverter maps the reply onto a Java record, Haunting. 
return chatClient.prompt()
        .system(SYSTEM_PROMPT)
        .user(trimmedTrace)
        .options(OllamaChatOptions.builder()
                .model(model)
                .temperature(0.4)
                .disableThinking()
                .numPredict(400))
        .call()
        .entity(converter);

That looks simple. Getting there was not, and the failures taught me more than the success did.

Ghost #1: "structured output is unavailable"

My first version asked Ollama to enforce a JSON Schema for the answer. Ollama replied with HTTP 501 {"error":"structured output is unavailable"} for this Gemma 4 build. Spring AI treated that as a transient error and retried with growing waits, 10 seconds, then 50, so my first request simply hung. I dropped the enforced schema and let BeanOutputConverter put the format instructions into the prompt and parse the reply. The structure still held.

Ghost #2: the request that never ended

Then I typed something that was not a stack trace into the séance box: "give me a new error". Six minutes later it was still summoning. ollama ps showed the model stuck on Stopping.... Nothing limited how long an answer could be.

I added a cap of 400 tokens. Now real stack traces came back empty: No content to map due to end-of-input.

The cause: Gemma 4 thinks silently before it answers, and that reasoning counts towards the token budget. On nonsense input it reasoned forever. With a cap, it spent the whole budget thinking and never wrote the JSON. One line, disableThinking(), fixed both problems and made answers faster.

Ghost #3: garbage in

The real fix for nonsense input was to never send it to the model at all. The séance now checks for at least one stack frame (at com.example.Foo.bar(Foo.java:42)) before calling Gemma. Anything else gets an instant refusal from the ghost of Applet: "You knock, but bring no bones. The dead answer only to stack traces."

Smaller decisions that mattered

  • Facts and role-play live in separate fields. The joke never leaks into the fix.
  • RuntimeException, not Exception. A browser asking for favicon.ico raises NoResourceFoundException. If I caught every Exception, every 404 would wake the model.
  • A fallback answer. If the model fails, the handler still responds instead of crashing inside the crash handler.
  • textContent, never innerHTML. Model output is never treated as HTML on the page.
  • Tests without a model. The controller tests mock GhostService, so GitHub Actions runs them on every push without Ollama.

Where the ghost stops

I pasted a trace from a bug in my own Expense Tracker: two Lombok @Data entities, AppUser and Expense, whose generated hashCode() methods call each other until the stack overflows. The ghost of Vector found the loop between the two classes immediately. But its fix was generic, because the trace never mentions Lombok. The real fix, @EqualsAndHashCode.Exclude on the relationship, was mine. The ghost is a good colleague, not an oracle, and I think that is the honest way to use these tools.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because stack traces are not harmless. They contain package names, class names, file paths, sometimes values. Pasting your company's stack traces into a hosted AI service means your company's code leaving the building. With an open-weight model on my own machine, nothing leaves. That is not a feature I bolted on. It is the reason the project exists.

What open made possible here:

  • It works offline and costs nothing to run. No API key, no rate limit, no bill per crash.
  • I could see inside it when it broke. When a request hung, ollama ps showed me the model stuck on Stopping..., and I restarted it myself. When answers came back empty, I could turn thinking off with one flag. With a closed API, I would have been looking at a timeout and guessing.
  • Swapping is one line. The model name lives in application.yml. If 12B is too weak for someone's traces, they can try gemma4:26b. Spring AI's ChatClient hides the provider, so the same code could point at a hosted model if a team chose to.

To be fair to closed models: a large hosted model would probably write better fixes for unusual traces. But for this job, explaining everyday exceptions on a developer's own laptop, a 12B open model was good enough, and its privacy was worth more than the extra quality.

My Agent Session

I built this pair-programming with Claude. Claude wrote most of the code. I decided what to build, ran and tested every step, hit every bug above on my own machine, chose the fixes, and reviewed the code until I could explain each part. I'm a junior Java developer, and working this way, fast with AI but understanding every line, is how I want to work.

The Spirit of It

The moment it landed was not a test passing. It was explaining the project to my partner, who does not write code.

I said: imagine an app that tells you every day which chair I sit in at class. One day I don't come. The app looks for me, finds nothing, and crashes. That is a NullPointerException. Java's message says what happened, in a language only programmers read. This app explains why, in plain words, through a ghost.

She understood it in one go. That's the point of the project: a crash is just a ghost of something you expected to be there.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 (12B) runs locally through Ollama and is the core of the app.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: the project is automated with GitHub Actions; every push runs the test suite on GitHub's runners.

Question for you: what is the most cursed stack trace you have ever met? Paste it in the comments and I will summon a ghost for it.

title: Accessible color palette for Shopify stores: contrast checked
description:
If you build or maintain Shopify stores for European customers, you have probably seen the same worry in client emails lately: "Is our store ready for the European Accessibility Act?"

Nobody can answer that with a color palette alone, and I will be clear about that below. But contrast is one of the most common, most visible and cheapest accessibility defects to fix, because you can fix it once, at the design-token level, and every page inherits the fix.

So I built a small free kit: two accessible color palettes (light and dark) where every pair is already measured, delivered as JSON tokens, CSS variables, a Tailwind config and a self-test page. In this post you get the palette, the setup for Shopify, and the 20-line script to verify any palette yourself, mine included.

What the rules actually ask for

For colors, the rules most teams care about come from WCAG 2.x, Level AA:

  • Text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background. Large text (24px regular, or about 18.66px bold) needs at least 3:1. See WCAG 1.4.3, Contrast (Minimum).
  • UI components and graphics (input borders, focus rings, icons that carry meaning) need at least 3:1 against adjacent colors. See WCAG 1.4.11, Non-text Contrast.

Why does this matter for EU stores? The European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) has applied since 28 June 2025 to a range of consumer-facing products and services, including e-commerce services. The technical reference most often used for websites is the harmonised standard EN 301 549, which points to WCAG 2.1 Level AA for web content. National rules and exemptions (for example for very small businesses) vary by country, so check your own situation with a qualified professional. This is not legal advice.

The five contrast mistakes I see most in store themes

  1. Placeholder text that is too light. A pale gray placeholder on white often fails 4.5:1.
  2. Light gray input borders. The border is what tells a user "this is a field", so it needs 3:1.
  3. Removed or invisible focus outlines. outline: none with no replacement leaves keyboard users lost.
  4. Brand-color buttons that were never checked in their hover state. The default passes, the hover does not (or the reverse).
  5. Error and sale colors on tinted backgrounds. Red on a pale pink badge looks fine on your monitor and fails the math.

(Disabled controls are exempt from the contrast requirements, which is why you will see greyed-out buttons that do not count.)

The fix at the token level

Instead of patching colors page by page, define every role once, as a pair that has been measured:

/* Minimalist Fashion, light */
[data-palette="fashion"] {
  --cpt-bg: #FAF8F5;
  --cpt-surface: #F0ECE6;
  --cpt-text: #1A1816;          /* 16.70:1 on bg   */
  --cpt-muted: #5A534B;         /*  7.14:1 on bg   */
  --cpt-primary: #1A1816;
  --cpt-on-primary: #FAF8F5;    /* 16.70:1 on primary */
  --cpt-link: #8A2D1C;          /*  8.01:1 on bg   */
  --cpt-border-strong: #8A8379; /*  3.53:1 on bg   */
  --cpt-focus: #2748C4;         /*  7.04:1 on bg   */
}

Two details make this robust:

  • Every foreground is measured on both backgrounds you actually use. A card (--cpt-surface) sits on the page (--cpt-bg), so text, muted text, links and messages are checked on both.
  • State colors are part of the pair list. The button label is checked on the default and the hover background.

Free palette: Contrast-Proof Tokens Lite

The free kit contains:

  • tokens.json: design tokens with 80 color pairs and their ratios (20 pairs × 2 palettes × light and dark)
  • variables.css: native CSS variables, palette switching and automatic dark mode
  • tailwind.config.js: copy-paste Tailwind config (v3.4+, v4 snippet in the comments)
  • test_page.html: a self-test page that recalculates every ratio in your browser

The two palettes:

  • Minimalist Fashion: warm paper-white and ink with a terracotta accent, for editorial, low-ornament stores.
  • SaaS Tools: crisp white and deep slate with an indigo primary and a teal accent, for dashboards and landing pages.

Download it free: https://payhip.com/b/6FTfQ?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=lite
Source: https://github.com/mohnadjib/contrast-proof-tokens-lite

Using it in a Shopify theme (Online Store 2.0)

  1. In the theme code editor, upload variables.css to Assets.
  2. In layout/theme.liquid, add this inside <head>: 
{{ 'variables.css' | asset_url | stylesheet_tag }}
  1. Pick a palette on the <html> tag: 
<html lang="{{ request.locale.iso_code }}" data-palette="fashion">
  1. Map your theme's selectors to the tokens in your custom CSS. For example: 
.my-primary-button {
  background: var(--cpt-primary);
  color: var(--cpt-on-primary);
}
.my-primary-button:hover {
  background: var(--cpt-primary-hover);
}
.my-input {
  border: 2px solid var(--cpt-border-strong);
  background: var(--cpt-bg);
  color: var(--cpt-text);
}
:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--cpt-focus);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Replace .my-primary-button and .my-input with your theme's real class names, and test on a duplicate of your live theme first.

Don't trust me: verify any palette in 20 lines

This is the exact WCAG formula. Paste it into your browser console or a Node file:

function channel(v) {
  v /= 255;
  return v <= 0.03928 ? v / 12.92 : Math.pow((v + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
}
function luminance(hex) {
  const h = hex.replace('#', '');
  const [r, g, b] = [0, 2, 4].map(i => parseInt(h.slice(i, i + 2), 16));
  return 0.2126 * channel(r) + 0.7152 * channel(g) + 0.0722 * channel(b);
}
function contrast(a, b) {
  const [la, lb] = [luminance(a), luminance(b)];
  return (Math.max(la, lb) + 0.05) / (Math.min(la, lb) + 0.05);
}

console.log(contrast('#1A1816', '#FAF8F5').toFixed(2)); // 16.70
console.log(contrast('#8A8379', '#FAF8F5').toFixed(2)); // 3.54 (the kit lists 3.53: it rounds down)

Two honest notes: use the exact value when you compare to a threshold (WCAG does not allow rounding up, so 4.499 is a fail), and remember that this checks the colors you pass in, not what is really rendered over a photo or gradient.

What color contrast will not fix

A verified palette removes one class of defects. It does not give your store:

  • keyboard navigation through menus, carts and modals
  • meaningful alt text and labels
  • a logical heading structure
  • accessible forms and error handling
  • reduced-motion support in your animations
  • accessible third-party apps and widgets

Color contrast is only one part of web accessibility. This kit does not guarantee that any website conforms to WCAG, EN 301 549 or the European Accessibility Act, and it is not legal advice. Test your real pages with real tools (and, when you can, with real users).

Your turn

If you build for a specific sector, tell me which one in the comments: it decides which palettes I add next. And if you find a pair that fails in your own check, tell me too. That is the whole point of putting the proof in the box.

Update: the full kit is out. It has 8 sector palettes (fashion, SaaS, jewelry, home, food, wellness, education, real estate), each in light and dark, 320 measured pairs, a palette-comparison page, a Shopify install guide and a command-line checker: Contrast-Proof Tokens, full kit. The two palettes from this free kit are included with identical colors.
