title: Building a Self-Hosted Prompt Library UI with TailwindCSS and Radix Dialog
description:
Building a Self-Hosted Prompt Library UI with TailwindCSS and Radix Dialog

When evaluating f/prompts.chat for internal deployment, the first friction point wasn't the backend—it was the UI layer for browsing, searching, and injecting prompts into existing AI workflows. The repository offers a clean prompt-sharing architecture, but integrating it into a production developer portal requires solving three specific UI problems:

  1. Accessible modal overlays for prompt preview without disrupting screen reader navigation
  2. Token-aware textarea components that provide visual feedback when prompt length approaches model limits
  3. CSS containment strategies to prevent layout thrashing when rendering thousands of prompts with dynamic Markdown content

The Broken Pattern: Direct DOM Manipulation for Modals

Our initial prototype used a naive approach—toggling display: none on a modal wrapper and manually managing focus with document.querySelector. This broke immediately:

// Anti-pattern: breaks screen reader focus trapping
const showPrompt = (id: string) => {
  document.getElementById('modal').style.display = 'block';
  document.getElementById('modal-content').focus(); // ❌ Lost context
};

Root cause: No focus restoration on close, no aria-modal="true" attribute, and animations triggered layout recalculations on every frame due to animating width/height directly.

Production Fix: Radix Dialog with TailwindCSS Transitions

Switching to Radix Primitives solved the accessibility contract while keeping TailwindCSS for styling:

import * as Dialog from '@radix-ui/react-dialog';
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

interface PromptModalProps {
  prompt: { id: string; title: string; content: string; tokens?: number };
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
}

export function PromptModal({ prompt, open, onClose }: PromptModalProps) {
  const textareaRef = useRef<HTMLTextAreaElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open && textareaRef.current) {
      textareaRef.current.select();
    }
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <Dialog.Root open={open} onOpenChange={onClose}>
      <Dialog.Portal>
        <Dialog.Overlay className="fixed inset-0 bg-black/50 data-[state=open]:animate-in data-[state=closed]:animate-out data-[state=closed]:fade-out-0 data-[state=open]:fade-in-0" />
        <Dialog.Content
          className="fixed left-[50%] top-[50%] z-50 w-full max-w-2xl translate-x-[-50%] translate-y-[-50%] rounded-lg border border-gray-200 bg-white p-6 shadow-lg data-[state=open]:animate-in data-[state=closed]:animate-out data-[state=closed]:fade-out-0 data-[state=open]:fade-in-0 data-[state=closed]:zoom-out-95 data-[state=open]:zoom-in-95 data-[state=closed]:slide-out-to-left-1/2 data-[state=closed]:slide-out-to-top-[48%] data-[state=open]:slide-in-from-left-1/2 data-[state=open]:slide-in-from-top-[48%]"
          aria-describedby="prompt-description"
        >
          <Dialog.Title className="text-xl font-semibold text-gray-900">
            {prompt.title}
          </Dialog.Title>
          <Dialog.Description id="prompt-description" className="sr-only">
            Prompt content for copying into your AI workflow
          </Dialog.Description>

          <TokenAwareTextarea
            ref={textareaRef}
            value={prompt.content}
            maxTokens={prompt.tokens}
            className="mt-4"
          />

          <div className="mt-4 flex justify-end gap-2">
            <button
              onClick={() => {
                navigator.clipboard.writeText(prompt.content);
              }}
              className="rounded bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-white hover:bg-blue-700 focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500 focus:ring-offset-2"
            >
              Copy to Clipboard
            </button>
            <Dialog.Close asChild>
              <button className="rounded border border-gray-300 px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-gray-700 hover:bg-gray-50">
                Close
              </button>
            </Dialog.Close>
          </div>
        </Dialog.Content>
      </Dialog.Portal>
    </Dialog.Root>
  );
}

Token-Aware Textarea with Visual Feedback

When integrating with AI gateways (we route through https://b-lost.com/v1 for multi-provider fallback), token limits vary by model. The textarea needs to warn users before they hit the ceiling:

import { forwardRef, useMemo } from 'react';
import { encode } from 'gpt-tokenizer'; // or tiktoken

interface TokenAwareTextareaProps {
  value: string;
  maxTokens?: number;
  className?: string;
}

export const TokenAwareTextarea = forwardRef<
  HTMLTextAreaElement,
  TokenAwareTextareaProps
>(({ value, maxTokens = 4096, className = '' }, ref) => {
  const tokenCount = useMemo(() => encode(value).length, [value]);
  const isNearLimit = tokenCount > maxTokens * 0.9;
  const isOverLimit = tokenCount > maxTokens;

  return (
    <div className={className}>
      <textarea
        ref={ref}
        value={value}
        readOnly
        rows={12}
        className={`w-full rounded border p-3 font-mono text-sm focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 ${
          isOverLimit
            ? 'border-red-500 bg-red-50 focus:ring-red-500'
            : isNearLimit
            ? 'border-yellow-500 bg-yellow-50 focus:ring-yellow-500'
            : 'border-gray-300 focus:ring-blue-500'
        }`}
        aria-describedby="token-count"
      />
      <div
        id="token-count"
        className={`mt-1 text-right text-xs ${
          isOverLimit ? 'text-red-600' : isNearLimit ? 'text-yellow-600' : 'text-gray-500'
        }`}
      >
        {tokenCount} / {maxTokens} tokens
        {isOverLimit && ' — exceeds model limit'}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
});

TokenAwareTextarea.displayName = 'TokenAwareTextarea';

CSS Containment for Prompt List Performance

Rendering 2,000+ prompts with Markdown preview caused 300ms layout recalculations. Adding contain: layout style to each card container dropped it to 45ms:

/* Tailwind arbitrary property */
.prompt-card {
  @apply rounded-lg border border-gray-200 p-4;
  contain: layout style;
}

For dynamic height cards with auto-rows-auto grid, use content-visibility: auto instead:

<div className="grid auto-rows-auto gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3">
  {prompts.map((p) => (
    <article
      key={p.id}
      className="prompt-card [content-visibility:auto]"
      style={{ contentVisibilityAutoStateCallback: true } as any}
    >
      {/* Card content */}
    </article>
  ))}
</div>

The Remaining Question: State Synchronization

f/prompts.chat's architecture assumes prompts are relatively static. But when integrating with live AI sessions, you need bidirectional sync—users might annotate prompts with execution results or pin favorites. Do you:

  1. Fork the prompt object into session-local state and accept drift?
  2. Extend the backend schema with user-specific metadata (breaking self-hosted simplicity)?
  3. Store deltas in localStorage and accept that shared devices lose context?

Each choice trades off data consistency, deployment complexity, and user experience. What's your approach when the upstream data model doesn't match your runtime needs?

title: Rebuilding this site as an F1-style dashboard
description:
My old portfolio was a long page you scrolled down, like most people's.

At that size the page is almost four screens tall. It had also broken quietly: the Xbox card said 0 games, next to a picture that no longer loaded.

I rebuilt it twice in a few days. The first rebuild was a gamer profile, and it didn't survive my own laptop. The second is the F1-style dashboard at siddharthabbineni.in. After that I moved the blog out to a site of its own, the one you're reading now.

I built all of it with Claude Code running Opus. I decided what I wanted and Opus did most of the typing.

The player profile, and why it went

The first version was a character sheet: a character build, a campaign timeline for my jobs, and a trophy cabinet with certifications and live Xbox and Steam achievements. On my 1440p monitor it looked great.

Then I opened it on a 1080p laptop with Windows set to 125%. That leaves the browser about 1536×730 pixels, and the page turned into a wall of text.

Three columns were all talking at once, and every panel was packed with small labels, chips and bullets. Nothing on the screen was more important than anything else. Making the text smaller to fit only made it worse.

Trying ideas before writing code

This time I didn't touch the code first. I asked Opus for rough screens of very different ideas: game menus, a magazine spread, a metro map, an F1 pit wall. I liked the metro map and the pit wall, so I mashed them together and drew my career as a line on the Nürburgring GP circuit.

I got a second opinion on that concept, and it made two points I agreed with. The section menu shouldn't be part of the career track, and the track shouldn't be a closed lap with a finish line, because my career hasn't finished yet. So the route became an open stretch of the circuit with the road carrying on past my current job.

The F1 dashboard

The site shows one section at a time, with F1 names and a plain line under each: Seasons (where I've worked), Driver profile, Podiums, Garage and Press. It uses the real F1 colours, and every button, tab and card has the same slanted cut as the nameplate.

On the track, grey is life before work, black is work, and red is my current job and the road after it. When you pick an older job, it and the stretch up to the next job turn teal. One job shows at a time, with a short summary, up to three numbers, a few bullets and the tools I used with their logos. That's far less text than before.

The buttons for moving between jobs took two goes. At first "Earlier" sat on the right and disappeared on the oldest job, so "Later" slid under the mouse. Clicking Earlier a few times in a row took me back to the newest job. Now each button has its own fixed spot and keeps it, even when the other one is hidden.

The header copies a driver's TV graphic: a picture on a red panel, with my first name small and my surname big, the way F1 shows "Max / VERSTAPPEN". It started as my photo. It's now a drawing of me in a helmet with SA on the side, which is also the little icon in your browser tab on both sites.

The Garage has my side projects, with my pull requests to other people's projects in a column that looks like a timing tower. One that hasn't been merged yet is marked "Under review", which is what the stewards say about an incident they haven't ruled on. The footer is a single "Team radio" line that flips between my two newest posts and two newest merged PRs.

You can get around without the mouse. The keys 1 to 5 open a section, and ↑ and ↓ change job. On a desktop the page never scrolls, so the mouse wheel steps through the jobs and then on to the next section. The animations use Motion, the library that used to be Framer Motion.

I worried that the logos would make the site heavy, since Simple Icons has 3,466 of them. I checked the production build: only the 14 I use reach the browser, about 15 KB in all.

Fitting on one screen

The whole design is 96 by 45.6 rem, and one line of CSS sets the size of a rem:

html {
    font-size: min(100vw / 96, 100dvh / 45.625, 20px);
}

At 1536×730 that's 16px, and at 1920×1080 it's 20px, where it stops. On bigger screens the page sits in the middle of a dark backdrop with a faint outline of the circuit.

I asked Opus for a Playwright script that opens every section at five laptop sizes, from 1280×600 to 1920×1080, and fails if anything scrolls or gets cut off. It checks all five jobs too, because each one has a different amount of text.

The track outline comes from Pitlane02's Nürburgring drawing on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

Moving the blog home

My two posts lived on dev.to, and the site pulled them in through its API. I moved them into my repo as markdown files, so a new post is a commit, a draft gets a staging preview, and the pages are built ahead of time.

At first the posts lived inside the dashboard, under Press. Next.js 16 with Cache Components surprised me a few times along the way:

  • dynamicParams isn't allowed any more. Unknown slugs call notFound() instead.
  • With Partial Prefetching on, you have to read params inside a <Suspense> boundary so the page can show its outline straight away.
  • Typed routes won't accept `/blog/${slug}` for a plain string. A small postHref() helper fixed it in one place.
  • The standalone build doesn't copy files you read with fs, so the posts folder has to go in outputFileTracingIncludes.
  • Running next build while next dev was still running confused the dev server, and every page started reloading itself about five times a second. Restarting it fixed that.
  • A 'use cache' function caches whatever it returns, failures included. My Xbox and Steam data is cached for six hours, so one rate-limited request would have emptied the Podiums section until the next refresh. Failures now call cacheLife('minutes') and get retried soon after.

Sharing a link

When I pasted a link into LinkedIn, the preview had a title and no picture. X was worse, showing the wrong title. Each page set its own Open Graph tags, and those replaced the site-wide ones, image included.

Now every section of the dashboard gets its own card, made at build time with Next's opengraph-image files and next/og. It has the same tab, slashes and nameplate as the site. The fonts had to be TTF files, because the renderer behind next/og can't read the WOFF2 files the site uses.

Digging up 2005

I had a blog long before dev.to. It started on Blogger, moved to WordPress on thesid.net, and died when my hosting ran out while I was moving countries. Luckily the Wayback Machine had saved it.

Its API lists every address it saved for a domain. For my two old domains that was about 1,300 addresses, and most were junk: client sites I used to host, and the crawler going round in circles. After removing duplicates I had 145 posts. Opus wrote a scraper that fetched them slowly, then a second script went looking for the images. Most image hosts from 2006 are gone (RIP echo.cx and ImageShack), so some pictures are lost for good.

I kept the posts exactly as I wrote them, typos and all. They're under Earlier sessions on this blog, one page per year. Reading 2006 me go on about BSNL and the new Iron Maiden album made the whole thing worth it.

The blog gets its own site

With 150 posts in it, the blog didn't fit the dashboard any more. The dashboard is built to fit on one screen, and a long post doesn't. I kept making the reader tighter, with smaller text, Older and Newer up in the tab row, and the title moving into the tabs once you scrolled past it, and it was still a long article in a box.

So the blog moved to blog.siddharthabbineni.in. Press on the dashboard is now a short feed of the three newest posts, and each one opens here. It reads a posts.json file the blog publishes at build time and caches it with 'use cache'. If the blog doesn't answer, Press says so and gives you the link.

I wanted it to feel like racing without copying the dashboard. Opus drew a few directions on a canvas. The first name was Night session, which I didn't like, so I picked Free practice. That's the session where drivers try things out, and that's most of what I write about. The look I picked is wet tarmac: dark asphalt with grain and puddles, worn white paint, and a chequered line under the title. New posts line up on a starting grid with the newest in P1. Inside a post, each heading is a lap, and the bar at the top lights them up as you read.

A few things changed after I lived with it for a day:

  • The header was far too tall. On a 1080p screen the title, blurb and tags took up most of the first screen, so I drew red lines on screenshots where I wanted them to stop. The home header is now about 256 pixels tall, and the tags moved to the end of each post.
  • The light mode background was too dark. Now it's pale concrete, and the white paint became charcoal, because white lines don't show up on concrete.
  • Search came back after I noticed it had gone missing in the redesign. It's a box in the header. Press / on any page to jump to it, and it searches titles, tags and the full text from an index made at build time. On the search page the footer stays put, since the results changing height made it jump up and down.

The blog is a plain static site. Next.js exports it as files, so route handlers like the RSS feed and the search index need dynamic = 'force-static'. Each post's share card gets drawn at build time into an og.png next to the post.

One repo, two sites

The repo is now split into apps/portfolio and apps/blog. Each has its own package.json and lockfile, and I skipped npm workspaces, since the two apps share nothing. Each one has its own GitHub workflow that only runs when its folder changes, so fixing a typo in a post doesn't rebuild the dashboard.

Both run on Azure Static Web Apps. My first apps were in West Europe for no good reason, so I deleted them and made new ones in East Asia, which is a lot closer to India. There are four now: the portfolio and the blog, each with a staging copy. Everything goes to staging first, and the staging sites tell search engines not to index them. Opus handled the Cloudflare DNS records through the API with a token that can only edit DNS for this one domain. Adding another subdomain later, like one for NuPrint, is one more app and one more record.

Phones, again

  • The Email button is gone. My resume has my email on it anyway. Resume and Blog moved to the end of the page, and a small pen icon next to the theme toggle opens the blog.
  • The Team radio line is now a bar stuck to the bottom of the screen.
  • Swiping used to work only on the tab row. Now a sideways swipe anywhere on the page moves to the next section, and the tabs scroll to keep the open one in view.
  • On a 360-pixel phone the pen and theme buttons wrapped onto their own line, so the photo, name and slashes shrink a little on small phones.

Seasons on a phone took the most work. Tapping a job used to open it in place while the old one stayed open, so the page jumped around and the job you tapped ended up somewhere different every time. I wanted an accordion: the open job folds up, the tapped one opens, and the page scrolls so the tapped one sits just under the tabs.

My first version did nothing at all. The fold animated height: 'auto' with Motion, and to measure that, Motion saves the scroll position, measures, and puts the scroll back with window.scrollTo. That cancelled my smooth scroll every time. I swapped Motion for a CSS grid row that goes from 0fr to 1fr, which folds just as well without measuring anything.

Then the tapped job landed anywhere from 16 to 19 pixels off. There were two causes. The page wasn't tall enough yet to scroll that far while the new job was still opening, so it now gets a temporary minimum height. And the browser's scroll anchoring was nudging the page as content above it folded away, so that's turned off until the fold finishes. Now it lands in the same spot every time. The first fold took 350ms, which was too quick to see what happened, so it takes 550ms now.

What I'd tell myself

  • Look at your site on the laptop people actually use, at the scaling they actually use.
  • Draw the screens before writing code. Throwing away a mockup takes seconds.
  • Less text on screen beats smaller text.
  • A dashboard and a blog want different layouts. Give long reading its own site.
  • If an animation fights your scrolling, find out what the library does when it measures.
  • Keep your writing somewhere you own.

First posted on my blog, Free practice.

title: NuPrint: printing without the phone app
description:
I have a little ZEITEL SC03h thermal printer. It's handy for labels, to-do lists and small notes, but using it meant going through the phone app. Even when whatever I wanted to print was already on my laptop, I had to send it to my phone first.

I wanted to get rid of that extra step. That was how NuPrint started.

It wasn't something I built in one stretch. I work full time and have other things going on, so I'd pick it up when I had time, make some progress, then leave it for a while. There were a few attempts before this one that didn't get very far.

Getting it to print

There wasn't any public documentation for the printer, so I started looking through the Android app with JADX. The app already knew how to talk to it; I needed to work out what it was sending.

A lot of that was digging through commands, checksums and the way images were converted into something the printer could understand. There were also a few things that weren't obvious at all. The Bluetooth service it advertised wasn't the one it used for printing, which explained why looking for the printing service wasn't finding it. Even the capitalisation of the model name mattered. Two names that looked almost identical needed different settings.

I did most of that initial digging myself. Eventually I gave what I had to Codex, and it got the remaining pieces working in about an hour. I had a small Python app that could actually print.

That was the point where it started moving again. I'd spent all this time figuring out the printer, and now there was something working to build on. From there, I planned the Rust app with Claude Code, and I've spent roughly the last month building it around my day job.

The Python version was basic. A little window, some text and image handling, and Bluetooth. The first test was a strip with a border and some text. It came out properly, and I kept that version around as a reference for the rewrite rather than trying to turn it into the finished app.

The Rust version

NuPrint is now a Rust app with a Tauri and React UI, plus a command-line tool. I kept the printing logic separate from the UI so both could use the same code, without tying the whole thing to one operating system.

The working Python version helped here. I could compare what the Rust code produced against output I already knew printed correctly. There are tests for that now, along with plenty of other checks that don't need the printer connected.

Getting a clean print was only part of it, though. I also had to think about what happens when Bluetooth disconnects or the app closes halfway through a job. I didn't want it automatically trying again when it had no way of knowing how much paper had already come out. Interrupted jobs are left for the user to check instead.

That also affected the wording in the app. Sending everything successfully isn't quite the same as knowing the print came out correctly, so I avoided simply calling that "printed".

There was some cleanup around saved jobs and logs too. A review caught text and PDF passwords being retained with jobs, which I fixed. Exported logs leave out identifying details by default.

A detour into Slint

Somewhere along the way I started wondering whether I could make the UI in Rust as well, without the web view.

I asked Opus about egui and Slint. The advice was to stay with Tauri for what I wanted, especially with the possibility of mobile later. But I still wanted to try Slint, and the shared core meant I didn't have to rewrite the printing side to do it.

So I had Opus build a Slint version of the UI. It got surprisingly far: printer discovery, previews, the queue, settings. It was usable enough that I kept working on it.

The fonts were the first thing that bothered me. Small text looked blurry and different from the other apps on my machine. Switching to Skia sorted that out, but then I got a different problem on Windows: the NVIDIA overlay decided this little printer app was a game. The window was also flickering on my HDR monitor.

Using Skia's software rendering fixed that. I looked at Qt as another option, but didn't take that further.

The oddest problem was moving the window between my monitors. They use different scaling settings, and the window kept getting bigger as I dragged it back and forth. Eventually it was wider than the screen. I traced that back to how Slint handled the scaling change and added a workaround to keep the size consistent.

I spent more time on fonts and window behaviour than I'd expected to spend on a printer app.

The Slint version ended up staying. Releases now include both versions, although Tauri is still the main app and the Slint one is less tested. They use the same printing core, so I don't have two separate implementations of the protocol to maintain.

Making it something other people could use

Once it was working on my machines, I started sorting out the repository, installers and releases. I put it under the MIT licence and set up pull requests and CI across Windows, macOS and Linux. Releases build installers for both apps, and everything has to pass before the release is published.

There were a few things to learn there too. I put a version override in an empty commit for release-please, only for GitHub to drop the commit during the rebase merge. The release came out with a different version than I'd intended. That override now goes on a commit that actually changes something.

I also had Opus review the code and help plan some cleanup. For performance work, the rule was to measure first and keep a change only if it made a useful difference.

Some changes were worth doing. Keeping the log file open instead of reopening it for every line helped, and limiting how many previews were being rendered at once brought memory use down quite a bit. Other ideas would have saved a few milliseconds on a print that spent far longer being sent over Bluetooth, so I left those alone.

I managed to confuse myself with the benchmarks as well. One change initially looked like it did nothing. It turned out that two copies of the repo were sharing a build directory, and I was testing the same old binary twice. Separate build directories gave me the comparison I'd meant to run.

Testing cancellation also turned up a Windows Bluetooth issue. Cancelling a scan could leave the next scan apparently finding nothing. That needed some recovery handling rather than just assuming another scan would work.

Signing, updates, and what's left

The installers still have the usual unsigned-app warnings. I haven't done Apple notarization, and I've applied to the SignPath Foundation for Windows signing but am still waiting on that.

The release builds do have GitHub attestations, so there's a way to verify where a download came from. The update files are signed too, although that's separate from getting rid of the operating system's installer warnings.

I've added in-app updates, with checking turned off unless you enable it or check manually. I didn't want a printer app going online without being asked. Updates also wait while something is printing, rather than restarting in the middle of a job.

A review caught a problem in the Slint updater's version checks, which is fixed. Adding updates also broke the Mac packaging on the first attempt because the app bundle wasn't being kept for the update step. That held up the release until I fixed the build.

I haven't watched an update install end to end yet. This is the first release with the updater in it, so that test comes with the next one.

As for printer support, I've used NuPrint with my SC03h on Windows and macOS. There's a Linux build, but I haven't tested it with the printer yet. The phone app listed other models with matching settings, so I've exposed those as experimental. I only own the one printer, and I don't want to imply I've tested hardware I haven't.

It's grown quite a bit from the Python test. AI helped me get past the point where the earlier attempts had stalled, and a lot of the work since then has been testing, reviewing and fixing things I wouldn't have thought about at the start.

NuPrint is open source under the MIT licence, with builds for Windows, macOS and Linux. If you have one of these little printers and try it, I'd be interested to hear how it works for you.

First posted on my blog, Free practice.

title: DORA Metrics for AI Agents: How We Built an Observability Engine in Pure Go
description:
The first phase of AI coding was dominated by awe at token generation speed: how many lines of code could Claude, Devin, or Antigravity produce in 60 seconds?

However, once autonomous coding agents enter production-grade engineering workflows, the fundamental question asked by Tech Leads and CTOs shifts dramatically:

"Are AI agents genuinely accelerating software delivery, or are they simply amplifying technical debt, rework rates, and pull-request chaos?"

To answer this question quantitatively rather than intuitively, we don't need to invent new software metrics. We need to leverage the gold standard of modern engineering: DORA Metrics (DevOps Research and Assessment).

In this article — consolidating releases DEL-020 through DEL-027 (v0.9.0) of the Pipeline-AI framework —, I share how we redesigned and implemented the four DORA metrics specifically for autonomous AI agents, building a zero-dependency telemetry engine in pure Go 1.24 stdlib, hardened with fuzz testing, rendered via an Interactive Generative UI Dashboard, and exposed directly to agents via the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

1. Why DORA Metrics for AI Agents?

Developed by Google Cloud / DORA, the four key metrics balance two essential software delivery forces: Throughput and Stability.

When human keystrokes are replaced by a team of specialized AI agents (Triage, Architecture, Test Writer, Dev Implementation, Code Review, Security, and QA), the four DORA metrics take on an entirely new meaning at machine speed:

DORA Metric Human Engineering Meaning Adaptation for Autonomous Agents (Pipeline-AI)
Deployment Frequency (DF) How often code reaches production (weekly or monthly). Number of fully validated micro-deliveries shipped per day at machine speed.
Lead Time for Changes (LT) Time from first commit to production deployment (days/weeks). Time elapsed from initial issue triage (pm-triage) to validated PR creation in git-delivery (measured in minutes).
Change Failure Rate (CFR) Percentage of deployments causing a production failure. Percentage of pipeline runs blocked by deterministic AI quality gates (doctor, sensor, validate) and calibrated semantic sensing (Jev / eval).
Time to Restore Service (MTTR) Mean time to recover from a downtime or production defect. Time required for the agent pipeline to resolve a blocked gate (STATUS: bloqueado) and restore a passing state (ok).

If an autonomous agent churns out 5,000 lines of code per hour but exhibits a 60% Change Failure Rate on test and security gates, it is not delivering velocity: it is creating cognitive pollution for human reviewers.

2. Telemetry Architecture in Pure Go (internal/metrics)

In Pipeline-AI, we maintain a strict invariant: Zero external dependencies. Introducing third-party telemetry collectors or SaaS vendor SDKs would increase supply chain risk and compromise air-gapped or containerized execution.

We implemented internal/metrics exclusively with the Go 1.24 standard library:

// internal/metrics/metrics.go
type DORAMetrics struct {
    DeploymentFrequency float64       `json:"deployment_frequency"` // Deploys per day
    DeploymentsTotal    int           `json:"deployments_total"`
    LeadTimeForChanges  time.Duration `json:"lead_time_for_changes"` // Average lead time
    ChangeFailureRate   float64       `json:"change_failure_rate"`   // Percentage (0.0 to 100.0)
    FailedDeployments   int           `json:"failed_deployments"`
    TimeToRestore       time.Duration `json:"time_to_restore"` // Mean time to recovery
    RestoresTotal       int           `json:"restores_total"`
}

Atomic & Fail-Safe Persistence

Agent telemetry must be fault-tolerant: if a process aborts midway through a write, metrics files must never become corrupt.

We enforce atomic file writes using temporary files and os.Rename, synchronized via sync.Mutex:

func Save(rootDir string, data *MetricsData) error {
    mu.Lock()
    defer mu.Unlock()

    stateDir := filepath.Join(rootDir, DirName)
    _ = os.MkdirAll(stateDir, 0755)

    tmpFile := filepath.Join(stateDir, fmt.Sprintf("%s.tmp.%d", FileName, time.Now().UnixNano()))
    if err := os.WriteFile(tmpFile, payload, 0644); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    // Atomic filesystem swap
    return os.Rename(tmpFile, targetFile)
}

If the metrics database is missing or empty, Load gracefully initializes default state structures. Telemetry must never fail the build.

3. Hardened with Native Fuzzing: 1.1M+ Executions

In LLM workflows, structured outputs can be interrupted, truncated, or injected with malformed tokens. To ensure our JSON parser never panics or triggers denial-of-service vulnerabilities, we built a native Go Fuzz Target:

// internal/metrics/metrics_fuzz_test.go
func FuzzParseMetrics(f *testing.F) {
    f.Add([]byte(`{"version":1,"events":[],"stages":[],"deliveries":[]}`))
    f.Add([]byte(`{"version":1,"deliveries":[{"delivery_id":"DEL-001","success":true,"lead_time":600000000000}]}`))
    f.Add([]byte(``))
    f.Add([]byte(`null`))
    f.Add([]byte(`{"corrupted": true`))

    f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, data []byte) {
        md, err := ParseMetrics(data)
        if err != nil {
            return // Handled errors are expected for corrupt input
        }
        if md == nil {
            t.Fatalf("ParseMetrics returned nil without error on valid input")
        }
    })
}

We verified the parser across 1,132,000+ continuous executions (go test -fuzz=FuzzParseMetrics -fuzztime=10s), confirming zero panics or unhandled edge cases.

4. Transparent Pipeline Runner Instrumentation

Rather than relying on agents to self-report when they begin or complete tasks, we instrumented the Pipeline Runner (internal/runner) at the engine level:

// Excerpt from internal/runner/runner.go
docStart := time.Now()
docResults, docOK := doctor.Collect(absRoot)
_ = metrics.RecordStageDuration(absRoot, deliveryID, "doctor", time.Since(docStart), docOK)

sensorStart := time.Now()
sensorRes, err := sensor.Run(absRoot)
_ = metrics.RecordStageDuration(absRoot, deliveryID, "sensor", time.Since(sensorStart), sensorStep.Status == StatusPass)

valStart := time.Now()
valStep := validate.Run(...)
_ = metrics.RecordStageDuration(absRoot, deliveryID, "validate", time.Since(valStart), validateStep.Status == StatusPass)

// Record overarching gate outcome
_ = metrics.RecordEvent(absRoot, metrics.Event{
    Type:       metrics.EventGate,
    DeliveryID: deliveryID,
    Timestamp:  time.Now().UTC(),
    Duration:   time.Since(runStart),
    Success:    allOK,
    Stage:      "runner",
})

This delivers zero-overhead passive observability: agents execute their assigned skills while telemetry data is persisted in real time.

5. CLI, Model Context Protocol (MCP) & Interactive Dashboard (Generative UI)

Telemetry data is immediately queryable via terminal CLI, an interactive visual HTML5 dashboard, and AI agents over MCP:

Terminal CLI: 

$ pipeline-ai metrics summary
Métricas DORA do Pipeline:
  Deployment Frequency:    3.50 deploys/dia (total: 20)
  Lead Time for Changes:   8m 42s
  Change Failure Rate:     5.0% (falhas: 1)
  Time to Restore Service: 4m 15s (restaurações: 1)

Structured JSON for Grafana, Datadog, or GitHub Actions:

$ pipeline-ai metrics summary -json
{
  "deployment_frequency": 3.5,
  "deployments_total": 20,
  "lead_time_for_changes": 522000000000,
  "change_failure_rate": 5.0,
  "failed_deployments": 1,
  "time_to_restore": 255000000000,
  "restores_total": 1
}

Native MCP Tool (pipeline_get_metrics):

AI agents invoke the MCP tool directly:

{
  "name": "pipeline_get_metrics",
  "arguments": {
    "dir": "."
  }
}

If an agent detects its Change Failure Rate climbing, it can autonomously adapt: allocating more reasoning tokens to test generation (test-writer), running calibrated semantic evaluations (pipeline-ai eval / pipeline_eval_semantic), or requesting additional guardrail checks.

Interactive Visual Dashboard (pipeline-ai dashboard & pipeline_render_dashboard):

Built in internal/dashboard (DEL-022), the framework also renders a self-contained HTML5/CSS3/SVG executive cockpit (dark mode, zero external JS dependencies, and XSS-safe):

$ pipeline-ai dashboard -output dashboard.html

Or inline in the IDE via the pipeline_render_dashboard MCP tool, visualizing the 4 DORA KPI cards, proportional stage latency bars, delivery timelines, and agent handoff inspection.

The Takeaway: Agent Reliability Engineering (ARE)

Generating code without telemetry is like driving a supercar with a disabled dashboard: you might feel fast, but you won't know the engine is overheating until it blows up.

By implementing DORA Metrics for AI Agent Pipelines, engineering teams achieve:

  1. Bottleneck Visibility: Concrete latency data per skill (TDD Red vs. Dev Green vs. Code Review).
  2. Defeating the Speed Mirage: Fast code that fails gates is immediately surfaced in the CFR metric.
  3. Auditable Industrial AI: Shifting from casual AI prototyping to hardened, measurable Agent Reliability Engineering (ARE).

The Pipeline-AI (v0.9.0) framework — including the telemetry engine, interactive visual dashboard, calibrated semantic sensor (Jev), official Google Antigravity Plugin, and complete 16-skill catalog — is open-source under the MIT license:

👉 GitHub: github.com/rodrigodosanjosoliveira/pipeline-ai

How is your engineering team measuring the real-world impact and reliability of AI agents? Let's discuss in the comments! 💬📊🚀

title: Ubuntu 27.04 development has begun with a release date of April 2027
description:
Development on Ubuntu 27.04 Tenacious T-Rex has officially begun, targeting an April 2027 release.

Explore what is planned for the upcoming cycle, including Linux 7.6 kernel integration, GNOME 52, Rust tooling like ntpd-rs, and maturing TPM-backed encryption.

The process officially opened on October 30, 2026, with automatic synchronization from the Debian community testing system. Over the next period, software packages will be continuously updated, building the foundation for the future stable release.

Release schedule

The official release of Ubuntu 27.04 is scheduled for April 22, 2027. A little earlier, on April 1 of the same year, the first test version is expected to be released for those who want to try the changes early.

What is expected to include

During development, those responsible plan major updates and additions to the software. Among them are:

  • The updated GNOME 52 graphical environment.
  • The Linux 7.6 kernel, which is the heart of the operating system.
  • More tools written in the Rust programming language, including a new time synchronization tool.
  • Acceleration in the development of a special version of the operating system based exclusively on standalone application packages, which will initially be offered as a test option.

Thoughts on artificial intelligence and security

The company is also looking at adding AI capabilities directly to the device. Plans include the possibility of integrating a voice dictation tool that would only be activated if the user chooses to do so, as well as ideas for AI features on the desktop, based on previous testing.

title: Modernizando Java legado com IA - o que funciona e o que dá errado
description:
Você herdou um sistema. Java 8, Spring 4 com metade da configuração em XML, Hibernate com hbm.xml, um pom.xml com dependências que não recebem atualização desde 2017 e um scanner de segurança apontando dezenas de CVEs. Ninguém do time original está mais na empresa. Não tem teste, ou tem uns vinte que ninguém roda porque metade quebra.

A tentação em 2026 é abrir um agente de IA, apontar para o repositório e pedir "migra isso para Java 21 e Spring Boot 3". Dá para fazer. O resultado compila, às vezes até sobe. E aí, três semanas depois, o financeiro reclama que um relatório está arredondando centavos diferente.

Esse post é sobre como usar IA nesse trabalho sem cair nisso: onde ela rende muito, onde ferramenta determinística é melhor, e o que precisa existir antes de qualquer linha mudar.

O problema real não é o código

Sistema legado não é sinônimo de código feio. Código feio que tem teste e documentação se refatora numa tarde. O que torna um sistema legado difícil é outra coisa:

  • Conhecimento perdido: regras de negócio que só existem no código, às vezes num if dentro de um service de três mil linhas, sem comentário nem ticket.
  • Nenhuma rede de segurança: sem teste, qualquer mudança é aposta.
  • Dependências mortas: bibliotecas abandonadas, versões fora de suporte, APIs do JDK que deixaram de existir.
  • Medo: ninguém mexe porque ninguém sabe o que quebra, então o sistema envelhece mais rápido.

Repara que digitar código não aparece na lista. O gargalo de uma modernização é entender o sistema, não escrever o código novo. E é justamente aí que a IA mais ajuda, muito mais do que na geração de código em si.

Fase 1: arqueologia

Antes de mudar qualquer coisa, use a IA para ler. Um modelo com janela de contexto grande, rodando como agente dentro do repositório (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot no modo agente, o que seu time usar), consegue fazer em uma hora o que levaria uma semana de leitura manual.

Coisas que valem pedir, uma por vez:

  • Mapa de módulos: quais pacotes existem, quem depende de quem, onde estão os pontos de entrada (servlets, controllers, jobs agendados, listeners de fila).
  • Fluxos de ponta a ponta: "siga o que acontece quando um pedido é cancelado, do endpoint até o banco, e liste cada efeito colateral". Esse tipo de pergunta revela as regras escondidas.
  • Tradução de configuração: XML do Spring, mapeamentos do Hibernate, web.xml, filtros. A IA explica o que cada bean faz e de onde vem cada injeção.
  • SQL e stored procedures: muita regra de negócio de sistema antigo mora no banco. Peça a explicação de cada procedure e quais tabelas ela altera.

O resultado dessa fase é documentação: um arquivo por módulo, diagramas em Mermaid, uma lista de regras de negócio encontradas. Revise tudo. A IA vai errar em alguns pontos, principalmente onde o código usa reflexão, configuração externa ou convenção que não aparece no fonte. Mas corrigir um documento errado é muito mais rápido que escrever do zero, e o ato de revisar já te ensina o sistema.

Guarde o que for confirmado num arquivo de contexto do projeto (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md ou equivalente). Toda sessão futura do agente começa sabendo o que você já descobriu, em vez de redescobrir e errar de novo.

Fase 2: travar o comportamento atual

Essa é a fase que todo mundo quer pular e a mais importante do post.

Você não vai migrar um sistema sem teste. Mas também não vai escrever testes unitários bonitos para código que você ainda não entende. O que você precisa é de testes de caracterização: testes que registram o que o sistema faz hoje, certo ou errado, e quebram se esse comportamento mudar.

A técnica também é chamada de golden master. Você roda o código atual com um conjunto de entradas, salva a saída, e o teste compara execuções futuras com essa saída salva:

class CalculoFreteCaracterizacaoTest {

    // Entradas reais, anonimizadas, tiradas de produção.
    static Stream<Pedido> pedidos() {
        return CarregadorFixture.ler("fixtures/pedidos.json");
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("pedidos")
    void freteContinuaIgual(Pedido pedido) {
        BigDecimal frete = new CalculoFreteService().calcular(pedido);

        // Compara com o valor gravado na primeira execução, contra o código antigo.
        assertEquals(Golden.valor("frete", pedido.getId()), frete.toPlainString());
    }
}

Repara no toPlainString(). Comparar BigDecimal com equals considera a escala (1.0 é diferente de 1.00), e é exatamente esse tipo de diferença que você quer pegar.

A IA é ótima para gerar esses testes em volume. Peça para ela identificar os caminhos de cada método crítico, montar entradas que cubram cada ramo e escrever o teste. Dois cuidados:

  • O teste trava o comportamento atual, inclusive os bugs. Se o agente "corrigir" algo enquanto escreve o teste, o teste deixa de servir. Deixe isso explícito no pedido.
  • Rode contra o código antigo primeiro. Todo teste de caracterização tem que passar antes de qualquer migração. Se não passa, ele está errado, não o sistema.

Com isso no lugar, você tem algo que não tinha antes: um jeito de saber se quebrou.

Fase 3: migração mecânica com ferramenta determinística

Agora sim, mudar código. E aqui vai a regra que mais economiza dor de cabeça: o que é mecânico vai para ferramenta determinística, e a IA fica com o que exige julgamento.

Trocar javax.persistence por jakarta.persistence em quatrocentos arquivos não exige inteligência. Exige consistência. Um LLM fazendo isso arquivo por arquivo vai acertar 98% e errar 2% de forma diferente a cada vez. Uma ferramenta de refatoração baseada em AST acerta 100%, ou falha de um jeito previsível.

A ferramenta padrão para isso no mundo Java é o OpenRewrite. Ele trabalha sobre a árvore sintática com tipos resolvidos, não sobre texto, e vem com receitas prontas para os saltos mais comuns:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.openrewrite.maven</groupId>
    <artifactId>rewrite-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version><!-- versão atual no Maven Central --></version>
    <configuration>
        <activeRecipes>
            <recipe>org.openrewrite.java.migrate.UpgradeToJava21</recipe>
            <recipe>org.openrewrite.java.migrate.jakarta.JavaxToJakarta</recipe>
        </activeRecipes>
    </configuration>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.openrewrite.recipe</groupId>
            <artifactId>rewrite-migrate-java</artifactId>
            <version><!-- versão atual --></version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</plugin>

mvn rewrite:dryRun   # gera um patch em target/rewrite/ sem tocar no código
mvn rewrite:run      # aplica

Para Spring Boot existe a família de receitas UpgradeSpringBoot_3_x no módulo rewrite-spring. Confira com mvn rewrite:discover quais estão disponíveis na versão que você instalou, porque a lista cresce a cada release.

Outra opção, se você está na AWS, é o Amazon Q Developer, que faz o salto de Java 8, 11 ou 17 para 17 ou 21 combinando receitas determinísticas com IA. A limitação prática é que o projeto precisa buildar com Maven, então projeto em Ant ou Gradle fica de fora.

Rode a migração em passos pequenos, um salto por vez, com os testes de caracterização entre cada um. Java 8 para 11 é um salto com problemas próprios (os módulos de JAXB, JAX-WS e CORBA saíram do JDK no 11). De 11 para 17 o encapsulamento forte das APIs internas do JDK quebra bibliotecas que usavam reflexão. De 17 para 21 costuma ser tranquilo. Fazer tudo de uma vez transforma três problemas conhecidos em um problema misterioso.

Fase 4: a IA no que sobra

As receitas cobrem talvez 70 a 80% do trabalho. O resto é onde a IA brilha:

  • Bibliotecas abandonadas: aquela lib de geração de PDF que parou em 2016 e não tem versão compatível. A IA sugere substitutos e reescreve as chamadas.
  • APIs removidas sem substituto direto: Nashorn saiu no Java 15, o SecurityManager foi depreciado no 17 e desativado de vez no 24. Código que dependia disso precisa ser repensado, não traduzido.
  • Erros de compilação e de runtime pós-migração: cole o stack trace, deixe o agente investigar. Ele lê o código ao redor, o changelog da dependência, e propõe a correção.
  • Código reflexivo e configuração por convenção: onde o OpenRewrite não enxerga porque a referência está numa string.

O fluxo que funciona com agente é sempre o mesmo loop curto:

  1. Uma tarefa pequena e bem definida ("faça o módulo de faturamento compilar no Java 17").
  2. O agente edita.
  3. Build e testes de caracterização rodam, de preferência pelo próprio agente.
  4. Você revisa o diff antes de aceitar.
  5. Commit. Próxima tarefa.

PRs pequenos não são preciosismo, são a única forma de a revisão humana continuar funcionando. Um diff de três mil linhas gerado por IA não é revisado, é aprovado. E aprovar sem revisar é como os bugs silenciosos chegam em produção.

Fase 5: modernizar de verdade

Compilar no Java 21 não é modernizar, é só sair da zona de risco. Depois que o sistema está estável na versão nova, vem a parte que melhora o código.

Um exemplo típico: um DAO com JDBC cru, do jeito que se escrevia em 2012.

public List<Cliente> buscarAtivos() {
    List<Cliente> lista = new ArrayList<Cliente>();
    Connection conn = null;
    PreparedStatement ps = null;
    ResultSet rs = null;
    try {
        conn = dataSource.getConnection();
        ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT id, nome, email FROM cliente WHERE ativo = 1");
        rs = ps.executeQuery();
        while (rs.next()) {
            Cliente c = new Cliente();
            c.setId(rs.getLong("id"));
            c.setNome(rs.getString("nome"));
            c.setEmail(rs.getString("email"));
            lista.add(c);
        }
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        throw new RuntimeException(e);
    } finally {
        // três blocos try/catch fechando rs, ps e conn
    }
    return lista;
}

Com um record e o JdbcClient do Spring 6.1:

public record Cliente(Long id, String nome, String email) {}

public List<Cliente> buscarAtivos() {
    return jdbcClient.sql("SELECT id, nome, email FROM cliente WHERE ativo = 1")
            .query(Cliente.class)
            .list();
}

Esse tipo de reescrita a IA faz muito bem, e o teste de caracterização garante que a lista devolvida continua igual. Mas tenha critério: record é imutável, então se algum lugar do sistema chama setNome no objeto devolvido, a troca quebra. É o tipo de coisa que você pede para o agente verificar antes, com uma busca por todos os usos.

Vale o mesmo para os outros recursos novos. Pattern matching e sealed ajudam onde existe hierarquia de tipos com instanceof espalhado. Virtual threads ajudam em código que bloqueia muito em I/O. Nenhum deles precisa estar em todo lugar só porque existe.

Para extrair partes do monólito, o padrão continua sendo o strangler fig: um módulo novo assume uma fatia do comportamento, o tráfego migra aos poucos, o código antigo morre por último. A IA ajuda a sugerir onde cortar, mapeando quais classes conversam entre si e quais tabelas cada fluxo toca. A decisão de onde fica a fronteira é sua, porque depende de coisas que não estão no código: time, deploy, quem é dono de qual regra.

Onde dá errado

Os problemas que aparecem quase sempre:

  • API alucinada: o modelo usa um método que existe em outra versão da biblioteca, ou que nunca existiu. O compilador pega a maioria. Os que passam costumam estar em código chamado por reflexão ou em configuração.
  • Mudança silenciosa de comportamento: o código compila, os testes unitários passam, e o resultado mudou. Os suspeitos clássicos são BigDecimal com escala diferente, equals e hashCode reescritos, fuso horário na troca de Date para java.time, e charset. Desde o Java 18 o charset padrão é UTF-8 em qualquer sistema operacional, então um new String(bytes) que rodava em Windows com Cp1252 passa a ler diferente. É exatamente para isso que existe a fase 2.
  • Ordem de iteração: código que dependia, sem saber, da ordem de um HashMap ou HashSet. A ordem nunca foi garantida, mas o código funcionava por coincidência e para de funcionar quando a implementação muda.
  • Diffs gigantes: já falei, mas repito porque é o erro mais comum. Agente com tarefa grande produz diff grande, e diff grande não é revisado.
  • Código proprietário saindo da empresa: mandar o código-fonte para uma API externa é decisão de compliance, não de desenvolvedor. Verifique o contrato do provedor (retenção de dados, uso para treino), e se o sistema processa dados pessoais, a LGPD entra na conversa. Muitas empresas resolvem com planos corporativos ou modelos rodando em nuvem própria.

Por onde começar amanhã

  • Rode um agente em modo só leitura e gere a documentação dos módulos. Revise e guarde no arquivo de contexto do projeto.
  • Escolha os cinco fluxos que mais doem se quebrarem e escreva testes de caracterização para eles.
  • Confirme que esses testes passam no código atual.
  • Configure o OpenRewrite e rode rewrite:dryRun só para ver o tamanho do patch.
  • Migre um salto de versão por vez, com os testes entre cada um.
  • Use a IA no que sobrar das receitas, sempre em tarefas pequenas, com build e teste no loop.
  • Revise todo diff. Se está grande demais para revisar, a tarefa estava grande demais.
  • Só depois de estável na versão nova, modernize o código de verdade.

O trade-off no fim é simples. A IA reduz drasticamente o custo de entender e de reescrever, mas não reduz em nada o custo de errar em produção. Se você não tem como saber que algo quebrou, a velocidade da IA só te leva mais rápido para o problema. Invista o tempo economizado na rede de segurança, e a migração que antes levava um ano de medo cabe em alguns meses de trabalho controlado.

title: The Best Hyperscaler Alternatives in 2026: AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Alternatives Compared
description:
The right alternative depends on what you are replacing (raw infrastructure, an app platform, or GPU capacity), and you do not have to leave the hyperscaler entirely. Control Plane runs the same workloads across hyperscalers and alternative providers from one platform.

Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR: What are the best alternatives to AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud?

Start by naming what you want to replace. A hyperscaler bill usually mixes three different things: virtual machines and storage, an application platform for deploying code, and GPU capacity for AI. Each has a different kind of alternative.

  • Raw infrastructure. Developer clouds and VPS or bare-metal providers give you servers and a smaller catalog of services.
  • An app platform. PaaS products take your code or container and run it, so you manage less.
  • GPU capacity. GPU clouds and neoclouds focus on AI hardware.
  • More than one of these at once. A multi-environment platform runs workloads across hyperscalers, infrastructure providers, and GPU clouds from one definition.

Control Plane ranks first because it is the only entry that runs one workload across hyperscalers and the infrastructure and GPU providers listed here. Infrastructure providers follow, then app platforms. The order is editorial, not a benchmark, and each description comes from the vendor’s own page, linked below.

  1. Control Plane: runs one workload across hyperscalers, infrastructure providers, neocloud GPU capacity, and your own servers.
  2. DigitalOcean: a cloud with an AI focus, covering agents, inference, and general cloud services.
  3. Hetzner: cloud servers in shared and dedicated resource plans for developers and teams.
  4. Akamai Cloud (Linode): cloud for applications and AI inference on a globally distributed platform.
  5. Vultr: cloud compute, cloud GPU, and bare-metal servers.
  6. OVHcloud: public cloud with compute, storage, databases, and managed Kubernetes.
  7. Render: an app platform for web services, databases, cron jobs, and workflows.
  8. Fly.io: hardware-virtualized machines and sandboxes for apps and agents.
  9. Heroku: a fully managed application platform built around dynos and add-ons.
  10. Railway: a repo-connected deployment platform with a visual canvas.

What are the three kinds of hyperscaler alternatives?

Type Examples Typical fit What you manage Typical trade-offs
Developer clouds and VPS or bare-metal providers DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Akamai Cloud, Vultr, OVHcloud Replacing virtual machines, storage, and networking Operating systems, deployment, scaling, and often databases and monitoring A smaller service catalog than a hyperscaler, so you assemble more yourself
App platforms (PaaS) Render, Fly.io, Heroku, Railway Deploying code or containers without running servers Application code and configuration Less control over infrastructure, and platform-specific conventions
GPU clouds and neoclouds for AI CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius Training and inference on GPU hardware Models, data movement, and the surrounding application stack GPU-focused catalogs, so general services and data may live elsewhere
Multi-environment platforms Control Plane Running one workload across hyperscalers, infrastructure providers, GPU clouds, and your own servers The workload definition, with the platform handling placement and routing One platform to adopt, replacing a separate toolchain for each provider

These are general patterns for each type. Check any provider’s specifics against its own documentation and SLA before you commit.

How do the options rank?

1. Control Plane

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into what Control Plane calls a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC).

It runs on Control Plane-managed compute in AWS, GCP, and Azure regions, on neocloud GPU capacity, and on your own servers. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, cron, and VM workloads. You can bring clusters you already run through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), or turn your own machines (bare metal or VMs) into managed locations with Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s). On Control Plane-provided compute, there is no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate. Many teams run it in a single cloud, not only across clouds.

A workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. You get failover without paying for idle standby capacity.

On Control Plane-provided compute, you pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, by the millicore and the megabyte, with no contracts or minimums. Control Plane’s Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory based on historical usage, within a minimum and maximum you set. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

Workloads can attach NVIDIA GPUs, and the pricing page lists models from T4 to B200. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API, and Control Plane ships its own Terraform and Pulumi providers, so it complements the infrastructure as code you already run.

For head-to-head comparisons, see Control Plane vs AWS, vs Render, vs Heroku, vs Fly.io, and vs DigitalOcean App Platform.

2. DigitalOcean

DigitalOcean’s homepage describes an “AI-Native Cloud” and “a unified stack for agents, inference, and cloud.” It lists serverless inference with intelligent routing and “80+ models,” a product called Agent Droplets, and DigitalOcean Managed Agents, which it says is in Public Preview. It also sells CPU and GPU Droplets, Managed Kubernetes, App Platform, managed databases, and storage and backups.

3. Hetzner

Hetzner describes its Cloud as a “cloud-hosting provider for developers & teams.” The page lists server plans with shared resources and with dedicated resources, a price calculator, networks, an API, and one-click apps. It states that the service is made in Germany and GDPR-compliant. Its cloud servers are available in Germany, Finland, Singapore, and the USA. Hetzner also sells S3-compatible Object Storage and Storage Box backup storage.

4. Akamai Cloud (Linode)

Akamai Cloud is presented as “Akamai Cloud for AI, Applications, and Agents.” Akamai says it lets you “run AI with rapid, GPU-powered inference and edge-native compute at global scale,” and that it “runs on one of the world’s most distributed platforms.” Access to NVIDIA GPUs is by request. The page also lists CPU compute, managed Kubernetes, managed MySQL and PostgreSQL databases, object and block storage, and backups.

5. Vultr

Vultr sells cloud compute, cloud GPU, and bare-metal servers. Its documentation also covers object and block storage, managed databases, Kubernetes, load balancers, and a container registry.

6. OVHcloud

OVHcloud’s Public Cloud page describes “over 50 OVHcloud infrastructure services and managed platforms.” It lists compute, storage, databases, and a secure network in 1-AZ or 3-AZ regions, with hourly, monthly, or long-term billing. It also offers managed Kubernetes and container management.

7. Render

Render calls itself “the cloud for builders.” Its page lists web services, Postgres databases, cron jobs, workflows, static sites, background jobs, key value stores, and private services. It describes load-based autoscaling, full-stack previews for each pull request, and managed Postgres with point-in-time recovery, read replicas, and high availability. For a direct comparison, see Control Plane vs Render.

8. Fly.io

Fly.io describes Fly Machines as “hardware-virtualized containers that launch instantly and run only when you need them.” It also offers hardware-isolated sandboxes for running untrusted or AI-generated code, storage options, and managed Postgres. The page says you can deploy from GitHub or its CLI. See Control Plane vs Fly.io for a comparison.

9. Heroku

Heroku describes a “fully managed application platform.” Apps run in dynos, which it calls “smart containers.” The page lists Heroku Postgres, a Key-Value Store, add-ons, buildpacks, team management, and fast rollback. See Control Plane vs Heroku for a comparison. In February 2026, Heroku moved to a sustaining engineering model focused on stability, security, reliability, and support rather than new features.

10. Railway

Railway calls itself “the all-in-one intelligent cloud provider.” You connect a repository, and the page says Railway handles configuration automatically. It offers a visual canvas, built-in networking, scaling, and logs, metrics, and traces. In October 2026, Railway disclosed a security incident, described in its preliminary report and in Control Plane’s guide to rotating keys or migrating.

Which cloud providers are best for full infrastructure control?

Control follows a spectrum, and each step toward more control adds operations work.

Level Example type Control Operations work
Most control Bare metal and VPS providers You choose the operating system, networking, and software Highest. You patch, scale, and recover.
Middle Managed Kubernetes on a cloud You control workloads and configuration Moderate. You run the workloads, the provider runs the control plane.
Least control PaaS You control code and settings Lowest. The platform runs the infrastructure.

Control Plane sits across this spectrum. Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK) lets you keep clusters you already run and add them as locations. Managed Kubernetes (MK8s) turns your own machines (bare metal or VMs) into managed Control Plane locations. You keep your own clusters and servers and manage them under one platform, so you do not give up hardware ownership to get one way of deploying. On Control Plane-provided compute, you can skip operating a cluster.

How do managed hosting platforms compare to hyperscalers for reliability, incident response, and SLAs?

Compare the same four things for every provider, including the hyperscalers.

  1. SLA scope and conditions. Read what the SLA covers. Many apply to specific services or configurations and require a minimum setup, such as more than one instance or location.
  2. Credits versus actual uptime. An SLA usually remedies a miss with service credits. Credits do not replace the revenue lost during an outage, so design for availability yourself.
  3. Multi-region options. Check whether you can run in more than one region or provider, and what that costs.
  4. Status page and incident transparency. Look at how the provider reports incidents, how quickly, and how much detail it gives afterward.

Hyperscalers also have major outages. Control Plane keeps a public record in its cloud outage tracker. Do not assume that size guarantees availability.

Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Those locations can be two regions of one cloud or locations on different providers. Take other vendors’ SLA figures from their own SLA pages.

What are common compute, storage, and networking service equivalents when moving off a hyperscaler?

The equivalents below are generic service types, not specific vendors’ products. Confirm that a provider offers a service on its own product page before you plan around it.

Hyperscaler service Generic equivalent elsewhere Migration note
Virtual machines VPS or bare-metal servers Re-create images and configuration, and plan for patching.
Managed Kubernetes Provider-managed or self-managed Kubernetes, or a platform that hides it Check version support and add-ons.
Object storage S3-compatible object storage Check API compatibility for your tools and libraries.
Managed databases Managed PostgreSQL or MySQL, or a self-run database Plan data transfer, backups, and failover testing.
Load balancers Provider load balancer or a reverse proxy Confirm health checks and TLS handling.
DNS Any DNS provider Lower the record lifetime before you cut over.
Secrets Secrets manager or an open-source secrets tool Rotate secrets as part of the move.
Monitoring Open-source monitoring and logging tools Rebuild dashboards and alerts.

You do not have to move everything. With Universal Cloud Identity, workloads running on Control Plane can keep using the hyperscaler services you depend on, such as storage or a managed database, while the compute moves. That lets you separate the move of compute from the move of data. Read how to run the same app on AWS, GCP, and Azure for a walkthrough.

What are good hyperscaler alternatives for small business apps needing databases, backups, and monitoring?

Developer clouds and PaaS platforms are often the simplest fit for small apps. They ship with fewer choices, and several bundle managed databases, backups, and monitoring into one product. Render’s page lists managed Postgres with point-in-time recovery and integrated logs and monitoring. Heroku’s page lists Heroku Postgres and app metrics. Fly.io’s page lists managed Postgres and storage options. Developer clouds such as DigitalOcean, Vultr, and OVHcloud list managed database and storage products on their own pages, and Hetzner lists object storage and backup storage.

Use this checklist for a small app:

  • Does the platform offer a managed database for the engine you use?
  • Are backups included, and can you restore to a point in time?
  • Does it include logs and metrics, or must you add a monitoring tool?
  • What do you pay when the app is idle?
  • How do you move off it if you outgrow it?

What is the simplest cloud platform alternative for small business apps needing predictable monthly pricing?

For most small apps, a PaaS or a developer cloud with plan-based pricing is the simplest fit. Read each vendor’s pricing page for the plan structure.

Control Plane works differently. On Control Plane-provided compute, it bills per millicore and megabyte reserved, with no contracts or minimums. That suits teams that want to pay for what a workload reserves and that expect load to vary. It is not a fixed monthly plan.

How do performance and networking differ between hyperscalers and alternative AI infrastructure providers?

The differences fall into four areas. None of them can be settled with a headline number, so test your own workload.

  • GPU availability. Hyperscalers and GPU clouds both limit capacity at times. A provider that specializes in GPUs may have different hardware and lead times. Check what you can get, for how long, and under what terms.
  • Interconnect options. Training across many GPUs depends on how the GPUs are connected inside the provider. Ask which networking options exist for the cluster size you need.
  • Data transfer between providers. Moving data between a hyperscaler and a GPU provider can add cost and time. Keep data close to compute where you can.
  • Global network reach. Inference serving users in many regions depends on where the provider has locations and how requests are routed.

Control Plane workloads can attach NVIDIA GPUs, and the pricing page lists models from T4 to B200. A GVC can include neocloud GPU capacity next to a hyperscaler region. Control Plane’s GPU Ocean lets you pull GPU capacity from any provider. For a comparison of GPU providers, see best GPU cloud providers in 2026.

Do you have to choose only one provider?

No. Many teams keep a hyperscaler for the services they depend on and add an alternative for cost, control, or GPU capacity. The risk is running a second stack: separate deployment pipelines, separate access control, and separate monitoring for each provider.

Control Plane addresses that risk. You define a workload once, and it runs in every location of a GVC. The locations can be two regions of one cloud or locations on different providers. A global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. That lets you run a hyperscaler and an alternative together, with one workload definition across both. For the step-by-step version, read how to run the same app on AWS, GCP, and Azure.

FAQ

What are good non hyperscaler options for running containerized web apps as a platform service?

Control Plane runs containerized workloads as a platform service on Control Plane-managed compute, with no Kubernetes cluster for you to operate. App platforms such as Render, Fly.io, Heroku, and Railway also run apps for you.

Which cloud providers are best for full infrastructure control?

Bare metal and VPS providers give the most control and the most operations work. Control Plane lets you keep your own clusters and servers through BYOK and MK8s, under one platform.

How do managed hosting platforms compare to hyperscalers for reliability, incident response, and service level agreements?

Compare SLA scope and conditions, credits versus actual uptime, multi-region options, and status page transparency. Hyperscalers also have major outages, as the cloud outage tracker records. Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

What are common compute, storage, and networking service equivalents when moving off a hyperscaler?

Virtual machines map to VPS or bare-metal servers. Object storage maps to S3-compatible storage. Managed databases map to managed PostgreSQL or similar. Load balancers, DNS, secrets, and monitoring each have generic equivalents, listed in the table above. Confirm a specific provider’s offering on its own page.

What are good hyperscaler alternatives for small business apps needing databases, backups, and monitoring?

Developer clouds and PaaS platforms are often the simplest fit. Check each for a managed database, backup and restore options, and built-in monitoring.

What is the simplest cloud platform alternative for small business apps needing predictable monthly pricing?

A PaaS or developer cloud with plan-based pricing is usually the simplest fit. Control Plane bills per millicore and megabyte reserved, with no contracts or minimums, which is a different model from a fixed plan.

How do performance and networking differ between hyperscalers and alternative AI infrastructure providers?

Compare GPU availability, interconnect options, data transfer between providers, and global network reach. Test your own workload rather than relying on a headline figure.

Do I have to leave AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud entirely?

No. You can keep a hyperscaler for the services you depend on and move compute elsewhere. Universal Cloud Identity lets workloads on Control Plane keep using hyperscaler services while compute moves.

Is Control Plane only for multi-cloud?

No. Many teams run it in one cloud. It also runs on your own servers and on premises.

Next steps

Name what you are replacing, shortlist one provider per job, and test one workload before you move more.
